title: From URL to First Pixels
shadowText:
Today we will talk about a classic interview question. What happens when you type a URL into the browser? The interviewer wants to know if you understand where the time goes before anything appears on the screen.

Let us start with the browser itself. A modern browser like Chrome is not one program. It is several processes. The browser process owns the address bar, navigation, and network access. The renderer process does the heavy page work. It parses the page, calculates style, does layout and paint, and it also runs your JavaScript. A separate GPU process draws the final layers to the screen.

Inside the renderer, there are a few threads you should know. The main thread runs JavaScript, parses HTML, and computes style and layout. There is only one main thread per page. So if your JavaScript runs for a long time, everything else on that thread has to wait. The compositor thread assembles frames. Here is a nice detail. It can scroll the page and run transform and opacity animations without the main thread. That is why those animations stay smooth even when JavaScript is busy.

Now let us follow the navigation in order. First, the browser parses the URL and checks if it must use HTTPS. Second, it does a DNS lookup, and then a connection handshake with TCP and TLS. With HTTP version three, the transport and encryption setup are merged, so there are fewer round trips. Every round trip costs latency. This is why preconnect hints and CDNs matter. Third, the browser sends the HTTP request and waits for the first byte from the server. We call this time to first byte. After that, the browser reads the response headers and picks a renderer process. Then the renderer streams the HTML. This is important. Parsing starts on the first bytes. It does not wait for the whole document.

Let us talk about how HTML becomes the DOM. The parser reads the bytes, makes tokens, and builds the DOM tree. It is forgiving, so bad nesting gets repaired by rules from the spec. But scripts change the flow. A classic script, without async or defer, blocks the parser. The browser stops, downloads the script, runs it, and only then continues. To help, the browser has a preload scanner. It looks ahead in the raw markup and starts downloads for images, styles, and scripts early. But it cannot see resources that JavaScript injects later, or a CSS background image.

Here are the script options. With defer, the script downloads in parallel and runs after parsing, in document order. With async, the script downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, in any order. Module scripts are deferred by default. A simple rule: use async for independent scripts like analytics, and defer for scripts that need the DOM.

Now CSS. The browser parses CSS into the CSSOM. CSS is render blocking. The browser will not paint until it has the stylesheets it knows about, so you do not see unstyled content. CSS is not parser blocking by itself. But a classic script after a stylesheet must wait for that stylesheet, because the script might read computed styles. So a slow stylesheet can delay JavaScript and, in the end, parsing. You can use a media attribute to make a stylesheet non blocking when it does not match, for example a print stylesheet.

Put these together and you get the critical rendering path. The DOM and the CSSOM combine into the render tree. Then come layout, paint, and composite. To make it shorter, inline the small critical CSS, defer your scripts, preconnect to important origins, preload the key image or font, compress and cache, and serve from a CDN.

One more point. DOMContentLoaded fires when the DOM is parsed and deferred scripts have run. The load event fires when everything is done, including images. Neither one tells you what the user sees. For that, measure First Contentful Paint and Largest Contentful Paint.

Let me finish with a short interview style summary. When I type a URL, the browser resolves DNS, connects, sends the request, and streams the HTML. The parser builds the DOM while the CSS builds the CSSOM. Blocking scripts and stylesheets can delay the first paint, so I use defer, critical CSS, and preloading. Then style, layout, paint, and composite put the first pixels on the screen.
passage:
A modern browser splits its work across several processes. The browser process handles the address bar and the network. The renderer process parses the page, computes style and layout, and runs JavaScript on a single main thread. A separate compositor thread can scroll the page and run transform and opacity animations even when the main thread is busy.

Navigation begins with URL parsing, a DNS lookup, and a TCP and TLS handshake, or a combined QUIC handshake with HTTP version three. The server then returns the first byte, and the renderer streams the HTML. The parser builds the DOM as the bytes arrive. A classic script blocks the parser, while defer and async let it download in parallel. A preload scanner looks ahead to start early downloads.

CSS becomes the CSSOM. It blocks rendering, so the browser waits for stylesheets before the first paint, and it can also delay scripts that follow it. To shorten this critical rendering path, inline small critical CSS, defer scripts, preconnect to key origins, and preload the main image. Measure real user experience with First Contentful Paint and Largest Contentful Paint, not just the load event.
prompt: Walk me through what happens between typing a URL and seeing the first pixels. Cover the browser processes, the network steps, how the HTML parser and CSS can block rendering, and two ways you would speed up the first paint.

title: Style, Layout, Paint and Composite
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the browser rendering pipeline. If you know which stage a change triggers, you understand the core of rendering performance. And interviewers love this topic.

Let us start with the five stages. Stage one is style. The browser matches selectors to elements and works out the final value of every property. The cost grows with the number of elements and the complexity of selectors. Stage two is layout, also called reflow. Here the browser calculates the size and position of every box, using the box model, flex, grid, and text flow. A small detail: an element with display none is not in the layout tree at all, but an element with visibility hidden still takes up space. Stage three is paint. The browser records drawing commands, like backgrounds, borders, text, and shadows. This is a list of instructions, not pixels yet. Stage four is raster. This turns those records into real pixels, in tiles, usually on the GPU and away from the main thread. Stage five is composite. The compositor thread stacks the layers in the right order and sends a frame to the GPU.

Now here is the key point. Different changes trigger different stages. If you change width, height, margin, font size, or you add nodes to the DOM, the browser needs layout, then paint, then composite. If you change only color, background color, or box shadow, it skips layout but still paints. And if you change transform or opacity on a composited layer, it can skip both layout and paint. It only needs to composite.

So what does that mean in practice? If you animate the left property, the browser runs layout and paint on every frame. If you animate transform with translateX, only compositing is needed, and it can even run on the compositor thread while JavaScript is busy. This is why transform is cheaper than top or left.

Next, layers. The browser promotes some elements to their own compositor layer. Examples are elements with three D transforms, will-change transform, video, canvas, and elements that animate transform or opacity. Layers make movement cheap, but each one costs GPU memory, because each is a texture. If you promote hundreds of elements, the page gets slower and can even crash on low end phones. So use will-change only on elements that are about to animate, and remove it afterwards. Also be careful about implicit compositing. An element that overlaps a composited layer may get promoted too, and the layer count can explode.

Now a very common problem: layout thrashing. Normally the browser batches style and layout work until the next frame. But when you read a geometry value, like offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect, or scrollTop, right after you changed something, the browser must run layout immediately. This is a forced synchronous layout. Imagine a loop where each step reads a width and then writes a width. That causes one full layout per iteration. The fix is simple. Read first, write later. Batch all your reads, then do your writes, or schedule writes inside requestAnimationFrame. In the DevTools Performance panel, you can spot forced layouts as purple Layout blocks with a red warning triangle.

There are also tools to limit the damage of a change. The contain property tells the browser that changes inside an element do not affect the outside, so layout and paint can be scoped. The content-visibility auto value skips style, layout, and paint for sections that are off screen, and you pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the scrollbar does not jump. Fewer DOM nodes and simpler selectors also help, and very long lists should be virtualized.

Finally, fonts and images. Web fonts can hide text for around three seconds by default. Using font-display swap shows a fallback font at once, and a metric matched fallback reduces the shift when the real font arrives. Images without width and height, or an aspect ratio, take no space until they load. Then they push content down, which is a layout shift and hurts CLS.

Here is a short summary for an interview. Layout recomputes geometry. Repaint redraws pixels without changing geometry. Composite only restacks existing layers. Transform and opacity are the cheapest to animate. Will-change is not free, because layers cost memory. And to avoid thrashing, I batch my reads before my writes.
passage:
The browser rendering pipeline has five stages. Style matches selectors and computes final property values. Layout calculates the size and position of every box. Paint records drawing commands. Raster turns those commands into pixels, usually on the GPU. Composite stacks the layers and sends a frame to the screen.

The cost of a change depends on the earliest stage it triggers. Changing width, margin, or the DOM requires layout, paint, and composite. Changing color or box shadow skips layout. Changing transform or opacity on a composited layer needs only compositing, and it can run on the compositor thread while JavaScript is busy. For this reason, animating transform is much smoother than animating the left property.

Compositor layers make movement cheap, but each layer uses GPU memory, so will-change should be applied sparingly and removed afterwards. Layout thrashing happens when code reads a geometry value after writing, which forces an immediate layout. Batching reads before writes avoids it. Containment, content visibility, smaller DOM trees, and virtualized lists further reduce the work, while explicit image dimensions and font display swap prevent layout shifts.
prompt: Explain the browser rendering pipeline and compare reflow, repaint, and composite. Say why animating transform is cheaper than animating left, and describe what layout thrashing is and how you would fix it.

title: The Frame and the Event Loop
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how the event loop and rendering work together. This is a favorite topic in front end interviews, because it explains why pages freeze and why animations stutter.

Let us start with the key idea. Rendering happens inside the event loop, on the main thread. At sixty frames per second, each frame has about sixteen point seven milliseconds. At one hundred twenty hertz, it is only about eight milliseconds. The browser needs part of that time for its own work. So in practice, you should keep your JavaScript under about ten milliseconds per frame.

Now let us walk through one turn of the loop. Step one: the browser runs one task from a task queue. A task can be a click handler, a setTimeout callback, or a network response. Step two: it runs all the microtasks. These are promise callbacks, queueMicrotask callbacks, and mutation observers. And note this: if a microtask queues another microtask, that one also runs, all before any rendering. Step three: if a frame is due, the browser runs the requestAnimationFrame callbacks. Then it does style, layout, and paint, and hands the frame to the compositor. Resize observers and intersection observers are handled around this step as well. Step four: if there is time left before the next frame, the browser runs requestIdleCallback work.

There are some important consequences. First, a long task is any task over fifty milliseconds. It blocks input and rendering, so the page feels frozen. Second, an endless chain of microtasks can starve rendering completely. That is different from a chain of setTimeout calls, which lets rendering happen between tasks. Third, setTimeout with zero does not mean the next frame. It means a later task, and that can run several times in one frame. Also, when timers are nested more than five levels deep, browsers clamp the delay to at least four milliseconds.

Let us talk about requestAnimationFrame. Its callbacks run right before the browser computes style and layout for the next frame. So this is the right place for visual updates. The callback receives a high resolution timestamp. You should base your animation on time, not on the number of frames, so it looks the same on fast and slow screens. Also, requestAnimationFrame pauses in background tabs, which saves battery. One warning: if you read a geometry value inside the callback after other code has written to the page, you still force a layout. So do your reads first.

What do you do when you have a lot of work? You break it up. If you split a long task into smaller pieces, the browser can render and respond to input in between. A common pattern is a loop that processes items, and every hundred items it awaits a small helper that yields to the main thread. That helper uses scheduler.yield when it exists, and falls back to a setTimeout of zero when it does not. The nice thing about scheduler.yield is that your work resumes ahead of other queued tasks.

There are other tools too. Web Workers run JavaScript on another thread, which is great for CPU heavy work like parsing or image processing, but they cannot touch the DOM. OffscreenCanvas lets a worker draw. And CSS animations of transform and opacity run on the compositor, so they do not depend on the main thread at all.

Now let us talk about the metric that captures all of this: Interaction to Next Paint, or INP. It measures the time from a user input to the next frame that is painted after it, and it roughly reports the worst interaction on the page. A good value is two hundred milliseconds or less. INP has three parts. The first is input delay, which happens when the main thread is busy as the user clicks. The second is processing time, which is your event handlers running. The third is presentation delay, which is the style, layout, paint, and composite for the new frame.

The fixes match the parts. Break up long tasks to reduce input delay. Keep handlers short, update the interface first, and defer analytics and heavy work. And keep the style and layout work for the next frame small.

Here is a short summary for an interview. In each turn, the browser runs a task, then all microtasks, then rendering if a frame is due. Long tasks and microtask floods block rendering. I use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates, I break up long work or move it to a worker, and I measure INP to know if the page feels responsive.
passage:
Rendering happens inside the event loop on the main thread. At sixty frames per second, a frame lasts about sixteen point seven milliseconds, and the browser needs some of that time itself, so JavaScript should stay under roughly ten milliseconds per frame.

Each turn of the loop runs a single task, then drains every microtask, including any that were queued by other microtasks. If a frame is due, the browser then runs requestAnimationFrame callbacks, followed by style, layout, paint, and composite. Remaining time can be used for idle callbacks. A task longer than fifty milliseconds is a long task and freezes the page, and an endless chain of microtasks starves rendering entirely. A setTimeout with a zero delay only schedules a later task, not the next frame.

To keep a page responsive, developers break long work into smaller pieces and yield to the main thread, move heavy computation to Web Workers, and rely on compositor driven animations. Interaction to Next Paint measures responsiveness through input delay, processing time, and presentation delay, and a good score is two hundred milliseconds or less.
prompt: Describe one turn of the browser event loop, from the task to the microtasks to the rendering step. Then explain what a long task is, how you would break one up, and what Interaction to Next Paint measures.

title: Rendering in React and Next.js
shadowText:
Today we will connect browser rendering to the frameworks you use every day, like React and Next.js. We will also learn a simple method to find out why a page is slow.

Let us start with a word that has two meanings. The word is render. A React render means React calls your components, builds a new element tree, and compares it with the previous one. This is called reconciliation, and it is JavaScript on the main thread. A browser render means style, layout, paint, and composite after the DOM changes. React commits only the differences to the DOM, and then the browser renders. This means a component can re-render in React with no DOM change, which wastes JavaScript time. And a tiny DOM change can still cause expensive layout, which wastes browser time. So you need to measure both. Use the React Profiler for the first one, and the DevTools Performance panel for the second.

Now let us see where React meets the frame. The useLayoutEffect hook runs after the DOM update but before the browser paints. Use it when you must measure layout and adjust right away, for example to position a tooltip. But it blocks painting, so keep it short. The useEffect hook runs after paint. Use it for subscriptions, fetching data, and logging. Concurrent rendering, with useTransition and useDeferredValue, lets React split its work into chunks and yield to the browser. This keeps typing responsive while a big list re-renders. And keys help reconciliation move existing DOM nodes instead of destroying and recreating them. That saves work in React and in the browser.

Next, server rendering and hydration. SSR and static generation send HTML that the browser can paint immediately, which improves First Contentful Paint and Largest Contentful Paint. Then hydration runs the component code in the browser to attach event handlers. Until hydration finishes, the page looks ready, but clicks may not respond. That shows up as poor INP. Streaming SSR with Suspense sends the shell first and fills in the slow parts later, so the browser can parse and paint sooner. React Server Components, used in the Next.js App Router, ship no JavaScript for server only components, so there is less to download, parse, and hydrate. A common bug is a hydration mismatch. This happens when the server HTML differs from the first client render, for example when you use the current time or the window object during render. React has to patch the DOM, and users may see a visible jump.

Now, preventing layout shift, which is measured by CLS. Give every image and video a width and height, or an aspect ratio. Next.js Image requires dimensions for this reason. Reserve space for ads, embeds, and banners that load late. Use font-display swap with metric matched fallbacks, and next/font does this for you. Animate with transform, not with properties that push other content around. And insert new content below the viewport, or in response to a user action, because shifts within five hundred milliseconds of an input do not count.

How do you diagnose a slow page? Here is a method. First, look at field data from real users, such as the Chrome UX Report, the web-vitals library, or Vercel Speed Insights. Lab tools can miss slow devices. Second, run Lighthouse for a quick report. Third, open the DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling, four or six times slower, to imitate a mid range phone. Look for long tasks on the main thread, count the Layout and Paint blocks and check if any are forced, and check the Frames track for dropped frames. Fourth, use the Rendering tab for paint flashing, layout shift regions, and layer borders. Fifth, use the Layers panel to see how many compositor layers exist and how much memory they use.

Finally, remember the targets. LCP should be two and a half seconds or less, INP two hundred milliseconds or less, and CLS zero point one or less. For LCP, improve server response time, preload the hero image, and avoid render blocking resources. For INP, break up long tasks, reduce hydration, and use transitions. For CLS, set dimensions and reserve space.

Here is a short summary for an interview. React render and browser render are different costs, so I measure both. I use server rendering for fast first paint, I watch hydration cost, and I fix layout shift with dimensions and reserved space. I start with field data, then use the Performance panel with throttling to find the real bottleneck.
passage:
The word render has two meanings. A React render computes a new element tree and compares it with the previous one, which is JavaScript work on the main thread. A browser render performs style, layout, paint, and composite after the DOM changes. A component may re-render without changing the DOM, and a small DOM change may still trigger expensive layout, so both costs need to be measured separately.

The useLayoutEffect hook runs before paint and suits synchronous layout measurement, while useEffect runs after paint. Server rendering sends ready HTML for a fast first paint, but hydration must finish before the page responds to clicks. Streaming, Suspense, and Server Components reduce the JavaScript that has to be hydrated. Hydration mismatches should be avoided because they force visible DOM patches.

To diagnose a slow page, start with field data from real users, then use Lighthouse and the DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling. Look for long tasks, forced layouts, and dropped frames. The goals are a Largest Contentful Paint of two and a half seconds or less, an Interaction to Next Paint of two hundred milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift of zero point one or less.
prompt: A product page has a fast Largest Contentful Paint but feels broken for its first two seconds. Explain how hydration can cause this, and walk through how you would diagnose and fix it using field data and the DevTools Performance panel.

title: Claude Code Slash Commands
shadowText:
Today we will talk about slash commands in Claude Code. If you type a slash at any time, a command menu opens. These commands trigger built in features, skills, and custom workflows. Let us group them by what you are trying to do.

We start with session and context. These are the commands you will use most. The clear command starts a fresh conversation with an empty context. The old one is still available through resume. The golden habit is to clear between unrelated tasks. A focused context gives better, faster, and cheaper answers. The compact command summarizes the conversation to free up context, and you can give it a focus hint. Use it when the context is filling up in the middle of a task. The context command shows what is using your context window. The resume command reopens a past session. The rewind command rolls back the conversation, the code, or both, to an earlier point. It is perfect when you say, that edit was wrong, undo the last few steps. And rename gives the session a readable name.

Next, code review and verification. The review command reviews a pull request. The code-review command reviews your current diff for bugs and cleanups, and it has levels from low to max. With the fix option it applies the findings, and with the comment option it posts them as inline pull request comments. The security-review command scans pending changes for problems like injection, auth issues, and data exposure. The simplify command looks for reuse and efficiency and applies cleanups, but it does not hunt for bugs. The verify command confirms a change works by building, running, and observing real behavior, and the run command launches the actual app. A nice combo: when you finish a feature, run code-review at a high level, then security-review, then verify. You catch bugs, security holes, and the question of whether it really runs.

For project setup and memory, init scans the repository and creates a starter CLAUDE.md file that describes the project. The memory command lets you edit CLAUDE.md files and see what Claude has remembered. And add-dir adds another working directory to the session.

Now planning and large scale work. The plan command enters plan mode. Claude explores and proposes a plan before touching any code. For anything non trivial, plan first, because reviewing an approach is much cheaper than redoing a wrong implementation. The goal command sets a condition, and Claude keeps working until it is met. The batch command orchestrates large changes across many subagents in isolated git worktrees. The deep-research command searches the web, cross checks sources, and returns a cited report. The loop command runs a prompt repeatedly, for example to poll a CI job. And schedule creates recurring cloud agents on a cron schedule.

For model and configuration, the model command switches the model, and the effort command sets reasoning effort from low up to max. The config command opens the settings screen. The fast command toggles fast mode. For tools and extensions, mcp manages MCP server connections, agents manages subagents, skills lists skills, hooks shows hooks, permissions manages allow and deny rules, and plugin manages plugins.

There are also diagnostics. The diff command opens an interactive viewer of uncommitted changes. The copy command copies a response to the clipboard. The usage command shows cost, plan limits, and activity. The doctor command diagnoses your installation and settings. The status command shows the version, model, and account. There are also commands for login, for IDE integrations, and for running a session in the background.

Finally, you can make your own commands. Put a markdown file in the commands folder inside your project's claude directory, or in your global one, and it becomes a slash command. The file can have a short description at the top, and the text of the file is the instruction. Arguments you type after the command are available through a variable called ARGUMENTS. Custom commands overlap with skills, but skills are richer and can be invoked automatically.

Here is a short summary for an interview. I clear context between tasks, compact when a task gets long, and use plan mode before bigger changes. I review my work with code-review, security-review, and verify. And I turn workflows I repeat into custom slash commands.
passage:
Slash commands in Claude Code are grouped by purpose. For managing sessions, the clear command starts fresh with an empty context, compact summarizes a long conversation to free space, resume reopens an earlier session, and rewind rolls back the conversation or the code. A good habit is to clear the context between unrelated tasks, because a focused session gives better and cheaper answers.

For quality, the code-review command checks the current diff for bugs, the security-review command scans for vulnerabilities, and verify and run confirm that the change really works in the running application. For larger work, plan mode proposes an approach before any code changes, while goal, batch, loop, and schedule support long running and parallel workflows.

Configuration commands switch the model and the reasoning effort, and others manage MCP servers, hooks, permissions, and plugins. Developers can also create custom commands by placing a markdown file in a commands folder. Arguments are passed in through a variable, so repeated workflows become reusable shortcuts.
prompt: Explain how you would use Claude Code slash commands to work on a large feature from start to finish. Cover managing context with clear and compact, planning first, reviewing the result, and creating a custom command.

title: Claude Code Shortcuts and Input Modes
shadowText:
Today we will talk about keyboard shortcuts and input modes in Claude Code. The terminal is your cockpit. If you learn these, you stop fighting the interface and start working faster.

Let us start with the four input prefixes. A single character at the start of your input changes its meaning. A slash means command. You can run a slash command or a skill, for example clear. An exclamation mark means shell mode. You can type a shell command like npm test, and it runs directly. The output is added to the session, so Claude can see it. An at sign means file mention. You type an at sign and a path, and it autocompletes the path and pulls that file into context. And a hash sign means memory. If you type hash and then a sentence such as always use pnpm, it saves a note to CLAUDE.md for future sessions. Here is the key point. The exclamation mark is great for quick checks, because Claude gets the output without you copying and pasting. And the hash sign is the fastest way to teach Claude a lasting rule.

Now the essential controls. Escape interrupts Claude in the middle of a response, and it keeps the work done so far. Pressing Escape twice clears the input draft, or opens the rewind menu if the input is empty. Shift plus Tab cycles permission modes, from default, to accept edits, to plan mode, and to bypass if it is enabled. This is the one to remember. It lets you switch between, ask me before every edit, and, go ahead and edit, and into plan mode, without typing a command. Control C clears the current input, and pressing it again exits. Control D also exits. Control L redraws the screen, which fixes garbled output. Control O toggles the transcript viewer. Control R searches your command history in reverse. Control V pastes an image from the clipboard. And Control T toggles the background task list.

There are also toggles that do not need typing. On Mac you use Option, and on Windows and Linux you use Alt. Option or Alt plus P switches the model without clearing your prompt. Plus T toggles extended thinking. Plus O toggles fast mode.

What about multiline input? When you write a long prompt, or paste a stack trace, you have several options. The universal fallback is a backslash followed by Enter, and it works in all terminals. Shift plus Enter works in many modern terminals, like iTerm two, WezTerm, Ghostty, Kitty, Warp, and Windows Terminal. For VS Code and Cursor, you run the terminal-setup command first. Control J works in any terminal. And Option plus Enter works on macOS.

For text editing, the shortcuts are like in bash or zsh. Control A and Control E jump to the start and end of the line. Control K deletes to the end of the line, and Control U deletes to the start. Control W deletes the previous word, and Control Y pastes the last deleted text. Alt plus B and Alt plus F move back and forward by one word.

If you like modal editing, you can turn on Vim mode in the config screen, under editor mode. Then the prompt has a real normal, insert, and visual split. Escape goes to normal mode. The keys i, a, o move to insert mode, and v starts visual mode. You get the usual movements, edits like dd and cw, and text objects such as inner word or inside quotes.

Finally, the transcript viewer, opened with Control O. It shows every tool call Claude made, so you can understand what it actually did. Inside it, the question mark shows help, the curly braces jump between user prompts, and the square bracket writes the conversation to your terminal scrollback so you can search it. The v key opens the conversation in your editor, and q or Escape exits.

Here is a short summary for an interview. I use slash for commands, exclamation for shell, at sign for files, and hash for memory. I press Escape to interrupt, and Shift plus Tab to change permission modes and enter plan mode. And I use the transcript viewer to check what Claude really did.
passage:
Claude Code gives special meaning to the first character of your input. A slash runs a command or skill. An exclamation mark runs a shell command directly and adds its output to the session so that Claude can see it. An at sign mentions a file and brings it into context. A hash sign saves a note to the CLAUDE.md file, which is the quickest way to teach Claude a lasting rule.

Several controls are worth memorizing. Escape interrupts a response while keeping the work done so far, and pressing it twice opens the rewind menu when the input is empty. Shift plus Tab cycles through permission modes, including plan mode. Control O opens the transcript viewer, which shows every tool call in detail, and Control R searches the command history.

For longer prompts, a backslash followed by Enter works in every terminal, and Control J works in any terminal as well. Readline style shortcuts handle editing, and Vim mode is available through the configuration screen for people who prefer modal editing.
prompt: Explain the four input prefixes in Claude Code and what each one does. Then describe how you would use Shift plus Tab, Escape, and the transcript viewer during a normal work session.

title: Claude Code Core Concepts
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the core ideas behind Claude Code. If slash commands are the what, these ideas are the how. They are the machinery that makes the tool feel like an engineer on your team, not just a chatbot.

Let us start with the memory file, called CLAUDE dot md. Think of it as a readme written for the AI. It is loaded automatically at the start of every session. So anything you put inside becomes a standing instruction, and you never repeat yourself. It can live in your project, or in a folder in your home directory for all your projects. Good content is your conventions, your architecture rules, and a short list of things not to do. For example, use one package manager, keep tests next to the source, and never edit generated files. You can create a first draft with the init command, and then you should prune it. Keep it tight, because it costs context in every session.

Here is the key point. Context is a budget, and the memory file spends it every time.

Next, subagents. A subagent is a fresh Claude instance with its own clean context. You give it a task, it does the work, and it returns only a summary. This matters for three reasons. First, parallelism, because you can search several modules at once. Second, context hygiene, because a subagent can read forty files and you only get the conclusion. Third, specialization, because some are tuned for exploration, planning, or review. A good mental model is worker threads. Use them when you need the verdict, not the file dump.

Now let us talk about skills. A skill is a reusable capability written in markdown. The important idea is that skills load on demand. Claude only sees a short description at first. The full instructions load only when the task matches. So you can have a big library of skills and pay almost nothing for the ones you are not using. A skill can be invoked automatically when its description matches, or you can call it by name. Custom commands are the simpler cousin. They are just prompt templates triggered by a slash name. Use skills when you want automatic invocation and richer behavior, and commands for quick shortcuts.

Then we have hooks. Hooks run your own shell commands automatically on lifecycle events. The important point is that the harness runs them, not Claude. So they are deterministic, and they even run in headless mode. Common uses are formatting a file after every edit, running tests after a command, blocking edits to protected paths, or sending a notification when a session ends. Here is a rule of thumb. If you want something to happen every time an event occurs, that is a hook, not a request to Claude.

After that, MCP, which stands for Model Context Protocol. It is an open standard that connects Claude Code to external systems. Think of databases, issue trackers, design tools, and internal APIs. They appear as first class tools. You configure servers in a JSON file, and you manage connections and sign in with the mcp command. Tool definitions are loaded on demand, so a large server does not bloat your context.

Finally, permission modes. They control how much Claude can do without asking. Default mode asks before edits and shell commands. Accept Edits mode auto approves file edits and safe file system commands, but still asks about risky ones. Plan mode explores and proposes, and it will not edit your source. Auto mode checks every action with background safety checks. And Bypass Permissions asks for nothing, so it belongs only in throwaway sandboxes. You can cycle modes live with Shift and Tab. For fine grained rules, you allow, ask, or deny specific tools in settings.

Let us summarize like an interview answer. Claude Code has a few core building blocks. The memory file gives persistent project rules. Subagents protect your context. Skills add reusable procedures that load on demand. Hooks guarantee automation. MCP connects outside systems. And permission modes balance speed against safety. I would choose each one based on whether I need memory, delegation, repeatability, determinism, integration, or control.
passage:
Claude Code is built from a small set of core concepts. The memory file, called CLAUDE dot md, is loaded at the start of every session and acts as standing instruction for the project, such as conventions, architecture rules, and prohibited actions. Because it consumes context in every session, it should be short and carefully maintained.

Subagents are fresh instances with their own context. They complete a delegated task and return only a summary, which allows parallel work and keeps the main conversation clean. Skills are reusable procedures written in markdown. They load on demand, so a large library costs almost nothing until a skill is actually needed.

Hooks run shell commands on lifecycle events and are executed by the harness, which makes them deterministic. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, connects Claude Code to external systems such as databases and issue trackers. Finally, permission modes range from Default, which asks before acting, to Plan, which only proposes, to Bypass Permissions, which should be reserved for disposable sandboxes.
prompt: Explain the difference between a skill, a hook, and a subagent in Claude Code. For each one, say what it does, when you would choose it, and why a hook is more reliable than simply asking Claude to do something every time.

title: Claude Code Headless Mode and Flags
shadowText:
Today we will talk about using Claude Code from the command line, and especially in headless mode. Claude Code is not only an interactive terminal. It is a tool you can pipe into, script around, and run in continuous integration. This is where it becomes automation.

Let us start with starting sessions. You can run claude on its own for an interactive session in the current folder. You can give it an opening prompt. You can continue the most recent session in the folder with the continue flag. You can resume a specific session by name or ID with the resume flag. If you want to branch from an old session without changing it, use the fork session flag, which gives you a new session ID. You can name a session so it is easy to find later. You can add extra directories the tool may access. And you can start inside an isolated git worktree, which is great for risky experiments.

Here is the key point. The print flag, dash p, is the automation workhorse. It runs one query and then exits. That makes it perfect for scripts, pre commit hooks, and CI. You can ask a one shot question about your code. You can pipe a log file into it and ask for the root cause. You can ask for machine readable output with the output format flag, using text, json, or stream json. And you can enforce a response shape with the json schema flag, so the final answer must match a JSON Schema you provide. That is very useful when another program has to parse the result.

For unattended runs, safety limits matter. The max turns flag caps how many agent steps are allowed. The max budget flag stops the run after you spend a certain amount of money. The verbose flag gives you turn by turn logging. A simple CI recipe is this. In a GitHub Action, run claude with print, ask it to review the diff for security issues, set a turn limit, request JSON output, and fail the job if it finds problems. Pair that with plan permission mode or a tight allow list, so it cannot change anything.

Now models and reliability. The model flag lets you choose opus, sonnet, haiku, or a full model ID. The effort flag controls how hard the model reasons, from low up to max. The fallback model flag gives a backup if the primary model is overloaded. A good cost instinct is this. Use the strongest model for hard architecture and debugging, a middle model for everyday edits and bulk work, and the smallest for cheap mechanical passes. You can also switch mid session with the model command, with no restart.

Next, permissions and safety. The permission mode flag starts you in default, accept edits, plan, auto, or bypass permissions mode. The dangerously skip permissions flag skips all prompts, and the name is a warning. Use it only in sandboxes. A related flag adds bypass to the Shift and Tab cycle without starting in it. For headless runs, you can delegate permission prompts to an MCP tool.

You can also shape the system prompt. Append system prompt adds your instructions to the default. System prompt replaces the whole thing, which is advanced. You can also load a prompt from a file. For extensions, you can pass MCP config files, use only the MCP config you passed, point to a settings file, choose which setting sources to load, and define subagents inline as JSON.

Finally, troubleshooting. Safe mode disables all customizations, including memory files, skills, plugins, hooks, and MCP, so you can isolate a problem. Bare mode skips heavy discovery for a faster start. The debug flag turns on logging, and you can filter categories such as api and mcp. For background work, the bg flag launches a background agent and returns a session ID right away. The remote flag creates a web session, and teleport pulls a web session into your local terminal.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Claude Code in print mode behaves like a normal Unix command. I can pipe input, get structured JSON, cap turns and budget, and restrict permissions. That lets me use it safely in CI for tasks like code review, triage, or documentation.
passage:
Claude Code can run non interactively, which makes it suitable for scripts and continuous integration. The print flag runs a single query and exits. Input can be piped in from other commands, and the output format flag can return plain text, JSON, or a stream of JSON events. The json schema flag forces the final answer to match a given schema, so that another program can parse it reliably.

Unattended runs need limits. The max turns flag caps the number of agent steps, and the max budget flag stops the run after a set amount of spending. Permission mode can be set to plan, or a narrow allow list can be used, so the run cannot modify anything. A typical pipeline asks Claude to review a diff for security problems and fails the job if findings are reported.

Other flags choose the model and reasoning effort, add a fallback model for overload, adjust the system prompt, and load extra tools. For diagnosis, safe mode disables all customizations so that a problem can be isolated quickly.
prompt: Walk me through how you would use Claude Code in a CI pipeline to review pull requests for security issues. Mention headless print mode, structured JSON output, limits such as maximum turns, and how you would keep it from changing any files.

title: Claude Code Best Practices Workflow
shadowText:
Today we will talk about best practices for working with Claude Code. The commands are easy. The workflow is what separates someone who occasionally uses the tool from someone whose output doubles. Let us go through the most important habits.

Let us start with the core loop. It has four steps. Explore, plan, code, and verify. First, explore. Let Claude read the relevant code before it changes anything. For example, ask it to read the authentication module and the user model, then explain how login works. No edits yet. Second, plan. Ask for an approach and tell it not to write code yet. Review the plan. Fixing a mistake in words is very cheap. Third, code. Approve the plan, switch to Accept Edits mode, and let it work. Fourth, verify. Run a code review, run the tests, or run the app. Never trust the word done without seeing it run.

Here is the key point. The biggest mistake is skipping the plan. A thirty second plan review can save you from twenty minutes of wrong implementation.

Next, context is a budget. The context window is finite, like memory. A bloated context makes answers slower, less accurate, and more expensive. So build a few habits. Clear the conversation between unrelated tasks. This is the number one habit. When you finish a bug, clear before you start the next feature. Compact the conversation in the middle of a long task when the window fills up. Use subagents for big reads, so they digest thirty files and report back a paragraph. Check the context command when things feel off. And do not paste huge files. Reference them by path, so Claude reads only what it needs.

Third, invest in the memory file early. Every correction you make twice belongs in CLAUDE dot md. Run init on day one, then prune the result. Capture your package manager, test command, code style, architectural boundaries, and paths that must never be touched. Keep it lean, because it loads every session, and dead rules cost you.

Fourth, write prompts like tickets, not tweets. Vague input gives vague output. Compare fix the bug with a strong version: users report that login fails with a server error on expired tokens, reproduce it in the auth test file, find the cause, fix it, and keep the test. Or compare add caching with: add an in memory least recently used cache, limited to a thousand entries with a five minute lifetime, to a getUser function, and invalidate it when updateUser runs. A good prompt gives the goal, the constraints, the relevant files, and how you will know it worked.

Fifth, review everything. Claude is fast and usually right, which is exactly why you must check it. Read the diff as if it were a colleague's pull request. Use the dedicated reviewers, and run a security review before anything touching authentication, input, or secrets. Actually run the code, because code that looks right is not code that works. Lean on git, and commit at green states so you can always roll back. There is also a rewind command for undoing within a session.

Sixth, match the tool to the job. Use the strongest model for gnarly debugging and design, a middle model for everyday edits, and the cheapest for mechanical sweeps. Use Default permission mode in unfamiliar code, Accept Edits once you trust the plan, Plan mode for design, and never Bypass on real repositories. Raise the effort level for hard reasoning and keep it low for trivial work.

Seventh, automate the repetitive. Use hooks for every time rules, like formatting or linting. Use skills and custom commands for multi step workflows. Use headless mode in CI. And make it a team sport by committing shared settings, hooks, permissions, and the memory file, while keeping personal preferences in a local ignored settings file.

When things go sideways, interrupt and redirect, or clear and restart. If responses get slow, check the context. If you suspect a plugin problem, use safe mode. If a bad edit landed, rewind or use git.

To summarize in an interview: I follow explore, plan, code, verify. I protect my context, encode conventions in the memory file, write specific prompts, and always review and run the result.
passage:
Effective use of Claude Code depends more on workflow than on individual commands. The reliable rhythm has four steps: explore, plan, code, and verify. Claude first reads the relevant code without making edits. Then it proposes an approach, which the developer reviews. Only after approval does it write code, and finally the result is checked by running tests or the application. Skipping the planning step is the most common and most costly mistake.

Context should be treated as a limited budget. Clear the conversation between unrelated tasks, compact it during long tasks, delegate large reads to subagents, and reference files by path instead of pasting them. Conventions that must be repeated belong in the project memory file, which should be kept short.

Prompts should read like tickets, stating the goal, the constraints, the relevant files, and how success will be measured. Every change should be reviewed like a colleague's pull request, and committing at working states makes rollback simple. Hooks, skills, and shared team settings remove repetitive work and keep behavior consistent.
prompt: Describe your ideal workflow for making a change with Claude Code. Cover the explore, plan, code, and verify steps, explain why skipping the plan is risky, and give one example of a weak prompt rewritten as a strong one.

title: How Claude Code Skills Work
shadowText:
Today we will talk about skills in Claude Code. We will cover what a skill is, where it lives, how to add one, and how it loads under the hood.

Let us start with the definition. A skill is a folder that contains a file named SKILL dot md. That file has two parts. At the top is YAML front matter, which holds metadata. Below it is a markdown body with the instructions. A skill teaches Claude a repeatable procedure, like how we deploy, how we write a database migration, or how we review a pull request. And Claude can pull it in on demand.

Here is the key idea, called progressive disclosure. Claude does not keep the whole skill in context all the time. It only sees the one line description until the skill is needed. So you can have fifty skills and pay almost nothing for the forty nine you are not using. If you know JavaScript, think of a skill as a lazily imported module. The description is the entry in the package index, and the body is only imported when something matches.

Now, where do skills live? There are four places. Personal skills live in your home folder, under dot claude, skills, and they are available in all your projects. Project skills live in the dot claude folder inside a repository, and you commit them to share with the team. Plugin skills live inside a plugin and are called with the plugin name, a colon, and the skill name. And nested skills can live inside sub packages of a monorepo, so each package can ship its own. One detail is easy to miss. The command name comes from the directory name, not from the name field in the front matter. So a folder called deploy staging gives you the command slash deploy staging. The name field is just a display label.

How do you add a skill? There is no scaffold command. You create the folder and the file by hand. For example, make a folder called changelog under the project skills folder, and write a SKILL dot md. In the front matter you put a name, a description, and maybe an allowed tools list. The description might say: draft a changelog entry from the staged git diff, and use it when the user asks for release notes. The body is a short numbered procedure. Look at the staged diff. Group the changes into added, changed, fixed, and removed. Write short imperative lines. Add them under the unreleased heading. Then show the diff and stop, without committing. After that, either Claude invokes it automatically, or you type the slash command. To check it loaded, type a slash and start typing the name. If it does not show up, check that the folder name matches and the YAML is valid.

Let us look at the front matter fields. The description is the one you should always write, because it is how Claude decides to use the skill. Write it carefully, and lead with the use case. It is capped at about fifteen hundred characters in the skill listing. The allowed tools field lists tools the skill can use without a permission prompt while it is active. The disable model invocation field, when true, makes the skill manual only. Use that for anything with side effects, like deploying or sending messages. The argument hint field gives an autocomplete hint. There are also optional fields. You can set a model or an effort level while the skill runs. You can run it in an isolated subagent context by setting the context to fork. You can limit activation to certain file paths. You can scope hooks to the skill, and choose bash or PowerShell for inline commands.

Finally, the loading model has three tiers. Tier one is metadata, the name and description of every skill, always in context and tiny. Tier two is the body, which loads when the task matches or when you type the command, and then stays in context for the rest of the session. Tier three is bundled files, such as templates, reference documents, and scripts. They are loaded or executed only when needed, so they never sit in context idle.

To summarize in an interview: a skill is a folder with a SKILL dot md file, loaded lazily in three tiers. The description controls automatic use, side effects should be manual only, and good skills keep context cost low.
passage:
A skill in Claude Code is a folder containing a file named SKILL dot md. The file has YAML front matter with metadata and a markdown body with instructions for a repeatable procedure, such as deploying a release or writing a changelog entry. Skills can be personal, stored in the home directory, or project level, stored in the repository and shared with the team. Plugins and nested packages can also provide their own.

The central idea is progressive disclosure. Claude always sees the short description of each skill, loads the full body only when the task matches or the user calls the skill by name, and reads bundled templates or scripts only when needed. This keeps context cost low even with a large library.

The description is the most important field, because it determines automatic invocation. Skills with side effects should disable model invocation so that they run only when called manually. Other fields can restrict tools, select a model, or run the skill in an isolated subagent.
prompt: Explain what a Claude Code skill is and how progressive disclosure keeps it cheap. Cover where a skill lives, what the front matter description does, and why a deployment skill should be manual only.

title: What a Docker Container Really Is
shadowText:
Today we will talk about what a container really is. We will skip the marketing version and look at how it actually works. This is a very common interview topic.

Let us start with a common mistake. People say a container is a lightweight virtual machine. That is wrong, and it will mislead you. A container is a normal Linux process. It is the same kind of process that runs your Node server or your dotnet app. The difference is that the kernel has been told to restrict what it can see and what it can use.

Here is the key point. There is no container object in the Linux kernel. A container is an emergent thing, built from two separate kernel features. Namespaces control what a process can see. Control groups, called cgroups, control what a process can use. Add a root file system made from the image layers, and you have a container. Everything Docker does on Linux is orchestration on top of those primitives.

Let us take namespaces first. A namespace wraps a global system resource so the process inside thinks it has its own isolated copy. If you know scoping in programming, it is the same mental model. The thing exists globally, but you can only reach what your scope exposes. Namespaces are scope, enforced by the kernel. There are several types. The pid namespace isolates process IDs, so your app sees itself as process number one and cannot see host processes. The net namespace gives the container its own network interfaces, IP addresses, routing table, and ports. This is why localhost inside a container is not the localhost of your machine. The mnt namespace gives it its own mount points and file system tree. This is why a container sees the image and not your host disk. The uts namespace lets it have its own hostname. The ipc namespace gives it its own shared memory. And the user namespace maps user IDs, so a process can be root inside the container while being unprivileged on the host. With user namespace remapping enabled, that is an important security layer.

You can prove this yourself. Run a shell in a small Alpine container and list the processes. Your shell is process one. On the host, that same process has some high number. Two views, one process. Half of all Docker confusion comes from forgetting that the container's view is not the host's view.

Now cgroups. Namespaces hide things, but they do not stop a runaway process from eating all the memory or using every CPU core. A process in its own namespaces can still starve the host. Cgroups add hard limits and accounting for CPU, memory, disk input and output, and the number of processes. For example, you can start a container with a memory limit of two hundred fifty six megabytes and half a CPU core. If the process goes over the memory limit, the kernel kills it for being out of memory. You can watch live usage across containers with the docker stats command, which works like top but for each container.

Why does this matter in production? Without a memory limit, one leaking container can take down the whole host and every neighbor with it. Setting a limit deliberately is a feature. A loud, attributable kill of one container is far better than silent degradation of the whole machine.

Finally, compare virtual machines with containers. A virtual machine virtualizes hardware. A hypervisor emulates the CPU, disks, and network cards, and each machine boots a complete guest operating system with its own kernel. A container shares the host kernel. There is no guest operating system at all. That is why containers start fast and use much less memory. The trade off is isolation. Containers share a kernel, so a kernel level problem can affect all of them, while virtual machines have a stronger boundary.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. A container is just a process with restricted visibility from namespaces and restricted resources from cgroups, running on a root file system from an image. It is not a virtual machine, because it shares the host kernel. And in production I always set memory and CPU limits.
passage:
A container is not a lightweight virtual machine. It is an ordinary Linux process whose view of the system and use of resources are restricted by the kernel. The Linux kernel has no single container object. A container emerges from two features: namespaces and control groups, together with a root file system built from image layers.

Namespaces control what a process can see. Separate namespaces isolate process IDs, the network stack, mount points, hostnames, inter process communication, and user mappings. This is why a containerized application sees itself as process one and has its own file system and its own idea of localhost.

Control groups control what a process can use. They enforce limits on memory, CPU, disk input and output, and the number of processes. Without a memory limit, one leaking container can exhaust the host. Unlike a virtual machine, which runs a full guest operating system on emulated hardware, a container shares the host kernel, which makes it faster and lighter but gives a weaker isolation boundary.
prompt: Explain what a Docker container really is and how it differs from a virtual machine. Cover namespaces, cgroups, the shared kernel, and why you should set memory limits in production.

title: Writing Good Dockerfiles
shadowText:
Today we will talk about writing Dockerfiles. A Dockerfile is a recipe that turns a base image plus your source code into a new image. Understanding layers and caching is about eighty percent of writing good Dockerfiles. The rest is knowing the instructions and a few security rules.

Let us start with the mental model. Each instruction that changes the file system produces a layer, which is a content addressed archive of changes. If the inputs to an instruction have not changed, Docker reuses the layer it computed before. If you come from Node, think of it as a memoized build graph, like an incremental compiler or a bundler cache. Get the order wrong and you bust the cache all the time. Get it right and rebuilds take seconds. A running container is the read only layer stack plus one writable layer on top.

Here is the key point. Put things that change rarely at the top, and things that change often at the bottom. A classic Node example goes like this. Start from a base image. Set the working directory. Copy only the package files. Run a clean install of dependencies. Then copy the rest of the source. Because dependencies change less often than your code, the install layer stays cached when you edit a source file.

Now the instructions. FROM sets the base image and starts a build stage. Always pin the tag. Use a full version like twenty point eleven point zero with alpine, not latest, and not even just twenty. Latest changes silently and destroys reproducibility. It is like using a star version in package dot json. For maximum determinism, you can also pin the digest, because a tag is only a label while a digest is the identity.

RUN executes a command at build time and creates a layer. It has a shell form and an exec form, where the exec form runs the program directly without a shell. The big rule is to chain related commands in one RUN. A later layer cannot truly delete bytes from an earlier one, it only hides them. So if you install packages in one layer and delete the cache in another, the image still carries the cache. Do the install and the cleanup in the same RUN, and you get real savings.

COPY versus ADD. Almost always use COPY. It is a plain, predictable copy from the build context. It can also set ownership, which avoids an extra layer, and it can copy from another build stage in a multi stage build. ADD has two surprising behaviors. It can fetch URLs, which is uncacheable and unverifiable, and it automatically extracts local archives, which is a trap when you wanted the archive as is. The only good use of ADD is deliberate extraction of a local tarball.

WORKDIR sets and creates the working directory. Always use it. Do not write RUN cd, because each RUN is a fresh shell, so the directory change does not carry to the next instruction.

ENV sets environment variables that are baked into the image and available at build time and at run time. They show up in docker inspect. Use ENV for non secret settings such as the environment name or the port. Never use it for secrets.

ARG sets build time variables that do not exist at run time. You can override them with the build arg flag. There are two details to remember. An ARG is scoped to a stage, so you need to declare it again after each FROM. And an ARG declared before the first FROM, which can parameterize the base image, is not visible inside the stage unless you redeclare it.

The comparison between ARG and ENV is a favorite interview question. Both are available during the build. Only ENV survives into the running container. ARG is set with build arg, and ENV is set in the Dockerfile or with the run flag.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Order instructions from least to most frequently changing so the cache works for me. Pin base image versions. Chain commands and clean up in the same layer. Prefer COPY over ADD, use WORKDIR, use ENV for plain config only, and never put secrets in ENV or build arguments.
passage:
A Dockerfile turns a base image and application source into a new image. Each instruction that modifies the file system creates a layer, and Docker reuses a layer when its inputs have not changed. Good Dockerfiles therefore place rarely changing steps first. For a Node application, the package files are copied and dependencies installed before the rest of the source, so that editing code does not invalidate the dependency layer.

The base image should be pinned to a specific version, because the latest tag changes without warning and harms reproducibility. Related commands should be chained in a single RUN instruction, since a later layer cannot remove bytes already stored in an earlier one. Cleanup must happen in the same layer as the installation.

COPY is preferred over ADD, which can fetch URLs and silently extract archives. WORKDIR should set the working directory instead of using cd. ENV values persist into the running container and are visible when the image is inspected, so they must not hold secrets. ARG values exist only at build time and must be declared again in each build stage.
prompt: Walk me through how you would write a Dockerfile for a Node application so that rebuilds are fast. Explain layer caching and instruction order, why you pin the base image tag, and the difference between ARG and ENV.

title: How Docker Networking Really Works
shadowText:
Today we will talk about Docker networking. Many developers treat it like magic. It is not magic. Let us make it simple.

Let us start with the mental model. Docker networking is just normal Linux networking with a friendly command line on top. Every container gets its own network namespace. When Docker creates a network, it builds a virtual switch inside the kernel, called a bridge. Then it plugs each container into that switch with a virtual cable. Containers on the same switch can talk to each other.

Here is the first key point. Inside a container, the word localhost means the container itself. It does not mean your laptop. If your app in a container tries to reach Postgres at localhost, it will look inside its own namespace and find nothing. This one fact causes half of all Docker networking confusion.

Now let us look at network drivers. A driver decides how containers are connected. The default driver is bridge. It creates a private network on one host. Containers get private addresses and reach the outside world through network address translation. For most work, this is what you want.

The host driver removes isolation. The container shares the network of the host, so port eighty in the container is port eighty on the host. It can be fast, but you lose separation. The none driver gives the container no network at all, only a loopback interface. That is useful for pure computation or strict isolation. The overlay driver spans many hosts, and it is used with Swarm. Macvlan gives a container its own address on the physical network, so it looks like a real machine. That is rare, and mostly for legacy systems.

Next, the default bridge versus a user-defined bridge. This is very important. On the default bridge, containers can reach each other only by IP address. There is no name resolution. On a user-defined bridge, Docker runs a built-in DNS server. So a container called db can be reached simply by the name db. That is why you should always create your own network for your apps. The old link flag is legacy, so do not use it.

Let us talk about ports. Publishing a port with the dash p flag opens a path from the host into the container. For example, host port eight thousand to container port three thousand. The EXPOSE instruction in a Dockerfile is different. It is only documentation. It tells readers which port the app uses, but it does not open anything. Publishing is what actually lets traffic in from outside.

What if a container needs to reach a service running on your host machine? Use the special name host dot docker dot internal. Do not use localhost, because that points back to the container.

DNS has a few more tricks. Docker's embedded DNS server listens at one twenty seven dot zero dot zero dot eleven inside the container. You can add extra names with a network alias. If several containers share the same alias, Docker answers with all of them in turn. That gives you a simple round robin, like poor man's load balancing.

Finally, debugging. Start by listing and inspecting networks to see which containers are attached. If the api cannot reach the database, check three things. Are both containers on the same user-defined network? Does the name resolve? Is the app listening on all interfaces rather than only on localhost? A very handy tool is the netshoot image. You attach it to the network and use tools like ping, curl and dig from inside.

Let us finish with a short summary you could say in an interview. Docker networking is built on Linux namespaces and virtual bridges. Use user-defined bridge networks because they give you DNS by container name. Publishing a port opens access from the host, while EXPOSE only documents it. And remember that localhost inside a container is the container itself.
passage:
Docker networking is standard Linux networking presented through a simpler interface. Each container runs in its own network namespace, and Docker connects those namespaces to a virtual switch in the kernel called a bridge. As a result, localhost inside a container refers to that container alone, not to the host machine.

Docker offers several network drivers. The bridge driver is the default and creates a private network on a single host. The host driver shares the host network and removes isolation. The none driver provides only a loopback interface. The overlay driver spans multiple hosts, and macvlan gives a container its own address on the physical network.

A user-defined bridge network is preferable to the default bridge because it includes an embedded DNS server, which lets containers find each other by name. Publishing a port makes a service reachable from the host, whereas the EXPOSE instruction merely documents the port the application uses. When a connection fails, verify that both containers share a network, that the name resolves, and that the application listens on all interfaces.
prompt: Explain the difference between publishing a port and using EXPOSE in a Dockerfile. Then explain why a container named api can reach a container named db by name on a user-defined bridge network, but not on the default bridge.

title: Docker Volumes and Persistent Storage
shadowText:
Today we will talk about storage in Docker. The big question is simple. Where does your data live so that it survives when the container is gone? Let us walk through it.

Let us start with the basic model. A container is made of read-only image layers, plus one thin writable layer on top. That writable layer belongs to the container. When you remove the container, the writable layer is deleted too. So you must never keep important data there. If you know Node.js, think of the container as the process and the writable layer as process memory. When the process exits, memory is gone. Volumes are like the disk. They stay.

Docker gives you three ways to move data in and out of a container. They are bind mounts, named volumes, and tmpfs mounts. The difference is where the bytes live and who manages them.

A bind mount maps a path on your host into the container. You control the path. It survives container removal, because it is simply your own folder. It is perfect for development, for example mounting your source code so changes appear instantly. But it is tied to one host path, so it is not portable.

A named volume is managed by Docker. Docker stores it in its own area on the host. It survives removing the container, and it lives until you explicitly remove the volume. It is the right choice for things the app owns, like a Postgres data directory. It is also easier to back up and move.

A tmpfs mount lives in memory only. It never touches the disk, and it disappears with the container. Use it for sensitive or throwaway data, like decrypted secrets or scratch files.

Here is a simple rule. If a human or an editor on the host needs to touch the files, use a bind mount. If the application owns the data and it must persist, use a named volume. If the data is sensitive or temporary, use tmpfs.

There are two famous gotchas with bind mounts. First, if the host path does not exist, the behavior can surprise you, and it differs from named volumes. A named volume that starts empty is filled from the image content at that path, while a bind mount simply hides what the image had there. Second, the permission mismatch. Files on the host belong to your user ID, while the process in the container may run as a different one. That leads to permission denied errors, and it is the number one pain with bind mounts. You can also mount read only, using the ro option, when the container should not change the files.

Now about syntax. The short dash v flag works, but the dash dash mount flag is clearer. It uses explicit keys like type, source and target, and it fails loudly if something is wrong instead of silently creating a folder. Volumes can also use drivers and plugins to store data on remote systems.

Backups matter too. A common approach is to run a temporary container that mounts the volume and an archive folder, then creates a tar file. You can restore the same way.

For hardening, you can run the container with a read-only root filesystem and add tmpfs mounts only for the folders that must be writable.

One more point about the writable layer. It is also slower than a volume, because it goes through the storage driver. So even for performance, heavy writes like database files belong in a volume. And remember that anonymous volumes exist too. They are named volumes with a random name, which makes them easy to lose track of, so give your volumes real names.

Let us finish with an interview-style summary. The writable layer is ephemeral, so persistent data belongs in volumes. Use bind mounts for development, named volumes for application data, and tmpfs for secrets and scratch space. Prefer the mount flag for clarity, and watch out for user ID mismatches on bind mounts.
passage:
A Docker container consists of read-only image layers and a thin writable layer on top. That writable layer is removed together with the container, so data that must outlive the container should be stored elsewhere. Docker provides three mechanisms for this purpose: bind mounts, named volumes, and tmpfs mounts.

A bind mount maps a host directory into the container and is well suited to development, where source changes should appear immediately. A named volume is managed by Docker, persists until it is explicitly removed, and is the appropriate choice for application data such as a database directory. A tmpfs mount stores data in memory only and is suitable for secrets and temporary files.

Two practical issues deserve attention. Bind mounts can cause permission errors when the user ID inside the container differs from the owner of the host files. In addition, the explicit mount flag is preferable to the short volume flag, because it is clearer and reports mistakes instead of silently creating directories.
prompt: Compare bind mounts, named volumes and tmpfs mounts. For each one, say where the data lives, whether it survives removing the container, and give one realistic use case, such as a Postgres database or source code during development.

title: Docker Compose Explained for Interviews
shadowText:
Today we will talk about Docker Compose. It is one of the most useful tools for local development. Let us go step by step.

Let us start with what Compose is. Compose lets you define a multi-container application in one YAML file. Without it, you would type many docker run commands, each with flags for ports, volumes, environment variables and networks. You would also need to remember the right order. With Compose, you describe the whole stack once, then run one command, docker compose up. To stop and clean up, you run docker compose down. A good analogy is a package dot json combined with a process manager, but for containers.

Here is an important detail. There are two versions. The old one is docker hyphen compose, a standalone tool that is now deprecated. The modern one is docker compose with a space. It is a plugin for the Docker command line and follows the Compose Specification. In the modern version, the version key at the top of the file is obsolete, so you can leave it out.

Now, what Compose is not. It is not a production orchestrator. It runs on a single host. It cannot schedule containers across machines or heal itself across nodes. For that you need Kubernetes or Swarm. It is also not a replacement for a Dockerfile. The Dockerfile builds the image, and Compose runs it. Compose is excellent for local development and small single-server setups.

The file itself has a few top-level keys. The main ones are services, networks and volumes. Under services, each container has its own definition, with fields like image or build, ports, environment, volumes and networks.

Now let us talk about a very common trap. The depends_on option controls start order, but started does not mean ready. A database container can be running while Postgres is still initializing. If your API starts and connects too early, it crashes. The fix is to define a health check on the database, then in the API service use depends_on with the condition service_healthy. There are three conditions: service started, service healthy, and service completed successfully. The last one is useful for one-time jobs like migrations. Still, a good application should also retry its connections, so do not rely on Compose alone.

Networking in Compose is easy. By default, Compose creates one network for the project, and every service can reach every other service by its service name. That gives you free DNS. For more control, you can define custom networks to isolate tiers. For example, the proxy can reach the API, the API can reach the database, but the proxy cannot reach the database.

Volumes are declared at the top level and then used inside services, so data survives when you run down. Profiles let you mark some services as optional, such as a debugging tool, and start them only when you ask. Override files let you layer configuration. A base file holds shared settings, and a second file adds development or production changes. Be careful with merge rules, because some fields are merged and others are replaced.

Among the most useful commands are up with the detached flag, down, logs, ps, exec and build.

Let us also review the commands you will use every day. Docker compose up with the detached flag starts the stack in the background. Docker compose logs follows output from services.
