Template literal types build string types with interpolation. Combined with mapped types, they power things like a type safe event emitter, where an event name generates a matching handler name. Be careful, because unions in template literals produce a cartesian product that can explode.

Declaration merging and augmentation. Interfaces with the same name merge. You can augment a third party module with declare module, for example to add a user property to the Express request. Declare global adds to the global scope, and dot d dot ts files describe things that exist at runtime but have no types.

Newer features. The satisfies operator checks that an expression conforms to a type without widening it, so you get validation and keep the precise inferred type. Const type parameters infer literal types as if the caller wrote as const. The using and await using declarations provide explicit resource management, disposing a resource automatically at the end of the scope.

Decorators. There are two incompatible systems. Legacy experimental decorators, enabled with a compiler flag, are what NestJS uses together with reflect metadata. Stage 3 decorators, standard since TypeScript five, take a value and a context object. Know which one your framework needs.

Type safe patterns. Branded types make two strings with different meanings, like user ID and order ID, non interchangeable. Phantom types carry compile time only information. Builder patterns can track in the type which fields have been set. And zod gives you a schema that does runtime validation and also infers the static type, so you define it once.

Finally the tsconfig. Strict mode is an umbrella for several flags, including strict null checks. Module resolution should match what actually runs your code: node sixteen or next for Node, bundler for bundlers. The paths option aliases imports, but it only affects type checking, not the emitted code. Project references split monorepos. And verbatim module syntax makes type only imports explicit.

To summarize for an interview: structural typing, discriminated unions, conditional types with infer, mapped types, branded types, satisfies, and a strict, well chosen tsconfig.
passage:
TypeScript is structurally typed, so a value is accepted when its shape matches, regardless of its declared name. Discriminated unions use a shared literal field to narrow types and make checks exhaustive, and as const keeps literal types narrow. Generics can be constrained, given defaults, and used in conditional types, where infer captures types and distribution applies to unions.

Mapped types, including the built in utility types, transform the keys of an existing type, and template literal types build string types that can be combined with mapped types. Interfaces merge, third party modules can be augmented, and the satisfies operator validates a value without widening its type.

Legacy decorators, used by NestJS, differ from the standard Stage 3 decorators. Branded types prevent mixing values of different meaning, zod unifies runtime validation with static types, and a strict tsconfig with the correct module resolution prevents many errors.
prompt: Explain structural typing in TypeScript and how it differs from nominal typing in C sharp. Then describe a discriminated union and how it supports exhaustive checking.

title: Node.js Production Patterns Deep Dive
shadowText:
Today we will talk about running Node.js in production: its architecture, parallelism, streams, error handling, configuration, profiling, HTTP details and the choice between Fastify and Express.

Start with architecture. Node is V8 plus libuv. V8 runs your JavaScript. Libuv handles network input and output asynchronously, and uses a thread pool for things like file system access, DNS and crypto. That pool has only four threads by default, a classic bottleneck: five concurrent file reads means the fifth waits. You can raise it with the UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE variable, set before the first input and output.

For CPU bound work, use worker threads. They give real parallelism, with separate JavaScript threads that can share memory if you opt in, and are best used as a pool, for example with Piscina. The cluster module takes a different approach: it forks multiple processes that share a server port, to use all cores for a web server. So worker threads are for CPU heavy tasks like hashing and image resizing, and cluster is for scaling a server across cores. In production, PM2 is a process manager built on cluster, adding restarts, logs and zero downtime reloads. In containers, scale with replicas instead.

Streams process data piece by piece, instead of loading everything into memory. There are four types: readable, writable, duplex and transform. The key concept is backpressure. A fast readable can produce data faster than a slow writable can consume. Without flow control, chunks pile up in memory. Using pipe, or better the pipeline function, handles this automatically, and pipeline also handles errors and cleanup. If you write on data handlers that call write without checking the return value, memory grows. Every stream has a high water mark, the buffer size at which backpressure applies. In a custom transform, the callback is the backpressure signal. Readable streams are also async iterables, so for await works. In HTTP, the request and response are streams, so you can stream a large file without blowing memory.

Error handling. Separate operational errors, expected failures such as a timeout or invalid input, from programmer errors, which are bugs. Do not swallow programmer errors and limp on. Funnel everything through one centralized error handler that decides whether to respond, log or crash. For unhandled rejections and uncaught exceptions, log and exit, then let the supervisor restart you, because after an uncaught exception the process state may be corrupt. AsyncLocalStorage carries a request ID through the call chain, so every log line can include it. And remember that JSON stringify of an error gives empty braces, because message and stack are not enumerable, so serialize errors deliberately.

Configuration follows twelve factor: store config in the environment. Use dotenv only for local development. Validate configuration with zod at startup and fail fast, since raw environment values are all strings or undefined. Secrets come from the platform or a secrets manager, and the app should not care where they come from.

Performance and profiling. Most Node performance work is finding the synchronous code that blocks the loop. Use the built in profiler, Clinic for diagnosis and flame graphs, or 0x for one command flame graphs. The most important health metric is event loop lag, measured with perf hooks. For precise timing, use process hrtime bigint, a monotonic clock, rather than Date now.

HTTP internals. Frameworks wrap the core request and response objects. Keep alive reuses connections to avoid repeated TCP and TLS handshakes, but can delay server close during shutdown. HTTP two adds multiplexing. In production, terminate TLS upstream, at a proxy or load balancer, not in Node.

Fastify versus Express. Fastify often benchmarks two to three times faster. It uses a fast router, schema based serialization, and encapsulated plugins instead of global middleware. With JSON schemas you get validation and TypeScript types from one definition, and fast serialization. Express still wins on ecosystem compatibility and team familiarity.

To summarize for an interview: know the thread pool limit, use worker threads for CPU work and cluster or replicas for scaling, respect backpressure with pipeline, separate operational from programmer errors, validate config at startup, monitor event loop lag, and terminate TLS upstream.
passage:
Node.js combines V8 for executing JavaScript with libuv for asynchronous input and output and a thread pool that defaults to four threads. CPU bound work belongs in worker threads, preferably pooled, while the cluster module or container replicas scale a server across cores. Streams process data in chunks, and the pipeline function manages backpressure and errors so that memory does not grow when a consumer is slower than a producer.

Production error handling distinguishes operational errors from programmer errors, centralizes handling, and exits on uncaught exceptions so that a supervisor can restart the process. Configuration is taken from the environment and validated at startup, and event loop lag is the key health metric.

Connection keep alive reduces handshake cost, TLS should be terminated upstream, and Fastify generally outperforms Express through schema based serialization and encapsulated plugins.
prompt: Explain backpressure in Node streams: what goes wrong without it, how pipeline helps, and what role the high water mark plays. Then say when you would pick worker threads and when you would pick cluster.

title: Prisma Drizzle And PostgreSQL Features
shadowText:
Today we will talk about databases in the TypeScript world: Prisma, Drizzle, and useful PostgreSQL features. If you know Entity Framework Core, many ideas will feel familiar.

Prisma is schema first. You write a schema dot prisma file, and Prisma generates a fully typed client. EF Core is code first, with C sharp classes as the source of truth. Migrations: migrate dev is for development. It can detect drift and offer to reset the database, so it is dangerous in production. Migrate deploy only applies existing migrations, and is what you run in CI and production. The Prisma client is a typed query gateway, but unlike a DbContext it has no change tracker and no unit of work. Every create or update is an immediate statement. And you rarely need manual DTOs, because Prisma infers the exact result type from your select and include.

Reading and writing. Include loads relations, and select picks fields, and at the same level they are mutually exclusive. Nested writes let you create a parent and children in one call. Upsert creates or updates. The N plus one problem happens in Prisma too: a loop that runs one query per parent record. The one is the query for the list, the N is one extra query per item. The fix is include, a join, or batching. For transactions, there are two forms. The array form runs several independent operations atomically. The interactive callback form lets you read, decide and write inside one transaction, but keep it short, because it holds a connection.

Raw SQL. When the query API cannot express something, such as window functions, CTEs or full text search, use query raw with the tagged template version, which parameterizes values and prevents injection. You lose some type safety unless you type the result. Client extensions replace the old middleware, and are used for things like soft deletes and audit fields. Connection pooling matters in serverless: each function instance opens its own pool and can exhaust the PostgreSQL connection limit. Use PgBouncer or Prisma Accelerate in front.

Drizzle is the SQL first alternative. Prisma generates a query engine and a heavier client and abstracts SQL away. Drizzle is lightweight, defines the schema in TypeScript with table builders, and its query builder looks like SQL, so you see what you get. It also has a relational query API. Prefer Drizzle on the edge and serverless, where cold start and bundle size matter, or when you know SQL well and want full control. Migrations use drizzle kit.

PostgreSQL features worth using. JSONB stores JSON in a binary, indexable form, good for flexible fields, but do not use it to avoid proper modeling. Full text search uses tsvector for documents and tsquery for queries, with a GIN index. CTEs name subqueries and can be recursive for trees. Window functions compute running totals and rankings without collapsing rows, unlike group by. Partial indexes index only some rows, and composite indexes depend on column order. A B tree index suits equality and range queries, while GIN suits JSONB, arrays and full text.

Use explain analyze to read query plans. It runs the query and shows real timings and row counts. Look for sequential scans on big tables, large gaps between estimated and actual rows, and expensive sorts.

Should you wrap Prisma in a repository? The honest answer is that Prisma is already a repository and unit of work. Wrapping it everywhere adds ceremony. Wrap it when you want domain focused interfaces, easier testing, or isolation from the ORM. Prefer specific repositories per aggregate over a generic one, and implement a unit of work with the interactive transaction.

To summarize for an interview: migrate dev versus migrate deploy, no change tracking in Prisma, fix N plus one with include, pool connections in serverless, choose Drizzle for SQL control and small bundles, and use Postgres features like JSONB, CTEs and window functions, verified with explain analyze.
passage:
Prisma is a schema first ORM that generates a typed client. Its migrate dev command is for development and may reset the database on drift, while migrate deploy applies existing migrations in production. Unlike Entity Framework Core, Prisma has no change tracker, so every write is an immediate statement, and result types are inferred from select and include.

The N plus one problem arises when one query for a list is followed by one query per item, and it is solved with include, joins or batching. Transactions come in an array form and an interactive form. In serverless environments, each instance opens its own connection pool, so a pooler such as PgBouncer is needed to avoid exhausting database connections.

Drizzle is a lightweight, SQL first alternative with a schema defined in TypeScript, well suited to edge environments. PostgreSQL offers JSONB, full text search, common table expressions, window functions and partial indexes, and explain analyze reveals how queries really execute.
prompt: Explain the difference between prisma migrate dev and prisma migrate deploy, and why running the first one in production is dangerous. Then explain how you would detect and fix an N plus one problem.

title: Clean Architecture With NestJS
shadowText:
Today we will talk about Clean Architecture with NestJS. We will see how the architecture ideas map onto Nest's building blocks, and how a request flows through the layers.

The problem is the fat controller. In a basic Express app, the route handler does validation, business rules, database access and external calls. The fix is one rule applied strictly: source code dependencies point only inward, toward the domain. NestJS makes this natural, because it ships an inversion of control container with dependency injection built in.

Core Nest concepts. A module groups providers and controllers and is the unit of dependency injection scope. A provider, marked injectable, is a class that Nest manages and injects. A controller handles HTTP. Provider scopes are default singleton, request scoped, and transient, similar to the ASP.NET lifetimes. The request lifecycle has a fixed order, which you should memorize because it decides where each concern belongs: middleware first, then guards, then interceptors before the handler, then pipes, then the controller handler, then interceptors on the way out, and exception filters if something fails. Guards answer whether a request is allowed. Pipes validate and transform input. Interceptors wrap the call for logging, caching or mapping. Filters shape errors.

There are four layers. The domain layer is plain TypeScript with no Nest decorators and no Prisma. It must be testable without mocks. It contains rich entities that hold behavior, not anemic data bags, value objects such as Email that are immutable and compared by value, domain events named in the past tense, domain exceptions that carry no HTTP status, and repository interfaces that speak only in domain types.

The application layer uses CQRS with the Nest CQRS package, which is the equivalent of MediatR. A command and its handler form the write side. A query and its handler form the read side, and for heavy read models the handler may skip the entity and read straight from the database. Merge object context and commit are how events recorded by an entity get dispatched. Data transfer objects are the contract at the boundary. Input DTOs are validated with class validator and class transformer, and output DTOs hide internals such as the password hash. Zod is a schema first alternative.

The infrastructure layer implements the interfaces. A Prisma module wraps PrismaClient as an injectable provider that follows the Nest lifecycle. The repository implementation translates between domain objects and database rows. External HTTP clients go through the HttpModule, and Redis is wrapped as a provider for caching and rate limits.

The presentation layer has thin controllers that just dispatch to the command and query bus. A global validation pipe, registered once, with the whitelist option stripping unknown properties, protects against mass assignment. A global exception filter is the single place that translates domain exceptions into HTTP status codes. API versioning is enabled once and then applied per controller or route.

The composition root is where it is assembled. An important trap: you cannot inject a TypeScript interface by type in Nest, because interfaces disappear at runtime, unlike in ASP.NET Core. So you bind the interface to the implementation with an injection token, usually a symbol or a string, and inject it with the Inject decorator. Also the emit decorator metadata option must be true in the tsconfig, or injection by type silently breaks.

Cross cutting concerns include structured logging with Pino through the nestjs pino package, AsyncLocalStorage for correlation IDs without passing parameters around, an exception filter that returns the RFC seventy eight oh seven problem details format, and audit fields stamped automatically through a Prisma client extension.

To summarize for an interview: dependencies point inward, the domain is plain TypeScript, use CQRS for application logic, implement repositories in infrastructure, keep controllers thin, bind interfaces with injection tokens, and centralize validation and error translation.
passage:
Clean Architecture in NestJS applies a single rule: dependencies point inward toward a framework free domain layer. The domain contains rich entities, value objects, domain events, domain exceptions and repository interfaces. The application layer uses the Nest CQRS package with command and query handlers and boundary DTOs validated by class validator. The infrastructure layer implements the repository interfaces with Prisma and wraps external services.

The request lifecycle runs through middleware, guards, interceptors, pipes, the handler and then exception filters. Controllers stay thin and dispatch to the bus, while a global validation pipe with whitelisting and a global exception filter translate input and errors at the boundary.

Because TypeScript interfaces do not exist at runtime, repositories are bound to their interfaces using injection tokens in the composition root, and the emit decorator metadata option must be enabled so injection by type works.
prompt: Explain why a TypeScript interface cannot be injected by type in NestJS, how injection tokens solve this, and where the repository interface and its Prisma implementation live in Clean Architecture.

title: Authentication And Security In NestJS
shadowText:
Today we will talk about authentication, authorization and security in NestJS. Authentication answers who are you. Authorization answers what are you allowed to do. In ASP.NET you wire these as middleware. In Nest, you wire them with guards and Passport.

Nest does not ship its own authentication. It wraps Passport, the standard Node library, which uses strategies. A guard is a class implementing CanActivate. It runs after middleware but before pipes and the handler, and decides whether the request proceeds. It is the Authorize attribute of Nest. Calling AuthGuard with the name jwt returns a guard that runs the matching strategy. Guards receive an execution context rather than the raw request, so you reach the request through it.

JWT basics: three base64url parts, header, payload and signature. The payload is encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it. Never put secrets in it. Use the Nest JWT module, registered asynchronously so the secret comes from configuration, never from a literal in code. Use two tokens. A short lived access token limits damage if stolen. A long lived refresh token lets the client renew. Refresh token rotation means every time a refresh token is used, it is invalidated and a new one is issued. Store only a hash in the database. If an old token is presented again, that signals theft, so revoke the whole session family. For secret rotation, support multiple keys, with a key ID in the header, so old tokens remain valid until they expire.

Passport strategies extend a base class and implement validate, and whatever validate returns is attached to the request as the user. The local strategy handles username and password at the login route. The JWT strategy is the workhorse, running on every protected request. A common production setup is a global JWT guard, so everything is protected by default, with a Public decorator to opt out routes like login. You can add custom strategies for API keys in machine to machine cases, and for OAuth providers like Google.

Authorization has layers. Role based access uses a Roles decorator and a roles guard that reads the user from the request. Guard order matters: JWT guard first, so the user exists, then the roles guard. Permissions based access is finer: roles map to permissions like users delete or orders read. Resource based authorization handles ownership questions such as is this the user's own order, which need the loaded resource. CASL lets you define attribute based rules, such as a user can update an order if the order's user ID equals their own ID.

Security best practices. Use helmet for secure headers like content security policy, no sniff, strict transport security, and frame protection against clickjacking. Use the throttler module for rate limiting, especially on login. Configure CORS with exact origins, never a wildcard with credentials. Use a global validation pipe with the whitelist option to strip unknown properties, which prevents mass assignment, also called over posting. Prisma parameterizes queries, which prevents SQL injection, unless you build raw SQL by concatenating strings.

Passwords: never use plain MD5 or SHA, because they are fast, which helps attackers. Use a slow, salted, adaptive hash. Both bcrypt and argon2 qualify, but argon2 is preferred because it is memory hard, which makes GPU attacks costly. Terminate TLS upstream at a proxy or load balancer. Keep secrets in environment variables loaded by the config module, never hard coded or committed.

To summarize for an interview: guards with Passport strategies, short access tokens with rotated and hashed refresh tokens, global guard with a public opt out, roles then permissions then resource checks, and the security basics: helmet, throttling, exact CORS, whitelist validation and argon2.
passage:
NestJS builds authentication on Passport strategies and guards. A guard implements CanActivate and decides whether a request may reach the handler, and the AuthGuard factory runs the strategy with a given name. A global JWT guard with a Public decorator makes routes protected by default.

Access tokens should be short lived and refresh tokens should be rotated on each use and stored only as hashes, so that reuse of an old token reveals theft. The JWT payload is encoded but not encrypted, so it must not contain secrets, and signing secrets can be rotated using key identifiers.

Authorization can be role based, permission based, resource based or attribute based with CASL. Further protections include helmet for headers, throttling against brute force, exact CORS origins, a whitelisting validation pipe against mass assignment, parameterized queries, and password hashing with a slow memory hard algorithm such as argon2.
prompt: Explain refresh token rotation and how it helps detect token theft. Then describe how you would build role based access control in NestJS using a Roles decorator and guards, including the order of guards.

title: Testing NestJS With Jest
shadowText:
Today we will talk about testing a NestJS application. If you know xUnit and Moq, the mapping is easy. Jest is the runner, jest fn is like Moq, and supertest is like the web application factory with an HTTP client.

Jest basics. Tests use describe, it and expect, nested and grouped explicitly. Lifecycle hooks such as before each and after all are the equivalent of the constructor, dispose and class fixtures in xUnit. A very common mistake: toBe checks reference identity, so use toEqual for objects and arrays. For test doubles there are three levels. Jest fn creates a standalone mock function. Spy on wraps an existing method and can call through. Jest mock replaces a whole module. In Nest code you rarely need module mocking for application and domain code, because dependency injection lets you pass fakes in. Know the difference between clear, reset and restore for mocks: clear resets calls, reset also removes implementations, and restore also restores the original for spies.

Fake timers let you control time, the equivalent of injecting a clock. Be careful when mixing fake timers with awaited promises, which can make a test hang unless you advance timers asynchronously. For TypeScript, you need a transform: ts jest does type checking but is slower, and swc jest is much faster but does not type check, so you run tsc separately.

Unit tests exercise one unit in isolation: no database, no HTTP, no real clock. Start with the domain. Entities and value objects have no dependencies, so tests are plain: create, call, assert, or expect a thrown domain exception. For value objects, test validation at construction and equality. For services with dependencies, use the Nest testing module with create testing module, which builds a small DI container where you provide mocks. CQRS handlers are just injectable classes with an execute method, so you test them directly with mocked repositories.

Integration tests use real collaborators and drive the app through its HTTP surface. Supertest makes real HTTP requests against the Nest app without binding a port. You can override providers: use override provider to swap a real service, and override guard to bypass authentication so a test can focus on the endpoint. Remember that an interface cannot be a DI token in Nest, so tests use the same token as production.

Database testing: do not use an in memory SQLite database to test repositories written for PostgreSQL. It gives false confidence, because it differs in constraints, types and behavior. Use Testcontainers for Node to start a real PostgreSQL container per test suite, apply the real migrations, and run your repository tests against it. For cleanup, you can truncate tables after each test, with restart identity and cascade, which is simple, or wrap each test in a transaction that rolls back, which is faster but harder with code that manages its own transactions.

Match the test type to the layer: domain gets pure unit tests, application gets unit tests with mocks, infrastructure gets integration tests with Testcontainers, and the API gets end to end tests. The test pyramid says to have many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a few end to end tests.

Best practices. Name tests as unit, state, and expected behavior. Test one concept per test. Use builders or object mothers instead of repeating construction, and faker for realistic data, but pin a seed so failures are reproducible. Keep tests independent and order agnostic, since Jest runs files in parallel and shared mutable state or a shared database will cause flaky tests. Know the five kinds of test doubles: dummy, stub, spy, mock and fake. And remember that coverage measures lines executed, not behavior verified, so ninety five percent coverage can still hide critical gaps.

To summarize for an interview: unit test the domain without mocks, use the Nest testing module for services, supertest for the API, real PostgreSQL in Testcontainers for repositories, keep tests independent, and treat coverage as a signal, not a goal.
passage:
Testing a NestJS application maps onto the xUnit and Moq world: Jest is the runner, jest.fn and spyOn create test doubles, and supertest drives the HTTP surface without binding a port. The toBe matcher compares references, so toEqual is used for objects, and fake timers require care when combined with awaited promises.

Domain entities and value objects are tested without mocks. Services and CQRS handlers are tested using the Nest testing module with mocked repositories, and integration tests can override providers or guards to focus on an endpoint.

Repository tests should run against a real PostgreSQL instance started with Testcontainers rather than SQLite, because an in memory substitute hides real constraint and type behavior. Tests must be independent and order agnostic, builders reduce duplication, and coverage measures executed lines rather than verified behavior. Together these practices keep a test suite fast, reliable and meaningful as the codebase grows.
prompt: Explain why you should test repositories against a real PostgreSQL container instead of SQLite, and describe how you would test a protected NestJS endpoint with supertest by overriding the authentication guard.

title: Microservices With NestJS And RabbitMQ
shadowText:
Today we will talk about microservices in the Node and NestJS world. If you know the .NET story, with MassTransit, Polly and YARP, you will see the same ideas with different tools.

Let us start with the trade offs. A monolith is one deployable unit with one database. Microservices are many units, each independently deployable. You draw service boundaries along bounded contexts from domain driven design. The most important rule is data ownership: each service owns its data, and no other service may touch its database. This also allows polyglot persistence, where each service picks the database that fits its access pattern.

NestJS has a package called microservices, which gives one programming model over several transports. The key distinction is between message pattern and event pattern. A message pattern is request and response: the caller waits for an answer. An event pattern is fire and forget: the publisher does not wait. You can build hybrid apps that expose an HTTP API to the outside and also listen on a message transport. To call another service you inject a client proxy. A classic gotcha: send and emit return lazy observables, so nothing leaves the process until something subscribes. Forgetting to subscribe, or to convert to a promise, means the message is never sent.

For synchronous calls you sometimes genuinely need an answer right now, for example validating a user. Use the Nest axios module, or the lighter got library which has retry built in. Protect these calls. A circuit breaker, with the opossum library, trips open after a failure threshold, so callers fail fast instead of piling up. Retry transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter, so many clients do not retry at the same moment. In Compose or Kubernetes, service discovery is DNS: a service is reachable by its name.

For asynchronous communication, RabbitMQ is the backbone. The AMQP model is: a publisher sends to an exchange, bindings route messages to queues using routing keys, and consumers read from queues. If no binding matches, the message is dropped. Consumers choose between auto acknowledge and manual acknowledge. Manual acknowledgement is safer because a crash before acknowledging causes redelivery. A dead letter queue catches messages that cannot be processed, so a poison message does not loop forever. Sagas coordinate a business transaction across services with local transactions and compensations. Choreography lets services react to each other's events. Orchestration uses a coordinator.

BullMQ is different. RabbitMQ is for messaging between services. BullMQ, on Redis, is for background jobs within or behind a service, with retries, delays, priorities and cron style repeatable jobs. For scheduled work, use BullMQ when you need durability and distribution across instances, and the Nest schedule package for simple in process timers. Bull Board gives you a dashboard, like Hangfire's.

An API gateway is the single entry point that routes, terminates TLS, and applies authentication and rate limits once. NGINX is the workhorse. The http proxy middleware library lets you build a gateway in code. A backend for frontend is a gateway tailored to one client type, such as web or mobile.

Observability. Use OpenTelemetry for Node, which auto instruments HTTP, Nest, the database client, Redis and the AMQP library, so one trace follows a request across services. Add correlation IDs with AsyncLocalStorage, structured JSON logs shipped to Loki or ELK, and health endpoints.

Resilience. Layer your defenses: timeout, retry with backoff and jitter, and a circuit breaker. Use idempotency keys for state changing operations, because at least once delivery and retries mean a request can arrive twice. And use the outbox pattern. The classic distributed bug is saving an order to the database and then publishing an event as two separate steps; a crash between them loses the event. Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, and have a relay publish it.

To summarize for an interview: data per service, message versus event patterns, subscribe to your observables, use manual acknowledgements and dead letter queues, use BullMQ for jobs, protect calls with circuit breakers and backoff, and use the outbox with idempotent consumers.
passage:
Microservices are split along bounded contexts, and each service owns its data, which allows each to choose a suitable database. NestJS provides a transport abstraction in which message patterns implement request and response, event patterns implement fire and forget, and client proxy calls return lazy observables that send nothing until subscribed.

RabbitMQ routes messages from exchanges to queues through bindings and routing keys. Manual acknowledgement protects against lost messages, and dead letter queues isolate poison messages. BullMQ on Redis serves background jobs, retries and scheduling inside a service, and sagas coordinate transactions that span services.

Synchronous calls should be protected with timeouts, retries using exponential backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers. Idempotency keys make retries safe, and the outbox pattern ensures that events are published reliably. A gateway centralizes authentication and rate limiting, and OpenTelemetry with correlation identifiers makes distributed behavior visible.
prompt: Explain the difference between a message pattern and an event pattern in NestJS microservices, why send and emit may silently do nothing, and how the outbox pattern prevents lost events.

title: Dockerizing And Deploying NestJS Apps
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the Node and NestJS specific parts of Docker and deployment: building images, shutting down gracefully, Compose, CI, hosting and production settings.

Start with the image. A NestJS app needs development dependencies like TypeScript and the Nest CLI to build, but not to run. So use a multi stage build. A common three stage pattern is builder, deps and runtime. The builder installs everything and compiles. The deps stage installs only production dependencies. The runtime stage copies the compiled output and the production modules. Always use npm ci in Docker, because it installs strictly from the lockfile and fails if it is out of sync. Your dockerignore must exclude node_modules, otherwise the host's modules, possibly built for another operating system, overwrite the ones in the image.

Signals. Use the exec form of CMD, with node and the file as separate array items. Then node is PID one and receives SIGTERM directly. With the shell form, a shell becomes PID one, eats the signal and never forwards it, so there is no graceful shutdown. Also npm start has the same problem.

Graceful shutdown. The drain order is: stop accepting new connections, finish in flight requests, close resources like database pools and queues, then exit. In plain Node you handle SIGTERM yourself, and remember keep alive connections can stop the server from closing. NestJS does much of this for you if you call enable shutdown hooks. Then Nest calls lifecycle hooks in order: on module destroy, before application shutdown, on application shutdown. Close connections in those hooks. Readiness must reflect shutting down: the endpoint should start failing as soon as shutdown begins, so the load balancer stops sending new traffic. In Kubernetes there is a subtlety: the pod is removed from endpoints and sent SIGTERM at about the same time, so use a pre stop sleep of a few seconds and set a termination grace period longer than your longest request.

Compose for local development. A bare depends on only waits for a container to start, not for Postgres to be ready. Use the condition service healthy together with a health check. In dev, build the stage that still has the Nest CLI and run the watch mode with a bind mount. For microservices, you add more app services on a shared network, and use a Compose override file for development tweaks, so the base file stays clean.

For CI with GitHub Actions, run tests in one job and build and push the image in another, so a failed test blocks the image. Use build cache backends to speed builds.

Deployment options form a ladder: a VPS with Docker and Nginx, platforms like Railway, Render or Fly, and orchestrators. Node specific tips: platforms inject a PORT variable, and you must bind to it. A hard coded port silently fails. For TLS, Caddy gives automatic certificates, or use Nginx with Let's Encrypt. Zero downtime combines graceful shutdown with rolling or blue green deployment.

Production considerations. Configuration comes only from environment variables, validated at startup, with no secrets baked into the image. Use the Terminus package for health endpoints, separating liveness from readiness. The Node specific footgun is memory: V8 sizes its heap without knowing about the container limit. Set the max old space size flag to a fraction of the container memory, around seventy five percent, leaving room for buffers and native memory. And size your Postgres pool carefully: each Node process opens its own pool, while Postgres has a hard connection limit, so replicas times pool size must stay below it.

To summarize for an interview: multi stage builds with npm ci, exec form CMD so signals arrive, enable shutdown hooks, readiness that fails during shutdown, health conditions in Compose, bind to the PORT, set the heap size, and budget database connections.
passage:
A NestJS image is built in stages so that compilers and development dependencies stay out of the runtime image. The build uses npm ci for reproducible installs, and a dockerignore keeps host node_modules out. The container command must use the exec form so that node is PID one and receives SIGTERM, because a shell or npm start would swallow the signal.

Graceful shutdown stops new connections, finishes in flight requests and closes resources, and NestJS supports it through shutdown hooks and lifecycle methods. Readiness must fail as soon as shutdown begins, and in Kubernetes a pre stop delay and a sufficient termination grace period prevent dropped requests.

In Compose, health conditions ensure dependencies are ready, not merely started. In production, platforms inject a PORT variable that the application must bind to, configuration comes from validated environment variables, the V8 heap should be limited to a fraction of the container memory, and the database pool size multiplied by the number of replicas must stay below the database connection limit.
prompt: Explain why the shell form of CMD or using npm start breaks graceful shutdown for a NestJS container, and describe the shutdown sequence you would implement including readiness and Nest shutdown hooks.

title: OOP Foundations And The Mental Model
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the foundations of object oriented programming. You have written classes for years, but this lesson is about the thinking behind them, and how to explain it clearly in an interview.

Start with the core idea. Object oriented programming is one answer to a question: how do you organize a large program? The answer is to bundle state and behavior together into objects. Compare a procedural bank account program, where data sits in one place and functions sit elsewhere, and anyone can change the balance directly, with an object version, where the account holds its own balance and offers methods like deposit and withdraw that protect the rules. OOP arose, from Simula and Smalltalk to C plus plus, Java and C sharp, because programs were getting too big to keep in your head, with scattered data and tangled functions.

A class is a blueprint, an object is an instance built from it. The class describes what state a kind of thing holds and what it can do. It is not the thing itself. Then there is identity versus equality. Identity asks whether two variables refer to the very same object. Equality asks whether two objects have the same values. Mixing them up is a common source of bugs. A useful mental model is the little machine: an object has internal state, a small public interface of buttons you can press, and behavior that keeps its own state valid.

The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Encapsulation hides internal state and exposes controlled operations. Abstraction exposes only what is essential and hides complexity. Inheritance lets a type build on another. Polymorphism lets different types respond to the same call in their own way. They are not four equal ideas: polymorphism is usually considered the most powerful, and inheritance is the most over used.

Why does abstraction versus encapsulation confuse everyone? They sound similar. The simple distinction: abstraction is about the design view, deciding what to show, while encapsulation is the mechanism of protecting the inside, such as private fields. Abstraction answers what does this do. Encapsulation answers how do I keep its insides safe.

Paradigms. Procedural code organizes around steps and functions. Functional code organizes around pure functions and immutable data. Object oriented code organizes around objects with state and behavior. None is best; each has a sweet spot. TypeScript and C sharp are multi paradigm, deliberately blending OOP with functional tools such as lambdas, LINQ and array methods. Objects versus functions is a false dichotomy. In practice, you use objects for things with identity and changing state, and functions for transformations.

For JavaScript developers, there is a nuance. In classical languages like C sharp, a class is a compile time blueprint. In JavaScript, objects are linked through prototypes, and class syntax is sugar over that. C sharp will feel stricter: static typing, enforced access modifiers and explicit overriding.

A common gotcha: a class is not an object. The class is defined once, objects are created many times with new. Another: data bag classes with public fields and no behavior are not real encapsulation.

To summarize for an interview: OOP bundles state and behavior to manage complexity. Know class versus object, identity versus equality, the four pillars and how they relate, the difference between abstraction and encapsulation, and be able to say that modern languages mix paradigms.
passage:
Object oriented programming organizes a program by bundling state and behavior into objects, in response to the difficulty of managing large programs where data and functions are scattered. A class is a blueprint and an object is an instance built from it, and identity, whether two references point to the same object, differs from equality, whether two objects hold the same values.

The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Encapsulation protects internal state, while abstraction decides what to expose, which is why the two are often confused.

Procedural, functional and object oriented styles each suit different problems, and TypeScript and C sharp deliberately combine them. Objects suit entities with identity and changing state, and functions suit transformations. JavaScript implements classes on top of prototypes, whereas C sharp enforces stricter typing and access rules.
prompt: Explain the difference between abstraction and encapsulation, and between object identity and equality. Give a short example of how bundling state and behavior in an object improves on a procedural design.

title: Classes Objects And Members
shadowText:
Today we will talk about classes, objects and their members, comparing TypeScript and C sharp. Let us go through the main ideas.

A class is a blueprint, and an object made with new is an instance. Every class is built from four kinds of members: fields, properties, methods and constructors. In TypeScript, a class is a real runtime construct that desugars to a constructor function and prototype. In C sharp it is a compile time type in the common language runtime.

Fields and properties. A field is raw storage. A property is a controlled access point that looks like a field from outside but runs code. C sharp has auto properties with get and set, the init accessor for set only at construction, and computed properties. TypeScript uses fields, or getter and setter accessors. Both languages let you assign defaults at the field declaration, which runs before the constructor body.

Methods are functions that belong to a class and operate on the instance state through this. C sharp supports expression bodied members, using an arrow to shorten simple methods. C sharp has true method overloading, multiple methods with the same name and different parameters. TypeScript only has overload signatures over a single implementation, because JavaScript has no overloading.

Constructors. A constructor runs on new, and its job is to leave the object in a valid initial state. TypeScript has parameter properties: adding an access modifier to a constructor parameter declares and assigns the field in one step. C sharp twelve added primary constructors, with parameters on the class header in scope across the class. Constructors can chain to another constructor in the same class or to the base class. C sharp also has object initializers, which set properties after construction in one expression, similar to object literals.

The keyword this refers to the current instance. In JavaScript and TypeScript, this is decided by how a function is called, not where it is defined, so passing a method as a callback loses it. Fix this with an arrow function or bind.

Static members belong to the class, not to instances. There is one copy, shared by all. C sharp also has fully static classes that cannot be instantiated and are used for utility functions.

Object lifetime. New allocates memory, runs the constructor, and gives you a reference. Neither language has manual free; the garbage collector reclaims unreachable objects. When an object owns an operating system resource, such as a file or connection, waiting for the garbage collector is not enough. C sharp has IDisposable and the using statement, and newer JavaScript has the using declaration for explicit resource management.

Reference versus value semantics is the biggest difference between the languages. In JavaScript, every object is a reference. Assigning copies the reference, so both names point to the same object. C sharp lets you choose: a class is a reference type, a struct is a value type, copied on assignment. By default, two class instances are equal only if they are the same object. Records in C sharp provide structural equality, comparing by values. A classic bug is thinking you have a copy when you have an alias, so mutating one changes the other.

One more gotcha: TypeScript private is erased at runtime, so plain JavaScript can still read it.

To summarize for an interview: know the four member kinds, properties versus fields, constructor shortcuts, the this trap in JavaScript, static members, deterministic cleanup, and the difference between reference and value semantics.
passage:
A class defines fields, properties, methods and constructors, and an object is an instance created with new. TypeScript classes are runtime constructs built on prototypes, while C sharp classes are compile time types. C sharp offers auto properties, init accessors, expression bodied members, true method overloading and primary constructors, whereas TypeScript provides parameter properties and overload signatures over a single implementation.

In JavaScript and TypeScript, the value of this depends on how a function is called, so detached methods lose it. Static members belong to the class itself. Objects that own operating system resources need deterministic cleanup, through IDisposable in C sharp or the using declaration in modern JavaScript, because garbage collection timing is unpredictable.

JavaScript treats all objects as references, so assignment creates aliases. C sharp distinguishes reference types such as classes from value types such as structs, and records provide structural equality. Confusing an alias with a copy is a classic source of bugs.
prompt: Explain reference semantics versus value semantics using JavaScript and C sharp as examples. Include what a class and a struct do on assignment and how records change equality.

title: Encapsulation And Protecting Invariants
shadowText:
Today we will talk about encapsulation, the first pillar of object oriented programming. The one line idea: an object guards its own state and exposes controlled operations, so it can never be put in an invalid state.

Encapsulation has two ideas welded together. First, hide internal state. Second, expose a controlled interface. The anti example is the anemic object: public fields that anyone can change, with logic living elsewhere. Nothing protects anything. The object cannot defend itself.

Access modifiers are the mechanism. C sharp has six levels: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal and private protected. All are enforced by the compiler and the runtime. TypeScript has public, private and protected too, but they are compile time only. After compilation they are erased, and plain JavaScript can read a private field, as can a cast to any. JavaScript added true private fields in ES2022 with the hash prefix, enforced by the engine itself. So the comparison is: TypeScript private is checked by the compiler only, JavaScript hash private is checked at runtime, and C sharp private is checked by both. Remember this: TypeScript private is a lie at runtime.

Properties, getters and setters give controlled access. A computed property has no backing field and derives its value from other state, which avoids keeping redundant data in sync. If you must allow writes, put validation in the setter. The most useful move is read only from outside, writable inside. And watch the smell: a getter and setter pair that only reads and writes a field is not encapsulation. It is a public field wearing a costume.

Protecting invariants is the point of the whole pillar. An invariant is a statement that must be true for the object's whole life, such as a balance never going below zero. There are three techniques. One, validate in the constructor, so the object is born valid and no invalid instance can exist. Two, make mutations go through methods that enforce rules: call loan dot return, instead of setting a returned date field directly. Three, fail loudly on invalid transitions. A loan is a small state machine, going from active to returned. Illegal transitions, like returning twice, must throw rather than silently continue.

Information hiding scales up. Every public member is a promise you have to keep, because changing it later breaks callers. Keep the public surface small. Across modules, in TypeScript you control visibility with what you export, and in C sharp with internal, which limits access to the assembly.

Immutability is encapsulation's force multiplier. If state cannot change after construction, there are no setters to corrupt it. In C sharp, use readonly fields, init properties, records, and the with expression, which creates a modified copy without changing the original. TypeScript has readonly, as const and Object freeze, each weaker: readonly is compile time only, as const affects types, and Object freeze is shallow. Immutability also removes bugs from aliasing and shared state.

Gotchas: TypeScript private, protected and readonly are erased at runtime, so JSON stringify and the debugger can see them.

To summarize for an interview: hide state, expose behavior, validate at construction, route all changes through methods, throw on illegal transitions, know that only C sharp and JavaScript hash private are truly enforced, and prefer immutability where you can.
passage:
Encapsulation means an object hides its internal state and exposes only controlled operations, so that its invariants always hold. C sharp enforces access modifiers in the compiler and at runtime, TypeScript private and protected exist only at compile time and disappear in the emitted JavaScript, and JavaScript hash private fields are enforced by the engine.

Invariants are protected by validating in the constructor so that no invalid instance exists, by changing state only through methods that enforce rules, and by throwing on illegal state transitions. A getter and setter pair that merely exposes a field is not encapsulation, and the public surface of a class is a contract that should stay small.

Immutability strengthens encapsulation because there are no setters to corrupt state. C sharp provides readonly, init, records and the with expression, while TypeScript provides readonly, as const and the shallow Object.freeze.
prompt: Explain what an invariant is and show how you would protect one in a Loan class using constructor validation, methods that enforce rules and exceptions on illegal transitions. Mention how TypeScript private differs from JavaScript hash private.

title: Inheritance And Its Trade-offs
shadowText:
Today we will talk about inheritance, the most over used pillar of object oriented programming. We will see how it works in TypeScript and C sharp, and why it so often hurts.

Inheritance lets you derive a specialized type from a more general one, and the derived type gets the base type's members. It models an is a relationship. The relationship must hold behaviorally, not just sound true in English. The classic warning sign is a subclass that has to throw not supported for inherited methods, or one that breaks the base class's promises. That violates substitutability.

Syntax: TypeScript uses extends, and C sharp uses a colon. What the subclass can see depends on access modifiers: private members are hidden, protected members are visible to subclasses but not to outside callers, and public members are visible to all.

Construction. A derived object is built base part first. In TypeScript you must call super before using this, and in C sharp you call the base constructor in the constructor header. For a chain of three levels, construction walks down to the base and then unwinds back up. Field initializers and constructors run in a defined order, and calling an overridable method from a base constructor is dangerous, because the subclass is not yet initialized.

Overriding means a subclass replaces an inherited method, and the version that runs is chosen by the actual runtime type of the object, not the variable's declared type. In C sharp, overriding is explicit opt in: methods are non virtual by default. The base must say virtual or abstract, and the subclass must say override. The new keyword hides the base method instead of overriding it, and then the version called depends on the variable's type, which is almost never what you want. In TypeScript and JavaScript, every method is effectively virtual, because methods live on the prototype and a subclass method simply shadows the base one. Do not confuse overriding, overloading and shadowing.

How is the right method found? C sharp builds a virtual method table per type, an array of function pointers, one slot per virtual method, so the call goes through a table lookup. JavaScript walks the prototype chain from the object up. Protected members are how a base class offers extension points to subclasses without making them public.

Controlling inheritance. C sharp has sealed, which forbids deriving from a class, or further overriding a method. TypeScript has no sealed keyword, only conventions. The opposite is an abstract base class, which cannot be instantiated and can declare abstract members that subclasses must implement.

Now the cost of inheritance. It is the tightest coupling in object oriented design. The fragile base class problem: a harmless change in the base class silently breaks subclasses you did not even open. Deep hierarchies add coupling and cognitive load at every level. Joe Armstrong's quote captures it: you wanted a banana, but you got a gorilla holding the banana, and the entire jungle. The usual fix is composition over inheritance: give an object the behavior it needs as a collaborator, a has a relationship, instead of an is a one.

Gotchas: C sharp methods are non virtual by default, JavaScript methods are always virtual. If you override in C sharp without virtual on the base, you only hide the method.

To summarize for an interview: inheritance models is a, must preserve substitutability, uses virtual and override in C sharp, dispatches on the runtime type, and should be limited because of fragile base classes. Prefer composition when in doubt.
passage:
Inheritance derives a specialized type from a general one and models an is a relationship that must hold behaviorally. TypeScript uses extends and C sharp uses a colon, and construction proceeds from the base class to the derived class. Protected members form extension points for subclasses without becoming public.

In C sharp, methods are non virtual by default, so overriding requires virtual in the base and override in the subclass, while the new keyword only hides the base method. In JavaScript and TypeScript every method is overridable because it lives on the prototype chain. The method that runs is chosen by the runtime type, through a virtual method table in C sharp and prototype lookup in JavaScript.

Sealed classes and abstract classes control inheritance, but inheritance creates tight coupling, including the fragile base class problem and unwieldy deep hierarchies. Composition, which gives an object collaborators instead of a parent, is usually the safer design.
prompt: Explain the fragile base class problem and why inheritance is considered tight coupling. Then compare how overriding works in C sharp with virtual and override against how it works in JavaScript and TypeScript.

title: Polymorphism In TypeScript And C Sharp
shadowText:
Today we will talk about polymorphism, which means many forms. One name, one interface, many concrete behaviors, with the right one chosen for you. People say that object oriented programming equals inheritance. The deeper truth is that polymorphism is what makes it powerful, and inheritance is just one way to get it.

There are three kinds. Subtype polymorphism, also called inclusion or runtime polymorphism, works by overriding a base method and calling it through a base reference. Ad hoc polymorphism is overloading, where the same name has different implementations chosen by argument types. Parametric polymorphism is generics, where one piece of code works over many types.

Let us start with subtype polymorphism, the main event. You have a variable typed as the base type holding an object that is actually a subtype. When you call a method, the one that runs is chosen by the actual object, not the declared type of the variable. The compiler only lets you call members visible on the declared type, but the runtime picks the implementation. The classic example is shapes: a list of shapes, each with an area method, and a loop that sums the areas without knowing which shape is which. In the media library example, the base item declares a late fee calculation, and each item type, a book, an audiobook or a DVD, overrides it. The billing code just calls the method and never switches on the type.

Ad hoc polymorphism, overloading. C sharp has true overloading: several methods with the same name and different parameter lists, and the compiler picks one at compile time. JavaScript has no real overloading, since a second function with the same name replaces the first. TypeScript fakes it with overload signatures over a single implementation that uses union types and checks. C sharp also supports operator overloading, so a type can define what plus or double equals means. JavaScript and TypeScript do not.

Parametric polymorphism is generics. Subtype polymorphism is one piece of code for many subtypes. Generics are one piece of code for many types, with type safety. You can have generic classes and generic methods. A bare type parameter can do almost nothing, since you cannot call an area method on an unknown type, so you add constraints that say T must be at least this: for example, T must implement a certain interface.

How does dynamic dispatch work under the hood? In C sharp, each class with virtual methods has a virtual method table, an array of function pointers, one slot per virtual method, and each object points to its class table. A call is an index into the table. In JavaScript, there is no table. A method call is a property lookup that walks the prototype chain until it finds the method. For ordinary application code, the cost is negligible compared to input and output.

Polymorphism only works if a subtype is truly usable wherever the base type is expected. That requirement is the Liskov Substitution Principle. Imagine the base fee method promises a non negative fee that never decreases as the days increase. A subclass that returns a negative fee, or lowers it after a threshold, breaks the contract, and callers that relied on the promise break. A safe override must not demand more from callers, that is, not strengthen preconditions, and must not promise less in return, that is, not weaken postconditions.

Gotchas. In C sharp, forgetting to mark the base method virtual means your override does not work as polymorphism. In TypeScript, all methods are virtual, so this does not arise.

To summarize for an interview: polymorphism comes in three kinds, subtype, ad hoc and parametric. The runtime picks the implementation from the actual object. C sharp uses virtual tables, JavaScript uses the prototype chain. And subtypes must honor the base contract, or polymorphism turns into bugs.
passage:
Polymorphism allows one interface to have many concrete behaviors. Subtype polymorphism selects an overridden method according to the actual runtime object rather than the variable's declared type, so code such as late fee billing can call one method without switching on type. Ad hoc polymorphism is overloading, which C sharp supports directly and TypeScript emulates with overload signatures, while parametric polymorphism is provided by generics with constraints.

Dynamic dispatch uses virtual method tables in C sharp and prototype chain lookup in JavaScript, and the cost is usually negligible in application code.

Polymorphism is safe only when subtypes are substitutable for their base type. A valid override must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions of the base method, which is the essence of the Liskov Substitution Principle. In interviews, a good answer names the three kinds, explains that the runtime selects the implementation, and warns that overrides must respect the base contract.
prompt: Explain subtype polymorphism using a late fee calculation for different item types, and say how the runtime decides which method runs. Then explain why a subclass that breaks the base contract violates substitutability.

title: Abstraction Interfaces And Abstract Classes
shadowText:
Today we will talk about abstraction, interfaces and abstract classes. Abstraction is the discipline of modeling the essential and hiding the incidental. You decide what a thing does and let callers ignore how.

First, abstraction versus encapsulation, which people constantly mix up. They are related, as both involve hiding, but they answer different questions. Encapsulation hides one object's insides to protect its state. Abstraction hides which concrete type you are talking to, so you depend on a contract. Encapsulation is about protection. Abstraction is about simplification and substitution.

An interface is a contract: a set of members a type promises to provide, with no implementation. In C sharp, interface names start with a capital I, such as ILoanPolicy. The big divergence is nominal versus structural. In C sharp, a class must explicitly declare that it implements an interface. In TypeScript, typing is structural: any object with the right shape satisfies the interface, with no declaration needed. A type can implement many interfaces in both languages, which is the key to composing capabilities.

An abstract class sits between a plain class and an interface. It can provide real implementation for some members, while leaving others abstract for subclasses to fill. You cannot instantiate one, because it has unfilled holes. In C sharp, filling an abstract member requires the override keyword, while TypeScript simply redeclares it. A common use is the template method pattern: the base class owns the skeleton of an algorithm, such as computing a due date, and delegates one step, like the loan period, to subclasses.

Interface or abstract class? The decision is contract versus identity. Use an interface to define a capability that unrelated types can share. Use an abstract class when subclasses are truly one kind of thing and share real code or state. Both languages allow only single inheritance of classes but multiple interfaces. That is the structural reason behind the advice to prefer interfaces for public abstractions: they do not use up your single inheritance slot, they do not force shared state, and they are easier to mock in tests.

Default implementations. What if you add a member to an interface after many implementations exist? Since C sharp eight, an interface member can have a body, a default interface method, which implementers get for free and may override. TypeScript interfaces have no runtime presence, so they cannot carry code. The gap is filled with an abstract base class, a helper function, or a mixin.

The principle that makes this pay off is program to an interface, not an implementation. Depend on abstractions, not on concrete classes. In real frameworks, a dependency injection container wires the contract to a concrete class at runtime, so your code never uses new on the implementation. The canonical industrial example is the repository interface: the domain or application layer defines it, the infrastructure layer implements it with a database, and the business code stays free of database details. This carries straight into Clean Architecture.

Gotchas. Abstraction is not encapsulation. And do not create an interface for every class with only one implementation unless there is a reason, such as a boundary or testing seam.

To summarize for an interview: abstraction models the essential; interfaces are contracts, nominal in C sharp and structural in TypeScript; abstract classes mix contract and shared code; prefer interfaces for public abstractions; and program to interfaces so you can swap implementations.
passage:
Abstraction models what is essential and hides the incidental, so callers depend on a contract instead of a concrete type. It differs from encapsulation, which protects one object's internal state. An interface is a contract without implementation, declared explicitly in C sharp, which is nominal, and satisfied by shape in TypeScript, which is structural.

An abstract class can combine shared implementation with abstract members that subclasses must fill, and it cannot be instantiated. The template method pattern uses this to fix an algorithm's skeleton while subclasses supply the varying steps. Because a class can inherit from only one base but implement many interfaces, interfaces are usually preferred for public abstractions.

C sharp supports default interface methods, whereas TypeScript fills the gap with helper functions, abstract bases or mixins. Programming to an interface allows dependency injection to supply implementations, as in the repository interface defined by the domain and implemented by infrastructure.
prompt: Explain the difference between an interface and an abstract class and when you would choose each. Also explain nominal versus structural typing as it applies to interfaces in C sharp and TypeScript.

title: SOLID Principles Explained
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the SOLID principles. They are five design principles, assembled by Robert Martin, that push code toward being easy to change and test. The goal was never to obey five rules. The goal is code you can change safely and cheaply. Let us go through them.

S is the Single Responsibility Principle. A class should have only one reason to change, and a reason to change means one actor, one stakeholder who can demand a change. The before picture is a god class, such as a library service that applies business rules, formats output, saves to the database and sends notifications. The after picture splits it by reason to change: a loan policy for the rules, a repository for persistence, a notifier for messages, and a loan service that orchestrates them. You gain cohesion and testability. A gotcha: SRP is about actors, not verbs. Two methods can live together if the same stakeholder changes them.

O is the Open Closed Principle. Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. The bad example is a switch statement on item type inside a late fee function: every new item type means editing the function. The good version uses polymorphism. Each item type owns its fee rule, and adding a magazine is a new file with nothing existing touched. The same idea works through the strategy pattern, such as a loan policy interface.

L is the Liskov Substitution Principle. If S is a subtype of T, objects of T can be replaced with objects of S without breaking the program. The famous rectangle and square example is misunderstood. The point is not that a square is not a rectangle in math. The point is that a mutable square cannot honor a rectangle's contract, where setting the width does not change the height. The fixes are to make them immutable, to drop the false is a relationship, or to use a common abstraction. A domain trap: a reference book that cannot be checked out, but inherits a checkout method, which then throws. Callers break.

I is the Interface Segregation Principle. No client should depend on methods it does not use. A fat interface for media items forces an ebook to implement physical condition methods that make no sense. Split it into small role based interfaces, and let each type implement just the roles it fills. This is more natural in TypeScript, where structure matters, while C sharp requires explicit declaration.

D is the Dependency Inversion Principle. High level modules should not depend on low level modules. Both should depend on abstractions. In the before picture, a loan service creates a concrete Postgres repository with new, so business policy depends on Postgres. In the after picture, the service depends on a repository interface. The often missed point is who owns the interface: the high level module owns it. If the interface lives next to the Postgres code, the dependency still points the wrong way. DIP makes dependency injection natural, and it creates the seams tests plug fakes into.

How do they fit together? They form a chain. SRP gives small focused classes. OCP lets you extend them through abstractions. LSP makes sure the extensions are safe. ISP keeps abstractions lean. DIP wires it all through interfaces. The same idea appears at three scales: classes, dependency injection containers, and Clean Architecture.

A caution: SOLID is a means, not an end. Applying it blindly leads to needless abstraction. Apply it when you feel the pain of change.

To summarize for an interview: one reason to change, extend with polymorphism instead of editing switches, subtypes must honor contracts, small client specific interfaces, and depend on abstractions owned by the high level code.
passage:
The SOLID principles guide code toward changeability. The Single Responsibility Principle says a class should have one reason to change, meaning one stakeholder, so a god class is split into collaborators. The Open Closed Principle says to extend behavior through polymorphism or strategies instead of editing switch statements.

The Liskov Substitution Principle requires subtypes to honor the base contract, and the rectangle and square example shows how a false is a relationship breaks callers. The Interface Segregation Principle prefers small, role based interfaces over fat ones.

The Dependency Inversion Principle states that high level and low level modules should both depend on abstractions, and that the high level module should own the abstraction. This makes dependency injection natural and supplies the seams for testing. The five principles reinforce each other, but they are heuristics and should be applied where change causes real pain.
prompt: Explain the Dependency Inversion Principle using a loan service and a Postgres repository, including who should own the interface. Then explain the Open Closed Principle using a switch statement for late fees as the bad example.

title: Design Patterns And Their Overuse
shadowText:
Today we will talk about design patterns. A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. The classic catalogue is the 1994 Gang of Four book. Let us see the main ones, and, just as important, when not to use them.

First, how to think about patterns. They are discovered, not installed. You do not start a feature by picking a pattern. You write the simplest thing that works, feel a specific pain, such as a switch statement that keeps growing, and then reach for the pattern that relieves it. Learn the problem each pattern solves, not just its diagram.

Creational patterns control how objects are created. The factory method defers the choice of the concrete class to one method, so callers depend on an abstraction. The abstract factory does this for families of related objects. The builder constructs a complex object step by step, avoiding constructors with ten positional arguments. The singleton guarantees exactly one instance with global access, but dependency injection usually replaces it, because global state is hard to test.

Structural patterns compose objects into larger structures. The adapter wraps one interface to match another. The decorator adds behavior dynamically by wrapping an object that implements the same interface, such as adding logging or caching around a repository. The facade provides one simple interface over a complicated subsystem. The proxy is a stand in with the same interface that controls access, for lazy loading, access control or caching. The composite treats single objects and groups uniformly through a common interface, as in a file system of files and folders.

Behavioral patterns describe collaboration. The strategy defines interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the algorithm varies independently from the client, such as different late fee policies. The observer creates a one to many dependency, so when a subject changes, its observers are notified, which is the basis of event emitters. The command turns a request into an object that can be stored, queued, logged or undone. The template method defines an algorithm skeleton in a base class and lets subclasses override steps. The state pattern lets an object change behavior when its internal state changes, with each state as an object.

You are already using most of these. Dependency injection containers use factories. Express middleware is a chain of decorators or responsibility. Event emitters are observers. Array sort with a comparator is a strategy. Recognizing them is what turns writing framework code into understanding it.

The anti pattern is pattern overuse. Once you learn the catalogue, every problem looks like it needs one. The result is needless indirection, many tiny classes, and code that is harder to read. A sane procedure: write the simplest direct code first, wait for the pain, name the pattern that fits, apply the smallest version, and stop. A pattern is a response to a problem, not a goal. Asking where can I use the observer pattern is the wrong question. Ask what problem am I having.

To summarize for an interview: know a few patterns from each family, say the problem each solves, mention that DI replaces singleton, that decorator and strategy are very common, and always add that patterns should be applied only when a real problem appears.
passage:
A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem. Creational patterns such as factory method, abstract factory, builder and singleton control object creation, although dependency injection usually replaces the singleton. Structural patterns, including adapter, decorator, facade, proxy and composite, determine how objects are combined.

Behavioral patterns such as strategy, observer, command, template method and state describe how objects collaborate. Many are already present in everyday frameworks, for example event emitters as observers and comparators as strategies.

Patterns should be discovered in response to a specific pain, not applied up front. Overuse produces needless indirection and unreadable code, so the sensible approach is to write the simplest code first, wait for the problem, and then apply the smallest suitable pattern. In interviews, naming the problem a pattern solves, and admitting when a simple function is enough, shows good judgment.
prompt: Pick any two design patterns, such as strategy and decorator, and explain the problem each one solves with an example. Then explain why overusing patterns is itself an anti pattern.

title: Composition Anti Patterns And Real World OOP
shadowText:
Today we will talk about composition, common anti patterns, and how to apply object oriented design in the real world.

Start with composition over inheritance. Inheritance models is a: a book is a library item. Composition models has a: an item has a fee policy and a format. Has a beats is a more often than you think. In a library example, a hierarchy of item, book, audiobook and DVD looks clean at first. Then it strains: a book that is also available as an ebook, items with different fee rules cutting across the hierarchy, and a class explosion.
