The refactoring is to make an item have the parts that vary: a format and a fee strategy. You then compose behavior by plugging in collaborators. When you want to share behavior across unrelated classes without a common base, TypeScript has mixins, and C sharp uses interfaces plus delegation.

Common anti patterns. The god object does everything and violates single responsibility. The anemic domain model has entities that are bags of getters and setters, with all logic in services, which is OOP in syntax but procedural in practice. The yo yo problem is bouncing up and down a deep inheritance chain to understand one method. Deep inheritance, more than two or three levels, multiplies coupling. Leaky abstractions force you to know the implementation to use them correctly. Primitive obsession models domain concepts with raw strings and numbers instead of types, so a function taking two strings can easily be called with swapped arguments. The fix is value objects such as email, money or member ID, which validate themselves.

Blending object oriented and functional styles. A pure function has no side effects and returns the same output for the same input, so it is trivially testable. Modern C sharp and TypeScript are multi paradigm. Immutable objects, pure functions and objects can coexist. Choose records and functions over classes and methods when the thing is mostly data, when behavior is a transformation, or when you need cheap copies. C sharp has records, pattern matching and LINQ. TypeScript has discriminated unions, which solve the same problem as pattern matching on record types.

Domain modeling brings the pillars together. An entity has an identity that persists through change, such as a member. A value object has no identity and is defined by its values, such as money. An aggregate is a cluster of objects treated as a unit with one root that enforces invariants. Polymorphic policies combine abstraction and polymorphism: a loan policy interface with several strategy implementations, so rules change without touching the loan code.

Testing object oriented code. Good object oriented code is testable code, thanks to encapsulation and dependency inversion. Encapsulation gives a small public surface, so you test behavior through it, not private details. Dependency inversion gives seams, so you replace a repository or clock with a test double through an interface.

Finally, when not to use object oriented programming. It is a tool, not a religion. For plain data transformation, scripts, or simple handlers, a class can be pure ceremony. Prefer functions when there is no state or identity to protect. Composition is not no inheritance either: use inheritance when the is a relationship truly holds and is stable.

To summarize for an interview: prefer composition, name the anti patterns, replace primitives with value objects, blend functional ideas, model entities, value objects and aggregates, and use classes only where they earn their keep.
passage:
Composition models a has a relationship and is often preferable to inheritance, which models is a. When a hierarchy strains under cross cutting variations, an item can instead hold collaborators such as a format and a fee strategy. Behavior can also be shared across unrelated classes through mixins in TypeScript or interfaces with delegation in C sharp.

Common anti patterns include the god object, the anemic domain model, the yo yo problem, deep inheritance, leaky abstractions and primitive obsession, which is cured by value objects that validate themselves.

Modern C sharp and TypeScript blend object oriented and functional styles, using immutability, pure functions, records and discriminated unions where they fit. A rich domain model distinguishes entities, value objects and aggregates, and polymorphic policies keep rules replaceable. Encapsulation and dependency inversion make such code easy to test, and classes should be used only where they provide real value.
prompt: Explain why composition is often preferred over inheritance, using an example where a class hierarchy of library items becomes strained. Then name two anti patterns and how you would fix them.

title: Arrays Hashing And Prefix Sum Problems
shadowText:
Today we will talk about classic array and hash map interview problems. The main idea in all of them is trading a little memory for a lot of speed, using a hash map, a set or a running sum. Let us go through the most important ones.

Start with Two Sum. Given numbers and a target, return the indices of two numbers that add up to the target. Brute force checks every pair, which is quadratic. The better way: scan once, and for each value ask whether you have already seen the target minus that value. Store each value and its index in a map. That is linear time and linear space. Traps: if you insert before checking, an element can pair with itself. And checking truthiness of the stored index fails when the index is zero, so compare with undefined. If the array is sorted, two pointers solve it with constant extra space.

How does a hash map work internally? It stores entries in an array of buckets. A hash function turns the key into a number, and the number modulo the capacity picks the bucket. Collisions, two keys in one bucket, are handled by chaining, where each bucket holds a small list, or by open addressing, where you probe the next free slot. The load factor is entries divided by buckets, and when it passes a threshold, often around three quarters, the table rehashes into double the size. That is linear, but amortized away. Lookup is constant on average when keys spread evenly, and linear in the worst case. In JavaScript, a Map compares keys by SameValueZero, so objects are compared by reference, and two different arrays with equal contents are different keys. To key by a pair, build a string. Plain objects turn keys into strings and inherit keys like proto, so prefer Map for arbitrary keys.

Group anagrams. Anagrams share a canonical key. You can sort the letters of each word, costing k log k per word, or count the letters in a twenty six slot array and join the counts into a string, costing k per word. Use a separator in the join, otherwise counts like one and eleven are ambiguous. The twenty six slot approach assumes lowercase letters only, so lowercase the input first. The total is n times k.

Prefix sums. A prefix sum array stores the sum of everything before each position, so any range sum is a subtraction in constant time. To count subarrays whose sum equals k, keep a map of how many times each prefix sum has occurred. A subarray ending here sums to k if an earlier prefix equals the current sum minus k. Seed the map with the empty prefix, zero seen once, or you miss subarrays starting at index zero. A sliding window does not work here because negative numbers break monotonicity, but prefix sums work for any integers.

Product of array except self, without division. For each position, the answer is the product of everything on its left times the product of everything on its right. Fill the left products in one pass, then multiply in the right products in a reverse pass. That is linear time and constant extra space. Division fails because of zeros.

Longest consecutive sequence in linear time. Sorting is n log n. Instead, put all numbers in a set, and only start counting from numbers whose predecessor is missing, meaning they begin a run. Each number is then visited by the inner loop at most once, so the total is linear.

Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum. At each index, the best subarray ending here either extends the previous one or starts fresh: current equals the max of the value and current plus the value. Track the best overall. It is linear time and constant space, and is a one dimensional dynamic programming. Trap: starting the best at zero returns the wrong answer for an all negative array, and empty input needs a guard.

To summarize for an interview: use a map for complements, know hash map internals and collisions, use prefix sums with a map for subarray counts, build answers from the left and right passes, use a set to find run starts, and use Kadane for the maximum subarray.
passage:
Many array problems are solved by trading memory for speed. Two Sum scans once while a map records the values already seen, giving linear time. A hash map stores entries in buckets chosen by a hash function, handles collisions by chaining or open addressing, and rehashes when the load factor grows, so lookup is constant on average and linear in the worst case.

Grouping anagrams uses a canonical key, either sorted letters or a separated letter count. Prefix sums allow constant time range sums, and combined with a map of earlier prefixes they count subarrays that sum to k, including those that start at index zero, for any integers including negatives.

Product of array except self multiplies a left pass by a right pass without division, the longest consecutive sequence uses a set and starts counting only at run beginnings, and Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum subarray sum by deciding at each index whether to extend or restart.
prompt: Solve Two Sum aloud using a hash map. State the time and space complexity and mention two traps, such as pairing an element with itself and checking a stored index of zero. Then explain how a hash map handles collisions.

title: Big O Complexity And Amortized Analysis
shadowText:
Today we will talk about complexity analysis, the language every algorithm interview uses. We will cover Big O, growth classes, space, amortized cost and common costs in JavaScript.

First, what does Big O measure? Big O is an upper bound on growth: for large inputs, the function grows no faster than a constant times the bound. Big Omega is a lower bound, and Big Theta is a tight bound, both at once. In interviews people say Big O loosely to mean the tight bound for the worst case. You should say which case you mean. Worst case is the guarantee, for example quicksort is quadratic in the worst case. Average or expected case is different: quicksort with random pivots is n log n expected. Amortized is the average over a sequence of operations: push on an array is amortized constant, even though an occasional resize copies everything. To simplify: drop constants, keep the dominant term, and keep separate inputs separate. A trap: two nested loops over different arrays are n times m, not n squared.

Order the common classes from fastest to slowest: constant, like a map lookup; logarithmic, like binary search; linear, one pass; n log n, efficient sorting; quadratic, comparing every pair; exponential, all subsets; and factorial, all permutations. For a million items, log n is about twenty steps, n log n about twenty million, and n squared a trillion, which is too slow. Use input limits to pick an approach. A machine does roughly one hundred million simple operations per second. So with n up to about ten or twelve, factorial brute force is fine. Up to twenty or twenty five, exponential with bitmasks. Up to a few thousand, quadratic. Up to a hundred thousand or a million, n log n or linear. And with a billion, you need logarithmic or constant solutions.

Space complexity is the extra memory used as input grows, usually excluding the input, and you should say whether you exclude the output. The recursion stack counts. A depth first search on a tree of height h uses h stack space, log n for a balanced tree and n for a degenerate one. In JavaScript, deep recursion throws a maximum call stack error at roughly ten thousand frames, and V8 does not optimize tail calls. For very large inputs, convert to a loop with an explicit stack.

Amortized analysis, explained with a dynamic array. Amortized cost is the total cost of a sequence divided by the number of operations, a worst case guarantee over the sequence, not a probability. A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. A push that triggers a resize copies the existing elements. Over n pushes the copies total less than two n, so the total is linear and each push is amortized constant. If it grew by a fixed amount instead of doubling, the copies would total quadratic time. Geometric growth is what makes it work. Other examples are hash map insertion with rehashing and a queue built from two stacks.

Common JavaScript costs. Push and pop are amortized constant. Shift and unshift are linear, because they re index every element. Splice is linear. Includes, indexOf and find are linear scans. Slice and spread are linear copies. Map and Set operations are constant on average. Sort is n log n, using TimSort, which is stable. String concatenation in a loop is often fine in V8, but not guaranteed, so collect parts and join. Two traps: using shift as a queue in breadth first search makes it quadratic, so use a head index instead. And sort without a comparator sorts numbers as strings, so ten, nine, one becomes one, ten, nine. Always pass a numeric comparator.

Finally, analyze loops carefully. If the outer loop doubles i each time up to n, and the inner loop runs i times, the total is one plus two plus four up to n over two, which is less than n. So it is linear, not n log n. The pattern: when the inner bound depends on the outer variable, sum the inner work instead of multiplying. Related: an inner loop from i to n is quadratic, a halving loop is logarithmic, merge sort's recurrence is n log n, and a recurrence that branches into two calls of size n minus one is exponential.

To summarize for an interview: state the case, simplify properly, use input limits to choose the approach, count the stack as space, understand amortized doubling, and know the costs of common JavaScript operations.
passage:
Big O describes an upper bound on growth, Big Omega a lower bound and Big Theta a tight bound, and it should be accompanied by the case being discussed: worst, average or amortized. Constants are dropped, the dominant term is kept, and independent inputs remain separate, so nested loops over two different arrays cost n times m.

Growth classes range from constant and logarithmic through linear and n log n to quadratic, exponential and factorial, and input limits indicate the feasible class, since a machine performs about one hundred million simple operations per second. Space complexity counts extra memory including the recursion stack, and deep recursion in JavaScript can overflow the call stack.

Amortized analysis shows that pushing onto a doubling dynamic array costs constant time per operation on average, because resizing copies total less than twice the number of pushes. In JavaScript, shift and splice are linear, Map and Set operations are constant on average, and sort without a comparator orders numbers as strings.
prompt: Explain amortized analysis using a dynamic array that doubles its capacity, and why growing by a fixed amount would not give constant amortized cost. Then name two JavaScript array operations that are linear and often misused.

title: Dynamic Programming Classic Problems
shadowText:
Today we will talk about dynamic programming, one of the most feared interview topics. The good news is that there is a repeatable method, and a small set of classic problems cover most cases.

How do you approach a dynamic programming problem? Use five steps. One, define the state: what does dp of i, or dp of i and j, mean, in words. Two, find the transition: how a state is computed from smaller states. Three, set the base cases. Four, decide the order, so dependencies are ready, or let memoized recursion handle it. Five, find which state holds the final answer. The signals that a problem is dynamic programming: count the number of ways, minimum or maximum cost, is it possible, choices at each step, and a brute force that recomputes the same sub state.

Memoization versus tabulation, with climbing stairs. You can climb one or two steps at a time. The ways to reach step n equal the ways to reach n minus one plus the ways to reach n minus two. Top down memoization writes the recursion and caches results. It is easy to write from the recurrence and computes only the needed states. Bottom up tabulation fills a table from the base cases. It avoids recursion limits and allows space optimization, keeping only the last few values. Both are linear time.

Coin change: the fewest coins to make an amount. The state is the fewest coins for amount a. The transition: one plus the minimum of the state for a minus each coin that fits. Time is amount times number of coins, and space is the amount. Why greedy fails: with coins one, three and four and amount six, greedy picks four, one and one, which is three coins, but the best is three plus three, two coins. Greedy works only for canonical systems like real currencies. If you count the number of ways instead, the coin loop must be outside, so each combination is counted once and not once per ordering.

Longest common subsequence of two strings. The state is the LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j of b. If the last characters match, it is the diagonal value plus one. Otherwise it is the maximum of the value above and the value to the left. Time and space are n times m, and space can drop to two rows. It is used in diff tools and DNA alignment. Edit distance, with insert, delete and replace, is the same grid with three transitions, used in spell checkers and fuzzy search.

The zero one knapsack: maximize value within a weight limit, each item at most once. The state is the best value with capacity w using the items seen so far. For each item, iterate the capacity downwards, so the item is not reused in the same pass. The trap: iterating upwards turns it into the unbounded knapsack, where each item is reusable. The cost is items times capacity, which is pseudo polynomial: fine for capacity up to about a million, useless at a trillion. Partition equal subset sum and target sum are knapsack in disguise.

House robber, where you cannot take two adjacent houses: the best at i is the maximum of skipping, which is the best at i minus one, or taking, which is the best at i minus two plus the value. Linear time and constant space. Longest increasing subsequence: the quadratic dynamic programming looks at all earlier smaller values. The n log n version keeps, for each length, the smallest possible tail, and uses binary search to place each number. Trap: the tails array is not itself a subsequence; only its length is the answer.

Grid problems, like unique paths with obstacles. If movement is only right or down, every cell depends on the cell above and the cell to the left. Time is rows times columns, and space is one rolling row. But if movement can go in all four directions, dependencies form cycles, so it is a graph problem for breadth first search or Dijkstra, not a grid dynamic programming problem.

To summarize for an interview: state the five steps, compare memoization and tabulation, explain why greedy fails for coin change, know the LCS grid, remember the downward loop for zero one knapsack, and recognize a grid dynamic programming from a graph problem.
passage:
Dynamic programming solves a problem by defining a state, a transition from smaller states, base cases, an evaluation order and the state that holds the answer. Memoization writes the recursion with a cache and computes only the needed states, while tabulation fills a table bottom up, avoids recursion limits and allows space optimization.

Coin change shows why greedy choices can fail: with coins one, three and four, six is made with two coins, not three. The longest common subsequence uses a grid in which matching characters extend the diagonal value, and edit distance uses the same grid with three transitions.

In the zero one knapsack, iterating capacity downwards prevents reusing an item, whereas iterating upwards gives the unbounded version. House robber and the longest increasing subsequence are classic one dimensional problems, and a grid dynamic programming works only when movement avoids cycles, otherwise the problem is a graph search.
prompt: Explain how you would approach a dynamic programming problem using the five steps, and demonstrate with coin change. Include why a greedy approach fails for coins one, three and four with amount six.

title: Graph Basics and Traversals
shadowText:
Today we will talk about graphs. Graphs come up often in interviews, so let us go through the main ideas in simple words.

Let us start with how to represent a graph. There are two common ways. The first is an adjacency list. For each node, you store a list of its neighbours. The space is order V plus E, where V is the number of nodes and E is the number of edges. Checking if a specific edge exists costs the degree of the node, and walking through the neighbours costs the degree as well. The second way is an adjacency matrix. It is a table with V rows and V columns. The space is V squared, but checking for an edge is constant time. Here is the key point. Use an adjacency list for sparse graphs, which is most real graphs. Use a matrix for dense graphs or when V is small. In an interview you usually build an adjacency list from an edge list, and for an undirected graph you add each edge in both directions.

Next, breadth first search and depth first search. Breadth first search, or BFS, uses a queue and explores in rings of growing distance. This is why it finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph. Depth first search, or DFS, uses recursion or a stack and goes deep first. You use it for reachability, counting components, cycle detection, topological sort, and exploring all paths with backtracking. Both take order V plus E time. For space, BFS may hold a whole level of the graph, and DFS holds the current path.

A classic example is the number of islands problem. You have a grid with ones for land. You scan every cell. When you find land that you have not visited, you count one island and flood fill it with DFS or BFS, marking every connected land cell as visited. The total work is the size of the grid, because each cell is visited a constant number of times.

Now topological sort. A topological order lists the nodes of a directed acyclic graph, a DAG, so that every edge goes from an earlier node to a later one. It exists only if there is no cycle. The course schedule question asks if you can finish all courses given prerequisites. That is the same as asking if the graph has a cycle. Kahn's algorithm solves it with BFS. You compute the in-degree of every node, put all nodes with in-degree zero in a queue, and repeatedly remove one, reducing the in-degree of its neighbours. If you process every node, you can finish all courses. If some nodes are never processed, there is a cycle.

You can also detect a cycle in a directed graph with DFS using three colours. White means not visited. Grey means it is on the current DFS path. Black means finished. If you ever reach a grey node, you have followed an edge back into the current path, and that is a cycle.

Let us talk about Dijkstra's algorithm. It finds shortest paths from one source in a graph with non-negative edge weights. The idea is to always expand the unvisited node with the smallest known distance, usually with a priority queue, and relax its edges. It fails when there are negative edge weights, because a node that you already finalized might later get a shorter path. For negative weights, you need Bellman-Ford instead.

Finally, union-find, also called disjoint set union. It tracks which elements belong to the same group with two operations. Find returns the representative of a group. Union merges two groups. With two optimizations, path compression and union by rank or size, the cost per operation is almost constant. It is perfect for counting connected components and detecting cycles in undirected graphs.

Here is a short interview summary. I choose an adjacency list for sparse graphs. I use BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and DFS for components, cycles, and ordering. I use Kahn's algorithm or DFS colouring for dependency problems, Dijkstra for non-negative weights, and union-find for grouping.
passage:
A graph can be stored as an adjacency list, which uses space proportional to the nodes plus the edges, or as an adjacency matrix, which uses space proportional to the square of the number of nodes but answers edge queries in constant time. Most real graphs are sparse, so the adjacency list is the usual choice.

Breadth first search uses a queue and visits nodes in rings of increasing distance, so it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Depth first search uses recursion or a stack and suits reachability, connected components, cycle detection, and backtracking. Both run in time proportional to the nodes plus the edges. Counting islands in a grid is a typical flood fill problem.

For directed acyclic graphs, a topological order can be built with Kahn's algorithm, which repeatedly removes nodes with no incoming edges. If some nodes remain, the graph has a cycle. Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths when all weights are non-negative, and union-find groups elements almost in constant time using path compression and union by size.
prompt: Compare breadth first search and depth first search on a graph. Explain when you would choose each one, how topological sort answers the course schedule question, and why Dijkstra's algorithm needs non-negative weights.

title: Greedy Algorithms and Heaps
shadowText:
Today we will talk about greedy algorithms and heaps. These two topics often appear together in interviews, because many greedy solutions use a heap.

Let us start with greedy. A greedy algorithm makes the best local choice at each step. When is it correct? It is correct when the problem has the greedy choice property. This means that some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice, and what remains is a smaller problem of the same kind. To convince an interviewer, you do not just say it works. You give a short argument. The usual one is an exchange argument: take any optimal solution, and show that you can swap in the greedy choice without making it worse. You should also try a small counter example, to show you have thought about where greedy might fail.

Let us see three examples. First, merging overlapping intervals. You sort the intervals by start time. Then you walk through them. If the next interval starts before the last merged one ends, you extend the end. Otherwise, you start a new interval. The cost is order n log n because of the sorting. Second, the minimum number of meeting rooms. Sort the start times and the end times separately, and sweep through. Every start needs a room, but if a meeting ended before the current start, you can reuse that room. Third, the jump game. You want to know if you can reach the last index. You track the furthest index you can reach so far. If the current index is beyond that, you are stuck. Greedy is enough here because reaching a further index is never worse than reaching a nearer one.

Now let us talk about heaps. A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array. The children of index i are at two i plus one and two i plus two, and the parent is at i minus one, divided by two, rounded down. In a min-heap, every parent is smaller than or equal to its children, so the smallest value is always at the root. Insert adds the value at the end and bubbles it up. Removing the minimum takes the root, moves the last element to the top, and sinks it down. Both cost order log n. Peeking at the minimum is constant time.

A very common question is to find the k-th largest element. There are three approaches. Sorting costs order n log n. A min-heap of size k costs order n log k and uses order k space. You keep the k largest values, and the root is your answer. Quickselect has an average time of order n, but the worst case is order n squared. In an interview, the heap is the safe answer, and quickselect is a good follow up.

Another heap problem is merging k sorted lists. You push the head of each list into a min-heap. Then you repeatedly pop the smallest node, add it to the result, and push that node's next. With N total nodes and k lists, the cost is order N log k.

Finally, the median of a data stream. You keep two heaps. A max-heap holds the lower half of the numbers, and a min-heap holds the upper half. You keep them balanced so that their sizes differ by at most one. Then the median is either the top of the bigger heap, or the average of both tops. Adding a number costs order log n, and reading the median is constant time.

Here is a short interview summary. I use greedy when I can justify it with an exchange argument. For intervals, I sort first. For top k problems, I use a heap of size k. And for streaming medians, I use two heaps, one for each half.
passage:
A greedy algorithm picks the best local option at each step. It is correct when the problem has the greedy choice property, meaning some optimal solution begins with that choice and the rest is a smaller problem of the same type. The standard way to justify it is an exchange argument, together with a check against small counter examples.

Common greedy problems include merging overlapping intervals after sorting by start time, counting the meeting rooms needed by sweeping sorted start and end times, and the jump game, where tracking the furthest reachable index is enough.

A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array, with the smallest value at the root in a min-heap. Insertion and removal cost logarithmic time. A min-heap of size k finds the k-th largest element in order n log k time, merging k sorted lists costs order N log k, and two balanced heaps maintain the median of a stream.
prompt: Explain how you would find the k-th largest element in an array. Compare sorting, a min-heap of size k, and quickselect, and then describe how a heap-based idea helps merge k sorted lists.

title: Approaching Coding Problems
shadowText:
Today we will talk about something every candidate needs: how to approach a coding problem you have never seen. Interviewers care about your process as much as your final code.

Let us start with a repeatable sequence. You should spend about the first five to ten minutes on the first few steps. Step one is to clarify. Restate the problem in your own words. Ask about the input size, the value ranges, duplicates, empty input, and whether the data is sorted. Step two is to work through a small example by hand. Step three is to start with a simple brute force idea, and say its time and space cost out loud. Step four is to look for the bottleneck, and think about which pattern can improve it, like a hash map, two pointers, a sliding window, sorting, or a heap. Only then do you code. After coding, you test with your examples and edge cases, and you state the final complexity. Talking while you think is a strong signal.

A good interviewer will often follow up with a different question: where do these ideas show up in real work? It helps to have examples ready. Trees appear in the DOM and the CSS object model. Graphs appear in dependency resolution, build tools, and routing. Queues appear in the event loop and in job systems. Hash maps appear in caches and in lookup tables. Heaps appear in schedulers and priority queues. Tries appear in autocomplete. If you can point to these, you show that you understand why the topic matters for a web developer.

Now let us look at some common traps. Trap number one: someone says, this is order n, right? Look at a loop over an array, and inside it a call to includes on another array. The answer is no. The includes call scans the other array, so the whole thing is order n times m. A hidden linear call inside a loop is the most common complexity mistake in real code. The fix is to put the other array into a set first, and then the lookup is constant on average.

Trap number two: creating a grid with new Array of three, and fill with new Array of three filled with zero. This looks fine, but fill puts the same inner array reference in every row. If you set the first cell of the first row to one, every row shows one in the first column. The fix is to build each row separately, for example with Array.from and a function that creates a new row each time.

Trap number three: the claim that recursion and iteration are interchangeable, so a recursive depth first search is fine. In theory they are interchangeable, because any recursion can use an explicit stack. But in JavaScript the call stack is limited, usually to around ten thousand frames. A very deep input, like a long linked structure or a huge grid, can cause a stack overflow. In those cases you use an explicit stack in a loop. Also, JavaScript engines do not guarantee tail call optimization.

Trap number four: the claim that hash map lookups are constant, so the solution is order n. That is true on average, and it assumes that hashing the key is constant. It breaks when the keys are long strings or composite keys, because hashing then takes time proportional to the key length. It also breaks with many collisions, in the worst case. So you should say average constant time, and mention key size when it matters.

Here is a short interview summary. I clarify first, then solve a small example, then give a brute force solution and improve it. I name the pattern, code carefully, and test edge cases. And I watch for hidden costs, shared references, deep recursion, and the real meaning of constant time lookups.
passage:
A good approach to an unfamiliar coding problem follows a repeatable sequence. First clarify the problem and ask about input size, duplicates, and empty input. Then solve a small example by hand, describe a brute force solution with its cost, and look for the bottleneck. After choosing a pattern such as a hash map, two pointers, or a heap, write the code, test it with edge cases, and state the final complexity. Thinking aloud shows the interviewer your reasoning.

It also helps to connect data structures to real work. Trees appear in the DOM, graphs in dependency resolution, queues in the event loop, and heaps in schedulers.

Several traps are worth remembering. A call to includes inside a loop makes the code quadratic. Using fill with one array shares a single row between all rows of a grid. Deep recursion can overflow the JavaScript call stack, so an explicit stack is safer. Finally, hash map lookups are constant only on average, and long keys make hashing cost more.
prompt: Walk me through how you approach a coding problem you have never seen before. Then describe two common complexity or correctness traps, such as a hidden linear call inside a loop, and how you would avoid them.

title: Linked Lists and LRU Cache
shadowText:
Today we will talk about linked lists. They look simple, but they are a favourite for interviews because they test how well you handle pointers and edge cases.

Let us start with the comparison. When is an array better, and when is a linked list better? With an array, access by index is constant time. With a singly linked list, it is linear, because you must walk from the head. Inserting or deleting at the front is linear for an array, because everything shifts, but constant for a linked list. Inserting in the middle is constant for a linked list only if you already have the node. Finding that node still takes linear time. Arrays are also friendlier to the CPU cache, because the memory is contiguous. So in practice, arrays win most of the time. Linked lists are useful when you do many insertions and removals at known positions, like in queues and in an LRU cache.

Now, reversing a singly linked list. The iterative way uses three pointers. You keep a previous pointer, starting at null, and the current pointer, starting at the head. At each step you save the next node, point current to previous, and then move both forward. When current becomes null, previous is the new head. This takes linear time and constant space. The recursive way reverses the rest of the list first, then makes the next node point back to the current one. It also takes linear time, but it uses linear stack space.

Next, detecting a cycle with Floyd's algorithm, also called the tortoise and hare. You move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps. If there is a cycle, they will meet inside it. If the fast pointer reaches null, there is no cycle. To find where the cycle starts, after they meet you reset one pointer to the head. Then you move both one step at a time. The place where they meet again is the start of the cycle. It uses constant extra space.

Now, merging two sorted lists. The trick is a dummy node. You create a fake head, keep a tail pointer, and compare the two current nodes, attaching the smaller one to the tail each time. At the end, you attach whatever list remains. The dummy node avoids special code for the empty result at the start, and you simply return the dummy's next node.

Removing the n-th node from the end in one pass uses two pointers. Move the fast pointer n steps ahead. Then move fast and slow together until fast reaches the last node. Now slow is just before the node you want to remove. A dummy node again helps when you need to remove the head itself.

The last topic is an LRU cache with constant time get and put. You need constant time lookup, which suggests a hash map. You also need constant time to move an item to most recent, and to evict the least recent item. That suggests a doubly linked list. The map points from each key to its node in the list. On every get or put, you move that node to the front. When the cache is over capacity, you remove the node at the back, and delete its key from the map. Using a doubly linked list is important, because you need to unlink a node in constant time, and for that you need its previous pointer.

Here is a short interview summary. Arrays are better for random access, and linked lists are better for cheap inserts and removals when you hold the node. For list problems, I use a dummy node and two pointers. And for an LRU cache, I combine a hash map with a doubly linked list.
passage:
Arrays give constant time access by index and good cache behaviour, while a singly linked list gives constant time insertion and deletion at the front but linear time access. Linked lists are useful when many insertions and removals happen at known positions.

Several classic problems use pointer techniques. Reversing a list iteratively keeps a previous and a current pointer and runs in linear time with constant space. Floyd's algorithm detects a cycle with a slow pointer and a fast pointer and can also find where the cycle begins. Merging sorted lists and removing the n-th node from the end are simplified by a dummy node and by two pointers.

An LRU cache with constant time get and put combines a hash map with a doubly linked list. The map finds the node, the list keeps the usage order, and the node at the back is evicted when capacity is exceeded.
prompt: Explain how to design an LRU cache with constant time get and put. Say why you need both a hash map and a doubly linked list, and what happens during a get, a put, and an eviction.

title: Recursion, Sorting and Binary Search
shadowText:
Today we will talk about recursion, backtracking, sorting, and binary search. These are core tools, so let us go step by step.

First, how to write a correct recursive function. Ask three questions. What is the base case, the smallest input that you can answer directly? A missing or unreachable base case causes infinite recursion. What is the recursive step, and does it move toward the base case? And what do you combine or return from the smaller answers? Also think about the depth, because deep recursion can overflow the stack.

Now backtracking. Generating all subsets is a good example. Each element is either in or out, so you get a binary decision tree with two to the power n leaves. The complexity is order n times two to the n, because each subset must be copied. For permutations, you choose an unused element at each step. If the input has repeated values, you sort first, and you skip a value if it equals the previous one and the previous one was not used in the current path. That avoids duplicate permutations.

In combination sum, you find all combinations that add up to a target, and candidates can be reused. You backtrack with a start index, so combinations are generated in non decreasing order, and you avoid two three and three two as different answers. You prune when the remaining sum becomes negative. In word search, you run DFS from each cell, mark a cell as visited on the way down, and unmark it on the way back. This choose, explore, undo pattern is the heart of backtracking.

Now sorting. Insertion sort is order n in the best case, order n squared in the worst case, uses constant space, and is stable. It is good for tiny or almost sorted inputs. Merge sort is always order n log n, uses order n extra space, and is stable. Quicksort is order n log n on average, uses little extra space, and is not stable. Its worst case is order n squared. That happens when the pivot is repeatedly the smallest or largest element, for example with a sorted input and a bad pivot choice. A random or median of three pivot makes it very unlikely. Heap sort is order n log n in all cases with constant extra space, but it is not stable.

Merge sort works by splitting the array in half, sorting each half recursively, and merging the two sorted halves with two pointers. Quicksort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller values are left and larger values are right, and then sorts both sides.

Now binary search. Most bugs are off by one errors. A simple way to avoid them is to use a half open range, from low up to but not including high, and one clear invariant. The lower bound variant finds the first index where the value is greater than or equal to the target. You set the middle, and if the value there is less than the target, you move low to middle plus one. Otherwise, you move high to middle. The loop ends when low equals high.

A powerful extension is binary search on the answer. When you cannot search the input directly, but you can ask whether a certain answer X is feasible, and feasibility is monotonic, you can binary search over X. For example, the minimum ship capacity to deliver all packages within D days. For a given capacity, you simulate loading the packages in order and count the days. If it fits, try a smaller capacity. If not, try a larger one. The search range goes from the heaviest package up to the total weight.

Here is a short interview summary. For recursion, I define the base case first. For backtracking, I choose, explore, and undo. I know the trade offs between the sorting algorithms, especially stability and the quicksort worst case. And I use half open binary search, even on the answer when feasibility is monotonic.
passage:
A correct recursive function has a reachable base case, a recursive step that moves toward it, and a clear way to combine the smaller results. Backtracking problems such as subsets, permutations, combination sum, and word search follow a choose, explore, and undo pattern. Subsets take time proportional to n times two to the power n, and duplicate values are handled by sorting and skipping repeats.

Among sorting algorithms, insertion sort is simple and stable but quadratic, merge sort is always n log n and stable but needs extra space, quicksort is fast on average but degrades to quadratic with poor pivots and is not stable, and heap sort is n log n with constant extra space but not stable.

Binary search is easiest to write with a half open range and a single invariant. The lower bound variant returns the first index whose value is at least the target. The same idea works on the answer itself, as in the minimum ship capacity problem, whenever feasibility is monotonic.
prompt: Compare merge sort and quicksort in terms of time, space, and stability, and explain what causes the quicksort worst case. Then explain what binary search on the answer means, using the minimum ship capacity problem.

title: Stacks, Queues and Rotated Search
shadowText:
Today we will talk about stacks, queues, and a few related interview problems. These structures are simple, but the problems can be clever.

Let us start with searching a rotated sorted array, like four, five, six, seven, zero, one, two. You want the target in order log n time. The key observation is this: at any middle point, at least one half of the array is sorted. So you check which half is sorted by comparing the ends. Then you check whether the target lies inside that sorted half. If yes, you search there. If not, you search the other half. Each step cuts the range in half, so it is logarithmic.

Next, valid parentheses. Is the string with round, square, and curly brackets balanced? You use a stack. When you see an opening bracket, you push it. When you see a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opening bracket, so you pop it. If it does not match, or the stack is empty, the string is invalid. At the end, the stack must be empty. The time is linear.

Now, a stack that returns the minimum in constant time. The idea is to store, with each element, the minimum of the stack at that point. So each item holds its value and the smallest value up to and including it. When you push a new value, its minimum is the smaller of the value and the previous minimum. Then push, pop, top, and get minimum are all constant time.

Another favourite is implementing a queue with two stacks. You have an inbox stack and an outbox stack. To enqueue, you push onto the inbox. To dequeue, if the outbox is empty, you pour everything from the inbox into the outbox, which reverses the order, and then pop from the outbox. A single dequeue can cost linear time. But each element is moved at most once from the inbox to the outbox, so the amortized cost is constant. That is the answer interviewers want to hear.

Now the monotonic stack. It is a stack whose elements stay in increasing or decreasing order. When a new element breaks the order, you pop elements until the order is fine again. Each element is pushed once and popped once, so the whole thing is linear. A good example is the daily temperatures problem. For each day, you want to know how many days until a warmer one. You keep a stack of indices of days that are still waiting for a warmer day, with decreasing temperatures. When a new day is warmer than the day on top, you pop that day and set its answer to the difference in indices. Then you continue until the stack top is not colder. Finally, push the current day.

The last one is the sliding window maximum in linear time. You keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. For each new element, first remove indices from the back while their values are smaller than the new value, because they can never be the maximum again. Then add the new index. Also remove the front index if it has left the window. The front of the deque is always the index of the maximum of the current window. Each index enters and leaves the deque once, so the total time is linear.

Here is a short interview summary. A rotated array always has one sorted half, which allows binary search. Brackets are matched with a stack. A min stack stores the running minimum. Two stacks make a queue with constant amortized cost. And monotonic stacks and deques solve next greater element and window maximum problems in linear time.
passage:
To search a rotated sorted array in logarithmic time, observe that at any middle point at least one half is sorted. Check whether the target lies in the sorted half, and continue in that half or in the other one.

A stack validates balanced brackets: push each opening bracket and, on a closing bracket, require that the top of the stack is its partner. A min stack stores with every element the smallest value seen so far, so the minimum is available in constant time.

A queue can be built from two stacks. Elements are pushed onto an inbox, and when the outbox is empty, they are poured across, which reverses their order. A single dequeue may be linear, but the amortized cost is constant. A monotonic stack, which keeps elements in sorted order by popping, solves problems such as daily temperatures, and a monotonic deque of indices gives the sliding window maximum in linear time.
prompt: Explain how to implement a queue using two stacks and why dequeue is constant time amortized. Then describe how a monotonic stack solves the daily temperatures problem in linear time.

title: Binary Tree Essentials
shadowText:
Today we will talk about binary trees. Trees are very common in interviews, and most tree problems use recursion, so let us go through the main patterns.

Let us start with traversals. There are three depth first orders. In-order visits left, then the node, then right. For a binary search tree, this gives the values in sorted order. Pre-order visits the node first, then left, then right. It is useful for copying a tree and for serialization. Post-order visits left, then right, then the node. It is useful when a node needs the results of its children, like computing a height, or deleting a tree. The fourth traversal is level order, which uses a queue and visits the tree level by level. All of them take linear time. The space is the height of the tree for depth first, and the width for level order.

For level order traversal, you process one level at a time. You keep the current level in a list. For each node in it, you record its value and collect its children into the next level. Then the next level becomes the current one. This gives you a list of lists, one for each level.

Now, validating a binary search tree. A common mistake is to compare each node only with its direct children. That is wrong. Every node must sit inside a range, a minimum and a maximum, inherited from its ancestors. You start with no limits at the root. Going left, the maximum becomes the parent's value. Going right, the minimum becomes the parent's value. If any node falls outside its range, the tree is invalid. Another approach is to do an in-order traversal and check that the values are strictly increasing.

Next, the lowest common ancestor. In a general binary tree, you use post-order. If the current node is one of the targets, return it. Otherwise, ask the left and right sides. If both sides find something, the current node is the lowest common ancestor. If only one side finds something, pass that result up. In a binary search tree, it is simpler. Starting at the root, if both values are smaller, go left. If both are larger, go right. Otherwise the current node is the answer.

Why do balanced trees matter? The cost of a binary search tree operation is proportional to its height. If you insert sorted data into a plain tree, you get a tree shaped like a linked list, with height n, and every operation becomes linear. Balanced trees keep the height logarithmic. AVL trees and red-black trees keep a binary tree balanced with rotations, and they are used in ordered maps and sets in many standard libraries. B-trees have many keys per node and a low height, so they need few disk reads, and that is why databases and file systems use them.

To serialize and deserialize a binary tree, you use pre-order with explicit null markers. The output fully describes the shape of the tree. For deserialization, you read the values in the same order, and use the markers to know when a branch ends.

Finally, the diameter of a binary tree, which is the longest path between any two nodes. The longest path through a node equals the height of its left side plus the height of its right side. You compute heights in post-order and update a global best value on the way. The time is linear.

Here is a short interview summary. I choose the traversal by the problem. For binary search tree validation, I pass down a range. For lowest common ancestor and diameter, I use post-order. And I remember that balance keeps the height logarithmic.
passage:
The depth first traversals of a binary tree are in-order, pre-order, and post-order. In-order gives sorted values for a binary search tree, pre-order suits copying and serialization, and post-order suits problems where a node needs results from its children. Level order uses a queue and returns the values level by level. All of these take linear time.

To validate a binary search tree, each node must fall inside a minimum and maximum range inherited from its ancestors, not only compare with its direct children. The lowest common ancestor can be found with post-order recursion in a general tree, and by simple comparisons in a binary search tree. The diameter equals the largest sum of left and right heights through any node.

Balanced trees matter because operations cost time proportional to the height. Sorted insertions into a plain search tree create a tree as tall as a list. AVL and red-black trees keep the height logarithmic, and B-trees keep it very low for disk based storage.
prompt: Explain how to validate a binary search tree and why comparing a node only with its children is not enough. Then say why balanced trees matter and where AVL, red-black, and B-trees are used.

title: Tries, Bits and Two Pointers
shadowText:
Today we will talk about a mix of useful techniques: tries, bit tricks, Bloom filters, two pointers, and sliding windows. Each one solves a family of interview problems.

Let us start with the trie, also called a prefix tree. It stores strings character by character, and each path from the root spells a prefix. Insert, search, and starts-with all cost time proportional to the length of the word, not to the number of words stored. Each node has links to its children and a flag that says whether a word ends there. Tries are perfect for autocomplete and prefix search. The trade off is memory, since many nodes can be needed.

Now bit tricks. A few are worth knowing. X and one tells you whether a number is odd. X and x minus one clears the lowest set bit, and if the result is zero for a positive x, then x is a power of two. X and negative x isolates the lowest set bit. Xor is also useful, because a number xored with itself is zero, which finds the single non duplicated value in an array where every other value appears twice.

Next, a Bloom filter. It is a bit array with k hash functions, and it answers whether an item is in a set with either definitely not, or probably yes. Adding an item sets k bits. A lookup checks those bits. If any bit is zero, the item was never added. If all are one, it was probably added, but there can be false positives. There are no false negatives. It uses very little memory, so you can use it as a quick check before an expensive lookup, like checking a database or a cache.

Now two pointers. This works when moving a pointer safely discards candidates, usually because the data is sorted or the problem is monotonic. Take pair with sum target in a sorted array. Put one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, the left value can never work with anything else on the right side, so move the left pointer up. If the sum is too big, move the right pointer down. It is correct because each move discards a value that cannot be part of any answer. The time is linear.

Three sum builds on that. You sort the array, fix the first number, and run the two pointer pair search on the rest. You skip duplicate values at each level to keep the triplets unique. The time is order n squared. Container with most water uses the same idea. The area is the smaller height times the distance. You start with the widest pair and always move the shorter line inward, since moving the taller line can only make the area smaller or equal.

Now the sliding window. For a variable size window there is a template. Expand the right side by one and add that element to the window state. While the window is invalid, remove elements from the left. Then record the best answer. For the longest substring without repeating characters, you keep a set or a map of characters in the window. When a repeated character appears, you shrink from the left until the duplicate is gone. For the minimum window substring, you keep a count of what is still needed. You expand until the window is valid, then shrink while it stays valid, tracking the smallest window.

A fixed size window is simpler. For the maximum sum of k consecutive elements, you do not re-add k numbers for each window. You add the element entering and subtract the one leaving. That makes it order n and not n times k.

Here is a short interview summary. I use a trie for prefix problems, bit tricks for powers of two and duplicates, and a Bloom filter when I accept false positives. I use two pointers on sorted or monotonic data, and the sliding window when I need the best contiguous range.
passage:
A trie stores strings character by character, so insertion, search, and prefix checks cost time proportional to the word length. It is ideal for autocomplete. Useful bit tricks include checking oddness with and one, testing for a power of two with x and x minus one, and finding a single unpaired value with xor.

A Bloom filter is a bit array with several hash functions. It can say that an item is definitely absent or probably present, with false positives but no false negatives, which makes it a cheap guard in front of expensive lookups.

Two pointers work when moving a pointer safely discards candidates, as in pair sum on a sorted array, three sum, and container with most water. The sliding window technique expands on the right and shrinks on the left to find the best contiguous range, as in the longest substring without repeated characters, while a fixed window updates its sum in constant time per step.
prompt: Explain when two pointers work and why they are correct for finding a pair with a target sum in a sorted array. Then describe the sliding window template using the longest substring without repeating characters.

title: HTML Fundamentals and Parsing
shadowText:
Today we will talk about HTML fundamentals. These questions look easy, but interviewers use them to see if you understand how the browser really works.

Let us start with the DOCTYPE. What does it actually do? It switches the browser into standards mode. Without it, the browser uses quirks mode, which imitates bugs from the nineties. For example, tables do not inherit some font settings, and the box model can behave differently. So always put the DOCTYPE at the very top of the page.

Next, is the anchor element an inline element? Can it wrap a div? It displays as inline by default, and yes, it can wrap a div. The anchor has a transparent content model. This means it can contain whatever its parent is allowed to contain. So inside a div, it may hold block content. This is how whole card links are made. The only rule is that you must not nest interactive elements, like a button inside a link.

What happens when the parser meets invalid nesting? The HTML parser follows a fixed error recovery algorithm from the spec. This means every browser repairs the same broken markup in the same way. It does not throw an error. The danger is that the repaired result may not be what you meant.

This leads to the question: why validate HTML if the browser fixes it anyway? Because the fix may be different from your intention. Validation catches duplicate ids, which break label for, aria-labelledby, and fragment links. It also catches wrong nesting, missing alt text, and invalid attributes. A related follow up: why is a br with a slash valid but a div with a slash not? In HTML, the trailing slash is ignored. On a void element like br, that is harmless. On a div, the parser sees an opening tag that is never closed, and everything after it ends up inside that div.

Now global attributes and data attributes. Global attributes work on every element. Examples are id, class, hidden, lang, dir, tabindex, title, inert, contenteditable, draggable, and popover. Data attributes, which start with data and a dash, let you store small custom values on an element, to be read from JavaScript or CSS. Use them for hooks and small bits of state, not for secrets, and not for data that should be visible to users or search engines.

When must you use HTML entities? Only the less than sign and the ampersand must be escaped in text content. Inside an attribute, you must escape the quote character that you use to wrap the value. If you declare meta charset utf-8, you can write most characters like accents and emoji directly.

Let us talk about headings and the document outline. Use one h1 for the main topic of the page, and nest h2 to h6 by structure, never by visual size. The old HTML5 outline algorithm, where each section would restart heading levels, was never implemented by browsers. Screen reader users navigate by headings, so skipping levels or using headings only for style hurts accessibility.

Lists and tables: choose by meaning. Use ul for items where order does not matter, ol for steps and rankings, and dl for term and description pairs. Use a table only for real tabular data, with caption, th, and scope attributes, so assistive technology can announce the relationships. Do not use tables for layout.

And links: the anchor can do more than navigate. A fragment link like hash pricing jumps to an element with that id. The download attribute suggests saving a file. A mailto or tel link opens email or a phone app. And target blank should be used with care, together with rel noopener.

Here is a short interview summary. DOCTYPE gives standards mode. The anchor can wrap block content. The parser repairs mistakes the same way everywhere, but validation catches what you did not intend. I use headings for structure, the right list or table element for the content, and data attributes for small hooks.
passage:
The DOCTYPE switches the browser into standards mode, while its absence triggers quirks mode, which emulates old bugs. The anchor element is inline by default, but because it has a transparent content model it can wrap block content such as a div, as long as it does not contain other interactive elements.

The HTML parser uses a fixed error recovery algorithm, so every browser repairs invalid nesting identically. Even so, validation is valuable because the repaired result may differ from the intended one, and it also catches duplicate ids and missing alternative text. A trailing slash is ignored in HTML, so a self closed div is actually an unclosed div.

Global attributes such as id, class, lang, and hidden apply to every element, and data attributes store small custom values. A page should have one h1 and nested lower headings by structure. Developers should choose ul, ol, dl, or table according to meaning, and use only the less than sign and ampersand as mandatory entities in text.
prompt: Explain what the DOCTYPE does, how the HTML parser handles invalid nesting, and why you should still validate your HTML. Also say why an anchor element can wrap a div.

title: Modern CSS and HTML Features
shadowText:
Today we will talk about modern features in HTML and CSS. Interviewers like to ask about these, because they show if you keep up with the platform.

Let us start with media. For images, you should always give width and height attributes, so the browser can reserve space before the image loads. You write meaningful alt text that describes what the image shows. You wrap an image and its caption in a figure with a figcaption. For video and audio, you use the controls attribute, provide captions with a track element, and avoid autoplay with sound.

Now native CSS nesting. You can nest rules inside a parent rule, using the ampersand to refer to the parent. It is similar to Sass, but there are differences. It is part of the real cascade, it works in the browser at runtime, and the syntax has been relaxed so the ampersand is optional for element selectors. Unlike Sass, you cannot build class names by joining strings, so there is no ampersand underscore title trick.

What can the has selector do, and what does it cost? It selects an element based on its descendants, following siblings, or state. It is the long missing parent selector. For example, you can style a card that contains an image, or a form group that contains an invalid input. The cost is that the browser must check the subtree, so avoid very broad uses, like has on the body or on the root with a complex inner selector.

Logical properties: why bother? Physical properties like margin-left are fixed to the screen. Logical ones, like margin-inline-start, follow the writing mode and direction. So a layout automatically works for right to left languages such as Arabic, without writing extra rules.

Next, three image helpers. Aspect-ratio sets a box shape, like four to three, without hacks. Object-fit controls how an image fills its box, with cover cropping to fill and contain fitting inside. Object-position chooses which part stays visible.

Content-visibility auto lets the browser skip layout and paint for off screen sections until they come near the viewport. It is a large win for long pages. Pair it with contain-intrinsic-size so the scrollbar does not jump.

Now at supports and progressive enhancement. You write a baseline that works everywhere, for example flex, and then use at supports to enhance with grid in browsers that have it. This way, older browsers still get a usable layout.

The popover API lets you create menus and tooltips with an attribute. A button with popovertarget opens an element with the popover attribute. The browser handles showing it on the top layer, closing on outside click, and closing on escape. Together with anchor positioning, which ties an element's position to another element, you can build dropdowns with almost no JavaScript.

Scroll snapping makes carousels feel native. On the container you set scroll-snap-type, such as x mandatory, and on the children you set scroll-snap-align. Overscroll behavior can stop the scroll from chaining to the page.

A few other features worth naming: starting-style with transition-behavior allow-discrete lets you animate from display none, for entry and exit of popovers and dialogs. Container queries let components respond to their container size, not the viewport. And the dialog element gives you a built in modal with focus handling.

Here is a short interview summary. I use native nesting and logical properties for maintainable code, has for parent based styling with care, content-visibility for long pages, and popover for simple overlays. And I wrap newer features in at supports so the baseline always works.
passage:
Modern HTML and CSS reduce the need for JavaScript and hacks. Images should carry width, height, and descriptive alt text, and captions belong in figure and figcaption. Native CSS nesting works at runtime and follows the cascade, but unlike Sass it cannot concatenate class names. The has selector acts as a parent selector, although broad uses can be costly.

Logical properties such as margin-inline-start follow the writing direction, so layouts adapt to right to left languages. Aspect-ratio, object-fit, and object-position control image boxes cleanly. Content-visibility auto skips rendering work for off screen sections, and works best with contain-intrinsic-size.

Progressive enhancement uses at supports to add newer layouts on top of a baseline. The popover API and anchor positioning build menus and tooltips with little script, scroll snapping provides carousels, and starting-style allows animation from display none.
prompt: Pick three modern CSS or HTML features, for example the has selector, logical properties, and the popover API. Explain what each one does, the problem it solves, and any cost or limitation you should mention.

title: CSS Animation and Performance
shadowText:
Today we will talk about CSS animation. The key questions are what to animate, how to make it smooth, and how to keep it accessible.

Let us start with transitions versus keyframe animations. A transition runs when a property value changes, for example on hover or when a class is toggled. It goes from one state to another, and it needs a trigger. A keyframe animation uses at keyframes to define several steps. It can run when it is applied, can loop, can alternate, and can have many stages. Use transitions for simple state changes, and keyframes for sequences, loops, and loaders.

Why are transform and opacity cheap, but left and height expensive? Animating left, top, width, height, or margin changes geometry. So every frame the browser has to run layout and paint on the main thread. Transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor on the GPU. They skip layout and paint. So they stay smooth even when the main thread is busy. The rule is simple: animate transform and opacity whenever you can.

Timing functions control the feel. Ease-out starts fast and stops gently. It is best for elements entering, because they respond instantly. Ease-in starts slowly, and fits elements leaving. Ease-in-out suits movement across the screen. Linear is for constant things like progress and spinners. Keep interface animations short, usually between one hundred and three hundred milliseconds.

How do you animate elements in and out of display none? Historically, you could not, because display switches instantly. Now you can use transition with the display property and the allow-discrete behavior, together with the starting-style rule for the entry state. This lets toasts, dialogs, and popovers fade in and out without JavaScript timing tricks.

How do you make animation accessible? Respect the prefers-reduced-motion media query. When the user asks for reduced motion, remove parallax, large movement, zooming, and autoplay. Keep subtle fades, because opacity is generally fine. Never rely on animation alone to communicate important information. And avoid flashing content, since it can trigger seizures.

A skeleton loader is a good practical example. You show grey blocks that match the shape of the content, with a gentle shimmer animation, instead of a spinner. This reduces perceived waiting time and prevents layout shift. Mark the skeleton as aria-hidden, and announce the loading state to assistive technology in another way, for example with a live region.

Scroll-driven animations are a newer feature. You define a normal keyframe animation, for example a progress bar that scales from zero to full width. Then you link its timeline to the scroll position with animation-timeline scroll or view. So the progress bar grows as you scroll, and there is no JavaScript scroll listener. Some browsers still need a fallback.

The last question is a good follow up: why can a transform animation still jank? There are several reasons. It may be driven from JavaScript, for example requestAnimationFrame updating style.transform, so it shares the main thread with scripts. It may cause many layers to be created, which uses a lot of GPU memory. It may force layout by reading geometry in the same frame. Or the element may be very large or have an expensive filter or shadow to repaint. The way to find out is the DevTools Performance panel and the Layers panel.

Here is a short interview summary. I animate transform and opacity, not layout properties. I use ease-out for entering and keep durations short. I respect reduced motion. And I check the DevTools when an animation still feels rough.
passage:
A CSS transition runs when a property changes, while a keyframe animation defines multiple steps and can loop on its own. Animating transform and opacity is cheap because the compositor can handle them without running layout or paint, whereas animating left, top, width, or height forces layout and paint on the main thread every frame.

Timing functions shape the feel: ease-out suits elements entering, ease-in suits elements leaving, and linear suits spinners. Modern CSS can animate from display none using the allow-discrete transition behavior together with starting-style, and scroll-driven animations link a timeline to scroll position without JavaScript.

Accessible animation respects the prefers-reduced-motion setting, avoids flashing, and never carries essential meaning alone. A transform animation can still jank if it is driven from JavaScript, creates too many layers, or triggers forced layout, so it should be checked in the Performance panel.
prompt: Explain why animating transform and opacity is smoother than animating left or height. Then describe how you would make an animation accessible and what could still make a transform animation janky.

title: Web Performance with HTML and CSS
shadowText:
Today we will talk about web performance from the HTML and CSS side. We will cover Core Web Vitals, and the practical steps to improve them.

Let us start with the three Core Web Vitals. Largest Contentful Paint, or LCP, measures how long it takes for the largest visible element to render. Good is two and a half seconds or less. Interaction to Next Paint, or INP, measures responsiveness to user input. Good is two hundred milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift, or CLS, measures unexpected movement. Good is zero point one or less. These are judged at the seventy fifth percentile of real users, so field data matters more than a lab test on your fast laptop.

How do you speed up LCP from HTML and CSS? First, make the hero image discoverable early. Use a real image element, not a CSS background, and add fetchpriority high, or a preload. Second, preconnect to important origins, like your CDN. Third, inline a small amount of critical CSS for above the fold content, and load the rest without blocking. Fourth, avoid render blocking scripts, and use defer. And fifth, improve server response time and caching.

What causes layout shift? Images and video without dimensions. The fix is width and height attributes, or CSS aspect-ratio. Late loading ads, embeds, and banners. The fix is to reserve space. Web fonts swapping in. The fix is font-display swap with a fallback font adjusted to match the metrics. And content inserted above existing content. The fix is to insert it in response to user actions, or below the viewport.

Font loading strategy: preload the one or two critical font files in woff2 format, with the crossorigin attribute. Use font-display swap or optional. Subset the fonts to the characters you need, prefer a variable font to many separate files, and adjust the fallback with size-adjust to reduce shift.

Lazy loading done right: add loading lazy to images and iframes that are below the fold. But never lazy load the LCP image, because that delays it. And always keep width and height so there is no shift when the image arrives.

How do you reduce CSS cost at scale? Measure first. The DevTools Coverage tab shows unused bytes in each stylesheet, and the Performance panel shows long Recalculate Style and Layout blocks. Then split CSS by route, remove dead code, keep selectors simple, avoid huge DOM trees, and use content-visibility for long pages.

How do you profile a janky interaction? Record in the DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling, four to six times slower, to imitate a mid range phone. Find the long task, longer than fifty milliseconds, after the interaction. Look at what ran inside it: JavaScript, style recalculation, layout, or paint. Then fix the biggest part.

And a follow up: what makes up INP, and where does CSS hurt it? INP for one interaction is the input delay, which is when the main thread is busy as the user taps, plus the processing time of event handlers, plus the presentation delay, which is the style, layout, and paint of the next frame. CSS hurts in the last part. A large DOM, expensive selectors, and heavy effects make the next frame slow.

Here is a short interview summary. I know the three vitals and their thresholds. For LCP, I make the main image discoverable and remove blocking resources. For CLS, I reserve space. For INP, I keep the main thread free and the next frame cheap. And I always measure before I optimize.
passage:
The Core Web Vitals are Largest Contentful Paint, with a good value of two and a half seconds or less, Interaction to Next Paint, with a good value of two hundred milliseconds or less, and Cumulative Layout Shift, with a good value of zero point one or less. They are judged on real user data at the seventy fifth percentile.

To improve LCP, use a real image with high fetch priority or a preload, preconnect to key origins, inline critical CSS, defer scripts, and improve server response. To prevent layout shift, give media dimensions or an aspect ratio, reserve space for embeds and ads, and use font-display swap with a metric adjusted fallback.

Fonts should be preloaded in woff2 format, subset, and preferably variable. Lazy loading suits below the fold content but not the LCP image. CSS cost is reduced by measuring unused code with the Coverage tab, splitting by route, and simplifying selectors. Janky interactions are found by profiling with CPU throttling and looking for long tasks.
prompt: Name the three Core Web Vitals with their good thresholds. Then explain how you would improve LCP and prevent layout shift on a content page using only HTML and CSS changes.

title: Scalable CSS Architecture
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how to organize CSS in a large codebase. This is a favourite senior level topic, because small projects hide the problems that big ones expose.

Let us start with BEM. It stands for Block, Element, Modifier. For example, card is the block, card double underscore title is an element, and card double dash featured is a modifier. Every selector is a single class, so specificity stays flat and low. That solves the problem of selectors fighting each other, and it makes the code easy to search. The weakness is long class names, and it relies on discipline, because nothing enforces the convention.

Now compare the main approaches. Naming conventions like BEM have no runtime cost, and are simple and framework neutral, but they are not enforced. CSS Modules scope class names automatically at build time, with no runtime cost, but sharing styles takes more care. CSS in JS gives scoping and dynamic styles, but it can add runtime cost. Utility first CSS, like Tailwind, keeps styles next to the markup and gives consistency, but markup can get verbose. Pick based on the team and the tooling.

How do you prevent specificity wars? First, declare layer order once with at layer, for example reset, tokens, base, components, utilities, and overrides. A later layer wins over an earlier one, no matter the specificity. Second, use single class selectors for components. Third, avoid ids and important in component code. Fourth, keep the structure of selectors shallow. And fifth, use where to lower the specificity of selectors you want to be easy to override.

Design token architecture: tokens are named design decisions, organized in tiers. Primitive tokens hold raw values, like a blue 600 colour. Semantic tokens give them meaning, like color action primary, which points to a primitive. Component tokens are specific, like button background. Changing a theme, or supporting dark mode, then means changing the semantic layer, not every component. Native CSS custom properties make this work at runtime.

How do you refactor legacy CSS safely? First, take an inventory: use Coverage to find dead CSS, a linter to find specificity hotspots, and list the important declarations and id selectors.
