Second, build a safety net with visual regression tests. Third, work in small steps. Put legacy code into a low priority layer, and write new code in higher layers. Fourth, delete dead code gradually, and measure the result.

Global versus local styles: where is the line? Global styles are for the reset, tokens, typography defaults, focus styles, element defaults such as links, buttons, and form controls, and small utilities like a visually hidden class. Everything else, such as layout details and component looks, should be local to the component.

Is Sass still needed? Native CSS now covers variables, nesting, colour mixing, calc, layers, and media range syntax. Sass still helps with loops, maps, mixins, and functions that generate code. Many teams now use plain CSS with a small amount of tooling.

A follow up: how does at scope differ from nesting or BEM? At scope lets you limit where styles apply, with a root and an optional lower boundary. For example, style images inside a card, but not inside nested slot content. It gives scoping in plain CSS, with proximity based resolution, and no naming convention needed.

Here is a short interview summary. I keep specificity flat with single classes and layers. I organize tokens in tiers. I refactor legacy code step by step with tests. And I choose a scoping approach that matches the team, whether it is BEM, modules, utilities, or at scope.
passage:
BEM names classes as block, element, and modifier, so every selector is a single class and specificity stays flat. Its weakness is verbosity and the need for team discipline. Other approaches include CSS Modules, which scope names at build time, CSS in JS, which adds dynamic styling at some runtime cost, and utility first CSS, which keeps styles in the markup.

To avoid specificity wars, declare the layer order once with at layer, prefer single class selectors, avoid ids and important, and use where to reduce specificity. Design tokens should be organized in tiers, from primitive values to semantic names to component tokens, so that themes and dark mode change only the semantic layer.

Legacy CSS is refactored safely through an inventory, visual regression tests, and small steps, often placing old code in a low priority layer. Global styles should be limited to resets, tokens, and element defaults, and at scope offers native scoping with a clear boundary without relying on naming rules.
prompt: Explain how you would prevent specificity problems in a large CSS codebase. Cover cascade layers, single class selectors, and a tiered design token system, and mention one approach for refactoring legacy CSS safely.

title: Cross-Browser Compatibility
shadowText:
Today we will talk about cross browser compatibility. The web platform is much more consistent than before, but you still need a clear strategy.

Let us start with two ideas that are often confused. Progressive enhancement means you start with a baseline that works everywhere, which is semantic HTML and basic CSS. Then you add enhancements for browsers that support more. Graceful degradation is the reverse. You build the full experience first, and then make sure it fails nicely in older browsers. Progressive enhancement is usually the safer mindset, because the core content and function never depend on a new feature.

What is Baseline? It is a cross vendor label, shown on MDN, caniuse, and web.dev, that tells you when a feature works in the current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari. A feature can be newly available, meaning it just reached all four, or widely available, which is after about thirty months. It helps teams decide when a feature is safe to use without fallbacks.

Feature detection in CSS and HTML: in CSS, use at supports. You can test a property and value, a selector, or use the not keyword for a fallback. In JavaScript, you check if the API exists before you use it. Never detect the browser by its user agent string, because it is unreliable. Detect the feature itself.

Vendor prefixes and polyfills: prefixes like webkit and moz were for experimental features. Vendors now ship experiments behind flags, so you should not write prefixes by hand. Use a tool like Autoprefixer, driven by a browser list, which adds only what you need. Polyfills add missing JavaScript behaviour, but they cost bytes, so load them only when the feature test fails.

Which cross browser differences do you still meet? On iOS, every browser uses WebKit, so features ship with Safari releases. You should test on real Safari. Form controls and date pickers look different. Viewport units on mobile are affected by the browser toolbar, so use the dynamic viewport units. Scrollbar styling, and some newer features, vary between browsers. The mitigation is to test early, use feature queries, and keep fallbacks.

How do you debug a cross browser layout bug? First, reproduce it in the failing engine with a minimal test case. Strip the page down to the smallest HTML and CSS that still shows the bug. Then compare computed styles and box sizes in the developer tools of both browsers. Check for a missing reset or a different default. Check if a feature is unsupported, and look it up on MDN or caniuse. Then fix it with a feature query or a simpler approach, and add a test or a comment so the fix is not removed later.

A follow up: what is the Interop project? It is an annual collaboration among Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, and others. They pick focus areas, such as the has selector or container queries, and work to make them behave the same in every engine. They publish test results, which makes the platform more predictable.

Here is a short interview summary. I prefer progressive enhancement. I use Baseline and at supports to decide what is safe. I let tools handle prefixes. I test on real Safari. And I debug with a minimal test case in the failing browser.
passage:
Progressive enhancement starts with a baseline of semantic HTML and basic CSS that works everywhere, then adds capabilities where they are supported. Graceful degradation builds the full experience first and handles failures afterwards. Progressive enhancement is generally safer because essential content never depends on a new feature.

Baseline is a cross vendor label showing when a feature works across the current versions of the major browsers. Feature detection should use at supports in CSS and API checks in JavaScript, never user agent sniffing. Vendor prefixes should come from a tool such as Autoprefixer, and polyfills should load only when a test shows they are needed.

Persistent differences include the WebKit requirement on iOS, form control styling, and mobile viewport units. Cross browser layout bugs are debugged by building a minimal test case, comparing computed styles, and checking support data. The Interop project helps by aligning behaviour across engines each year.
prompt: Compare progressive enhancement with graceful degradation, and explain how you would use Baseline and at supports to adopt a newer CSS feature safely. Then describe how you would debug a layout bug that appears only in Safari.

title: Front-End Security Basics
shadowText:
Today we will talk about security in HTML and CSS. A front end developer needs to know how markup choices can create vulnerabilities, and how the browser helps defend.

Let us start with cross site scripting, or XSS. It happens when user controlled data is inserted into the page as markup instead of text. Then an attacker can run script in your page. HTML choices that cause it include using innerHTML with user data, building markup by joining strings, and putting untrusted data into attributes like href or event handlers. The fix is to treat data as text. Use textContent, use frameworks that escape by default, validate link protocols, and sanitize any rich HTML with an allow list.

What does Content Security Policy add? It is an HTTP header that tells the browser which sources may run or load. Even if an attacker injects markup, inline scripts without the right nonce or hash will not run, and scripts from unknown origins will not load. CSP is a second line of defence. It does not replace proper escaping.

Next, target blank and rel noopener. A page opened with target blank used to get access to window.opener, so it could redirect your original tab to a phishing page. This is called reverse tabnabbing. Modern browsers now treat target blank as noopener by default, but it is still good practice to add rel noopener, and noreferrer if you do not want to send the referrer.

How do you embed third party content safely with an iframe? Use the sandbox attribute and allow only what is needed, for example allow scripts and allow popups. Use the allow attribute to grant specific features. Set a strict referrer policy. And prefer the provider's privacy friendly embed domain when it exists.

What is clickjacking? An attacker loads your site in an invisible iframe over a decoy button, so the user's click lands on your Delete account or Pay button. You prevent it by telling the browser not to allow framing. Use the Content Security Policy directive frame-ancestors, or the older X-Frame-Options header.

Can CSS be a security risk? Yes, if attackers can inject it. They can exfiltrate data with attribute selectors and background URLs. For example, a selector that matches an input value starting with a letter can trigger a request to the attacker's server. They can also cover the page with a fake interface. So never allow untrusted CSS, and restrict styles with your CSP.

Third party scripts, integrity, and privacy: use Subresource Integrity, which adds a hash to the script tag so the browser refuses a modified file. Load third party code only from trusted sources, keep the list short, and review what data they collect. Use the referrer policy and consent rules to protect user privacy.

A follow up: how would you render untrusted rich HTML, like an email preview? Use layers of defence. Sanitize with an allow list, using a library like DOMPurify, and strip scripts, event handlers, and javascript links. Render it inside a sandboxed iframe without script permission. Apply a strict CSP. Block remote images or proxy them, to avoid tracking. And never trust only one layer.

Here is a short interview summary. I treat data as text, not markup. I add CSP as a second layer. I use rel noopener, sandboxed iframes, and frame-ancestors. I use Subresource Integrity for third party files. And for untrusted HTML, I sanitize and isolate.
passage:
Cross site scripting occurs when untrusted data is inserted into a page as markup rather than text. Developers prevent it by using textContent, framework escaping, protocol validation for links, and allow list sanitization for rich content. A Content Security Policy adds a second layer by restricting which scripts may run, but it does not replace escaping.

Links that open in a new tab should use rel noopener to prevent reverse tabnabbing. Third party iframes should use the sandbox attribute with minimal permissions, a strict referrer policy, and only the features they need. Clickjacking is prevented with the frame-ancestors directive or the X-Frame-Options header.

Injected CSS can also leak data through attribute selectors and background requests, so untrusted styles should never be allowed. Subresource Integrity protects against modified third party files. Untrusted rich HTML, such as an email preview, should be sanitized, rendered in a sandboxed iframe, and protected by a strict policy.
prompt: Explain what cross site scripting is and how HTML choices can cause it. Then describe how a Content Security Policy, a sandboxed iframe, and sanitization together protect a page that shows untrusted rich HTML.

title: The Critical Rendering Path
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the critical rendering path. This is how the browser turns HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels, and it is a very common interview topic.

Let us walk through it. Step one: bytes become tokens, and tokens become the DOM. The HTML parser streams the bytes, builds nodes step by step, and does not wait for the whole document. Step two: the CSS is parsed into the CSSOM. Step three: the DOM and CSSOM combine into the render tree, which contains only visible elements. Then the browser does layout, to compute sizes and positions, then paint, to record the drawing, and then composite, to assemble layers into the final image.

Is CSS render blocking? Is it parser blocking? CSS is render blocking. The browser will not paint until all the stylesheets in the head are loaded, to avoid a flash of unstyled content. CSS is not parser blocking by itself. The HTML parser keeps going. But a classic script after a stylesheet must wait for it, because the script may ask for computed styles. So a slow stylesheet can delay the script, and in the end the parsing.

Next, async versus defer versus module. A normal script pauses parsing, downloads, and runs immediately. A script with async downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives, so the order is not kept, and it can pause the parser when it runs. A script with defer downloads in parallel and runs after parsing, in order, before DOMContentLoaded. Module scripts behave like defer by default. A simple rule: async for independent scripts like analytics, defer for scripts that need the DOM.

DOMContentLoaded versus load. DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is fully parsed and all deferred and module scripts have run. It does not wait for images, iframes, or most stylesheets that do not block scripts. The load event fires when everything is finished, including images and iframes. Neither tells you what the user sees. For that, use paint metrics.

Now, reflow, repaint, and composite. A geometry change, like width, height, margin, top, or font size, runs layout, then paint, then composite. It is the most expensive. A change to colour, background, or shadow skips layout but runs paint and composite. A change to transform or opacity can skip both, and only composite. That is why they are best for animation.

What creates a compositor layer? Elements get their own layer through three D transforms such as translateZ zero, will-change on transform or opacity, video, canvas, and some fixed or sticky positioned elements. Is will-change a free performance boost? No. Each layer uses GPU memory, and too many layers slow the page and can crash low end devices. Use will-change only on elements that are about to animate, and remove it afterwards.

A follow up: what is the preload scanner? While the main parser is blocked on a script, a secondary preload scanner reads ahead through the raw HTML and starts fetching the images, stylesheets, and scripts it finds. This is a big speed up. But it can only see what is in the markup. Resources that JavaScript injects, or that are referenced only from CSS, such as background images, are discovered late. That is why the main image should be a normal image tag, and why you can use preload for important late discovered files.

Here is a short interview summary. HTML builds the DOM, CSS builds the CSSOM, and together they make the render tree, then layout, paint, and composite. CSS blocks rendering, and scripts can block parsing, so I use defer. I animate transform and opacity, and I use will-change carefully. And I make key resources visible to the preload scanner.
passage:
The critical rendering path begins with the HTML parser turning bytes into tokens and then into the DOM, while CSS becomes the CSSOM. These combine into a render tree of visible elements, followed by layout, paint, and composite. CSS blocks rendering but not parsing, though a classic script after a stylesheet waits for it.

A normal script pauses the parser. An async script downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it arrives in any order, and a defer script runs after parsing in document order. Module scripts defer by default. DOMContentLoaded fires after parsing and deferred scripts, while load fires after all resources finish.

Geometry changes trigger layout, paint, and composite, color changes trigger paint and composite, and transform and opacity only composite. Layers cost GPU memory, so will-change should be used sparingly. The preload scanner reads ahead in the markup to start downloads early, but it cannot see resources hidden in CSS or injected by scripts.
prompt: Walk me through the critical rendering path from HTML bytes to pixels. Explain whether CSS blocks rendering and parsing, and compare async and defer scripts.

title: Semantic HTML and Accessibility
shadowText:
Today we will talk about semantic HTML and accessibility. These topics show whether a developer builds for all users, not only for the mouse and the screen.

Let us start with div, section, and article. A div is a generic wrapper for styling or layout, and it has no meaning. A section is a thematic group of content that normally has a heading. An article is a self contained piece that makes sense on its own, like a blog post or a comment. Choose the element that matches the meaning, and use a div only when nothing else fits.

Next, button or link? Links navigate. They change the URL, go to another page, or jump to an anchor. Buttons act. They submit a form, open a dialog, toggle something, or delete something. If you use a div with a click handler, you lose keyboard support, focus, and the right role for screen readers. A good question to ask is: does this change where I am, or does it do something?

How is an accessible name computed? The browser follows a priority order from the accessible name specification, and it stops at the first one that produces text. First is aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then native sources such as a label element, alt text, or the content of the element, and finally the title attribute as a last resort. Every interactive element needs a name, otherwise a screen reader just says button, with no hint.

Now hidden, inert, and aria-hidden. The hidden attribute makes an element display none. It is not visible, not in the accessibility tree, and not focusable. The inert attribute makes an element and its children non interactive and not focusable, even if they are still visible. This is useful behind a modal dialog. Aria-hidden true removes an element from the accessibility tree only. It is still visible and, importantly, still focusable. So never put aria-hidden on something that can receive focus.

How do you manage focus correctly? Tab order follows the DOM order. Visual reordering with CSS order, row-reverse, or grid placement does not change it, which makes the tab order confusing. So keep the DOM order logical. Never remove the focus outline without a clear replacement, and use focus-visible for keyboard users. Avoid positive tabindex values. When you open a dialog, move focus into it, trap it there, and return it to the trigger when it closes. The native dialog element does much of this for you.

What are the WCAG essentials you check in every review? WCAG 2.2 level AA is the usual legal and contract target. Check text contrast, which is four point five to one for normal text. Make sure everything works with a keyboard. Provide text alternatives for images. Make sure forms have labels and clear errors. Do not use colour alone to give meaning. Support zoom and reflow, and respect reduced motion. Make touch targets large enough.

How do you test accessibility? Automated tools like axe-core, Lighthouse, and WAVE catch roughly a third of issues, like missing names, low contrast, and invalid ARIA. The rest need manual testing. Use only the keyboard to go through the page. Test with a screen reader, such as NVDA, VoiceOver, or TalkBack. Zoom to two hundred percent and check reflow. And include real users with disabilities when you can.

A follow up: when is ARIA necessary? When HTML does not have the widget you need, for example tabs, combobox, tree, and grid, and for live regions that announce updates. The first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA if a native element does the job. Bad ARIA is worse than no ARIA, because it changes what assistive technology announces.

Here is a short interview summary. I choose elements by meaning, buttons for actions and links for navigation. I make sure every control has an accessible name, I keep the DOM order logical, and I manage focus. I test with automation, a keyboard, and a screen reader, and I use ARIA only when native HTML is not enough.
passage:
Semantic HTML gives elements meaning that browsers and assistive technology can use. A div is only a generic wrapper, a section groups related content under a heading, and an article is a self contained piece. Links navigate, while buttons perform actions, and native elements bring keyboard support and correct roles for free.

The accessible name of a control is computed in a fixed priority: aria-labelledby, aria-label, native labels or alternative text and content, and finally the title attribute. The hidden attribute removes an element entirely, inert makes it non interactive, and aria-hidden only removes it from the accessibility tree. Focus order follows the DOM, so visual reordering with CSS can confuse keyboard users.

Reviews should check WCAG 2.2 level AA essentials, such as contrast, keyboard operation, text alternatives, labels, and reflow. Automated tools find only about a third of problems, so manual keyboard and screen reader testing is required. ARIA should be used only when native HTML cannot express the widget.
prompt: Explain when you would use a button versus a link, and how the browser computes an accessible name. Then describe how you would test a page for accessibility beyond running an automated tool.

title: CSS Layout, Positioning and Stacking
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the foundations of CSS layout. These ideas explain many of the strange bugs that developers meet, so they are very popular in interviews.

Let us start with the box model and box-sizing. By default, with content-box, the width sets only the content. Padding and border are added on top, so a box with width two hundred and padding twenty is actually two hundred forty wide. With border-box, the width includes the padding and the border. This is easier to reason about, so most projects set border-box on everything.

Now margin collapsing. In normal block flow, vertical margins that touch merge into one margin equal to the larger value, not the sum. This happens between siblings, and between a parent and its first or last child if nothing separates them. It does not happen with horizontal margins, with flex or grid items, with floats, with absolutely positioned elements, or when the parent has padding, a border, or creates a new formatting context.

What is a block formatting context, or BFC? It is an independent layout region. Floats inside it are contained, floats outside it do not overlap it, and margins do not collapse through its edge. Things that create a BFC include the root element, floats, absolutely positioned elements, display flow-root, overflow other than visible, and flex or grid items. The cleanest way to create one is display flow-root.

The containing block is the rectangle that an element's position and percentage sizes are measured against. For normal elements it is the content box of the nearest block parent. For absolutely positioned elements, it is the nearest ancestor that is positioned, or has a transform. This is why percentages surprise people. A percentage height only works if the parent has a defined height, and percentage padding refers to the width of the containing block.

Compare the position values. Static is the default, in flow, and offsets are ignored. Relative stays in flow but can be shifted from its original place, and it becomes an anchor for absolute children. Absolute is removed from the flow and placed relative to its containing block. Fixed is placed relative to the viewport. Sticky behaves like relative until a scroll threshold, and then sticks.

Why does sticky stop working? Go through a checklist. First, you did not set a threshold like top. Second, an ancestor has overflow hidden, auto, or scroll, which becomes the scroll container. Third, the sticky element has no room to move, because its parent is as tall as the element. Fourth, the element is a flex item that stretches, so it has no space to move. Fix these and sticky usually works.

Stacking contexts and z-index. Z-index only competes inside the same stacking context. A stacking context is flattened into a single layer when compared with others. So z-index nine thousand nine hundred ninety nine inside a context with a low order can still be under an element in a higher one. Contexts are created by position with z-index, opacity below one, transform, filter, isolation isolate, and more. To debug, find the ancestors that create contexts. The isolation property is a clean way to create one on purpose.

Overflow values: visible is the default and content spills out. Hidden clips content, but it can still be scrolled by code, and it creates a block formatting context. Scroll always shows scrollbars. Auto shows them when needed. Clip clips without creating a scroll container. Are floats still relevant? Only for their original purpose, which is wrapping text around an image, with shape-outside for curved shapes. For page layout, use flexbox or grid.

Here is a short interview summary. I use border-box, I know when margins collapse, I use flow-root for containment, and I understand containing blocks. For sticky and z-index bugs, I check ancestors for overflow and stacking contexts.
passage:
The box model describes how width, padding, border, and margin add up. With content-box, width covers only the content, while border-box includes padding and border, which is why border-box is the common default. Vertical margins between block elements collapse to the larger value, except in flex and grid layouts or when a new formatting context, padding, or border separates them.

A block formatting context is an independent layout region that contains floats and stops margin collapsing, and display flow-root creates one cleanly. The containing block is the reference rectangle for positioning and percentages. Position values include static, relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky, and sticky fails when no threshold is set, when an ancestor clips overflow, or when it has no room to travel.

Z-index competes only within a stacking context, and contexts are created by transforms, opacity, filters, isolation, and positioned elements with z-index. Overflow controls clipping and scrolling, and floats are now used mainly for wrapping text around images.
prompt: Explain why position sticky sometimes does not work and why a very large z-index sometimes fails. Cover overflow on ancestors, stacking contexts, and how you would debug each problem.

title: Forms and Validation
shadowText:
Today we will talk about HTML forms and validation. Forms are everywhere, and small details here have a big effect on usability and security.

Let us start with what gets submitted. Only successful controls are submitted. A control must have a name attribute, it must not be disabled, and checkboxes and radio buttons must be checked. If you forget the name, the value silently disappears. The method decides where the data goes. Get puts it in the URL, and post puts it in the request body.

What is the default type of a button? It is submit, when it is inside a form. So a Cancel button or a Show password button inside a form will submit it unless you set type button. This is a very common bug. Always set the type explicitly.

Disabled versus readonly. A disabled control is not submitted, is not focusable, and cannot be used, and it is often styled as greyed out. A readonly control is submitted, is focusable, and can be selected and copied, but its value cannot be edited. Use readonly when the user should see and copy the value, and disabled when the field is not applicable right now.

How should labels be associated? Every control needs a label. The explicit way uses a label with a for attribute that matches the input id. It works everywhere and survives restructuring. The implicit way wraps the input inside the label. Both make the label clickable and give the input its accessible name. A placeholder is not a label. It disappears when typing, and often has low contrast.

How does native constraint validation work? Attributes declare constraints, such as required, type email, url, or number, min, max, step, minlength, maxlength, and pattern. The browser checks them on submit, blocks invalid submissions, and shows messages. In CSS you can use user-invalid and user-valid, which apply only after the user interacts. In JavaScript, you use the validity property, setCustomValidity, and reportValidity.

What does good validation UX look like? Validate on blur or on submit, not on every keystroke, and clear errors as soon as they are fixed. Put the message next to the field, in text that says what to do. Connect it to the field with aria-describedby, and mark the field with aria-invalid. On submit, move focus to the first error or to a summary. Do not rely on colour alone, and keep what the user typed.

Which input types and attributes improve mobile experience? Use type email, tel, url, and search for the right keyboard. Use inputmode numeric or decimal for number keyboards without the spinner behaviour. Use autocomplete attributes so the browser can fill in names, addresses, and one time codes. Use enterkeyhint to change the label of the enter key.

Is client side validation a security measure? No. It is only for user experience. Anyone can edit the page, turn off JavaScript, or send requests with curl. The server must always validate and sanitize again.

A follow up: submit versus requestSubmit. The form.submit method skips constraint validation and never fires the submit event, so your handlers and validation are bypassed. The requestSubmit method behaves like a click on a submit button. It runs validation and fires the event. For custom form controls, the best approach is to build on native elements, or use form associated custom elements, so they take part in forms and validation properly.

Here is a short interview summary. Controls need a name to be submitted. Buttons default to submit. Every field needs a real label. I use native validation with good error messages, mobile friendly input types, and always validate again on the server.
passage:
Only successful form controls are submitted: they need a name, must not be disabled, and checkboxes and radios must be checked. A button inside a form defaults to type submit, so non submitting buttons need type button. A disabled control is not submitted or focusable, while a readonly control is submitted and focusable but cannot be edited.

Every control should have a label, associated either with the for attribute or by wrapping, and a placeholder is not a replacement. Native constraint validation uses attributes such as required, type, min, max, and pattern, and can be extended with the validity API. Good validation messages appear near the field, are linked with aria-describedby, and are shown on blur or submit.

Input types, inputmode, and autocomplete improve the mobile experience. Client side validation improves usability but is never security, because requests can be forged, so the server must validate everything. The requestSubmit method triggers validation and the submit event, whereas submit does not.
prompt: Explain what makes a form control get submitted, why a button inside a form may submit unexpectedly, and why client side validation is not enough. Then describe good validation UX.

title: Cascade, Specificity and Units
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the cascade, specificity, inheritance, and CSS units. This is the core of how CSS decides what to apply, and it is a classic interview area.

Let us start with the cascade. When several rules compete, the browser resolves the conflict in order, and each step only runs if the previous one tied. First is origin and importance. From weakest to strongest, you have user agent styles, user styles, author styles, then the important versions in reverse order. Next come cascade layers. Then specificity. Then the order of appearance, where the later rule wins.

How is specificity calculated? As a three part tuple, A, B, C, compared from left to right, and not as a base ten number. A counts id selectors. B counts classes, attributes, and pseudo classes. C counts element types and pseudo elements. So one id beats any number of classes, and eleven classes never beat one id. Inline styles beat all selectors, and the universal selector adds nothing.

How do is, where, not, and has affect specificity? The is, not, and has selectors take the specificity of their most specific argument, even if a less specific one matched. The where selector always has zero specificity. That makes where perfect for default styles that are easy to override.

What are cascade layers, and why do they matter at scale? The at layer rule lets you set precedence by intent rather than by selector weight. You declare the order once, for example reset, base, components, and utilities. A later layer wins over an earlier one, no matter how specific the selectors are. Unlayered styles beat layered ones. This helps you mix third party code and your own code with no specificity fights.

When is important legitimate? For utility classes that must always win, like visually hidden. For overriding inline styles from third party code. And in a user stylesheet for accessibility. Otherwise it is a sign of a design problem, and it makes later overrides harder.

Which properties inherit? Text and font properties inherit by default, like color, font, line-height, letter-spacing, and text-align. Box properties such as margin, padding, border, and background do not. The global keywords are: inherit, which takes the parent value, initial, which resets to the spec default, unset, which acts as inherit or initial depending on the property, and revert, which goes back to the earlier origin.

How do custom properties resolve? They inherit, and var is substituted at computed value time on the element where it is used. The classic bug is that a custom property is computed where it is declared if it refers to others, and redefining a value on a child does not change a parent's calculation. Also, invalid values at computed time become the guaranteed invalid value, so the property falls back to its inherited or initial value instead of the previous rule.

Which units should you use? Px for borders, hairlines, and shadows. Rem relative to the root font size, for font sizes and spacing, which respects user settings. Em relative to the current font size, good for padding inside a component that should scale. Percent relative to the parent. Ch for text measure, like a line length of sixty five characters. And viewport units for large layout parts, with dynamic variants on mobile.

And the math functions. Calc mixes units. Min and max choose the smaller or larger. Clamp takes a minimum, a preferred value, and a maximum, which is perfect for fluid type and container widths.

A follow up: does a long selector slow the page? Browsers match selectors from right to left, so they find every match of the last part and then check ancestors. Modern engines are fast, so selector length is rarely the problem. The larger costs are huge DOM trees and broad changes that force many elements to recalculate.

Here is a short interview summary. The cascade goes by origin, layers, specificity, then order. Specificity is a tuple. I use layers and where to keep it low. I use rem, em, ch, and clamp with intent.
passage:
The cascade resolves conflicts in order: origin and importance, then cascade layers, then specificity, and finally the order of appearance. Specificity is a tuple counting ids, then classes, attributes and pseudo classes, then element types, compared from left to right. The is, not, and has selectors take the weight of their most specific argument, while where has zero specificity.

Cascade layers let developers set precedence by intent, so later layers win regardless of selector weight. The important keyword is legitimate mainly for utilities, third party overrides, and user preferences. Text properties inherit by default, while box properties do not, and the keywords inherit, initial, unset, and revert control this behaviour.

Units should be chosen with purpose: px for hairlines, rem for scalable sizing, em for component relative spacing, ch for text width, and viewport units for large layout. The functions calc, min, max, and clamp support fluid layouts and typography.
prompt: Explain the order in which the cascade resolves conflicts, how specificity is calculated, and how cascade layers and the where selector help keep specificity under control in a large project.

title: Selectors, Colour and Flexbox
shadowText:
Today we will talk about selectors, colour, and flexbox. Flexbox is one of the most asked topics, so we will spend most of our time there.

Let us start quickly with selectors. The descendant combinator matches any element inside another. The child combinator matches only direct children. The adjacent sibling combinator matches the element right after another, and the general sibling matches any later sibling. Relational selectors such as has let you select by what an element contains. Choose the narrowest selector that expresses your intent.

For colour, modern CSS has better tools. The oklch colour space has perceptually even lightness, so changing lightness gives predictable results. The color-mix function mixes two colours, which is great for hover states and soft backgrounds from one brand colour. Gradients, shadows, and borders can be layered, and custom properties keep it consistent.

Now flexbox. The main axis follows flex-direction. In a row it is horizontal, in a column it is vertical. Justify-content distributes space along the main axis. Align-items aligns items on the cross axis, which is perpendicular. Align-content distributes whole lines when items wrap. Gap adds space between items. Remember that these swap when you change the direction.

What does flex one actually mean? It is the shorthand for grow one, shrink one, and basis zero. The items start from a size of zero and share all the free space equally. This differs from the default, which is grow zero, shrink one, basis auto, where items are sized by content or width, and can shrink but never grow. The keyword flex auto means grow one, shrink one, basis auto. And flex none means no growing or shrinking.

Walk through the grow and shrink algorithm. First, compute each item's hypothetical size from the flex basis, or from the width if the basis is auto, or from the content if both are auto. Second, add them up and compare with the container. If there is free space, distribute it by the grow factors. If there is not enough space, remove the overflow by the shrink factors, weighted by the base size. Finally, clamp by min and max sizes, and repeat if an item hits a limit.

Why does my text overflow instead of truncating? Flex items have min-width auto, and in a column min-height auto, which resolves to their min-content size. So an item cannot shrink below its longest unbreakable word. The fix is to set min-width zero on the flex item, or use overflow hidden, and then apply text-overflow ellipsis. This is the most common flexbox bug.

Flex-basis versus width. On the main axis, flex-basis wins over width when it is not auto. Both are still limited by min and max width. Prefer flex-basis for flex items, because it expresses the starting size in the flex context.

Some real world patterns. To push the last nav item to the end, give it a margin-inline-start auto. To center something, use justify-content center and align-items center. For a sticky footer, make the page a column with min-height of the viewport, and let main grow. For equal height cards, the default align-items stretch works. Stretch makes items as tall as the line, unless they have a fixed height or align-self. Baseline aligns the text baselines, which is nice for mixed font sizes.

And a follow up. Margins of flex items never collapse. Auto margins absorb free space before justify-content runs. And the order property changes visual order only, not the DOM or tab order, which affects accessibility.

Here is a short interview summary. Flexbox is one dimensional. I think in main and cross axes. Flex one means share space from a zero basis. For overflow problems, I set min-width zero. And I use auto margins and gap for common patterns.
passage:
Selectors can combine elements through descendant, child, and sibling combinators, and relational selectors such as has choose elements by their content. Modern colour tools include the oklch colour space, which has perceptually even lightness, and color-mix for deriving variants from a single brand colour.

In flexbox, the main axis follows flex-direction, justify-content distributes space along it, and align-items works on the cross axis. The shorthand flex one means grow one, shrink one, and a basis of zero, so items share free space equally. The algorithm computes base sizes, distributes free space by grow factors or removes overflow by shrink factors, and clamps results by minimum and maximum sizes.

Text overflows in flex items because min-width auto prevents shrinking below the content size, and setting min-width zero fixes it. Flex-basis takes priority over width on the main axis. Margins never collapse in flex layouts, auto margins absorb free space, and the order property changes only visual order, not the accessibility order.
prompt: Explain what flex one means and walk through how flexbox distributes grow and shrink space. Then explain why long text in a flex item overflows instead of truncating, and how to fix it.

title: CSS Grid in Practice
shadowText:
Today we will talk about CSS Grid. Grid is the best tool for two dimensional layouts, and interviewers like to ask about its details.

Let us start with the explicit and implicit grid. The explicit grid is made of the tracks you define with grid-template-columns, grid-template-rows, and grid-template-areas. The implicit grid is created automatically when items need more rows or columns than you defined. You control the size of implicit tracks with grid-auto-rows and grid-auto-columns. A good habit is to set grid-auto-rows, so extra rows do not collapse to content size by surprise.

How does the fr unit work, and why does one fr overflow? The fr unit takes a share of the space left after fixed and content sized tracks. But one fr is really minmax auto, one fr. The auto minimum means a track cannot shrink below its min-content size, so a long word or a wide image can push the grid wider than its container. The fix is minmax zero, one fr, or setting min-width zero on the item.

Auto-fill versus auto-fit. Both create as many columns as fit. They differ only when there are fewer items than columns. With repeat auto-fill and minmax two hundred, one fr, the empty columns stay and keep their space. With auto-fit, the empty columns collapse to zero, so the items stretch to fill the row. A responsive card grid usually uses auto-fit or auto-fill with minmax, and needs no media queries.

Placement: you can place items by grid lines, with grid-column and grid-row, using start and end numbers or a span. You can also name areas with grid-template-areas, and give items grid-area names. This makes a dashboard layout readable, like a picture of the layout in the CSS. With named areas you can change the layout in a media query by redefining only the template.

Auto placement and dense. By default, items fill the grid row by row and never go back to fill holes left by larger items. Setting grid-auto-flow dense lets the browser backfill holes with later, smaller items. The trade off is that the visual order no longer matches the DOM order, which hurts keyboard and screen reader users. Use it for decorative galleries, not for ordered content.

What is subgrid and what does it solve? A nested grid normally has its own independent tracks. So card titles, bodies, and buttons in adjacent cards do not line up. With subgrid, the child grid uses the tracks of its parent, so items in different cards align across rows. It solves aligned card layouts without fixed heights or JavaScript.

Grid versus Flexbox. Ask yourself: do rows and columns need to align? Then use grid. Should the content size decide the layout, like a toolbar or a row of tags? Then use flexbox. Grid is layout first, where you define the structure and place content into it. Flexbox is content first. Often you use both, grid for the page and flexbox inside components.

A follow up on alignment. Justify-items and justify-self work in grid, unlike in flexbox. Place-items center is a shorthand for align-items and justify-items, and it centers content in each cell. Place-content centers the whole grid inside its container. Gap works with both flexbox and grid. And you can use minmax, fit-content, and min-content to create flexible but bounded tracks.

Here is a short interview summary. I define the explicit grid and set auto sizes for the implicit one. I use minmax zero for fr tracks to avoid overflow. I use auto-fit with minmax for responsive grids, named areas for page layout, subgrid for aligned cards, and dense only when order does not matter.
passage:
CSS Grid is a two dimensional layout system. The explicit grid comes from the template properties, while the implicit grid is created automatically when items need extra tracks and is sized with grid-auto-rows and grid-auto-columns. The fr unit shares the remaining space, but because one fr behaves like minmax auto, one fr, wide content can cause overflow, which minmax zero, one fr prevents.

With repeat and minmax, auto-fill keeps empty columns, while auto-fit collapses them so items stretch. Items can be placed by lines, spans, or named areas, and named areas make page layouts easy to read and rearrange. The dense auto-flow mode fills holes but breaks the match between visual and DOM order.

Subgrid lets nested elements share the tracks of their parent, so card parts align across cards. Grid suits layouts where rows and columns must align, while flexbox suits content driven, one dimensional layouts, and the two are often combined.
prompt: Compare CSS Grid and Flexbox and say when you would choose each. Then explain how auto-fit with minmax creates a responsive card grid, and what subgrid adds for card layouts.

title: Responsive Design Techniques
shadowText:
Today we will talk about responsive design. This covers viewport settings, breakpoints, responsive images, and units that behave well on mobile.

Let us start with the viewport meta tag. It sets the width to the device width and the initial scale to one. Without it, mobile browsers lay out the page on a wide virtual canvas, often about nine hundred eighty pixels, and then shrink it to fit the screen. Your media queries would then look wrong, and text would be tiny. So every responsive page needs this tag in the head.

Mobile first versus desktop first. In a mobile first approach, the base styles are for small screens, and you add complexity with min-width media queries as the screen grows. In desktop first, you start wide and remove things with max-width queries. Mobile first is usually better. It makes you prioritize content, it keeps the base CSS simple, and mobile devices download less overridden code.

How do you choose breakpoints? By content, not by devices. Widen the browser until the layout looks wrong, for example the lines become too long or the cards are stretched too far. That is where you add a breakpoint. Device sizes change all the time. Also, many layouts need fewer breakpoints when you use flexible tools like auto-fit grids, clamp, and flex wrap.

Container queries versus media queries. Media queries ask about the viewport. Container queries ask about the component's container, so the same card can adapt when it is in a narrow sidebar or in a wide main area. To use them, you set container-type on the parent, and write a container rule for the child. This makes components truly reusable.

How does the browser pick from srcset and sizes? In srcset, you list image files with their widths, like four hundred w and eight hundred w. In sizes, you tell the browser how wide the image will be displayed at different viewport sizes. The browser knows the layout width and the device pixel ratio, so it calculates the needed pixels and picks the smallest file that is good enough. It may also choose a file already in the cache. Without sizes, the browser assumes the image is the full viewport width.

When do you need the picture element? For art direction, where you want a different crop at different sizes, and for format fallback, like serving AVIF or WebP with a JPEG fallback. For simple resolution switching, srcset on an image is enough.

One hundred vh versus dvh, svh, and lvh. On mobile, the browser toolbars grow and shrink while you scroll. The unit 100vh equals the largest viewport, with toolbars hidden, so content can be cut off at first. The svh unit is the smallest viewport, lvh is the largest, and dvh is dynamic and changes as the toolbars move. Use dvh for full screen sections, and be aware that dvh can cause relayout while scrolling.

Responsive typography. Keep the root font size at one hundred percent, to respect the user's setting. Use rem for sizes, and clamp for fluid scaling, with a minimum, a preferred value mixing rem and viewport width, and a maximum. Including a rem part in the preferred value keeps zoom working for accessibility.

Finally, user preference and capability media features. Use hover hover and pointer fine to apply hover effects only on devices that really have them. Use pointer coarse to make touch targets bigger. Prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, and prefers-contrast adapt to the user's settings. A follow up on container queries: container-type inline-size applies containment on the inline axis only, so the container's height still comes from its content. Container-type size contains both axes, so you must give it an explicit height.

Here is a short interview summary. I always set the viewport tag, design mobile first, choose breakpoints by content, and use container queries for components. I give the browser srcset and sizes, use dvh carefully, and make type fluid with clamp.
passage:
Responsive pages need the viewport meta tag, otherwise mobile browsers lay out the page on a wide virtual canvas and shrink it. A mobile first approach writes base styles for small screens and adds complexity with min-width queries. Breakpoints should be chosen where the content starts to look wrong, not at specific device widths.

Media queries respond to the viewport, while container queries respond to the size of a component's container, which makes components reusable. For images, srcset lists the available files and sizes describes how wide the image will be displayed, so the browser can pick the best file. The picture element is needed for art direction and format fallback.

On mobile, 100vh includes the hidden toolbar area, so dvh, svh, and lvh give better control. Fluid typography uses clamp with a rem part, and media features such as hover, pointer, and the prefers family adapt the interface to device capabilities and user settings.
prompt: Explain how you would build a responsive layout. Cover the viewport meta tag, mobile first design, container queries versus media queries, and how srcset and sizes help the browser choose an image.

title: Types, Coercion and Equality
shadowText:
Today we will talk about JavaScript types, coercion, and equality. These basics are asked in almost every interview, and the details are where people make mistakes.

Let us start with the data types. JavaScript has eight types. Seven are primitives: undefined, null, boolean, number, bigint, string, and symbol. The eighth is object, and that includes arrays, functions, dates, and more. Primitives are immutable and are compared by value. Objects are compared by reference.

How does typeof behave? It mostly returns what you expect, with a few quirks. Typeof null returns the string object. This is a historical bug from the first implementation, and it was never fixed, so never use typeof to check for null. Typeof of a function returns function, even though functions are objects. Typeof of an array returns object, so use Array.isArray for arrays. And typeof of an undeclared variable returns undefined, without throwing an error.

Null versus undefined. Undefined means no value was assigned. You get it from a missing property, a missing argument, an uninitialised variable, or a function with no return. Null means an intentional empty value, set by the developer. A common convention is to use null when you want to say there is deliberately nothing, and to let undefined be the default.

How does type coercion work? Operators convert their operands using abstract operations: ToPrimitive, ToNumber, ToString, and ToBoolean. The plus operator is special. If either operand is a string after ToPrimitive, it does string concatenation. Otherwise, it adds numbers. Other arithmetic operators always convert to numbers. When an object becomes a primitive, ToPrimitive first looks for a Symbol.toPrimitive method, then calls valueOf and toString in an order that depends on the hint. This is why an array plus an array gives a string.

Double equals versus triple equals versus Object.is. Triple equals is strict and does no coercion. Its only oddities are that NaN is not equal to NaN, and positive zero equals negative zero. Double equals is loose and coerces using the abstract equality algorithm. For example, null equals undefined, but neither equals anything else. A string and a number are compared as numbers. Object.is is like strict equality, except that NaN is the same as NaN, and positive zero is different from negative zero. In practice, use triple equals, and use double equals only for the check against null, which covers both null and undefined.

Why is zero point one plus zero point two not equal to zero point three? JavaScript numbers are IEEE seven five four sixty four bit doubles. Zero point one and zero point two cannot be stored exactly in binary, so the sum is zero point three with a tiny error at the end. For money, do not use floating point. Store the amount in integer cents, or use a decimal library, or BigInt for large integers. For comparisons, check if the difference is smaller than Number.EPSILON.

NaN and isNaN. The global isNaN function converts its argument first, so isNaN of the string abc is true. Number.isNaN checks only whether the value is really NaN, so it is false for a string. Prefer Number.isNaN. Also remember that NaN is the only value that is not equal to itself.

And the primitive wrapper trap. If you create new Boolean with false, you get an object, and any object is truthy. So an if on it will run. The same applies to new String and new Number. Their typeof is object. Avoid constructors with new for primitives. Use the plain function form, like Number of a string, for conversion.

Here is a short interview summary. There are seven primitives and objects. Typeof null is a known bug. Plus can concatenate or add depending on the types. I use triple equals, I use Number.isNaN, and I never use floating point for money.
passage:
JavaScript has seven primitive types, undefined, null, boolean, number, bigint, string, and symbol, plus the object type. The typeof operator has quirks: typeof null returns object, arrays also report object, and functions report function. Undefined means a value was never assigned, while null is an intentional empty value.

Operators convert operands through ToPrimitive, ToNumber, ToString, and ToBoolean. The plus operator concatenates when either operand becomes a string, and otherwise adds. Strict equality performs no coercion, loose equality applies the abstract equality algorithm, and Object.is differs from strict equality only for NaN and signed zero.

Numbers are sixty four bit floating point doubles, so zero point one plus zero point two is not exactly zero point three, and money should be stored in integer cents or handled by a decimal library. Number.isNaN is safer than the global isNaN because it does not coerce, and wrapper objects created with new are always truthy.
prompt: Explain why zero point one plus zero point two is not equal to zero point three in JavaScript, and how you would handle money. Then compare double equals, triple equals, and Object.is.

title: ES Modules and CommonJS
shadowText:
Today we will talk about JavaScript modules. We will compare ES modules with CommonJS, and cover loading, cycles, tree shaking, and code splitting.

Let us start with the key differences. ES modules use import and export. They have a static structure, so tools can analyze them without running the code. They load asynchronously, they are always in strict mode, and they export live bindings. CommonJS uses require and module.exports. It loads synchronously, it is evaluated when it is called, and it exports a copy of the values at that moment. This static structure is what makes tree shaking possible.

What are live bindings? With ES modules, an imported name is a read only view of the variable in the exporting module. Imagine a module that exports a variable count and a function inc which increases it. After you import both and call inc, the imported count shows the new value. With CommonJS, you would get the old value, because you copied it when you required the module. You cannot assign to an imported binding, but you can see changes made by the exporter.

How are ES modules loaded? In three phases. The first is construction. The engine fetches and parses every module in the dependency graph and builds module records. No code runs yet, and import specifiers are resolved. The second is instantiation. The engine allocates memory for all the exports and connects the imports to them. The third is evaluation. The code runs, from the deepest dependencies upward, and each module runs only once.

Circular dependencies. In ESM, a cycle works if no module uses an imported binding during its own evaluation before the other module has finished evaluating. Accessing a let or const binding too early gives a temporal dead zone error. Function declarations are hoisted, so they can be used. In CommonJS, a cycle gives you a partially filled exports object, which is a common source of undefined values. The best fix is to remove the cycle, by extracting shared code into a third module.

Default versus named exports. Which do I prefer? Named exports give consistent names across the codebase, better auto import and refactoring support, and clearer tree shaking. Default exports allow any name at each import, which hurts search and consistency. Many teams prefer named exports, and keep defaults for things like framework route files that require them.

Tree shaking. Bundlers like Rollup, webpack, esbuild, and Vite remove unused exports by using the static structure of ESM. It fails when you use CommonJS, when modules have side effects at the top level, when you re-export a whole namespace in a way the bundler cannot analyze, or when the package does not declare side effects properly. The sideEffects field in package.json helps bundlers know which files are safe to drop.

Dynamic import and code splitting. The import function returns a promise of the module namespace, and creates a split point in the bundle. Use it for routes, heavy libraries, and features that are not needed at first load, for example a chart library loaded when the user opens a report. It reduces the initial bundle size and improves load performance.

Dual packages and interop in Node. Node decides the module type by file extension, dot mjs for ESM and dot cjs for CommonJS, or by the type field in package.json. ESM can import CommonJS, and the module exports become the default import. CommonJS cannot use a static import of ESM, and older Node versions needed a dynamic import for it. Publishing a dual package needs care, to avoid loading two copies of the same code.

Here is a short interview summary. ESM is static, asynchronous, and has live bindings, so it enables tree shaking. CommonJS is dynamic and copies values. I avoid circular dependencies, prefer named exports, and use dynamic import for code splitting.
passage:
ES modules use import and export, have a static structure, load asynchronously, always run in strict mode, and export live bindings. CommonJS uses require and module.exports, loads synchronously, and exports a copy of values at the time of the call. The static structure of ESM is what makes tree shaking possible.

ES modules load in three phases: construction, where the module graph is fetched and parsed, instantiation, where memory for exports is allocated and imports are linked, and evaluation, where code runs once per module. A cycle between modules works only if no module uses an imported binding too early, and the usual fix is to extract shared code.

Named exports provide better tooling and consistent naming than default exports. Tree shaking fails with CommonJS, with top level side effects, and with unclear package declarations. Dynamic import returns a promise and creates a split point for code splitting. In Node, the file extension or the type field decides the module system, and dual packages need careful design.
prompt: Compare ES modules and CommonJS. Explain live bindings, the three phases of ES module loading, and why ES modules make tree shaking possible while CommonJS usually does not.

title: DOM Events and Browser APIs
shadowText:
Today we will talk about events and browser APIs in JavaScript. These are the tools for building interactive pages, and many interview questions come from here.

Let us start with event propagation. A DOM event travels in three phases. First is capture. The event moves from the window down through the ancestors to the target's parent. Second is the target phase, at the element itself. Third is bubble, where the event moves back up through the ancestors. By default, listeners run in the bubble phase. If you pass the capture option, the listener runs on the way down. You can stop propagation, but do it rarely, because it can break other code, like analytics.

What is event delegation, and how do you implement it? You attach one listener to a common ancestor, and handle events from many children, even the ones added later. In the handler, you look at event.target, and use closest with a selector to find the element you care about. It saves memory and handles dynamic lists well. One note: events that do not bubble, such as focus and blur, need focusin and focusout instead.

Now addEventListener options and cleanup. You can pass passive true, which promises that you will not call preventDefault, so the browser can scroll without waiting for your handler. You can pass once, to run only one time. And you can pass a signal from an AbortController. When you call abort, all listeners that share the signal are removed. That is a clean way to clean up in components, instead of keeping references to every handler.

Reflow versus repaint, and layout thrashing. Changing geometry, like width, position, font, or adding nodes, forces layout. Changing only visual style, like colour or visibility, forces repaint. Layout thrashing happens when you alternate between writing styles and reading geometry, such as offsetHeight, in a loop. Each read forces a fresh layout. The fix is to batch all reads first and all writes after, or to use requestAnimationFrame.

Which observer should you use? IntersectionObserver watches the visibility of an element against the viewport or a root, and is used for lazy loading images, infinite scroll, and view tracking. ResizeObserver watches element size changes, which is great for components that depend on their size. MutationObserver watches changes in the DOM tree, like added nodes or attributes. These are better than scroll handlers and polling, because they are asynchronous and efficient.

Storage options in the browser. Cookies hold about four kilobytes each, are strings, and are sent to the server with every request, so they suit sessions, but should be marked HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite. Local storage holds around five megabytes, is synchronous, persists across sessions, and is readable by any script on the origin. Session storage is the same but lasts only for the tab. IndexedDB is asynchronous, holds much more, and supports structured data. The Cache API stores network responses, often with service workers. Never store sensitive tokens in local storage if you can avoid it.

Custom events and communication between components. You can dispatch a custom event with a name like cart colon add, and a detail object with the data. Set bubbles true, so ancestors can listen, and composed true to cross a shadow DOM boundary. This keeps components decoupled, since the sender does not need to know who listens.

And the critical rendering path with script loading. HTML becomes the DOM, CSS becomes the CSSOM, and together they form the render tree, then layout, paint, and composite. CSS blocks rendering. Classic scripts block the parser, while defer runs after parsing in order, and async runs as soon as it downloads.

Here is a short interview summary. Events go capture, target, bubble. I use delegation for lists, passive listeners for scroll, and AbortController for cleanup. I use observers instead of scroll polling, avoid layout thrashing, and choose storage according to size, security, and lifetime.
passage:
A DOM event moves through the capture phase down the ancestors, the target phase, and the bubble phase back up. Event delegation attaches one listener to a common ancestor and uses event.target and closest to handle children, including ones added later. Events that do not bubble, such as focus, need focusin and focusout.

Useful listener options include passive, which lets scrolling proceed without waiting, once, and signal, which allows many listeners to be removed together by aborting an AbortController. Layout thrashing is caused by alternating geometry reads and style writes, and it is solved by batching reads before writes. IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, and MutationObserver watch visibility, size, and DOM changes without polling.

Browser storage options differ in size and security: cookies are small and are sent with each request, local and session storage are synchronous string stores readable by scripts, and IndexedDB is asynchronous and larger. Custom events with bubbles and composed allow decoupled communication between components.
prompt: Explain event propagation and event delegation, and show how you would use delegation on a dynamic list. Then compare cookies, local storage, and IndexedDB, including their security implications.

title: Memory Management and Leaks
shadowText:
Today we will talk about memory in JavaScript: where values live, how garbage collection works, and how to find leaks. Senior interviews often ask about this.

Let us start with the stack and the heap. Conceptually, the stack holds call frames, with local slots and return addresses. The heap holds objects, the context of closures, and other dynamic data. Primitives may live in frames, but engines can place them anywhere, so the model is a conceptual one. What matters is that variables hold either primitive values or references to objects on the heap.

How does garbage collection work? Modern engines use reachability, which is tracing, not reference counting. They start from roots, such as the global object, the current call stack, and active closures. Everything reachable from the roots stays alive. Everything else can be collected. This handles cycles well, because two objects that point to each other, but are unreachable from the roots, are both collected. V8 uses generational collection. Most objects die young, so the young generation is cleaned often and cheaply, while the old generation is cleaned less often, with incremental and concurrent marking to avoid long pauses.

What causes memory leaks in JavaScript? A leak is memory that is still reachable but no longer needed. Common sources include forgotten timers and intervals, which keep their callbacks alive. Event listeners that are never removed. Global variables, created by accident. Caches and maps that grow without a limit. Detached DOM nodes that are removed from the page but still referenced from JavaScript. And closures that hold large data. The fixes are to clear timers, remove listeners, often with an AbortController, limit cache size, and use WeakMap and WeakSet for data attached to objects.

There is a subtle one: the shared closure context leak. Imagine a function that creates a huge array, and then creates two inner functions. One uses the array, and the other does not. In some engines, both closures share one context object. So even the function that does not use the array keeps it alive, as long as that function is alive. The lesson is to keep large data out of scopes that long living closures share, or set it to null when finished.

How do you find a memory leak? There is a process that interviewers like to hear. First, reproduce with a repeatable action, such as opening and closing a modal twenty times, or navigating between routes. Second, observe the trend. In Chrome DevTools, use the Performance monitor to watch the heap, or the Memory panel. Third, take heap snapshots before and after, force a garbage collection, and compare them. Look for objects whose count keeps growing. Fourth, inspect the retainers, which show what keeps an object alive. Fifth, fix it, and measure again.

Shallow versus retained size. Shallow size is the memory held by the object itself. Retained size is the memory that would be freed if the object were collected, including everything that is only reachable through it. A small object can have a very large retained size, so retained size is the number to sort by when you hunt for leaks.

When should you use WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry? Rarely. They fit caches of expensive objects that can be rebuilt, or releasing external resources as a backup. The timing of garbage collection is not guaranteed, and callbacks may never run, so you must never rely on them for program logic.

Here is a short interview summary. The engine frees memory that is unreachable from roots. A leak is memory that is reachable but unneeded. The usual causes are timers, listeners, caches, detached nodes, and closures. I find leaks by repeating an action, comparing heap snapshots, and reading the retainers.
passage:
Variables hold primitive values or references to objects on the heap, and call frames live on the stack. Modern engines use tracing garbage collection based on reachability from roots such as the global object and the call stack, so cycles are not a problem. V8 uses generational collection with incremental and concurrent marking to reduce pauses.

A memory leak is memory that is still reachable but no longer needed. Typical causes include forgotten timers and event listeners, accidental globals, unbounded caches, detached DOM nodes, and closures that retain large data. Fixes include clearing timers, removing listeners, bounding caches, and using weak collections.

To find a leak, repeat an action many times, watch the heap trend, take heap snapshots, force collection, compare them, and inspect the retainers. Retained size is more useful than shallow size, because it shows what would be freed. WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry are rarely appropriate, since collection timing is not guaranteed.
prompt: Describe how JavaScript garbage collection works and list the common causes of memory leaks. Then walk through how you would find a leak in a single page app using Chrome DevTools.

title: Functional Programming and Immutability
shadowText:
Today we will talk about functional programming ideas in JavaScript, and why immutability matters in modern user interface code.

Let us start with the core ideas. First, pure functions and referential transparency. A pure function gives the same output for the same input, and has no side effects. So a call can be replaced by its result. Second, immutability. Instead of changing data, you create new data. Third, functions are values. You can pass them, return them, and store them. This leads to higher order functions like map, filter, and reduce, to function composition, and to currying and partial application. Together these make code easier to test and reason about.

Why does immutability matter in UI frameworks? React, Redux, Angular with OnPush, and memoised selectors detect change by reference equality. They check whether the previous value is the same object as the next one. If you mutate an object in place, the reference stays the same, so the framework thinks nothing changed, and the screen is not updated. If you create a new object, the reference changes, and the framework updates, while unchanged branches keep the same reference and can be skipped. Immutability also makes undo, time travel debugging, and concurrent rendering safer.

const versus Object.freeze versus deep freeze. The const keyword prevents rebinding the variable. It does not stop you from changing the object. Object.freeze makes the object's own properties read only, but only at the first level. Nested objects can still be changed. A deep freeze walks through the nested objects and freezes each one. Freeze fails silently in sloppy mode and throws in strict mode. It is useful in development, to catch accidental mutation, but it has a cost, so it is not usually used in production for large data.

What are the trade offs of immutability at scale? With manual spread syntax, there is no dependency and it is explicit, but deep updates are verbose and it is easy to miss a level. With a library like Immer, you write code that looks like mutation on a draft, and it produces an immutable result, with structural sharing. The cost is some extra overhead and learning. With persistent data structure libraries, you get efficient updates, but the data needs conversion. Modern array methods, like toSorted, toSpliced, and with, return new arrays without changing the original.

Reduce based patterns. Reduce is powerful, but it can be hard to read. A common use is grouping and summing. For example, with a list of orders, each with a customer and a total, you can reduce into an object that maps each customer to the sum of their totals. Start with an empty object as the initial value, and in each step add to the entry for that customer. Always provide the initial value, so an empty array does not throw. If the reduce gets complicated, a simple loop or a Map may be clearer.

Functors, monads, and Maybe: do you need them? Arrays and Promises already behave like functors, because they have map, and like monad like containers, because flatMap and then flatten nested results. A Maybe type wraps a value that might be missing, and lets you chain operations without checking for null at every step. In JavaScript, optional chaining and nullish coalescing already solve most of this. So you rarely need to build these abstractions, but knowing the idea helps you understand Promises and libraries.

Here is a short interview summary. I prefer pure functions and immutable updates, because UI frameworks depend on reference equality. Const does not make an object immutable, and freeze is shallow. For deep updates, I use spread carefully or Immer. And I use functional tools, but not at the cost of readability.
passage:
Functional programming in JavaScript emphasizes pure functions, immutability, and functions as values. A pure function returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects, which makes code easier to test. Higher order functions such as map, filter, and reduce, together with composition, support this style.

Immutability matters in UI frameworks because React, Redux, and memoised selectors detect change by comparing references. Mutating an object in place leaves its reference unchanged, so updates can be missed. The const keyword prevents rebinding only, Object.freeze is shallow, and a deep freeze must walk nested objects.

At scale, manual spread updates are explicit but verbose for deep structures, while Immer allows mutation style code that produces immutable results with structural sharing. Reduce is useful for grouping and summing, and should always have an initial value. Arrays and Promises already behave like functors, so custom monads are rarely needed.
prompt: Explain why immutability matters in React and Redux. Compare const, Object.freeze, and deep freeze, and describe two ways to update nested state immutably.

title: Diagnosing JavaScript Performance
shadowText:
Today we will talk about performance in JavaScript applications. The most important skill is a clear method for finding and fixing a slow page.

Let us start with how to approach a ticket that says the page is slow. Step one: define slow with a metric and a user journey. Is it load time, measured with LCP and time to first byte? Is it responsiveness, measured with INP and long tasks? Or is it visual stability? Step two: reproduce it on a realistic device and network, using throttling. Step three: measure, using field data if you have it, then the Performance panel. Step four: find the biggest bottleneck. Step five: fix one thing, and measure again to prove it helped. Without a measurement, you are only guessing.

Load performance techniques. For a large JavaScript bundle, use code splitting by route, dynamic import, tree shaking, and remove unused dependencies. For slow server responses, use caching and a CDN. For render blocking resources, use defer and preload. For large images, use modern formats, correct sizes, and lazy loading. For third party scripts, load them late, or remove them. Also compress with Brotli, and cache static files with long lifetimes and hashed names.

Runtime performance techniques. Pick the right data structure. A Set lookup is constant time, while includes on an array is linear, and inside a loop that turns a linear solution into a quadratic one. Avoid unnecessary work in hot paths. Debounce or throttle events like input and scroll. Break up long tasks, or move heavy work to a Web Worker. Avoid layout thrashing. Virtualize long lists. And memoize expensive calculations, but only when you have measured a problem.

Reading a flame chart. In the Performance panel, the horizontal axis is time, and the vertical axis is the call stack, with callers above callees. Wide bars are functions that took a long time. Look for the widest bars at the bottom, called self time, because that is where the work really happens. Long tasks are marked in red. Purple blocks are layout, and green blocks are paint. Zoom in on the interaction you care about, and ask what ran, and why.

Measure correctly: micro benchmarks lie. The engine optimizes code differently when it is hot, dead code may be removed, and a tiny test does not reflect real data. Use the performance mark and measure functions to time real operations in the real app. Run many iterations, ignore the first run, and test on a slow device. Prefer measuring the full user journey over a tiny function.
