Network optimization from JavaScript. Deduplicate requests that are in flight by caching the promise. Cache responses, for example with stale while revalidate. Cancel requests that are no longer needed, with AbortController. Batch small requests. Prefetch data that the user is likely to need next. And use pagination or streaming for large data.

String and array performance traps. Repeated string concatenation in a hot loop is fine in modern engines, but building an array and joining it is predictable. Avoid creating huge temporary arrays with chained map and filter on large data, when one loop would do. Avoid deleting properties from objects in hot paths, since it can change the object's shape and slow property access.

Here is a short interview summary. I start with a metric and a measurement, find the biggest bottleneck, fix one thing at a time, and measure again. For load, I reduce and split the bundle. For runtime, I choose better data structures, break up long tasks, and avoid layout thrashing.
passage:
Diagnosing a slow page starts with defining slow by a metric and a user journey, such as LCP for loading, INP for responsiveness, or layout shift for stability. The next steps are to reproduce the problem on a realistic device with throttling, measure it, find the largest bottleneck, fix one thing, and measure again.

Load performance improves through code splitting, tree shaking, caching, compression, deferred scripts, optimized images, and fewer third party scripts. Runtime performance improves by choosing suitable data structures, such as a Set instead of repeated array searches, debouncing events, breaking up long tasks, using Web Workers, and virtualizing long lists.

In a flame chart, time runs horizontally and the call stack vertically, so wide bars and large self time reveal expensive functions. Micro benchmarks can mislead, so measure real operations in the real application. Network work can be reduced by deduplicating, caching, cancelling, and prefetching requests.
prompt: A user reports that the page is slow. Walk me through how you would investigate. Cover choosing a metric, measuring with DevTools, reading a flame chart, and two examples of fixes for load and runtime performance.

title: JavaScript Security Basics
shadowText:
Today we will talk about security for JavaScript applications. Every developer should know the common attacks and the standard defences.

Let us start with cross site scripting, or XSS. It means an attacker gets their script to run in your origin. There, it can read the DOM, call your APIs with the user's session, and steal data. The main types are stored, reflected, and DOM based. The root cause is treating data as code. The defences: escape output by context, use frameworks that escape by default, avoid innerHTML and dangerous APIs like eval, use textContent, sanitize any rich HTML with an allow list library, and add a Content Security Policy as a second layer.

CSRF, or cross site request forgery. An attacker tricks a logged in user's browser into sending a state changing request to your site, and the browser attaches the cookies automatically. The defences are SameSite cookies, set to Lax or Strict, anti CSRF tokens, checking the Origin header, and requiring custom headers for API calls. Also never change state with GET requests.

Prototype pollution. Unsafe deep merge or set by path utilities let an attacker write to Object.prototype through keys like double underscore proto, constructor, or prototype. Then every object in the app can inherit unexpected properties, which can lead to logic bypasses or even code execution. The defences are to reject those keys, to use Object.create null or Map for dictionaries, to freeze the prototype in sensitive places, and to keep dependencies updated.

Where should you store auth tokens in the browser? Local storage and session storage are exposed to any script, so one XSS bug can steal the token. HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript, so they resist theft by XSS, but they need CSRF protection through SameSite and tokens. In memory storage is safe from persistence, but is lost on refresh. A common good design uses a short lived access token in memory and a refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie.

Other common vulnerabilities. ReDoS happens when a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking, like nested repetition, runs on attacker input and blocks the event loop. Avoid nested quantifiers and limit input length. Open redirects happen when you redirect to a user supplied URL. Validate against an allow list. Insecure deserialization, path traversal, and server side request forgery also appear in Node code. And always validate input on the server.

Supply chain security. npm dependencies run install scripts and ship code into your bundle. Controls include committing lockfiles and using npm ci in builds, auditing dependencies, pinning versions, reviewing new packages, using Subresource Integrity for CDN files, and limiting install scripts. Be careful with typosquatting names, and keep the number of dependencies small.

A secure headers checklist. Content-Security-Policy to restrict sources. Strict-Transport-Security to force HTTPS. X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff. Referrer-Policy such as strict origin when cross origin. Permissions-Policy to limit browser features. Frame protection with frame-ancestors. And cookies with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite.

Here is a short interview summary. XSS is solved by escaping and sanitizing, with CSP as a backup. CSRF is solved with SameSite cookies and tokens. I block prototype pollution keys. I prefer HttpOnly cookies for tokens. I watch regular expressions and dependencies, and I set secure headers.
passage:
Cross site scripting lets an attacker run script in your origin, where it can read the page and act as the user. It is prevented by treating data as text, escaping by context, avoiding innerHTML and eval, sanitizing rich HTML with an allow list, and adding a Content Security Policy as a second layer.

Cross site request forgery tricks a logged in browser into sending a state changing request, and is countered with SameSite cookies, anti forgery tokens, Origin checks, and by never changing state with GET. Prototype pollution comes from unsafe deep merge utilities that accept keys such as proto, and is prevented by rejecting those keys and using Maps or prototype free objects.

Auth tokens in local storage can be stolen by XSS, while HttpOnly cookies resist theft but need CSRF protection. Other risks include regular expression denial of service, open redirects, and supply chain attacks, which are reduced with lockfiles, audits, and Subresource Integrity. Secure headers such as CSP, HSTS, and nosniff add further protection.
prompt: Explain what XSS and CSRF are and how you defend against each. Then discuss where you would store an authentication token in a browser app and why. Mention at least one other attack.

title: Testing and Maintainable JavaScript
shadowText:
Today we will talk about testing, debugging, and keeping a JavaScript codebase maintainable over time.

Let us start with the levels of testing. Unit tests cover one function or module, with dependencies faked. They are very fast, and run in milliseconds, with tools like Vitest or Jest. They catch logic errors. Integration tests combine several parts, such as a component with its state and a mocked network. They are slower, but catch wiring problems. End to end tests drive a real browser through a full user flow, with tools like Playwright or Cypress. They are the slowest and most expensive, but they show that the whole system works. A healthy suite has many unit tests, a good number of integration tests, and a few critical end to end tests.

Testing async code, timers, and network. With fake timers, you can control time. For example, to test a debounce function, you enable fake timers, call the function many times, advance the time, and check that the callback ran once. For promises, return them or use async and await in the test, so the test waits. For network calls, mock the fetch layer, or use a tool that intercepts requests at the network level, so your code runs in a realistic way. Always clean up mocks between tests.

Mocks versus stubs versus spies versus fakes. A spy records calls on a real function, so you can check how it was used. A stub replaces a function with a fixed answer. A mock is a stub or spy with built in expectations. A fake is a working but simplified implementation, like an in memory database. Prefer fakes and real code when you can, because over mocking makes tests that pass while the real code is broken.

How do you debug a production only bug? Step one: gather evidence. Use error tracking, such as Sentry, with source maps uploaded privately, along with breadcrumbs, the user agent, and the app version. Step two: reproduce it. Use the same build, the same data, and the same browser or device. Step three: narrow it down. Use logs, feature flags, and bisecting between releases. Step four: fix it and add a test. Step five: add monitoring so you see it earlier next time. Do not debug by making random changes on production.

Design patterns in JavaScript, and which ones matter. The module pattern is now done with ES modules or closures, giving an encapsulated service with private state. The singleton comes for free from module caching. The observer pattern appears as events, and as pub sub. The factory pattern builds objects without exposing the details. The strategy pattern is just passing a function. The adapter wraps an API into the shape you need. The key is to use patterns to solve a real problem, not to add structure for its own sake.

Maintainability: what do you enforce on a team? Use TypeScript in strict mode, at least at module boundaries, and runtime validation with zod or valibot for external data, because types disappear at runtime. Use a linter and a formatter, enforced in continuous integration. Write small functions with clear names. Keep modules focused, and avoid circular dependencies. Review code in pull requests, and keep tests meaningful and not brittle. Document decisions, and remove dead code.

Here is a short interview summary. I use many unit tests, some integration tests, and few end to end tests. I control time and network in async tests, and I prefer fakes to heavy mocking. For production bugs, I gather evidence first. And I keep code maintainable with strict types, validation, linting, and reviews.
passage:
A balanced test suite has many fast unit tests, a moderate number of integration tests that check how parts work together, and a few end to end tests that drive a real browser through critical user flows. Async code is tested with fake timers, awaited promises, and mocked or intercepted network requests, with cleanup between tests.

A spy records calls on a real function, a stub replaces a function with a fixed answer, a mock adds expectations, and a fake is a simplified working implementation. Over mocking can hide real bugs, so fakes and real code are preferred where practical.

Debugging a production only bug starts with evidence from error tracking with source maps, then reproduction, narrowing down by logs, flags, or bisecting, and finally a fix with a test. Maintainable code relies on strict TypeScript, runtime validation of external data, linting, small focused modules, and careful code review.
prompt: Explain the difference between unit, integration, and end to end tests, and how you would test a debounced function. Then describe your process for debugging a bug that only happens in production.

title: How the V8 Engine Works
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how the V8 engine runs JavaScript, and what that means for writing fast code. This is a deeper topic, but it shows real expertise.

Let us start with the pipeline. The source code goes to the parser. V8 parses lazily, so it only pre-parses inner functions until they are called. The parser produces an abstract syntax tree. Then the Ignition interpreter turns it into bytecode and starts running it. While it runs, V8 collects feedback about types. Hot functions are then compiled by optimizing compilers, such as Sparkplug and TurboFan, into fast machine code, based on assumptions from the feedback. If an assumption breaks, for example a variable that was always a number is suddenly a string, V8 deoptimizes and goes back to the slower path.

What are hidden classes, also called shapes or maps, and inline caches? V8 gives each object a hidden class that describes its property layout. Objects created with the same properties, in the same order, share a hidden class. This lets V8 find a property at a fixed offset, instead of a dictionary lookup. Inline caches remember the hidden classes seen at each property access. If the site always sees one shape, it is monomorphic and very fast. A few shapes make it polymorphic, and many shapes make it megamorphic, which is slow. So initialize all properties in the constructor, in a consistent order, and avoid adding or deleting properties later.

Array element kinds. V8 tracks the kind of elements in an array. For example, packed small integers, then packed doubles, then packed general elements, and also holey versions when there are gaps. The kinds only move toward more general ones, never back. So creating arrays with holes, or mixing types, can make operations slower. Prefer packed arrays of one type when you care about speed, and avoid pre-sizing arrays with new Array of a large number if you will fill them gradually.

Engine versus runtime versus host. The ECMAScript engine, such as V8, provides the language: syntax, built in objects like Array, Promise, and JSON, and garbage collection. The runtime or host provides the environment APIs. In a browser, that includes the DOM, fetch, timers, and the event loop integration. In Node, it includes the file system, networking, and process. Things like setTimeout and console are not part of the language itself, but come from the host.

Multithreading in JavaScript. Each agent, meaning the main thread or a Worker, has its own heap and event loop. Objects are not shared by default, so there are no data races on normal objects. Workers communicate by passing messages, which are copied with structured cloning, or transferred, as with ArrayBuffers. For shared memory, you can use SharedArrayBuffer together with Atomics, which needs extra security headers in browsers. Most code uses a single thread with asynchronous APIs, and Workers for heavy computation.

Tail calls, recursion depth, and stack size. ES2015 specified proper tail calls, but only JavaScriptCore in Safari implements them. In V8, deep recursion throws a RangeError for exceeding the call stack, typically after around ten thousand frames, depending on the frame size. So for deep structures, use an iterative approach with an explicit stack.

A few other internals. Strings are UTF-16, so an emoji can have a length of two. Use the spread syntax or Intl.Segmenter to handle user perceived characters. Small integers have a fast representation, and numbers outside that range are boxed as doubles. And the garbage collector is generational, as we discussed.

Here is a short interview summary. V8 parses, interprets with Ignition, and optimizes hot code with TurboFan, using type feedback. Stable object shapes and consistent types keep code fast. The engine gives the language, the host gives the APIs, and JavaScript uses isolated threads with message passing.
passage:
V8 parses source code lazily into an abstract syntax tree, runs it as bytecode in the Ignition interpreter, and collects type feedback. Hot functions are compiled by optimizing compilers such as TurboFan into machine code based on that feedback, and V8 deoptimizes if an assumption breaks.

Hidden classes describe the property layout of objects, and objects created with the same properties in the same order share one. Inline caches use these shapes to speed up property access, so code stays fast when shapes are consistent and slows when many shapes appear. Arrays have element kinds, such as packed integers, doubles, or general values, and become more general but never less, so holes and mixed types can cost performance.

The engine provides the language and garbage collection, while the host provides APIs such as the DOM, timers, and the file system. Each thread or Worker has its own heap and event loop, communicating through messages or SharedArrayBuffer with Atomics. V8 has no proper tail calls, so deep recursion overflows the stack, and strings use UTF-16.
prompt: Explain how V8 executes JavaScript, from parsing and the Ignition interpreter to optimization. Describe hidden classes and inline caches, and how they affect the way you should create objects.

title: Strings, Dates, Errors and Binary Data
shadowText:
Today we will talk about some JavaScript topics that look small, but interviewers love them. We will cover Unicode strings, regular expressions, dates, the Intl tools, custom errors, and binary data.

Let us start with strings. Here is a surprising fact. The length of a single smiley emoji is two. Why? Because JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units. Characters outside the basic multilingual plane, like emoji, take two units. We call that a surrogate pair. And it gets more complex. A character that a user sees can be several code points. A thumbs up with a skin tone is a thumbs up plus a modifier. Even the letter e with an accent can be one code point or two. So to count code points, you spread the string into an array and take the length. To count what the user actually sees, use the Intl segmenter with grapheme granularity.

Now regular expressions. You should know the flags. G is global, i ignores case, m makes anchors work per line, s lets the dot match a newline, u turns on Unicode mode, y is sticky, d gives match indices, and v is the newer Unicode sets mode. Named groups let you read match dot groups dot year, which is much clearer than numbers. Lookarounds, ahead and behind, assert something without consuming characters. Interviewers also like to ask about catastrophic backtracking, where a badly written pattern takes exponential time on certain input.

Next, dates and time zones. Here is the key point. A Date is a UTC millisecond timestamp. Only the display uses the local zone. A date only ISO string, like the first of November, is parsed as UTC. But the same date with a time and no offset is parsed as local time. In a place like Dhaka, those two differ by six hours. Months in the constructor start at zero, so month ten is November. And Date is mutable, so setting the day changes the original object. For safety, always include an offset in your strings, or use the newer Temporal API where available.

Then the Intl object. It formats numbers and currency for a locale. It can show compact numbers, so one million two hundred fifty thousand becomes one point three M. It can produce relative time, like yesterday. It has plural rules, and a list formatter that produces phrases like A, B, and C. So you rarely need a heavy date or number library.

Now errors. The built in types include Error, TypeError for a wrong type or calling something that is not a function, ReferenceError for an unknown or not yet initialized binding, RangeError for invalid lengths or stack overflow, and SyntaxError, for example from bad JSON. AggregateError comes from Promise dot any. For your own code, create a custom class that extends Error, for example an HTTP error that stores a status code. Pass the options to super so you can use the cause property. Cause lets you wrap a low level error while keeping the original, which makes debugging much easier.

Finally, binary data. An ArrayBuffer is a block of raw bytes, and you cannot read it directly. Typed arrays, like Uint8Array or Float32Array, are views over a buffer with a fixed element type. They are fast, and they are used by WebGL, Web Audio, random number generation, and file and network bytes. A DataView is for mixed types and explicit byte order, which you need for binary protocols. Since a recent version of the language, buffers can also be resizable.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. JavaScript strings are UTF-16, so length is not the number of characters a person sees. Dates are UTC timestamps with tricky parsing, so I always include offsets. I use Intl for formatting, custom errors with cause for debugging, and typed arrays when I handle raw bytes.
passage:
JavaScript strings are sequences of UTF-16 code units, so an emoji has a length of two. Counting code points requires spreading the string, and counting characters that a user perceives requires the Intl segmenter. Regular expressions offer flags for global, case insensitive, multiline, Unicode, and sticky matching, as well as named groups and lookarounds.

A Date is a UTC timestamp that is displayed in the local zone. A date only ISO string is parsed as UTC, whereas a date and time without an offset is parsed as local time, which can cause surprises across zones. Months in the constructor are zero based. Intl provides locale aware formatting of numbers, currencies, plurals, lists, and relative times.

Custom errors should extend Error and use the cause option to keep the original failure. Binary data is handled with an ArrayBuffer, typed array views, and a DataView when mixed types or explicit byte order are needed.
prompt: Explain why the length of an emoji string is two in JavaScript and how you would count characters correctly. Then explain one common date parsing trap involving UTC and local time, and how you would avoid it.

title: Node.js Streams, Workers and Shutdown
shadowText:
Today we will talk about practical Node dot js topics that come up in senior interviews. We will cover streams and backpressure, three ways to use more than one core, graceful shutdown, async local storage, event emitter pitfalls, and some modern built in features.

Let us start with streams. A stream processes data in chunks instead of loading everything into memory. There are four types. Readable, writable, duplex, and transform. Here is the key point. Backpressure. When the consumer is slower than the producer, the write method returns false once its buffer passes the high water mark. A correct producer then pauses until the drain event. If you ignore this, everything gets buffered in memory, and a big file can crash your process. The easy and safe way is to use the pipeline helper, which handles backpressure and cleanup for you.

Next, how do you use more than one CPU core? There are three options. Worker threads run threads inside one process. Each has its own V8 isolate and event loop. They share memory only through SharedArrayBuffer, and they can transfer buffers without copying. Use them for CPU heavy work like parsing, image processing, or hashing. The cluster module runs multiple processes that share a server port, so you can use every core for an HTTP server. They do not share memory. And child process starts any external program or a separate Node process. Choose based on the problem. CPU bound work inside an app means worker threads. Scaling an HTTP server over cores means cluster, although in many production setups a process manager or container orchestrator does this instead.

Now graceful shutdown. This is a very practical topic. When your service receives a termination signal, you should not just die. The pattern is this. Keep a flag so you only shut down once. Stop accepting new connections by closing the server. Set a hard deadline timer, for example ten seconds, that forces an exit with an error code if cleanup takes too long. Mark that timer so it does not keep the process alive. Then wait for in flight work and close the database and the queue, using Promise dot allSettled so one failure does not block the others. Finally, exit with a success code. Orchestrators like Kubernetes send the signal and then wait, so this prevents dropped requests during deployments.

Next, AsyncLocalStorage. It solves a classic problem. How do you carry a request ID or a user ID through many layers of code without passing it everywhere? You create a store, and in a middleware you run the rest of the request inside that store with the data. Later, any function, such as your logger, can read the current store. The important part is that it survives across await boundaries. It is a clean way to get request scoped logging and tracing.

Then event emitter pitfalls. First, an error event with no listener throws and crashes the process, so always handle errors on streams, sockets, and emitters. Second, listeners run synchronously in the order they were registered, so a slow listener blocks emit. Third, the max listeners warning, which defaults to ten, usually signals a leak, for example adding a listener on every request and never removing it. And the once helper from the events module gives you a promise for a single event.

Finally, modern built ins worth naming. The built in test runner, the watch flag, the env file flag for loading environment variables, a native fetch and WebSocket client, the experimental permission model, and in newer versions, a built in SQLite module and running TypeScript files by stripping types. Always check the exact Node version your team uses before relying on these.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. I respect backpressure by using pipeline, I choose workers, cluster, or child processes by workload, I always implement graceful shutdown with a deadline, I use AsyncLocalStorage for request context, and I never leave an emitter without an error handler.
passage:
Node streams process data in chunks instead of loading it fully into memory. The four stream types are readable, writable, duplex, and transform. When a consumer is slower than a producer, the write method returns false after the buffer passes the high water mark, and the producer should wait for the drain event. The pipeline helper handles this automatically.

To use multiple cores, worker threads run CPU heavy work in separate isolates within one process, the cluster module runs several processes that share a server port, and child processes launch external programs. A graceful shutdown stops accepting new connections, sets a hard deadline, waits for in flight work, closes databases and queues, and then exits.

AsyncLocalStorage carries request context, such as a request identifier, across asynchronous boundaries. With event emitters, an error event without a listener crashes the process, listeners run synchronously, and a growing listener count usually indicates a leak.
prompt: Describe how you would implement a graceful shutdown for a Node HTTP service. Explain what you do when the termination signal arrives, why you set a hard deadline, and how backpressure in streams relates to memory safety.

title: Scope, Hoisting and Closures
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how JavaScript runs your code, and about three core ideas: hoisting, scope, and closures. These are among the most common interview topics.

Let us start with the execution context. It is the environment in which code runs. There is one global context, one for each function call, and one for each module or eval. Each one is created in two phases. In the creation phase, the engine builds the lexical environment, which holds let, const, class, and function bindings, and the variable environment, which holds var. It also binds this and sets a reference to the outer scope. Then, in the execution phase, the code runs line by line.

This leads to hoisting. Here is the key point. Every declaration is hoisted, but they behave differently. A var is hoisted and starts as undefined, and it is function scoped. A let or const is hoisted too, but it stays uninitialized until its declaration runs, and it is block scoped. A function declaration is hoisted with its whole body, so you can call it before it appears. A class is like let. It is in the temporal dead zone until evaluated.

The temporal dead zone is the span from the start of a block until the let, const, or class declaration is evaluated. Touching the binding in that span throws a ReferenceError. This actually proves that let is hoisted. If it were not, the code inside the block would read the outer variable with the same name. Instead you get an error. Default parameters can fall into the same trap, if one parameter refers to a later parameter.

Next, lexical scope versus dynamic scope. JavaScript uses lexical scope. Which variables a function can reach depends on where the function is written, not where it is called. If an inner function is defined at the top level, it sees the global variable, even if you call it from inside another function that has a variable with the same name. The exception is this, which is dynamic.

Now closures. A closure is a function together with references to the variables of the scope where it was created. The function keeps those variables alive even after the outer function has returned. A classic example is a counter. A function called createCounter has a local variable count, and it returns an object with an increment method and a getter. Nobody outside can touch count directly, so you get private state. Practical uses are private data, factories, memoization, debounce, once, and event handlers that remember their setup.

There is also the classic loop problem. If you use var in a loop and schedule timers that print the index, you see the final value three times, because there is only one function scoped variable. If you use let, each iteration gets a new binding, and you see zero, one, two. Before let existed, the fix was an immediately invoked function or passing the value as an argument.

What about strict mode? It makes JavaScript safer. Assigning to an undeclared variable throws, instead of creating a global. This is undefined in plain function calls. Writing to read only properties throws. Duplicate parameter names and octal literals become syntax errors, and the with statement is not allowed.

Finally, the scope chain. When you use a name, the engine walks outward through environments until it finds it. Modern engines resolve most lookups ahead of time, so deep nesting costs very little. What hurts is sloppy mode eval and with, because they can add bindings at runtime and force slow dynamic lookup.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Declarations are hoisted, but let and const are in the temporal dead zone until they run. Scope is lexical. A closure is a function plus its surrounding variables, and it powers private state and many patterns. And I prefer let and const with strict mode.
passage:
Every piece of JavaScript code runs inside an execution context, which is created in two phases. During creation, the engine builds the environments for variables and functions, binds the value of this, and links to the outer scope. During execution, the code runs in order.

Hoisting applies to all declarations, but with different results. A var starts as undefined and is function scoped. Let and const are block scoped and remain in the temporal dead zone until their declaration is evaluated, and accessing them earlier throws a ReferenceError. Function declarations are hoisted with their bodies.

JavaScript uses lexical scope, meaning that a function sees the variables from where it was written, not where it is called. A closure is a function that keeps references to the variables of its creating scope, even after that scope has finished. Closures provide private state, factories, and memoization. In loops, let creates a fresh binding per iteration, which avoids the classic var problem. Strict mode adds safety by turning silent mistakes into errors.
prompt: Explain what a closure is and give a practical example, such as a counter with private state. Then explain the classic loop problem with var and timers, and why let fixes it.

title: Web Platform and TypeScript Types
shadowText:
Today we will talk about two groups of topics. First, browser networking and caching. Second, the TypeScript type system. Both are common in front end and full stack interviews.

Let us start with fetch. The first detail people miss is that fetch rejects only on a network failure or an abort. A server error like four hundred and four or five hundred does not reject. So you must check the ok property. Second, a response body can be read only once. If you call the json method twice, it throws, so clone the response if two consumers need it. Third, cookies. By default, cookies are sent only to the same origin. For cross origin cookies you need credentials set to include, and the server must also allow credentials and name a specific origin.

Now CORS. It is enforced by the browser, to decide whether page code may read a cross origin response. It does not protect your server. Before some requests, the browser sends a preflight request using the OPTIONS method. A request is simple, with no preflight, only if the method is GET, HEAD, or POST, uses only safelisted headers, and has a content type of plain text, multipart form data, or url encoded form. So a JSON POST triggers a preflight, and so does any custom header like Authorization.

Next, real time options. Short polling pulls on a schedule and is fine for low frequency checks. Long polling holds the request open and is mostly a legacy fallback. Server sent events go one way, from server to client, over normal HTTP, with built in reconnect and resume. WebSocket is two way, supports binary, and suits chat and games, but you must handle reconnection yourself.

Then service workers. A service worker is a background script that proxies network requests, works only over HTTPS, runs on its own thread, and has no DOM access. Its lifecycle is install, waiting, and activate. A new version waits until old tabs close, unless you force it, which can mix old pages with new assets. For HTTP caching, give hashed asset files a very long max age and the immutable flag. Give the HTML a no cache directive so deployments are picked up. Use private or no store for personalized API responses, and use ETag for cheap revalidation.

Now TypeScript. Any turns off type checking for a value, and it spreads silently. Unknown means it could be anything, so you must narrow it before use. Use it for parsed JSON, catch variables, and external input. Never is the type with no values. It appears for functions that always throw, and for impossible branches in exhaustiveness checks.

Narrowing with discriminated unions is a favorite. You define a union where each member has a common literal field, like status, with values ok, error, or loading. In a switch on that field, TypeScript narrows each branch. In the default branch you assign the value to a variable of type never, so adding a new status later causes a compile error. That is exhaustiveness checking.

Generics with constraints let you relate inputs to outputs. For example, a pluck function takes a list of items of type T and a key K that extends the keys of T, and returns a list of T at K. Asking for a missing key is an error. A good rule is that a type parameter should appear at least twice. Utility types such as Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record, ReturnType, and Awaited transform existing types.

Last, structural typing. TypeScript compares shapes, not names. An object with extra properties is assignable if it comes from a variable. But a fresh object literal with extra properties triggers the excess property check.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Fetch does not reject on HTTP errors. CORS is a browser rule, with preflight for non simple requests. I choose SSE or WebSocket by direction. And in TypeScript I prefer unknown over any, discriminated unions with never checks, and generics that relate types.
passage:
The fetch function rejects only on network failure or abort, so the ok property of the response must be checked for HTTP errors. A response body can be read once, and cross origin cookies require both credentials include on the client and an explicit allow credentials policy on the server. CORS is enforced by the browser, and a preflight request is sent for anything other than simple requests.

For real time updates, polling is simple, server sent events provide a one way stream with automatic reconnection, and WebSocket provides two way communication including binary data. Hashed static assets can be cached for a long time, while HTML should always be revalidated.

In TypeScript, unknown requires narrowing before use and is safer than any. Discriminated unions with a never based exhaustiveness check catch missing cases at compile time. Generic constraints relate inputs to outputs, and typing is structural, comparing shapes instead of names.
prompt: Explain what triggers a CORS preflight request and why a JSON POST with an Authorization header needs one. Then compare unknown with any in TypeScript and say when you would use each.

title: The this Keyword and TypeScript Choices
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the this keyword, which is a classic interview topic, plus a few TypeScript design choices.

Let us start with TypeScript. Interface versus type. An interface can be merged, which means you can declare it twice and the parts combine, and it can be extended. A type alias handles unions, intersections, mapped types, and conditional types. Both work for object shapes, so pick one convention per code base. For enums, prefer a union of string literals, or a constant object, because they produce no extra runtime code and have no reverse mapping surprises. And the satisfies operator checks that a value matches a type while keeping its more precise inferred type.

Here is an important point. Types vanish at runtime. TypeScript checks code, not data. An API can still return an id of null while your type says number. So at boundaries, validate external data at runtime. A good approach is to use a schema library, like Zod, and derive the static type from the schema, so the two can never drift apart.

Now, how is this determined? The key sentence is this. This is set by how a function is called, not where it is defined. Arrow functions are the exception. There are rules in priority order. First, new binding. When you call a function with new, this is the newly created object. Second, explicit binding, using call, apply, or bind, where this is the object you pass. Third, implicit binding. When you call obj dot method, this is the object left of the dot. Fourth, the default. In sloppy mode it is the global object, and in strict mode it is undefined.

Call, apply, and bind. Call runs the function immediately with arguments listed one by one. Apply runs it immediately with arguments in an array. Bind does not run it. It returns a new function with this fixed and optionally some arguments pre filled, which is partial application. Interviewers often ask you to implement them. For call, you temporarily put the function on the context object under a unique symbol key, call it, and then delete it in a finally block. For bind, you return a function that calls the original with the fixed context and the preset arguments followed by the new ones, and you should handle use with new.

Arrow functions versus regular functions. An arrow function has no own this, it uses the one from the surrounding scope. It has no arguments object, so use rest parameters. It cannot be used with new. It has no prototype. It cannot be a generator. And super and new dot target are taken from the surrounding scope too. So an arrow function is a bad choice for an object method or a constructor.

A very common bug is a class method losing this. If you take a method from an instance and call it alone, for example as an event handler, this is undefined, because class bodies are strict. A fix is a class field written as an arrow function, which is bound for each instance. The trade off is that each instance gets its own copy of the function, which costs memory and makes it harder to mock on the prototype.

Finally, callbacks. In a normal event listener, this is the element. In an arrow listener, it is the outer this. Many array methods accept a thisArg as the second argument. And passing a method to setTimeout loses this, so wrap it in an arrow function.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. This depends on the call site, following new, explicit, implicit, and default rules, and arrow functions capture it lexically. I fix lost this with bind, arrow wrappers, or arrow class fields, and I validate runtime data instead of trusting types.
passage:
In JavaScript, the value of this depends on how a function is called, not where it is defined. The rules, in priority order, are new binding, explicit binding with call, apply, or bind, implicit binding through the object before the dot, and finally the default, which is the global object in sloppy mode and undefined in strict mode.

Call and apply invoke a function immediately, with arguments passed individually or as an array. Bind returns a new function with a fixed this and optionally preset arguments. Arrow functions have no own this, no arguments object, and no prototype, and they cannot be used with new, so they take this from the surrounding scope.

When a class method is passed as a callback, it loses its this. The usual fixes are binding it, wrapping it in an arrow function, or defining it as an arrow class field. TypeScript types disappear at runtime, so external data should be validated with a schema.
prompt: Explain how the value of this is determined in JavaScript, covering the four binding rules and how arrow functions differ. Then show how you would fix a class method that loses this when passed as an event handler.

title: Prototypes, Classes and Inheritance
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how objects inherit in JavaScript. We will cover the prototype chain, classes, the new operator, older inheritance patterns, and when to prefer composition.

Let us start with the prototype chain. Every object has an internal link called prototype, which you can read with Object dot getPrototypeOf. When you look up a property and it is not on the object, the engine follows the link to the next object, and then the next, until it reaches null. Reads walk the chain. Writes create an own property on the object you are writing to, unless a setter or a read only property is found up the chain.

People often confuse three names. The internal prototype link is what every object has. The double underscore proto property is an old accessor that reads and writes that link. Prefer Object dot getPrototypeOf and Object dot setPrototypeOf. And the prototype property on a function is a normal property that exists on regular functions. It becomes the internal link of objects created with new on that function.

So what does new do? Here are three steps. First, create a new object whose prototype is the function's prototype property. Second, call the function with this bound to that object. Third, if the function returns an object, use that. Otherwise return the new object. Interviewers often ask you to implement it. You create the object with Object dot create, apply the function, and check the result.

Are ES6 classes real classes? Mostly they are syntax over prototypes, but with real differences. Class bodies are always strict. Class declarations stay in the temporal dead zone until evaluated. Calling a class without new throws. Methods are not enumerable, and they cannot be used as constructors. And extends sets up two chains: one between the prototypes for instances, and one between the constructors so static members are inherited.

Before classes, inheritance was done by hand. You wrote a constructor, called the parent constructor with call to copy instance properties, set the child prototype with Object dot create of the parent prototype, and repaired the constructor property. You use Object dot create, and not simply assign the parent prototype, because assigning would let changes on the child affect the parent.

Now, composition versus inheritance. Deep class hierarchies couple the child to the parent's internals. This is the fragile base class problem. They also force a single way to classify things. When behaviors vary independently, build objects from small capabilities instead. For example, make a function that adds a fly method, another that adds a swim method, and compose a duck from both. This is more flexible than a tree of classes.

About instanceof. It checks whether the right side's prototype appears anywhere in the left side's chain. You can customize it using the Symbol dot hasInstance method. It can fail across realms. An array that comes from an iframe is not an instance of the array of the parent window, so use Array dot isArray. It can also be wrong if someone reassigns the prototype after creating the object.

Finally, why not change built in prototypes? It affects every array in the realm, including third party code. It can collide with future standard names. There is a famous case where an old library had added a method called flatten, which forced the standard to use the name flat instead. If enumerable, it also shows up in for in loops. Only polyfill real standard methods, only when missing, and define them as non enumerable.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Objects inherit through the prototype chain. New links the object, runs the constructor, and returns it. Classes are mostly syntax with stricter rules. I prefer composition for varying behavior, and I never modify built in prototypes.
passage:
Every JavaScript object has an internal prototype link. When a property is not found on an object, the engine follows the chain of links until it finds the property or reaches null. Reading walks the chain, while writing normally creates an own property on the receiving object.

The new operator creates an object linked to the constructor's prototype property, calls the constructor with this bound to that object, and returns the result if it is an object, otherwise the new object. ES6 classes are largely syntax over this mechanism, but they are always strict, cannot be called without new, define non enumerable methods, and link both instance and static inheritance.

Deep inheritance hierarchies create tight coupling, known as the fragile base class problem, so composition of small capabilities is often preferable. The instanceof operator checks the prototype chain and fails across realms, where Array dot isArray is more reliable. Built in prototypes should not be modified, because changes affect all code and may collide with future standards.
prompt: Explain what the new operator does step by step and how the prototype chain is used when a property is read. Then say when you would prefer composition over class inheritance.

title: Objects, Arrays and Modern Syntax
shadowText:
Today we will talk about everyday JavaScript data handling. We will cover copying, destructuring, spread and rest, optional chaining, property order, array methods, property descriptors, and a quick timeline of language features.

Let us start with copying. A shallow copy copies only the top level. You can do it with the spread syntax, Object dot assign, or slice on arrays. Nested objects are still shared references, so changing a nested value changes both copies. A deep copy duplicates everything. The old trick of stringifying to JSON and parsing back is limited. Dates become strings, maps and sets become empty objects, undefined and functions are dropped, and cycles throw an error. The modern option is structuredClone, which handles dates, maps, sets, and cycles, but not functions. For special needs, you can use a library or write your own.

Next, destructuring. You can pull values out of objects and arrays, rename them, set defaults, go into nested objects, and collect the rest. A default applies only when the value is undefined, not when it is null. You can skip array items with extra commas. You can even swap two variables in one line with array destructuring. In function parameters it gives you named options with defaults.

Spread and rest use the same three dots, but have opposite jobs. Spread expands an iterable or an object into elements. Rest collects the remaining elements into an array or an object. Object spread copies only own enumerable properties, and it reads getters. Later keys win, so putting defaults first and user options last is a common pattern.

Optional chaining and nullish coalescing are very useful. A question mark followed by a dot reads a property only if the left side is not null or undefined, and otherwise gives undefined instead of throwing. You can use it for method calls and indexes too. Two question marks give a fallback only for null or undefined. This is different from double pipe, which also replaces zero, empty string, and false, and that is often a bug. There are also logical assignment forms, such as nullish assignment, which sets a value only if it is nullish.

Now property order. Own keys are ordered like this. First integer like keys in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols in insertion order. Object dot keys and for in skip symbols and non enumerable keys, and for in also walks inherited keys. Reflect dot ownKeys returns everything.

For arrays, know which methods mutate. Push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill, and copyWithin all change the original. Concat, slice, map, filter, flat, and flatMap return new arrays. The newer methods toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, and with give non mutating versions. Also know at, find last, and the short circuit methods some and every.

Getters and setters let you compute properties. You can inspect and control a property with descriptors, which have value, writable, enumerable, and configurable. Object dot freeze blocks adding, changing, or deleting, but only at the top level.

Finally, the timeline. ES2015 brought let and const, arrows, classes, modules, promises, template literals, destructuring, maps and sets, symbols, generators, and proxies. ES2017 added async and await. ES2018 added object rest and spread and async iteration. Later years added optional chaining, nullish coalescing, and the non mutating array methods.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. I know the difference between shallow and deep copies and I use structuredClone. I use nullish coalescing instead of double pipe for defaults, I know which array methods mutate, and I remember that freeze is shallow.
passage:
A shallow copy, made with spread, Object dot assign, or slice, duplicates only the top level, and nested objects remain shared. A JSON round trip is a limited deep copy that loses dates, maps, sets, functions, and cycles, whereas structuredClone handles most data types except functions.

Destructuring extracts values with renaming, defaults, nesting, and rest, and defaults apply only to undefined. Spread expands values and rest collects them. Optional chaining safely reads nested properties, and nullish coalescing provides a fallback only for null and undefined, unlike the double pipe operator, which also replaces zero, empty strings, and false.

Own keys are ordered with integer keys first, then strings in insertion order, then symbols. Some array methods mutate the original, such as sort and splice, while newer methods like toSorted return copies. Property descriptors control whether a property is writable, enumerable, or configurable, and Object dot freeze locks an object only at its top level.
prompt: Compare shallow and deep copying in JavaScript. Explain the limits of the JSON round trip trick, what structuredClone does better, and why using double pipe for defaults can be a bug.

title: Functional Patterns in JavaScript
shadowText:
Today we will talk about functional programming patterns in JavaScript, which interviewers often ask you to implement by hand. We will cover higher order functions, currying, composition, memoization, debounce, throttle, once, and pure functions.

Let us start with the basics. In JavaScript, functions are first class values. You can store them in variables, pass them as arguments, and return them. A higher order function either takes a function as an argument or returns one. Examples are map, filter, reduce, addEventListener, debounce, middleware, and higher order components in React.

A popular exercise is to implement map, filter, and reduce. For map, you loop over the array, call the callback with the value, the index, and the array, and build a new array. A careful version preserves holes by checking whether the index exists. For reduce, the tricky part is the initial value. If none is given, you use the first existing element and start from the next. If the array is empty and there is no initial value, you throw a TypeError.

Next, currying and partial application. Currying transforms a function of three arguments into a chain of three functions that each take one argument. Partial application fixes some arguments and returns a function waiting for the rest. Bind can do that. A typical curry helper checks whether enough arguments have arrived, compared with the function's length. If yes, it calls the function. If not, it returns another function that collects more arguments.

Function composition. Compose runs functions from right to left, and pipe runs them from left to right. Both can be written using reduce. A nice example is a slugify function made by piping three small steps: trim and lowercase, remove unwanted characters, and replace spaces with hyphens. You can write an async version of pipe too, by awaiting each step.

Now memoization. It caches the result of a function for given arguments. A simple version uses a Map and a key built from the arguments, often by stringifying them. A better version limits the cache size, for example with a least recently used policy, by deleting and re inserting a key whenever it is read. The pitfalls matter. Memoization only makes sense for pure functions. The key must be correct, since stringifying can fail for functions or cycles. An unbounded cache is a memory leak. And async functions need care, because you might cache a rejected promise.

Debounce versus throttle. Here is the key point. Debounce runs a function once after the calls have stopped for a given wait. It suits search as you type, the end of a resize, and autosave. Throttle runs a function at most once per interval during a stream of events. It suits scroll, mouse move, and analytics pings. A debounce can have a leading option, which runs immediately on the first call.

The once helper is short. It keeps a done flag and a stored result. On the first call it runs the function and saves the result, then drops the reference so it can be garbage collected. Later calls return the saved result.

Finally, pure functions. A pure function gives the same output for the same input and has no observable side effects. No input and output, no changing its arguments or outside state, and no time or random calls. Pure functions are easy to test, cache, and run in parallel. In real systems, keep an impure shell for network, database, and user interface work, around a pure core for business logic.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Functions are values, so I can compose and cache them. I can implement map, reduce, curry, pipe, memoize, debounce, and once from scratch, and I design systems with a pure core and a thin impure shell.
passage:
In JavaScript, functions are first class values, and a higher order function takes a function as an argument or returns one. Common examples are map, filter, reduce, event listeners, middleware, and debounce. Implementing reduce correctly requires handling the optional initial value and empty arrays.

Currying turns a function of several arguments into a chain of single argument functions, while partial application fixes some arguments in advance. Compose and pipe combine functions from right to left or from left to right. Memoization caches results for repeated inputs, and it is safe only for pure functions with a well defined cache key and a bounded cache size.

Debounce delays a call until events stop, which suits search boxes, while throttle limits the call rate during continuous events such as scrolling. A pure function returns the same result for the same input and has no side effects, and good designs keep a pure core of business logic inside a thin layer that performs input and output.
prompt: Explain the difference between debounce and throttle, and give one real use case for each. Then describe how you would implement a memoize function and name two pitfalls to watch for.

title: The Event Loop Explained
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the event loop. It answers one of the most common questions: JavaScript is single threaded, so how does async work?

Let us start there. The engine, like V8, runs one call stack on one thread. But the host environment, which is the browser or Node dot js, provides other parts. Web APIs or libuv do the waiting for timers, network, and file input and output, on other threads or in the operating system. When they finish, they queue a callback. The event loop moves a queued callback onto the stack only when the stack is empty. So your JavaScript is single threaded, but the waiting is not.

Now the key question. Microtasks versus macrotasks. The microtask queue holds promise reactions, such as then, catch, and finally, plus await continuations, queueMicrotask, and mutation observers. The microtask queue runs after the current script or task finishes, and whenever the stack empties. It is drained completely, even if new microtasks are added while draining. Macrotasks, also called tasks, come from timers, user events, network callbacks, and message channels. The loop takes one task, runs it, drains all microtasks, possibly renders, and then takes the next task. So promises always run before the next timer.

How does await work? Await x is roughly the same as wrapping x in a resolved promise and attaching the rest of the function as a then callback. Code before the first await in an async function runs synchronously. Everything after it is a microtask. So if you log S1, call an async function that logs A1, awaits, then logs A2, and then log S2, the order is S1, A1, S2, A2.

Can microtasks starve the loop? Yes. Because the queue drains completely, a microtask that always schedules another microtask blocks rendering, input, and timers. The page freezes, like an infinite loop, even though no single function runs long. To yield, use a timer, a message channel, or the scheduler API.

Why is setTimeout with zero not zero milliseconds? The delay is a minimum. The callback must wait for the current task and all microtasks, and then for its turn. Browsers clamp nested timers to at least four milliseconds, and they throttle timers in background tabs. Node treats zero as one millisecond.

Node has its own loop phases through libuv. In order: timers, pending callbacks, idle and prepare, poll for input and output, check, which runs setImmediate, and close callbacks. Between callbacks, Node drains the process dot nextTick queue first, and then the promise microtasks. Inside an input and output callback, setImmediate always runs before a zero millisecond timer, but from the main module the order can vary.

Where does requestAnimationFrame fit? Its callbacks run before the next paint, after microtasks, once per frame. Use it for visual work. A timer of sixteen milliseconds drifts and can cause jank. RequestIdleCallback runs when the frame has spare time. It suits low priority work, but it may never run on a busy page, so pass a timeout.

Finally, long tasks. Any task over fifty milliseconds hurts the Interaction to Next Paint metric. Options are to split work into chunks and yield between them, move heavy work to Web Workers and communicate with messages or transferred buffers, or move work off the critical path by lazy loading.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. One thread runs the stack, the host does the waiting, and the loop feeds callbacks. Microtasks run to completion before the next macrotask, await splits a function at the first await, and I avoid long tasks by chunking or using workers.
passage:
JavaScript engines run a single call stack on one thread, while the host environment, such as the browser or Node, performs waiting for timers, network, and file operations outside that thread. When the operations finish, callbacks are queued, and the event loop moves them onto the stack only when it is empty.

There are two kinds of queues. The microtask queue contains promise reactions and await continuations, and it is drained completely after each task and whenever the stack empties. Macrotasks, such as timers and user events, are processed one at a time, with microtasks drained between them. Therefore a promise callback always runs before the next timer. A microtask that keeps scheduling more microtasks can starve rendering.

A timeout of zero is only a minimum delay. Node has its own phases, with timers, poll, and check, and it drains the nextTick queue before promise microtasks. Long tasks over fifty milliseconds hurt responsiveness and should be split into chunks or moved to workers.
prompt: Explain the JavaScript event loop, including the difference between microtasks and macrotasks. Use a short example with a promise and a setTimeout to show which runs first and why.

title: Promises and Async Patterns
shadowText:
Today we will talk about promises and async code in JavaScript. We will cover promise guarantees, chaining, combinators, parallel versus sequential code, error handling, a concurrency limiter, retries, and stale responses.

Let us start with what a promise is. It represents a future value. It starts pending, and then becomes either fulfilled or rejected. Together those are called settled. Here is the key point. A promise settles only once. Later calls to resolve or reject are ignored. And handlers always run asynchronously, as microtasks, even if the promise is already settled. That removes a whole class of bugs where code sometimes runs synchronously and sometimes does not.

Chaining. Each then returns a new promise. It resolves with the value the handler returns, or rejects with what it throws. If you return a promise, the chain waits for it. A catch can recover from an error by returning a value, and then the chain continues as fulfilled. Finally runs at the end for cleanup, such as hiding a spinner.

Now the combinators. Promise dot all fulfills when all fulfill, giving results in input order. It rejects on the first rejection, but the others keep running. Promise dot allSettled waits for everything and never rejects, and it reports each status. It is good for batch jobs where you want to report partial failures. Promise dot race settles with the first result, whether success or failure. Promise dot any fulfills with the first success and rejects only if all fail, with an AggregateError. Interviewers often ask you to implement all. You create a results array, count the remaining items, resolve each item with Promise dot resolve, store the value at its index, and resolve when the counter hits zero. Reject at the first failure.

Sequential versus parallel. If you await two one second calls one after the other, it takes two seconds. If you start both and await Promise dot all, it takes one second. There is a famous trap. Using forEach with an async callback does not wait. The promises are dropped, the caller continues, and errors go unhandled. Use a for of loop with await for sequential work, or Promise dot all with map for parallel work.

Error handling. Try and catch around await catches rejections. But it does not catch an error thrown inside a callback that is not awaited, like a timer. An async function never throws synchronously. It returns a rejected promise. Unhandled rejections fire an event in browsers and crash the process by default in modern Node, so always handle or return your promises.

Concurrency limiter. If you run fetch on ten thousand URLs at once, you open too many sockets, hit rate limits, and spike memory. A promise pool starts a fixed number of workers. Each worker takes the next index, awaits the job, stores the result, and repeats. Because JavaScript is single threaded, reading and incrementing the index is safe.

Retry with exponential backoff. On failure, wait longer each time, doubling the delay up to a maximum, and add random jitter so many clients do not retry together. Stop after a limit, if the error is not retryable, or if an abort signal fires.

Race conditions in the interface. If a user types a, then ab, the response for a might arrive last and show wrong results. Fix it by aborting the previous request with an AbortController, or by ignoring responses that are not the latest.

Finally, Promise dot withResolvers, from a recent standard, gives you a promise with its resolve and reject functions in one call. It is useful for bridging event based APIs.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Promises settle once and run handlers as microtasks. I use all for independent parallel work, allSettled for partial failures, never forEach with async, a pool for large batches, backoff with jitter for retries, and abort signals for stale requests.
passage:
A promise represents a future value. It is pending until it settles once, either fulfilled or rejected, and its handlers always run asynchronously as microtasks. Each then call returns a new promise, so chains can transform values, recover from errors with catch, and clean up with finally.

Promise dot all rejects at the first failure while the other operations continue, allSettled reports every outcome, race settles with the first result, and any waits for the first success. Independent operations should be started together and awaited with Promise dot all, because awaiting them one by one is slower. A forEach loop with an async callback does not wait for its promises.

Errors thrown inside non awaited callbacks are not caught by try and catch, and unhandled rejections can crash a Node process. Large batches should be limited with a concurrency pool, transient failures retried with exponential backoff and jitter, and stale interface requests cancelled with an AbortController.
prompt: Compare Promise dot all, allSettled, race and any, and say when you would use each. Then explain why forEach with an async callback is a bug and how you would fix it.

title: Iterators, Generators and Collections
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the lower level building blocks of modern JavaScript. We will cover iterators, generators, async iterators, symbols, maps and sets, weak references, and proxies.

Let us start with the iteration protocols. An iterable is an object with a method under Symbol dot iterator that returns an iterator. An iterator is an object with a next method that returns an object with value and done. Anything iterable works with for of, spread, destructuring, Array dot from, Promise dot all, the Map constructor, and yield star. Plain objects are not iterable. You can make your own class iterable, for example a Range class that goes from a start number to an end number, by writing that method.

Generators make this much easier. A function with a star returns a generator object, which is both an iterator and an iterable. Each yield pauses the function and keeps its local state. Calling next resumes it, and the value you pass to next becomes the result of the paused yield expression. An example is an ID generator that loops forever, yielding the next number, and resets if you pass true. Generators are useful for lazy sequences, custom iteration, and step by step control flow.

Async iterators and for await of. An async generator can yield values over time. A common example is paginating an API. The generator fetches a page, yields every item, and moves to the next URL. The caller uses for await of, and if it breaks early, no further pages are fetched. That gives you backpressure for free. Node streams and web readable streams are async iterable.

Symbols. A symbol is a unique, immutable primitive used as a property key that cannot collide with others. Symbol keys are skipped by for in, Object dot keys, and JSON stringify. They are still visible through getOwnPropertySymbols, so they are not truly private. Symbol dot for uses a global registry. Well known symbols customize language behavior, such as iterator, hasInstance, and toPrimitive.

Map versus Object. A Map accepts any value as a key, including objects and functions. An object only accepts strings and symbols, and numbers become strings. A Map keeps pure insertion order, has a size property in constant time, and has no inherited keys, while objects can have prototype pitfalls. A Map is usually better for frequent adding and removing. A Set stores unique values and gives fast membership checks, unlike searching an array.

Now weak collections. A WeakMap and a WeakSet hold their keys weakly. If nothing else references the key object, it can be garbage collected and the entry disappears. Keys must be objects. They are not iterable and have no size. A typical use is attaching metadata to DOM elements without causing leaks. WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry are advanced tools, and you should avoid relying on their timing.

Finally, Proxy and Reflect. A proxy intercepts basic operations, such as get, set, has, delete, apply, and construct. Reflect provides the default behavior for each one, so your trap can forward correctly, including the receiver. A simple reactive system wraps an object in a proxy, and on each set it forwards the change with Reflect and then notifies listeners. Proxies power reactivity in some frameworks, validation layers, and logging.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Iterables follow a simple protocol, generators build iterators with pause and resume, and async generators suit paginated data. I choose Map and Set for dynamic keys and uniqueness, weak collections to avoid leaks, and proxies for interception.
passage:
An iterable is an object that has a method under Symbol dot iterator, and that method returns an iterator, which is an object with a next function producing a value and a done flag. Iterables work with for of loops, spread, destructuring, and many built in functions, while plain objects are not iterable.

Generators, declared with a star, pause at each yield and keep their local state, which makes lazy sequences and custom iteration simple. Async generators combined with for await of are well suited to paginated data and streams, because stopping the loop stops further fetching.

A symbol is a unique primitive that is useful as a collision free property key. A Map accepts any type of key, preserves insertion order, and has a constant time size, which makes it better than an object for dynamic collections. WeakMap and WeakSet hold keys weakly and allow garbage collection. A Proxy intercepts operations such as reads and writes, and Reflect supplies the default behavior.
prompt: Explain how generators work and how they relate to the iterator protocol. Then give an example of when an async generator with for await of is a good fit, such as reading a paginated API.

title: JavaScript Tricky Output Questions
shadowText:
Today we will talk about tricky JavaScript questions, the kind where the tempting answer is wrong. For each one, I will give the correct answer and the reason. This is great practice for explaining your thinking out loud in an interview.

Let us start with typeof null. The tempting answer is the string null. The correct answer is object. Why? In the first engine, values were tagged with type bits, and null, which was the null pointer, carried the object tag. The language kept this because fixing it would break the web. To check for null, use triple equals against null.

Next, an empty array double equals not an empty array. The tempting answer is false. The correct answer is true. Here is why. The not operator runs first. An empty array is truthy, so its negation is false. Then you compare an empty array with false using loose equality. The boolean becomes zero. The array becomes an empty string, and then zero. Zero equals zero. The tempting answer assumes loose equality compares truthiness, but it actually compares coerced primitives.

Third, zero point one plus zero point two equals zero point three. The tempting answer is true. The correct answer is false, because the sum is zero point three, then fifteen zeros, then four. IEEE seven fifty four doubles cannot represent zero point one or zero point two exactly, and the errors do not cancel. But zero point five plus zero point two five equals zero point seven five is true, because those are exact binary fractions.

Fourth, does const make values immutable? If you declare an array with const, you can still push to it, but reassigning it throws a TypeError. Const blocks reassignment of the binding, not mutation of the value.

Fifth, an arrow function as an object method. If an object has a property n and a method written as an arrow that returns this dot n, calling it does not return the property. The arrow takes this from where the object literal was written, never from the object. In a browser script it is the window, so you get undefined. In an ES module, this is undefined, so reading n throws a TypeError.

Sixth, parseInt with map. Mapping the strings one, seven, and eleven with parseInt gives one, NaN, and three. Why? Map passes the value, the index, and the array. So parseInt gets radix zero for the first, which means automatic, radix one for the second, which is invalid, and radix two for the third, so eleven in binary is three. The fix is to map with Number, or pass radix ten explicitly.

Seventh, does Promise dot all cancel the others when one fails? No. Promises are results, not tasks. Promise dot all just stops waiting and rejects early. The other operations keep running. To really stop work, share an abort signal and abort it in the catch block.

Eighth, try and catch around setTimeout. If you throw inside a timer callback, the catch does not run. The callback runs later on a fresh call stack, after the try block finished. Catch inside the callback, or use promises with await.

Ninth, an async function returning one. Logging the call shows a promise that is fulfilled with one, not the number. An async function always returns a promise, even for a plain return or a synchronous throw.

Tenth, forEach with async. The tempting belief is that it saves items one by one and the caller waits. In reality all saves start at once, the caller continues immediately, and rejections go unhandled. Use for of with await for sequential work, or Promise dot all with map for parallel work.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. Many surprises come from coercion, floating point math, and the way this and async code work. When I answer, I say the result and then give the reason, because the reasoning shows real understanding.
passage:
Several JavaScript results surprise developers. The typeof operator returns object for null because of an early engine design that tagged null with the object type bits. An empty array compared loosely to its own negation is true, because the negation is false and both sides are coerced to the number zero. Adding zero point one and zero point two does not equal zero point three, since binary floating point cannot represent those decimals exactly.

A const declaration blocks reassignment but not mutation. An arrow function used as an object method takes this from its surrounding scope rather than from the object. Mapping with parseInt fails because map passes the index as the radix.

Promises represent results, not tasks, so Promise dot all does not cancel the remaining operations when one rejects. An error thrown inside a timer callback is not caught by an outer try block, an async function always returns a promise, and forEach does not wait for async callbacks.
prompt: Pick two tricky JavaScript outputs, for example mapping with parseInt and an array compared to its own negation. For each one, say what a beginner would expect, give the real result, and explain the reason.

title: More JavaScript Gotchas and Myths
shadowText:
Today we will talk about more JavaScript gotchas and some common myths. Like before, each one has a tempting answer that is wrong, so let us learn the reasons.

Let us start with creating arrays. Calling Array with the number three does not give an array containing three. A single numeric argument is a length. So you get an array with three empty slots. Array dot of three gives an array containing three. And if you call map on the empty array, it does not fill it with indexes, because holes are not undefined values, and methods like map and forEach skip them. The result is still empty slots.

Second, this inside setTimeout in a method. Imagine a counter object with a start method that sets a timer using a regular function that increments this dot count. You might expect the count of the counter to increase. It does not. The callback is a regular function called by the timer, not by the counter, so implicit binding does not apply. This is the window in a browser, or a timeout object in Node. Use an arrow function instead.

Third, are object keys always strings? Suppose you create two different objects and use both as keys on a plain object. Reading the first key gives the second value. Both objects are converted to the same string, which is object Object, so the second write overwrites the first. If you need real object keys, use a Map.

Fourth, sort on numbers. Sorting one, ten, two, and twenty one without a comparator does not sort numerically. The default sort converts items to strings and compares code units, so ten comes before two. There is a second trap. Sort mutates the original array and returns the same array. Use toSorted with a comparator, or copy first.

Fifth, JSON stringify surprises. In objects, undefined values, functions, and symbols are omitted. In arrays they become null. NaN becomes null. Dates become ISO strings. And a BigInt throws a TypeError. So the belief that it round trips any object is false.

Sixth, is instanceof Array reliable? No. It fails for arrays from another realm, like an iframe, because each realm has its own Array prototype. Array dot isArray checks the internal marker and works across realms.

Seventh, is JavaScript pass by reference? No. It is always pass by value. For objects, that value is a reference, which some people call call by sharing. This matters because reassigning a parameter does not affect the caller, but mutating the object does. For example, a function that sets a property and then reassigns its parameter to a new object only leaves the property change visible to the caller.

Eighth, does await block the thread? No. It suspends only the current async function and returns control to the event loop. Other code keeps running. Only synchronous work, like long loops, huge JSON parsing, or synchronous file input and output, blocks.

Ninth, do Object dot freeze and const make state deeply immutable? No. Both are shallow. Const only stops reassigning the variable. Freeze only locks the top level properties. A nested object can still be changed, and maps, sets, and dates keep their internal state mutable.
