These are natural seams for modules or services. Aggregates enforce invariants in one transaction, like an order with its lines, and reference other aggregates by ID. Domain events, like order placed, decouple modules.

Multi tenancy. Shared tables with a tenant ID column are cheapest but give the lowest isolation, and rely on every query being scoped. Schema per tenant gives medium isolation and cost, but migrations multiply. Database per tenant gives the highest isolation, easy per tenant backup and data residency, at the highest cost, which suits enterprise and regulated customers.

Technical leadership. Write architecture decision records, short documents with context, decision, alternatives and consequences, so future engineers know why. In code reviews, look at correctness, failure modes and operability, not style, which you automate. Keep pull requests small, and ask what happens when this dependency is slow. Provide team standards, such as service templates with logging, metrics and health checks already in place.

To summarize: size resources and scale on the right signals, test your restores, start with a modular monolith, keep business logic independent of frameworks, and lead with written decisions.
passage:
On Kubernetes, memory requests should equal limits because exceeding memory causes an out of memory kill, CPU limits should be used carefully because throttling harms latency, and autoscaling should use request rate, event loop utilization or queue depth rather than CPU alone. Migrations should run as a single backward compatible job, and backups are only trustworthy if restores are tested regularly.

For architecture, most products should begin as a modular monolith with clear module boundaries and extract services only for concrete reasons such as independent scaling or ownership. Hexagonal architecture keeps business rules independent of frameworks through ports and adapters, and domain driven design supplies bounded contexts, aggregates and domain events.

Multi tenant systems trade isolation against cost, from shared tables with a tenant column to a separate database per tenant. Technical leadership relies on architecture decision records, focused code reviews, small pull requests and shared service templates.
prompt: Compare a modular monolith with microservices for a new product. Say when you would extract a module into its own service, and how architecture decision records help the team over time.

title: Production Mistakes And Event Loop Blocking
shadowText:
Today we will talk about common production mistakes in Node, and about what blocks the event loop. Let us start with a few statements that sound reasonable but cause incidents.

First: we will run migrations on app startup. With twenty replicas starting at once, twenty processes race to migrate. Long migrations delay readiness and fail deploys, and a failed migration crash loops every pod. Run migrations as one job with a lock, before the rollout.

Second: our container uses npm start, so SIGTERM works. Npm may not forward signals to Node, so the process is killed after the grace period instead of shutting down gracefully. Use the node command directly in the Docker CMD, in exec form.

Third: microservices will make us faster. Only if team boundaries, ownership and platform tooling are in place. Otherwise you get a distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together, with network calls where function calls used to be.

Now the event loop. What blocks it? Anything synchronous that takes long. CPU loops. JSON parse or stringify of multi megabyte payloads. Synchronous crypto like pbkdf2 sync and scrypt sync. The sync versions of zlib. File system sync calls after startup. Catastrophic regular expression backtracking, called ReDoS. Sorting huge arrays. Synchronous rendering of large pages. A rule of thumb is to keep any single callback under a few milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, so other requests are not delayed.

What is microtask starvation, and how is it different from nextTick starvation? The loop cannot advance while the microtask queue or the nextTick queue is non empty. Code that keeps adding to them never lets input and output run. But setImmediate does not starve the loop. Each immediate is queued for the next check phase, so timers and I O run in between. That is the standard way to yield during long work. Chunking work this way keeps the server responsive, but it does not make the total work cheaper. For heavy CPU work, use worker threads.

How do you measure event loop health in production? There are two key measures. Event loop delay, or lag, is how late a timer fires compared to when it should. Event loop utilization, or ELU, is the fraction of time the loop was busy running callbacks rather than idle in the poll phase. When you compute ELU, read the counter once and compare it with the previous reading, so every window is exactly contiguous. Reading it twice per tick leaves small gaps that skew short intervals. Export both as metrics, alert on sustained high values, and use ELU as an autoscaling signal, because it reflects real saturation better than CPU for these services.

A related point is that high event loop delay with low CPU can mean other things, like garbage collection pauses or a saturated thread pool. So check those too.

To summarize for an interview: run migrations as a separate job, start Node directly so signals work, do not adopt microservices without team structure, avoid synchronous long operations in request paths, yield with setImmediate or move work to workers, and monitor event loop delay and utilization.
passage:
Common production mistakes include running migrations at application startup, where many replicas race and a failure crash loops every pod; migrations should run once as a separate locked job before the rollout. Starting a container with npm start may prevent termination signals from reaching Node, so the command should launch node directly. Microservices help only when team boundaries and platform tooling exist, otherwise they form a distributed monolith.

The event loop is blocked by long synchronous work, such as large JSON operations, synchronous crypto and compression, synchronous file calls, catastrophic regular expression backtracking and sorting huge arrays. Microtask and nextTick queues starve the loop if they keep refilling, whereas setImmediate lets timers and input and output run between chunks.

Event loop health is measured with event loop delay and event loop utilization, and both should be exported as metrics and used for alerting and autoscaling.
prompt: Explain what can block the Node event loop, how setImmediate helps during long work compared with process.nextTick, and which two metrics you would use to monitor event loop health in production.

title: The Node.js Event Loop And Promises
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the Node event loop and promises. This is the most common deep topic in Node interviews, so let us make it clear.

Explain the event loop. Say this first: JavaScript runs one piece of code at a time on the call stack. When the stack is empty, the event loop picks the next ready callback, such as a timer that expired, a socket with data, or a setImmediate callback, and runs it. After every callback, Node drains two high priority queues: first the process nextTick queue, then the promise microtask queue. Only then does the loop move on.

Macrotask versus microtask. A macrotask is one callback scheduled by libuv, like one timer, one input and output completion, or one setImmediate. The loop runs them phase by phase. A microtask is a promise job or a queueMicrotask callback. Microtasks run as soon as the current callback finishes, before the next macrotask, and the queue is drained completely, including microtasks added while draining.

Browser versus Node. The browser follows the HTML standard, with one task per turn from several queues chosen by the browser, and rendering between tasks. Node has fixed phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check and close. Node also has the extra nextTick queue, which runs before promise microtasks.

Cancelling async work. Promises cannot be cancelled. The operation behind them can be, if it accepts an AbortSignal. Fetch, file reads, stream pipeline, events once, timers promises, child processes and most modern libraries support it. Cancellation is cooperative. CPU bound code that never checks the signal cannot be cancelled.

What is wrong with a timeout helper that races a promise against a timer? Three problems. The timer is never cleared, so on success it still fires later and keeps the process alive, and at scale thousands of timers pile up. The underlying work continues, so the request or query keeps holding a socket or pool connection. And the error is anonymous, so callers cannot tell a timeout from other failures. Use an AbortSignal with a timeout, and a typed error.

Promise combinators. All resolves when every input fulfils and rejects on the first rejection, so use it for parallel steps that must all succeed. AllSettled waits for everything and never rejects, which suits batch jobs where partial failure is fine. Race settles with the first input to settle, either way. Any resolves with the first fulfilment and rejects only if all fail, which suits trying several mirrors.

Error propagation. A rejection skips every then handler until it reaches a catch. A catch that returns normally recovers the chain, so the next then runs with the returned value. A common mistake is a catch in a service function that only logs the error. It resolves with undefined, so the caller thinks it succeeded. Rethrow, or let it propagate.

Unhandled rejections. Since Node fifteen, the default mode throws: an unhandled rejection becomes an uncaught exception, and the process crashes with exit code one if nothing handles the event. Before that it only printed a warning. A rejection is unhandled if no handler is attached by the time the microtask queue drains.

Floating promises. A promise you neither await nor return nor catch is floating. Its errors become unhandled rejections, and its work outlives the request. If it must not block the response, enqueue it to a durable job queue. If fire and forget is acceptable, make it explicit with void and a catch that logs. Enforce this with the no floating promises lint rule.

To summarize: nextTick, then microtasks, then the next macrotask; cancel with AbortSignal; choose the right combinator; never swallow errors; and never leave promises floating.
passage:
The event loop runs one callback at a time on the call stack. After every callback, Node drains the nextTick queue and then the promise microtask queue completely, before moving to the next macrotask such as a timer or an input and output completion. The browser event loop differs, since it has no nextTick queue and renders between tasks, while Node proceeds through fixed phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll, check and close.

Promises cannot be cancelled, but the underlying operation can be if it accepts an AbortSignal, and cancellation is cooperative. A naive timeout helper that races a promise against a timer leaves the timer running, lets the underlying work continue and produces an anonymous error.

Promise.all rejects on the first failure, allSettled never rejects, race follows the first settlement and any follows the first success. A catch handler that only logs turns a failure into a successful undefined result. Since Node fifteen, unhandled rejections crash the process by default, and floating promises should be awaited, queued or explicitly caught.
prompt: Explain the order in which Node runs process.nextTick callbacks, promise microtasks and timers after a callback finishes. Then describe why a timeout helper built with Promise.race and a timer is flawed.

title: Concurrency Patterns And Event Loop Phases
shadowText:
Today we will talk about concurrency in Node, and the phases of the event loop. Let us start with the basic idea.

Concurrency versus parallelism. Concurrency means many tasks in progress at once, interleaved at await points, on one thread. Parallelism means many tasks executing at the same instant on different cores. Node's main thread gives you concurrency. Worker threads, child processes and the libuv thread pool give you parallelism.

Sequential versus parallel awaits. If operations are independent, start them together and await with Promise all. A common mistake in reviews is using forEach with an async callback. Foreach ignores the returned promises, so nothing waits, and errors are unhandled. Use for of for sequential work, or Promise all with map for parallel work.

Implementing a concurrency limit. Start N worker loops that pull from a shared index. Because JavaScript is single threaded, incrementing the index cannot interleave with another worker. Results keep input order. The flaw an interviewer will probe: on the first error, the returned promise rejects like Promise all, but the other workers keep pulling and processing items. Add a stopped flag checked in the loop, or pass an AbortSignal.

Race conditions on a single thread. Any read, check, write sequence with an await in the middle can interleave with another request. Fixes from weakest to strongest: an in process mutex per key, which only protects one process and is useless with two or more replicas. An atomic conditional write in the database, which is correct across replicas. Select for update inside a transaction, or optimistic concurrency with a version column.

AsyncLocalStorage. It stores a value that follows the async call chain. Every callback, promise continuation and timer created inside run sees the same store. It is used by OpenTelemetry, Pino helpers and most tracing libraries, and it is how you carry a request ID without passing it everywhere. Since Node twenty four it is implemented on V8's async context frame and is cheaper than the old async hooks version. Be careful with libraries that lose context, like some connection pools and event emitters.

Now the phases of the loop. First, timers run setTimeout and setInterval callbacks whose threshold has passed. A delay is a minimum, never a guarantee, and zero is clamped to one millisecond. Second, pending callbacks run some deferred system callbacks. Then idle and prepare, internal. Third, poll retrieves new input and output events and runs their callbacks. Fourth, check runs setImmediate callbacks. Fifth, close callbacks run, such as a socket close event.

How long does the poll phase wait? Libuv computes a timeout before polling. It is zero if there are pending setImmediate callbacks. It is until the nearest timer if timers are scheduled. And it is indefinite if there are active handles, like a listening server, and nothing else to do. The loop exits when there are no active referenced handles or requests.

What keeps a Node process alive? Any referenced handle: a listening server, an open socket including keep alive connections, a setInterval, a child process, a file watcher, or an open database pool. Graceful shutdown is mostly about closing these in order. The trap is calling process exit to fix a hanging shutdown. It kills in flight requests and skips flushing logs.

Does the order of timers and I O depend on the Node version? In edge cases yes. Node eleven moved microtask draining to after every callback, to match browsers. Guaranteed: nextTick before promise microtasks in CommonJS, and setImmediate before setTimeout zero when both are scheduled from an I O callback. Not guaranteed: the order of setTimeout zero and setImmediate from the main module.

To summarize: concurrency is not parallelism, use Promise all with limits, protect read check write sequences in the database, use AsyncLocalStorage for context, and close handles instead of calling process exit.
passage:
Concurrency means many tasks are in progress and interleave at await points on one thread, whereas parallelism means tasks run at the same instant on different cores, which Node achieves with worker threads, child processes and the libuv pool. Independent operations should be started together and awaited with Promise.all, and an async callback inside forEach is a bug because its promises are ignored.

A concurrency limiter uses a fixed number of worker loops pulling from a shared index, but it must stop remaining workers after the first failure. Any read, check, write sequence that contains an await can interleave with other requests, and the robust fixes are atomic database writes, row locks or version checks, because an in process mutex does not protect multiple replicas. AsyncLocalStorage carries request context through the async call chain.

The event loop phases are timers, pending callbacks, poll, check and close. The poll phase waits according to pending immediates, timers and active handles, and a process stays alive while referenced handles remain, so shutdown should close them rather than call process.exit.
prompt: Explain the difference between concurrency and parallelism in Node, then describe how you would prevent a race condition where two requests read, check and write the same record at the same time.

title: Node Event Loop and Async Ordering
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the order in which Node runs asynchronous code. This is one of the most popular Node interview topics, so let us go step by step.

Imagine a file with five things. A setTimeout with zero delay, a setImmediate, a promise callback, a process.nextTick callback, and a normal console log called sync. What is the order? Here is the key point. The sync log always comes first, because the main script runs synchronously. Then Node drains the nextTick queue. Then it drains the promise microtask queue. So the fixed order is sync, nextTick, then promise. After that, the event loop starts. The timeout and the immediate can swap places when they are scheduled from the main module. The timer needs at least one millisecond to pass. If the process started fast, the timer is not due yet, and the immediate runs first. So that part depends on timing.

There is a nice twist. This order is for a CommonJS file. If you run the same code as an ES module, the result is sync, promise, nextTick. The reason is that an ES module is evaluated inside a promise job, so the microtask queue is drained before Node goes back to the nextTick queue. That is a good reason not to depend on nextTick running before promises.

When is setImmediate guaranteed to run before setTimeout with zero? Inside an I/O callback. When you are in the poll phase, the next phase is check, where immediates run. So the immediate runs before the loop wraps around to the timers phase. Inside an I/O callback, the order is always immediate, then timeout.

Now nextTick versus queueMicrotask. Process.nextTick uses Node's own queue, and it runs before promise microtasks. QueueMicrotask and promise then use the V8 microtask queue. QueueMicrotask is portable to browsers, Deno, and Bun, while nextTick is Node only. When is nextTick the right choice? When you want to make an API consistently asynchronous. For example, a class that extends EventEmitter can emit a ready event inside nextTick in the constructor, so that callers can attach their listeners after calling new and still receive the event. Otherwise, prefer queueMicrotask or plain promises. The Node docs themselves recommend that.

Why is setTimeout with zero never really zero? A delay below one millisecond is clamped to one. The callback runs in the timers phase of a later iteration, after the current callback and all its microtasks. And under load, timers drift. A hundred millisecond timer can fire at four hundred if the loop is busy. So never use timers as a clock. Compare timestamps from performance.now. Also, setInterval does not compensate for drift, and it can overlap with slow async work. For periodic async jobs, use a loop that waits, runs the task, and reschedules itself.

What does await actually do? It converts the value to a promise, suspends the async function, and returns control to the caller. When the promise settles, the rest of the function is scheduled as a microtask. The code before the first await runs synchronously. A common mistake is to think that an async function runs in the background. It does not. It runs on the same thread, and gives up the thread only at each await.

What does an async function return, and what does return await change? It always returns a promise. Returning a value resolves it, throwing rejects it, and returning a promise adopts that promise's state. The important difference is inside try and catch. If you return a promise without await, a rejection is not caught by your catch block. If you write return await, it is caught. Return await also keeps the async frame in stack traces, which helps in production. Outside a try block, the performance difference is tiny.

Two more details. Resolving a promise with another promise, or any object with a then method, takes extra microtask ticks. And that has a security side: if you resolve with external data that has a then key, it can hang or hijack the resolution, so validate shapes first. Also, the promise executor runs synchronously. If you log one, create a promise that logs two, resolves, and logs three, then log five, you get one, two, three, five, and then the then callback. Resolve does not stop the executor, and then callbacks are always asynchronous.

Finally, the error first callback style. The last argument is a function called once, with an error on failure, or with null and a result on success. The rules are: call the callback exactly once, always call it asynchronously, to avoid the so called Zalgo problem, and pass errors instead of throwing them. To convert, use the promise versions of fs, timers, and streams, or util.promisify for older libraries. Remember that promisify loses this, so bind the method first.

Here is a short interview summary. Sync code runs first, then nextTick, then promises, then the event loop phases. Timeout and immediate from the main module are timing dependent, but inside an I/O callback the immediate wins. And async functions are not background threads.
passage:
In Node, synchronous code runs first, then the process.nextTick queue drains, then the promise microtask queue drains, and only then does the event loop begin. When a timer and an immediate are scheduled from the main module, their order depends on process timing, but inside an I/O callback the immediate always runs first because the check phase follows the poll phase. In an ES module, promises run before nextTick, because module evaluation itself runs inside a promise job.

The nextTick queue is Node specific and runs before promise microtasks, while queueMicrotask is portable. NextTick is useful for making an API consistently asynchronous, such as emitting an event after a constructor returns. A timer delay of zero is clamped to one millisecond and drifts under load, so timers should never be used as a clock.

An await suspends an async function and schedules the rest as a microtask, but the function still runs on the same thread. Inside a try block, return await is needed so that the catch block sees a rejection. Callback APIs should call the callback exactly once and always asynchronously, and util.promisify converts them to promises.
prompt: Explain the order of sync code, process.nextTick, promises, setTimeout with zero, and setImmediate in Node. Say which parts are deterministic, which are not, and when setImmediate always wins.

title: Async Output Puzzles in Node
shadowText:
Today we will practice reading asynchronous Node code. Interviewers often show a small snippet and ask for the output. We will go through the common puzzles and the reasons behind them.

Puzzle one: nested ticks and promises. A promise then logs p1 and inside it schedules a nextTick that logs tick inside p1. A second then logs p2. Outside, there is a nextTick that logs tick1. The output is tick1, p1, p2, tick inside p1. Why? After the main script, the nextTick queue drains first, so tick1 prints. Then the microtask queue drains completely. P1 runs and queues a tick, and p2's reaction is queued as a microtask. Since p2 is a microtask, it runs before Node goes back to the nextTick queue. Only then does tick inside p1 run. The tempting wrong answer is tick inside p1 before p2, which assumes nextTick can interrupt the microtask queue. It cannot. The check happens between queue drains.

Puzzle two: async and await ordering. A function a logs a1, awaits b, and then logs a2. Function b logs b. Outside, we log start, set a zero timeout, call a, add a promise then, and log end. The output is start, a1, b, end, a2, then, timeout. Function a runs synchronously until its await. B runs synchronously and returns a resolved promise. The continuation of a is queued as a microtask before the then callback, because the await came first. Then end prints, microtasks run in first in, first out order, and finally the timers phase prints timeout.

Puzzle three: a timeout inside an immediate. In an immediate callback, we log immediate, then schedule a timeout and another immediate. The first immediate is always first. The other two can come in either order. The immediate scheduled during the check phase goes to the next iteration's check phase, so the loop passes through timers first. Whether the one millisecond timer is due depends on how long the iteration took. The right answer is: immediate first, and the rest depends on timing, so code must not rely on it.

Puzzle four: does try and catch catch errors from callbacks? If you put a setTimeout that throws inside a try block, nothing is caught, and the process crashes with an uncaught exception. The try block finished long before the callback ran, on a new, empty stack. The same is true for event listeners and for promises that you do not await. The fix is to wrap the inside of the callback, or to use promise APIs with await inside the try.

Puzzle five: does async make code non blocking? Imagine an async route handler that calls the synchronous pbkdf2Sync function. The answer is no. The async keyword only changes the return type. The synchronous call still blocks the event loop for hundreds of milliseconds. Use the asynchronous pbkdf2, which runs on the libuv thread pool, and remember the pool has four threads by default, so fifty concurrent hashes will queue.

Puzzle six: Promise.all with a shared database connection. Code takes one client, begins a transaction, runs many inserts with Promise.all, and commits. Is this parallel? No, and it has a worse bug. One PostgreSQL connection runs one query at a time, so the queries are queued. You get the complexity of Promise.all with sequential execution. When one insert fails, the others still run and fail with a message that the transaction is aborted. It also leaks the connection. If an insert fails, commit is never reached, nothing rolls back, and release is never called. A few failures exhaust the pool, and every request hangs. The fix is a try, catch, finally structure. Begin, run one statement that inserts all rows, for example with unnest and arrays, then commit. In catch, roll back, and in finally, always release the client. For very large batches, use COPY.

Last puzzle: why can a tight loop of awaits starve I O? If a loop awaits an async function that never does real I O, each await of an already resolved promise resumes in a microtask. Microtasks drain before the loop can reach the poll phase. So the loop behaves like a synchronous one. Insert an await of setImmediate from timers promises now and then, to yield to the event loop.

Here is a short interview summary. Microtasks drain completely before Node goes back to nextTick. Await continuations are microtasks. Try and catch does not cover later callbacks. Async does not mean non blocking. And a shared connection means sequential queries, so always release in finally.
passage:
Reading asynchronous output in Node depends on a few rules. After the main script, the nextTick queue drains, then the microtask queue drains completely, including microtasks queued by other microtasks, before Node returns to the nextTick queue. An await continuation is a microtask queued in the order the awaits were reached, and timers run later in the timers phase.

A try and catch block does not catch errors thrown later inside a timer callback, an event listener, or a promise that is not awaited, because the original stack is gone. The async keyword does not make code non blocking, since a synchronous call such as pbkdf2Sync still blocks the event loop, and the libuv thread pool has only four threads by default.

Using Promise.all on a single database connection does not run queries in parallel, and a failure can leak the connection. A correct transaction uses begin, one batched statement, commit, a rollback in the catch block, and release in finally. A loop of awaits that never performs real I O can also starve the event loop, so it should yield with setImmediate.
prompt: Explain why try and catch does not catch an error thrown inside a setTimeout callback, and why wrapping synchronous crypto in an async function does not make it non blocking. Add how you would fix both.

title: Memory Leaks and the V8 Heap
shadowText:
Today we will talk about memory in Node services: what a leak is, how to find one in production, and how the V8 heap and containers interact.

Let us start with the definition. A memory leak in a garbage collected runtime is memory that is still reachable from a GC root, but that the program will never use again. The garbage collector frees unreachable objects. A leak is a reference you forgot to drop. The usual suspects are these. An unbounded module level cache or map, keyed by user input. The fix is an LRU with a maximum size and a time to live. Listeners added per request and never removed. The fix is once, or off when the owner closes. Timers never cleared, like a setInterval per connection. Closures that capture a large scope. Growing arrays used as queues with no consumer. Promises that never settle, which you can fix with timeouts and abort signals. Small Buffer slices that keep a large parent alive. And libraries with unbounded metric labels. Node even warns you about this with MaxListenersExceededWarning. The fix is almost never to raise the limit to zero. Find out why listeners accumulate.

Now Buffers. Buffer bytes live outside the V8 heap, as external memory. Small buffers from allocUnsafe or from a string are carved out of a shared eight kilobyte pool. And subarray, or the old slice, returns a view of the same memory, not a copy. So if you read a two hundred megabyte file and keep a sixty four byte header slice in a cache, the whole file stays in memory. Copy the bytes you need with Buffer.from. Also a security note: allocUnsafe memory is not zeroed and may contain old data, so use it only when you overwrite every byte.

How do you find a leak in production? Step one: confirm it is a leak. Memory should keep rising across many major garbage collections under steady load. A sawtooth that returns to a stable baseline is normal. Step two: decide which memory is growing. Rising heapUsed means JavaScript objects. Rising external or arrayBuffers means Buffers. Only RSS rising points to native memory. Step three: capture heap snapshots, for example with writeHeapSnapshot on a signal, or the heapsnapshot flags, including one that captures before an out of memory crash. Step four: use the three snapshot technique. Take one at baseline, one after N requests, and one after another N. Objects allocated between the first and second that still exist in the third are the suspects. Step five: read the retainer chain to a GC root. The first object you own, like a module level Map, is the bug. Step six: fix it and prove it with a load test.

Be careful in production. A snapshot pauses the process for seconds and roughly doubles memory. Take it on one instance removed from the load balancer, never on all replicas. And snapshots contain user data and secrets, so treat them as sensitive files.

What are the fields of process.memoryUsage? RSS is all the RAM the process uses. HeapTotal is the reserved V8 heap. HeapUsed is the memory used by live and not yet collected objects. External is memory owned by C plus plus objects bound to JavaScript. ArrayBuffers is the bytes of Buffers and array buffers. A common mistake is to alert on heapUsed alone. The container is killed on RSS, and Buffers are not in heapUsed.

How is the V8 heap organised? The young generation has two semi spaces. Allocation is very fast. The scavenger copies live objects, and survivors are promoted to old space. The cost depends on survivors, not garbage, so short lived request objects are cheap. Old space uses mark sweep compact, mostly concurrent. There is also a large object space and a code space.

When does garbage collection hurt latency? When the allocation rate is very high, when the heap is near its limit, so V8 runs major collections back to back and throughput collapses, and when many objects live just long enough to be promoted. You see rising latency and CPU long before the crash.

Finally, heap limits in containers. The heap limit is not the process limit. RSS includes heap, external memory, native memory, and thread stacks. A one gigabyte container with a heap allowed to reach one gigabyte will be killed by the kernel, with exit code one hundred thirty seven and no JavaScript stack trace. So set max-old-space-size explicitly, about seventy to seventy five percent of the container, and monitor RSS. Raising the limit is not a fix for a leak. It only delays the crash.

Here is a short interview summary. A leak is reachable but unused memory. I find it with heap snapshots and retainer chains, I watch RSS and not only heapUsed, and I size the heap below the container limit.
passage:
A memory leak in a garbage collected runtime is memory that remains reachable from a root but will never be used again. Common causes in Node services are unbounded caches, listeners added per request, timers that are never cleared, closures that capture large data, unbounded queues, and Buffer slices that keep a large parent buffer alive. Buffer bytes live outside the V8 heap, so a small view can retain a very large file.

To find a leak in production, confirm that memory rises across many garbage collections, decide whether the heap, external memory, or native memory is growing, and capture heap snapshots from one instance taken out of the load balancer. Comparing three snapshots and following the retainer chain to a root reveals the owner of the leaked objects. Snapshots pause the process and contain sensitive data.

The V8 heap has a young generation collected by a fast scavenger and an old generation collected by mark sweep compact. Garbage collection hurts latency when allocation is heavy or the heap nears its limit. In containers the heap limit differs from the process limit, so max-old-space-size should be set explicitly with headroom, and resident memory should be monitored.
prompt: Walk me through how you would find a memory leak in a production Node service. Include how to tell which memory is growing, how to use heap snapshots safely, and one common cause of leaks.

title: Node Diagnostics and the Thread Pool
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how to diagnose a Node service, and about the libuv thread pool and DNS, which often explain strange slowness.

Let us start with the diagnostics toolbox that is built into Node. Match the tool to the question. If you ask where the CPU time goes, use the cpu-prof flag or the inspector with DevTools. It is a sampling profiler, so the cost is low to moderate. If you ask what is retaining memory, use heap snapshots. They are expensive, because they pause the process and need about twice the memory. If you ask where memory is being allocated, use the heap-prof flag, a sampling heap profiler with a low cost. To check if the event loop is healthy, use monitorEventLoopDelay and eventLoopUtilization from perf hooks, which cost almost nothing. To see what the process looked like when it crashed, use a diagnostic report. To time your own operations, use performance mark and measure. And to watch library calls without patching them, use diagnostics channel. On top of these, there are tools like Clinic.js, zero x flame graphs, and APM agents built on OpenTelemetry.

A diagnostic report is a JSON snapshot of the process: JavaScript and native stacks, heap statistics, libuv handles like open sockets and timers, the environment, and resource usage. Enable it for fatal errors and uncaught exceptions in production, so a crash leaves evidence. Be careful, because reports include environment variables, so restrict access. Diagnostics channel is a publish and subscribe API for instrumentation. Libraries publish named events, such as outbound request creation, and tracing tools subscribe without monkey patching. When nobody subscribes, the cost is nearly zero. The senior signal here is to decide before an incident what you will collect. During an incident, it is a bad time to find out that profiling needs a redeploy.

Now the libuv thread pool. What uses it? Most fs operations, dns.lookup, which means also http requests and net connect by default, the async forms of pbkdf2, scrypt, and random bytes, key pair generation, and async zlib. What does not use it? Network sockets, which use the operating system's readiness notification, timers, dns.resolve, which uses c-ares, and anything synchronous, which blocks the main thread instead.

What happens when the pool is saturated? It has four threads by default and one shared queue. If you start eight password hashes, they fill the pool for hundreds of milliseconds. A small file read that should take one millisecond then waits in the same queue. The production symptom is that event loop delay looks fine, CPU is moderate, but file reads, outbound connection setup, and hashing are all slow at once. That combination points at the pool.

How do you size UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE? The default is four and the maximum is one thousand twenty four. It is read once, when the pool is first used, so set it in the process environment before Node starts. Setting it inside your code only works if it runs before anything touches the pool, and not at all on Windows. More threads help when tasks wait, like slow disks or slow DNS. They help less for CPU bound work beyond the number of cores. A good answer: start from the default, measure queueing, raise it to about the core count for mixed workloads, and move heavy CPU work to worker threads or a separate service.

Finally, dns.lookup versus dns.resolve. Lookup uses the operating system's getaddrinfo on the thread pool, and honours the hosts file and OS caching. Resolve uses c-ares and talks to DNS servers directly on the event loop. Http, net, and fetch use lookup by default. Node has no built in DNS cache, so each new connection does a lookup, and slow DNS can occupy pool threads and slow down fs and crypto. The first fix is keep alive connections. Then use OS level caching or a lookup cache library, respecting the TTL. A version trap: since Node seventeen, lookup keeps the resolver's order, so localhost may resolve to the IPv6 address, and connecting to a server that listens only on IPv4 fails. Listen on both, use 127.0.0.1, or set the default result order to ipv4first. Also, long lived keep alive connections never re resolve DNS, so after a failover they may keep hitting the old IP. Recycle connections with a maximum lifetime.

Here is a short interview summary. I pick the diagnostic tool by the question. I know what uses the thread pool and what does not, I recognise pool saturation by its symptoms, and I treat DNS and keep alive as part of performance.
passage:
Node includes diagnostics for most questions: CPU profiles for time, heap snapshots for retained memory, a sampling heap profiler for allocations, event loop delay and utilization for loop health, diagnostic reports for crashes, and performance marks for timing operations. Garbage collection can be observed through a PerformanceObserver or the trace-gc flag, and diagnostics channel lets tools subscribe to library events without patching. Teams should decide what to collect before an incident.

The libuv thread pool has four threads by default and serves most file system calls, dns.lookup, async crypto functions such as pbkdf2, and async zlib. Sockets, timers, and dns.resolve do not use it. When the pool is saturated, unrelated work queues behind slow tasks, and the symptom is slow file reads, connection setup, and hashing while the event loop delay looks normal. The pool size is set through an environment variable before startup, and heavy CPU work belongs in worker threads.

dns.lookup uses the operating system and the thread pool, while dns.resolve queries DNS directly. Node has no built in DNS cache, so keep alive connections, OS caching, and lookup cache libraries reduce load. Recent versions keep the resolver's address order, which can make localhost resolve to IPv6, and long lived connections need a maximum lifetime so that they notice failovers.
prompt: Explain what runs on the libuv thread pool and what happens when it is saturated. Describe the symptoms you would see in production and how you would size and work around the pool.

title: Common Node Memory and Runtime Traps
shadowText:
Today we will go through several tricky statements about Node memory and runtime behaviour. Each one sounds reasonable, but each one hides a trap. Interviewers love these.

Trap one: heapUsed is eighty megabytes, so the service uses eighty megabytes. This is wrong. The resident set size, or RSS, can be several times larger. Buffers, which are external memory, native allocations, JIT code, thread stacks, and allocator fragmentation are all outside heapUsed. A service that streams files can show an eighty megabyte heap and nine hundred megabytes of RSS. Containers are killed based on RSS, so that is the number to alert on.

Trap two: setting process.env.UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE to sixteen in the middle of server.js. Does it cap the pool at sixteen threads? Usually not. The pool is created on first use. If the imports above already did file system work, the pool exists with four threads, and the variable is ignored. On Windows, it is ignored regardless. Set it in the process environment before Node starts.

Trap three: a cache built with a WeakMap, keyed by a user id string. Is it leak proof? Actually it throws. WeakMap keys must be objects, or non registered symbols, so setting a string key is a TypeError. Even with object keys, a WeakMap is not a cache. Entries disappear when the key object is collected, not by a time limit or size limit, and you cannot iterate or bound it. Use an LRU cache for caching. Use a WeakMap for metadata attached to objects you do not own.

Trap four: just call global.gc after each request to keep memory low. This is a bad idea. Global gc exists only with the expose-gc flag. Forcing a full collection on every request pauses the main thread each time, destroys throughput, and does not fix a leak, because leaked objects are still reachable. V8's heuristics are better than manual collection in production. The expose-gc flag belongs in tests that assert memory returns to a baseline.

Trap five: why is the second loop much slower? We create a million objects with an id and a price. The first loop sums the prices and is fast. Then we add a discount property to every second object, and the second loop is slower. The reason is hidden classes. Adding discount to only some objects gives the array two shapes, so the access to price becomes polymorphic. The fix is to initialise discount to zero for every object at creation. The effect is real but small, and the interview point is to understand why, not to hand tune every loop.

Trap six: our pods keep restarting with exit code one hundred thirty seven, but there is no error in the logs. Exit code 137 is 128 plus 9, which means SIGKILL. The kernel out of memory killer, or the orchestrator, killed the process for exceeding its memory limit. JavaScript never had a chance to log anything. Check the container memory metrics, comparing RSS to the limit, look at orchestrator events for OOMKilled, and check whether max-old-space-size leaves headroom for non heap memory. A real V8 heap out of memory error instead prints a fatal error message and exits with a different code.

Trap seven: the same code on two different Node versions behaves differently in memory or latency. Why? Different V8 versions change the JIT tiers, garbage collection heuristics, and default heap sizing. New libuv versions change I O internals, and updates to undici change how fetch handles connections. That is why runtime upgrades should go through load tests, and why a benchmark result should always state the Node version.

Here is a short interview summary. Alert on RSS, not only on heap. Set the thread pool size before startup. A WeakMap is not a cache. Do not force garbage collection in production. Keep object shapes consistent in hot paths. Exit code one thirty seven means the process was killed from outside, usually for memory. And always load test a runtime upgrade.
passage:
Several common beliefs about Node are traps. HeapUsed is not the memory footprint of a service, because Buffers, native allocations, JIT code, and thread stacks sit outside it, and containers are killed on resident set size. Setting UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE inside the code usually has no effect, because the pool is created on first use, and on Windows it is ignored, so it must be set in the environment before startup.

A WeakMap cannot take string keys, and it is not a cache, since entries vanish only when the key object is collected, so an LRU cache should be used instead. Forcing garbage collection after each request harms throughput and does not fix leaks.

Adding a property to only some objects creates several hidden classes and makes property access polymorphic, so fields should be initialised at creation. Exit code one hundred thirty seven means the process was killed by SIGKILL, usually by the out of memory killer, and runtime upgrades should be load tested because V8 and libuv behaviour changes between versions.
prompt: A pod keeps restarting with exit code 137 and no error in the logs, while heapUsed looks small. Explain what is happening, why heapUsed is misleading, and how you would investigate and fix it.

title: V8, Modules and Node Internals
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how V8 runs your code, how Node is layered, and how modules work in Node. These are classic senior level questions.

Let us start with how V8 turns JavaScript into machine code. V8 starts by interpreting bytecode. It watches which functions are hot and what types they see, and then it compiles hot code with faster, more speculative compilers. If a speculation turns out wrong, it throws the optimised code away and falls back. This is called deoptimisation. There are four tiers in current V8. Ignition parses to bytecode, interprets it, and collects type feedback. It starts instantly but is the slowest to run. Sparkplug is a baseline compiler that goes from bytecode straight to machine code without optimisation. Maglev is a mid tier optimising compiler that uses type feedback. TurboFan is the top tier, with inlining and escape analysis. It compiles slowly but produces the fastest code. This explains why benchmarks need warm up, and why the first requests after a deploy are slower.

What are hidden classes and inline caches? V8 gives every object a hidden class, also called a shape, that describes its property layout. Objects created the same way share a shape. So a property access that always sees one shape can be cached as a fixed offset. This is an inline cache. A site that sees two to four shapes is polymorphic and slower. More than that is megamorphic, and much slower. You can defeat this by creating the same properties in a different order, adding properties later, or deleting properties, which can push the object into slow dictionary mode. The practical rules: initialise all fields in the constructor, in the same order. Do not delete properties on hot objects. Keep hot functions monomorphic. And use a Map for dynamic keys. But do not apply these rules everywhere. In most services, the time goes to I O, serialisation, and database calls. Prove it with a profile first.

What is deoptimisation, and how would you notice it? Optimised code is built on assumptions, like x is always a small integer. When a string arrives, or an array gets a hole, V8 discards the optimised code. Repeated cycles of optimising and deoptimising show up as a function that is unexpectedly expensive in a CPU profile. In production you rarely trace deopts. You take a CPU profile, find the hot function, and reproduce it locally. Then you look for type instability, like ids that are sometimes numbers and sometimes strings, or sparse arrays. A note: saying that try and catch is slow is an outdated answer for modern TurboFan.

Now draw the line between V8, Node, libuv, and the operating system. V8 runs JavaScript and manages its heap and garbage collection, and it also owns the promise microtask queue. Libuv runs the event loop, timers, and asynchronous I O, and it provides the thread pool. Node glues them together, provides the process.nextTick queue, and provides the APIs you import, like fs, http, and Buffer. The operating system does the real reading, writing, networking, and thread scheduling. A common mistake is to say V8 has an event loop. It does not. The embedder, like Node, Deno, or Chrome, brings its own loop. That is why ordering puzzles do not port between runtimes.

Now CommonJS versus ES modules. CommonJS loads synchronously, and module.exports is a value copy at require time. ES modules are parsed and linked before any code runs, have live bindings, static analysis that allows tree shaking, and top level await. In CommonJS you have dirname and filename, while ESM uses import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename. In ESM you need full file paths with extensions. Node decides by the extension, or by the type field in package.json. For interop, ESM can import CommonJS. CommonJS can require an ES module since Node 22.12, as long as the module graph has no top level await. A common mistake is to think that ESM is just new syntax. Imports are hoisted, so conditional imports need await import.

How does require resolve and cache? It checks core modules first, then relative paths with extensions and index files, then walks up node_modules folders, honouring the exports field. It wraps the file in a function, runs it once, and stores module.exports in the cache by the resolved absolute path. That is why modules behave like singletons, and why two copies of a package are two different singletons.

Here is a short interview summary. V8 interprets, then optimises hot code, and deoptimises when assumptions fail. Stable shapes keep it fast. V8, libuv, Node, and the OS each have clear jobs. And ESM and CommonJS differ in loading, bindings, and caching.
passage:
V8 starts by interpreting bytecode with Ignition, collects type feedback, and compiles hot code through Sparkplug, Maglev, and TurboFan. If an assumption fails, for example a value that was always an integer becomes a string, V8 deoptimises and falls back. Warm up therefore matters for benchmarks. Hidden classes describe object shapes, and inline caches use them for fast property access, so objects should be initialised with the same properties in the same order and hot code should avoid delete and late additions.

The layers are clearly separated. V8 runs JavaScript, the heap, and promise microtasks. Libuv provides the event loop, timers, asynchronous I O, and the thread pool. Node supplies the nextTick queue and its core APIs, and the operating system performs the real I O and thread scheduling. V8 itself has no event loop.

CommonJS loads synchronously and exports a value copy, while ES modules are linked before execution, have live bindings, and support tree shaking and top level await. The require function resolves a path, runs the module once, and caches it by absolute path, so modules act as singletons. Circular dependencies return partially filled exports in CommonJS and can throw in ESM, so shared code should be extracted.
prompt: Explain how V8 compiles JavaScript through its tiers and what hidden classes and deoptimisation are. Then explain how V8, libuv, Node, and the operating system divide responsibility.

title: Node Packages, Exports and Monorepos
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how Node packages and modules behave in real projects: load order, package exports, monorepos, and dependency health.

Let us start with a classic trap. A config file reads the PORT environment variable at import time, and the server file imports the config first and then imports dotenv. The port is always three thousand locally. Why? ES modules evaluate imports in order, and imports are hoisted. So the config module ran before dotenv loaded the file. The fix is to load the environment first, for example with node and the env-file flag, or to import dotenv before the config module.

Next, JSON imports. In ES modules, importing a JSON file needs an import attribute that says the type is json. In CommonJS, require of a JSON file just works, and the result is cached. So if you change the imported object, the change is visible to every importer.

Now some output questions. First, module initialisation order. A file a logs a, then imports b, and then logs a end. File b logs b. In ESM the output is b, a, a end. Imports are linked and evaluated before the body of the importing module, no matter where the import line is. In CommonJS with require, the order would be a, b, a end. Second, cache and mutation. A counter module exports an object with n equal to zero. Two requires give you the same cached object, so after incrementing through one, the other shows one, and they are strictly equal. Third, an ES module cycle with a function declaration. Function declarations are hoisted and initialised during linking, so a function from the module that has not finished evaluating can still be called. If it was an arrow function in a const, calling it during evaluation would throw a ReferenceError. The lesson is to ask when each binding is read.

How would you structure a Node monorepo? Use workspaces from npm, pnpm, or Yarn to link local packages. A strict tool like pnpm catches undeclared dependencies. Use a task runner such as Turborepo or Nx to cache builds and tests and run only what changed. Set boundaries: apps depend on packages, packages never depend on apps, and enforce this with lint rules. Version internal packages with the workspace protocol, and use Changesets for publishable ones. Share one base TypeScript config with project references. The trade off to name: a monorepo makes atomic changes and shared tooling easy, but it needs build caching and ownership rules, or CI time and coupling will grow without limit.

How do you keep dependencies healthy and safe? Commit the lockfile, use npm ci in CI, and read lockfile diffs in reviews. Use Renovate or Dependabot, grouped and scheduled, with CI as the gate. Run npm audit or an OSV scanner in CI, and triage the results instead of blindly using force. Use fewer dependencies. Check maintenance, install scripts, and the transitive count, and ask if a ten line function would do. Use ignore-scripts where possible, and provenance and signature checks for supply chain trust.

Does tree shaking matter on the server? Less than in browsers, because there is no download cost. It matters for serverless cold starts and container size, where bundling with esbuild or Rollup can cut startup time. The static imports in ESM make it possible, and sideEffects false in package.json tells bundlers that unused modules can be dropped.

What does the exports field do? It is the only public surface of a package. An import of an internal path fails with a package path not exported error, so maintainers can refactor internals safely. Conditions are matched in object order, so put types first, then import and require, then default. The main field is only a fallback, and module is a bundler convention that Node ignores.

What is the dual package hazard? A package that ships both CommonJS and ESM builds can be loaded twice in one app, once through require and once through import. You get two module states, two caches, and instanceof checks that fail across them. Mitigations: ship ESM only, which is practical now that require of ESM works on supported Node lines. Or keep state in a single CommonJS core, with a thin ESM wrapper. And test both entry points.

Finally, dynamic import and top level await. Dynamic import lets you lazy load a heavy library only when needed. Top level await is fine for startup config, but here is the trap: it blocks evaluation of every module that imports that module. A slow network call at the top of a shared module delays the whole startup, and a hanging one hangs it. It also prevents require of that module graph.

Here is a short interview summary. ESM imports are hoisted, so load the environment first. The exports field controls the public surface. I watch for the dual package hazard, I keep dependencies few and audited, and I use top level await carefully.
passage:
In ES modules, imports are hoisted and evaluated before the body of the importing module, so a config module that reads an environment variable at import time runs before a dotenv import placed after it. The environment should be loaded first, for example with the env-file flag. ES modules need an import attribute for JSON, while CommonJS caches required JSON, so mutations are shared.

A healthy monorepo uses workspaces, a task runner with caching, enforced dependency boundaries, and consistent versioning, and it must manage build caching and ownership to avoid growing CI time. Dependencies are kept safe through committed lockfiles, npm ci, automated updates gated by CI, audits, and a preference for fewer packages.

The exports field defines a package's only public surface, with conditions such as types, import, and require matched in order. Shipping both CommonJS and ESM builds risks loading two copies of a package, which splits state and breaks instanceof checks. Top level await blocks every module that imports the file, so slow startup work should not be placed in shared modules.
prompt: Explain the dual package hazard and what the exports field does in package.json. Then describe how you would keep the dependencies of a large Node monorepo healthy and safe.

title: Module Traps and Stream Details
shadowText:
Today we will go through a set of trap questions about Node modules, Buffers, and streams. Each one is short, but each one teaches a real lesson.

Trap one: why is the logger configured twice? You have one version of a logger package at the top level, and another version nested inside the HTTP package. Two versions resolve to two paths, so two module instances with separate state. You can see the duplication with npm ls. The fix is to align the version ranges, use a peer dependency, or use overrides.

Trap two: the error that says dirname is not defined in ES module scope. ES modules have no module wrapper, so no dirname. Use import.meta.dirname in Node 20.11 and later. On older versions, use path dirname of fileURLToPath of import.meta.url.

Trap three: live bindings. A module exports a let count and a function inc that increases it. The main module imports both, calls inc twice, and logs count. In ESM, the output is two, because exports are live bindings. In CommonJS, destructuring would copy the value at require time and print zero. But you cannot assign to count from the main module, because imported bindings are read only.

Trap four: I will clear require.cache to hot reload config. This reloads that one module, but every module that already holds a reference to the old exports keeps it. Listeners and timers created by the old instance keep running. The result is leaks and split brain state. Reload configuration through an explicit API, or restart the process.

Now Buffers and encoding. A Buffer is a fixed length sequence of bytes, a Uint8Array subclass, used for binary data like file contents and network packets. Strings are text, and Buffers are bytes. Converting needs an encoding, utf8 by default, but also base64, hex, and others. For example, the euro sign has a string length of one, but three bytes. If you cut those bytes in the middle and decode them, you get the replacement character. This leads to the streaming trap. If you decode each chunk separately, multi byte characters that straddle a chunk boundary are broken. Use setEncoding on the stream, a StringDecoder, or TextDecoder with the stream option, which carry partial bytes to the next chunk. Other traps: body size limits must count bytes, not string length. Comparing secrets needs timingSafeEqual on equal length Buffers. And allocUnsafe memory is not zeroed.

Now partial reads. A file handle read may return fewer bytes than you requested, at the end of a file, on pipes, or on network file systems. If you process the whole buffer, you process garbage after the bytes read. Use subarray from zero to bytesRead, and loop until you have what you need.

Does destroy flush buffered writes? No. Destroy discards pending data. End flushes and then finishes. Use end for normal completion and destroy with an error for aborts.

What about cancelling a pipe chain when the client disconnects? With source pipe to response, when the client disconnects, the response is destroyed, but the source keeps reading, and the file is not closed. The fix is pipeline, which destroys every stream in the chain when any one closes early.

Three output questions. First, the event order for a small file stream: open, data, end, close. The end event means no more data, and close means the file descriptor was released. Second, a Writable with a high water mark of four, where each write takes ten milliseconds. Three writes of two bytes each return true, false, false. After the first, two bytes are buffered, below four. The second reaches four, the threshold, so write returns false, and later writes also return false until drain. Third, memory behaviour. If you listen to the data event of a ten gigabyte file and write each chunk to a slow socket, ignoring the return value, memory grows toward the file size. With pipeline, memory stays near the high water mark of each stream.

Here is a short interview summary. Two versions of a package mean two instances. ESM has live bindings and no dirname. Decode streamed text with a decoder. Read results may be partial. End flushes, destroy does not. And use pipeline so that errors and disconnects clean everything up.
passage:
Two versions of the same package resolve to two paths and therefore two module instances with separate state, which explains a logger configured twice. ES modules have no dirname, so import.meta.dirname is used, and their exports are live bindings that importers see change, while a CommonJS destructuring copies the value. Clearing the require cache to hot reload is unsafe because old references and timers survive.

A Buffer is a sequence of bytes, and text conversion needs an encoding. Multi byte characters can be split across chunks, so streamed text must be decoded with setEncoding, a StringDecoder, or TextDecoder in stream mode. Size limits must count bytes. A file read may return fewer bytes than requested, so only the bytes actually read should be used.

On streams, end flushes pending data while destroy discards it. A piped chain does not clean up the source when a client disconnects, whereas pipeline destroys every stream when one fails or closes. A write returns false when the buffer reaches the high water mark, and ignoring this signal lets memory grow toward the size of the file.
prompt: Explain why ES module imports are live bindings while CommonJS requires copy values, and why decoding streamed text chunk by chunk can corrupt multi byte characters. Describe the correct fix for each.

title: Streams, Backpressure and Large Files
shadowText:
Today we will talk about streams in Node: the four types, backpressure, pipeline, and how to process very large files safely.

Let us start with the four stream types. A Readable is a source, like a file read stream, an incoming HTTP request on the server, or standard input. A Writable is a sink, like a file write stream, an HTTP response, or standard output. A Duplex is both, independently, like a TCP socket. A Transform is a duplex where the output is computed from the input, like gzip, a hash, or a CSV parser. Why use streams? They keep memory constant regardless of data size, data starts flowing before it is all available, which lowers time to first byte, and they compose: read, parse, transform, compress, upload.

Now backpressure. A write call returns false when the internal buffer of the writable reaches the high water mark. A well behaved producer stops writing and waits for the drain event. If you ignore the return value, the buffer grows without limit. A fast disk read, piped by hand into a slow client, can buffer gigabytes in memory. The manual correct version pauses the readable when write returns false, and resumes it on drain. A common mistake is to think that high water mark is a hard limit. It is a threshold. Write still accepts the chunk and returns false, and only the cooperation of the producer keeps memory bounded.

Pipe versus pipeline. Both handle backpressure. But with pipe, an error in the source does not close the destination, cleanup is manual, and it leaks file descriptors on error. Pipeline forwards errors, destroys every stream when any one fails, returns a promise in the stream promises module, accepts async generators as stages, and supports cancellation through a signal option. Use the finished function when you only need to know that a single stream is done or failed.

Async iteration. Readable streams are async iterables, and pipeline accepts async generator functions as transform stages. Backpressure is automatic, because the consumer pulls. In object mode, a stream carries JavaScript values instead of bytes, and high water mark counts objects, with a default of sixteen, instead of bytes. A transform from bytes to rows usually has readable object mode true and writable object mode false. Tuning: a larger high water mark means fewer, larger chunks and more throughput, but the memory is multiplied by the number of concurrent streams. A thousand downloads with one megabyte buffers is a gigabyte before anything else.

File descriptor leaks. Every open file or socket uses a descriptor, and the process limit can run out, giving an EMFILE error, too many open files. If you open a file handle and a parse step throws, the handle is never closed. Use try and finally to close it. Other causes: streams that are never consumed or destroyed, pipe chains that fail without cleanup, and unbounded concurrency, such as Promise.all over fifty thousand files. Limit concurrency and prefer pipeline.

Safe path handling. To prevent path traversal, resolve the user path against a root and check that the result stays inside the root. A join of the root with dot dot segments can escape. A starts with check without the separator lets a sibling folder like uploads-old through. Symlinks inside the root can still point outside, so resolve with realpath and check again. Better, never use user input as a path. Store files under generated ids and keep the original name as metadata. Use restrictive file modes, run as a non root user, and consider Node's permission model. For temp files, use mkdtemp, clean up in finally, and also on startup.

Now the big question: process a twenty gigabyte CSV and load valid rows into PostgreSQL without running out of memory. Requirements: constant memory, backpressure from the database, bad rows reported but not fatal, resumable or idempotent, and visible progress. The design is a pipeline. Read stream, then a CSV parser, then an async generator that validates rows and groups them into batches of about a thousand, then a stage that inserts each batch. Each stage pulls only when the next is ready, so a slow database slows the file read instead of filling memory. Batching reduces round trips. Using ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on a natural key makes a re run after a crash safe. A faster option is COPY from standard input into a staging table, followed by one insert select with validation in SQL. And run it in a job worker, not in an API process, so a twenty minute import cannot starve request handling.

Here is a short interview summary. Streams give constant memory. I respect backpressure, I use pipeline for cleanup, I limit concurrency to avoid descriptor leaks, I never trust user paths, and I build big imports as batched pipelines in a worker.
passage:
Node has four stream types: readable sources, writable sinks, duplex streams that do both, and transforms that compute output from input. Streams keep memory constant, start data flowing early, and compose into pipelines. A write returns false when the buffer reaches the high water mark, and a producer should then wait for the drain event. The high water mark is a threshold, not a hard limit, so ignoring it lets memory grow.

Pipeline is preferred to pipe because it forwards errors, destroys every stream on failure, returns a promise, supports async generators, and allows cancellation. Descriptor leaks come from handles that are not closed on error and from unbounded concurrency, and path traversal is prevented by resolving paths against a root, checking containment, handling symlinks, and avoiding user supplied paths.

A twenty gigabyte CSV import can be built as a pipeline of file reader, parser, validating and batching generator, and database writer, so a slow database slows the read. Idempotent inserts make restarts safe, COPY into a staging table is faster, and the job should run in a worker process. Uploads and downloads should also stream with byte limits and cleanup.
prompt: Design a way to import a twenty gigabyte CSV file into PostgreSQL in Node without running out of memory. Explain streams, backpressure, batching, error handling, and where the job should run.

title: REST API Design and Handler Traps
shadowText:
Today we will talk about what makes a good REST API in production, and about several traps in Node request handlers and streams.

Let us start with four stream traps. Trap one: someone pipes a read stream into gzip, then into a write stream, and adds one error handler at the end. Does this handle errors? Only for the last stream. A missing input file emits an unhandled error on the read stream, which crashes the process, and the gzip and write streams stay open. Use pipeline. Trap two: a request handler collects data chunks into an array and concatenates them at the end. Why does memory still grow with streams? Because it buffers the whole body. It is a streaming API with buffering behaviour. Add a size limit, or process the body incrementally. Trap three: readFileSync in a handler that serves a five kilobyte template. It blocks the event loop on every request, and disk latency under load can reach milliseconds. Read it once at startup and keep it in memory, or use the async API. Trap four: we set the high water mark to one gigabyte so that the stream never pauses. That disables backpressure and promises up to one gigabyte of memory per stream. With concurrency, that is an out of memory crash waiting to happen.

Now, what makes a good REST API in production? First, resources and methods. Use nouns, the correct verbs, and correct status codes. For example, 201 with a Location header after creation, 204 for no content, 400 versus 422 for bad input, 401 versus 403 for authentication versus permission, 404, 409 for conflicts, and 429 with a Retry-After header. Second, validation at the edge. Use schemas, such as Zod or Ajv, for params, query, and body. Reject unknown fields on writes, and use one consistent error format, such as problem details from RFC 9457. Third, pagination. Use cursor, or keyset, pagination for large or changing data. Offset pagination gets slow and can skip or duplicate rows as data changes. Fourth, versioning. Prefer additive changes. Create a new version only for breaking changes, with a deprecation timeline using Deprecation and Sunset headers. Fifth, idempotency. PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition. Make POST safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key header. And add rate limits, authentication, request ids, and documentation, with OpenAPI generated from the same schemas you validate with. A common mistake is to return status 200 with an error body. Clients, proxies, retries, and monitoring all rely on status codes.

Now four trap questions about HTTP handlers. First: a raw HTTP server handler calls JSON.parse on an undefined variable. A ReferenceError thrown synchronously inside the handler is an uncaught exception. The whole process crashes, and every in flight request fails. Frameworks wrap handlers in try and catch. With the raw http module, you must do it yourself. Second: our body parser protects us from big uploads. Express JSON has a default limit of one hundred kilobytes, but raw parsers, custom parsers, and multipart libraries have their own limits, and a proxy may have buffered the whole body already. Check every layer: the proxy body size limit, the parser limit, the multipart file size, and streaming byte counters. Third: why did moving the API to HTTP/2 between the load balancer and Node not reduce the p99 latency? Because the p99 was dominated by handler time, meaning database and CPU, not connection setup. Protocol upgrades fix only transport problems. Measure where time is spent first. Fourth: does res.end mean the client received the response? No. It means Node handed the data to the socket. The kernel and network may still be sending, and the client may disconnect. The finish event fires when Node has finished writing, but HTTP has no end to end delivery acknowledgement.

Three behaviour questions. First, a handler that calls res.json twice. The client receives the first object. The second call throws an ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT error. Second, a client that disconnects after a hundred milliseconds from a handler that sleeps for a second. After a second, the handler logs that the response is not writable, and the send does nothing useful. But the handler still did its full second of work, which is why cancellation on disconnect matters. Third, three requests that arrive at the same moment, and a module level counter of in flight requests. The responses contain the values one, two, and three, because all three handlers increment before any await finishes. The point is that module level state is shared by all concurrent requests in the process.

Here is a short interview summary. Use pipeline for stream errors. Never buffer unbounded bodies. Use correct status codes, schema validation, cursor pagination, and idempotency keys. And remember that a thrown error in a raw handler can crash the process, and that shared state is shared across concurrent requests.
passage:
Several stream and handler mistakes are common in Node. Attaching an error handler only to the last stream of a pipe chain leaves earlier errors unhandled, so pipeline should be used. Collecting a request body into an array buffers it entirely, a synchronous file read inside a handler blocks the event loop, and a huge high water mark disables backpressure and risks running out of memory.

A good production REST API uses nouns and correct methods, accurate status codes such as 201, 204, 409, and 429, schema validation at the edge, a consistent error format, cursor pagination, additive versioning with a deprecation timeline, and idempotency keys for retried POST requests. Returning status 200 with an error body defeats clients, proxies, and monitoring.

With the raw http module, a synchronous exception in a handler crashes the process. Body limits must be checked at every layer, protocol upgrades do not fix slow handlers, and res.end only means the data was handed to the socket. Module level state is shared by all concurrent requests, and responding twice causes a headers already sent error.
prompt: Describe what makes a good REST API in production. Cover status codes, validation, cursor pagination, versioning, and idempotency, and explain why returning 200 with an error body is a mistake.

title: Proxies, CORS and the HTTP Request Path
shadowText:
Today we will talk about running Node behind a reverse proxy, CORS, compression, streaming responses, and the full life of an HTTPS request.

Let us start with what changes behind a reverse proxy. The remote address of the socket is now the proxy's IP. The real client IP is in the X-Forwarded-For header, but anyone can forge that header, unless you trust only headers added by your own proxies. In Express, set trust proxy to the number of hops, never to true blindly. Rate limiting by a spoofable IP is a bypass. The X-Forwarded-Proto header tells you the original scheme, which you need for redirects and secure cookies. Also remember that the proxy may buffer request and response bodies, add its own timeouts and body limits, and terminate TLS.

CORS misconceptions. CORS is enforced by browsers, not by servers. It does not protect your API from curl, scripts, or other servers. It only controls which web origins' JavaScript may read responses. It is not a CSRF defence on its own, because simple requests, like form posts, are sent without a preflight, and the browser just hides the response. The wildcard origin cannot be combined with credentials. And reflecting the request's Origin header back with Allow-Credentials true lets any site read authenticated responses. Use an explicit allow list. Preflight requests with the OPTIONS method happen for non simple methods, headers, or content types, and you can cache them with Access-Control-Max-Age.

Compression trade offs. Gzip or Brotli cut JSON and HTML size by seventy to ninety percent, but cost CPU. The production answer is to compress at the reverse proxy or the CDN, not in Node. Skip tiny responses, under about one kilobyte, and already compressed formats like images, video, and zip. Precompress static assets at build time. A security note: compressing secrets next to attacker controlled input over TLS enables BREACH style attacks, so avoid reflecting user input in pages that contain tokens.

Streaming responses and server sent events. Stream large results instead of building one huge JSON string. Use NDJSON, one JSON object per line, or a database cursor piped through a transform, with backpressure through pipeline. Server sent events use the text event stream content type. They are a simple one way push channel over plain HTTP, they reconnect automatically in browsers, and they are good for notifications and progress. WebSockets are for two way, high frequency messaging.

Now walk through one HTTPS request to a Node service behind a load balancer. The client does a DNS lookup. It does a TCP handshake with the load balancer. Then a TLS handshake, which usually terminates at the load balancer. The client sends the HTTP request. The load balancer forwards it on a new or reused connection to Node.
