A pricing engine models each rule as a strategy that returns explainable adjustments, makes order of application explicit, uses integer money, and stores marketer rules as data. Permission systems combine roles and policies and keep authorisation at the application boundary.

Interview rounds test different skills. Intermediate rounds test precise vocabulary and predictions, advanced rounds test contracts and patterns such as LSP, and senior rounds test requirement discovery, choosing the right variation point, and naming trade offs. Coding rounds reward one working vertical slice, review rounds reward prioritisation, and refactoring rounds reward characterisation tests and small steps.
prompt: Design an extensible payment integration that supports several providers. Describe the provider port, adapters, registry, idempotency, and how webhooks update order status, and mention one trade off.

title: OOP Interview Rounds and Revision Plan
shadowText:
Today we will talk about two more interview rounds for object oriented design, and a practical plan for revision before an interview.

Let us start with the low level design round. A typical prompt is to design a library management system. The interviewer evaluates several things. First is entity identification. A good tell is whether you separate a Book from a BookCopy, since one title has many physical copies. Second is where you place responsibilities. Third is relationships with multiplicities. Fourth is walking one use case as a sequence. Fifth is concurrency on checkout, because two people may borrow the last copy at the same time. And sixth is extensibility, such as fines and reservations.

The architecture discussion round might say: our monolith's services folder has two hundred files and every change breaks something. How would you restructure it? Strong answer points: find bounded contexts from change history and team ownership. Enforce module boundaries with dependency rules before splitting deployable units. Move business rules into domain objects. Introduce ports at the I O boundaries. Communicate across modules through interfaces or events. Use a strangler approach, replacing parts step by step. Measure with change coupling and lead time. And mention that microservices are not the first step.

If you only have a weekend, focus on the high priority concepts. One: encapsulation as invariant protection, not getters and setters. Two: composition versus inheritance, with a concrete example. Three: the Liskov principle as contracts, and the interface segregation and dependency inversion principles at boundaries. Four: Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Adapter, Factory, and State, which you should be able to code from memory. Five: what TypeScript enforces versus JavaScript, such as private versus hash private, interfaces being erased, and structural typing. Six: this binding and construction order. Seven: testing with fakes, and mocks versus stubs. Eight: one low level design problem end to end, like a parking lot or a library.

Here are last minute revision notes. The pillars in one line each: encapsulation protects invariants, abstraction hides decisions, inheritance shares a contract, and polymorphism lets callers ignore the implementation. SOLID in one line each: one actor per module, extend at predicted variation points, subtypes keep contracts, clients get role sized interfaces, and policy owns the abstractions. Pattern intent words: Adapter converts, Decorator adds, Proxy controls, Facade simplifies, Strategy swaps an algorithm, State swaps behaviour by state, Observer notifies, and Command turns a request into an object. TypeScript truths: types are erased, hash private is real, arrow function fields are per instance, classes are strict mode, and method parameters are bivariant. And the senior reflex: for every pattern you propose, say when you would not use it.

A six week preparation roadmap works well. Week one: explain each pillar aloud in sixty seconds, and solve the output questions without notes. Week two: refactor one real file from your work using SOLID, and write a short before and after note. Week three: implement twelve Gang of Four patterns from memory in TypeScript, with one test each. Week four: build a small hexagonal service with one use case, one port, two adapters, and contract tests. Week five: do two timed rounds of output and debugging questions, and review every miss. Week six: do three timed low level design challenges and two mock interviews with a peer.

Finally, a readiness checklist. Can you explain each pillar with a non textbook example and a trade off? Can you state each SOLID principle and show a violation and its fix? Can you predict outputs involving this, construction order, statics, and copying? Can you say which TypeScript and JavaScript features are compile time only and which are runtime? Can you implement the main patterns from memory? Can you design one low level problem within forty five minutes, including tests? Can you explain mocks, stubs, and fakes and write a contract test? Can you describe clean and hexagonal architecture and when it is overkill? And for every design choice, can you name an alternative and say why you did not pick it?

Here is a short interview summary. In a design round, I identify the right entities, place responsibilities, handle concurrency and extension, and always name trade offs. I prepare with a plan, practice aloud, and use the checklist.
passage:
In a low level design round such as a library management system, interviewers look for correct entity identification, such as separating a book from its physical copies, sensible placement of responsibilities, relationships with multiplicities, one use case walked through as a sequence, concurrency on checkout, and extensibility for features like fines and reservations.

An architecture round about a large monolith expects answers based on bounded contexts found from change history and team ownership, enforced module boundaries before splitting deployments, business rules moved into domain objects, ports at I O boundaries, and a gradual strangler migration. Microservices are not the first step.

With limited time, candidates should prioritise encapsulation as invariant protection, composition versus inheritance, the Liskov principle, the main design patterns, the difference between compile time and runtime guarantees in TypeScript, this binding, testing with fakes, and one complete design problem. A staged six week plan and a final checklist help ensure readiness, and every pattern proposed should come with a case where it would not be used.
prompt: You are asked to design a library management system in a low level design round. Describe the entities, their responsibilities and relationships, one use case, and how you would handle concurrent checkouts.

title: Objects, Identity and Lifecycle
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how objects work in JavaScript and TypeScript: what new does, identity versus equality, copying, immutability, initialization order, and relationships between objects.

Let us start with what new actually does. First, a new empty object is created, and its prototype is the class prototype. Second, for a base class, the class fields are defined on it, and then the constructor body runs with this bound to the object. Third, for a derived class, this does not exist until super returns, and the fields are defined right after that. Fourth, the object is returned, unless the constructor explicitly returns another object. So the instance owns its name and role fields. The greet method is shared through the prototype. And a static counter lives on the class, not on the instance, so reading count on the instance gives undefined.

Instance versus static members. Instance members live on each object for fields, or on the prototype for methods, and this refers to the instance. Static members live on the class itself, and this refers to the class it was called on. Subclasses inherit statics in JavaScript, but in Java static methods are hidden, not overridden. Statics are good for factories, constants, and pure helpers. The trap: a static mutable field is global state. It leaks across tests and requests.

Identity versus equality. Identity means the same object in memory. In JavaScript, use triple equals or Object.is. Equality means the same value by a domain rule. JavaScript has no built in structural equality, so you write an equals method. In Java, double equals is identity, equals is value equality, and overriding equals requires overriding hashCode. In C sharp, records get value equality generated. Two Money objects with the same amount and currency are different objects but equal values. In DDD terms, entities are equal by identity, and value objects by their attributes.

Shallow versus deep copy. Spread and Object.assign are shallow, give a plain object without the prototype, and copy only own enumerable properties. StructuredClone is deep, handles Map, Set, Date, and cycles, throws on functions, and drops private fields and the prototype. JSON stringify and parse turns dates into strings, drops undefined, functions, and Map and Set, and throws on cycles. A custom clone method is the only option that preserves invariants and type. The senior answer: for domain objects, prefer immutability so copying is rarely needed, and when needed, give the class a clone or with method.

Mutable versus immutable. Readonly in TypeScript prevents reassignment at compile time only. Object.freeze prevents changes at runtime, but is shallow, so nested objects stay mutable. In strict mode writes throw a TypeError, and in sloppy mode they fail silently. A readonly array type removes mutating methods from the type. Immutable objects are thread safe, cacheable, and safe to share. The cost is allocation on every change.

Initialization order for creating a derived object. The derived constructor starts, and code before super cannot use this. Then super runs the base field initializers and the base constructor body. Back in the derived class, the derived field initializers run, then the rest of the constructor body. Static fields and static blocks run once, when the class definition is evaluated. Java has the same shape. C sharp differs: derived field initializers run before the base constructor. JavaScript and Java have no deterministic destructors, so use try and finally, the using declaration with Symbol dispose in TypeScript 5.2, Java try with resources, or C sharp IDisposable.

Finally, object relationships. A dependency means A uses B briefly. An association means A knows B, held as a field, with independent lifetimes. Aggregation means A has B, but B is shared and outlives A, and B is passed in from outside. Composition means A owns B, B dies with A, and A creates B internally. Inheritance is is a, and realization is implements. In garbage collected languages, the difference between aggregation and composition is about ownership and who controls the lifecycle, not about memory. Interviewers want you to say which object creates and deletes the part. Bidirectional relationships double the places that must stay consistent, so make one side the owner and derive the other through a query. Circular dependencies between modules show up as undefined imports at load time, and the fix is to extract a shared abstraction or invert one dependency.

Here is a short interview summary. New creates an object linked to the prototype. Identity is not equality. Copying is shallow by default, so prefer immutable objects. Know the initialization order, and be able to say who owns each part in a relationship.
passage:
When new is used, JavaScript creates an object whose prototype is the class prototype, defines the fields, and runs the constructor. In a derived class, this exists only after super returns. Methods are shared through the prototype, instance fields belong to the object, and static members live on the class, where mutable statics act as global state.

Identity means the same object in memory, while equality means the same value by a domain rule, so classes need an equals method and, in Java, a matching hashCode. Objects are passed as a copy of the reference, so mutation through a parameter affects the caller. Spread is a shallow copy, structuredClone is deep but drops prototypes, and a custom clone preserves invariants. Freeze is shallow, and immutable objects avoid most copying problems.

Object relationships range from dependency and association to aggregation, where the part is shared, and composition, where the owner creates and deletes the part. The key question is who controls the lifecycle. Bidirectional relationships should have one owning side, and circular module dependencies are fixed by extracting a shared abstraction.
prompt: Explain what new does in JavaScript, and the difference between identity and equality. Then explain the difference between aggregation and composition using an Order, a Customer, and order lines.

title: SOLID Principles in Interviews
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the five SOLID principles. They are among the most common object oriented design interview topics, so let us explain each one with a clear example.

The first is the Single Responsibility Principle. A module should have one reason to change. More precisely, it should answer to one actor, meaning one group of stakeholders. It does not mean that a class does one thing, or has one method. Imagine an InvoiceService that calculates totals, which Finance cares about, renders a PDF, which Design cares about, saves to the database, which the DBA cares about, and sends email. Four actors can request changes. A tax rule change forces retesting of the PDF and email code, and two teams edit the same file and get merge conflicts. To refactor, list each method's actor, move each actor's code into its own class, like pricing, PDF renderer, repository, and mailer, and keep a thin coordinator for the workflow. The trade off: over splitting scatters one concept across ten files. Split when actors or change rates really differ. A tricky question: does a UserRepository with findById, findByEmail, save, and delete violate SRP? No. It has one actor and one reason to change, the storage schema.

The second is the Open Closed Principle. Software should be open for extension and closed for modification, so you add new behaviour by adding code, not by editing tested code. A bad example is a shipping cost class with a switch on the method name. Every new courier means editing that class and retesting everything. A better version uses a ShippingRate interface and a registry map. Adding a courier means registering a new rate. The misconceptions: OCP does not forbid editing code, since bug fixes are modifications. It targets predictable variation, and you cannot be closed against every change. In TypeScript, a discriminated union with an exhaustive switch is closed for extension but gives compile time safety. Use it when you own the cases and they change rarely. Use Strategy when third parties or plugins add cases.

The third is the Liskov Substitution Principle. If S is a subtype of T, any code that works with T must keep working with an S, without knowing it. This is behavioural subtyping, not just matching signatures. The contract rules: preconditions cannot be strengthened. Postconditions cannot be weakened. Invariants must be preserved. No new exceptions that the caller was not prepared for. And a subtype must not allow state changes that the base forbids. The classic bad example is Square extending Rectangle. Rectangle promises that width and height vary independently. Square weakens that, so code that sets width and height and expects an area gets a surprise. The fixes: make shapes immutable, so that a with width method returns a new shape, or drop the inheritance and let both implement a Shape interface. Real world violations: a read only repository that extends a repository and throws on save, a payment provider subclass that throws not supported for refunds, or a subclass that needs init called first. A detection test: if client code contains an instanceof check to avoid misbehaviour, LSP is probably broken.

The fourth is the Interface Segregation Principle. Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use. A bad example is a Printer interface with print, scan, and fax, where a basic printer throws not supported for scan. Better, use role interfaces: Printer, Scanner, and Fax, and let an office machine implement all three. The trade off is that over segregating creates one method interfaces everywhere. Segregate by client role, not by method. In TypeScript, structural typing gives you ISP almost for free, because a function can declare that it needs only the findById part of a repository.

The fifth is the Dependency Inversion Principle. High level policy should not depend on low level detail. Both should depend on abstractions, and the abstraction should be owned by the high level side. A bad SignupService creates its own Postgres pool and SMTP client, which makes it hard to test and swap. Better, the application layer defines a UserStore and a Notifier interface, and the service receives them in its constructor. Now the arrows from infrastructure point up into the domain, and Postgres and SMTP can change without touching the service. Do not confuse the three terms. Dependency Inversion is a principle about the direction of source code dependencies. Dependency Injection is a technique where dependencies are passed in. Inversion of Control is the broader idea that a framework calls your code. You can do DI without DIP, by injecting a concrete pool, and DIP without a container, by manual wiring. And every abstraction is indirection, so invert at real boundaries, like I O, third party services, and volatile policy, not between two stable in process classes.
passage:
The Single Responsibility Principle says a module should answer to one actor, or one group of stakeholders, so a class that mixes pricing, PDF rendering, persistence, and email has four reasons to change. The Open Closed Principle asks that predictable variation, such as couriers or payment providers, be added by writing new code rather than editing tested code, usually through a strategy interface and a registry, although a discriminated union is a reasonable choice when cases rarely change.

The Liskov Substitution Principle requires that subtypes honour the contract of their base type: no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions, preserved invariants, and no surprising exceptions. Square extending Rectangle and a read only repository that throws on save are classic violations. The Interface Segregation Principle prefers small role interfaces so that clients do not depend on methods they never use.

The Dependency Inversion Principle says high level policy and low level detail should both depend on abstractions owned by the policy side. It differs from dependency injection, a technique, and inversion of control, a broader idea. Abstractions add indirection, so they belong at real boundaries such as I O and third party services.
prompt: Explain the Liskov Substitution Principle using the Square and Rectangle example or a read only repository. Then explain how the Dependency Inversion Principle differs from dependency injection.

title: Creational Design Patterns
shadowText:
Today we will talk about creational design patterns: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, and Prototype. For each one, we will see the problem, the simple alternative, and the trade offs.

Let us start with Singleton. The problem: exactly one instance must exist and be globally reachable, such as a config, a connection pool, or a logger. The classic pattern has a private constructor and a static getter that creates the instance on first use. But in JavaScript there is a reality. An ES module is evaluated once per module graph, so exporting a constant instance is already a singleton, per process, or per bundle copy. Duplicated packages in node_modules can produce two. Why is the pattern criticised? It is hidden global state. It is hard to replace in tests, it creates invisible coupling, and it breaks under parallel test runners that share the module cache. The better alternative is to create one instance in the composition root and inject it. You get one instance without global access. DI containers call this singleton lifetime. A trap for Java: is a lazy singleton thread safe? Not without synchronisation. The idiomatic answers are an enum singleton, or the holder class idiom. Double checked locking requires a volatile field.

Next, Factory Method. The problem: a base workflow needs to create an object, but subclasses decide which concrete class. For example, an abstract report exporter has an export method that calls an abstract createWriter method, the factory method, and subclasses for CSV and PDF return the right writer. People often confuse this with a simple factory, which is just a function with a switch that returns instances. Simple factories are fine and more common. Factory Method specifically uses inheritance to defer the choice. When not to use it? If you only vary the created object, pass a factory function instead. That is composition, and it avoids a subclass per format.

Abstract Factory. The problem: create families of related objects that must match. Examples are a UI theme's button and dialog, or a cloud provider's storage, queue, and secrets. A cloud kit interface has methods for each, and an AWS kit and an Azure kit implement them. The trade off: adding a new family is easy, just add a new kit. But adding a new product type, like a cache, changes every kit. The factory interface itself is not closed for that axis.

Builder. The problem: constructing an object needs many optional parameters, ordered steps, or validation of the combination. This is the telescoping constructor problem. An HttpRequest class with a private constructor and a builder, where you chain method calls and then call build, is a typical example. But in TypeScript, an options object with defaults usually replaces a Builder. Use a Builder when construction has steps, cross field validation, or produces an immutable result from a mutable staging area. Test data builders are the most common legitimate use.

Prototype. The problem: create new objects by copying a configured instance, when construction is expensive or the caller does not know the concrete class. A document template with a clone method is an example. Do not confuse the Prototype pattern with JavaScript's prototype chain. Object.create shares behaviour by delegation, and does not copy state. The pitfall: shallow clones that share nested mutable state, which is the bug the pattern was meant to prevent.

How do you choose? If you need one shared instance, create it once in main and inject it. Singleton only rarely. To choose a class by input, use a map of constructors or a simple factory, and move to Factory Method or a registry if it grows. For matching families, use an object of factory functions, and Abstract Factory if it outgrows that. For many optional parameters, use an options object with defaults, and Builder if needed. To copy a configured object, use a clone method, and Prototype with a registry if needed.

Here is a short interview summary. For each creational pattern, I start with the simplest language feature, and only use the full pattern when the problem really appears. I avoid global singletons by injecting one instance from the composition root.
passage:
Creational patterns control how objects are made. A Singleton ensures one instance, but it is hidden global state that is hard to test, so a better approach is to create one instance in the composition root and inject it. In JavaScript, a module level constant is already effectively a singleton per module graph, and in Java lazy singletons need careful synchronisation.

Factory Method lets subclasses choose which concrete class a base workflow creates, though passing a factory function is often simpler. Abstract Factory creates families of matching objects, such as a cloud provider kit, making new families easy but new product types hard. Builder handles many optional parameters or stepwise construction, although a TypeScript options object often suffices.

Prototype creates objects by cloning a configured instance, and it should not be confused with JavaScript's prototype chain. Its main pitfall is shallow cloning that shares nested mutable state. In practice, start with the simplest option, such as an injected instance, a simple factory, an options object, or a clone method, and adopt the full pattern only when it is needed.
prompt: Explain why Singleton is criticised and what you would use instead. Then compare Factory Method with simply passing a factory function, and say when each is the better choice.

title: Structural Design Patterns
shadowText:
Today we will talk about structural design patterns: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, and Proxy. They are about how objects are put together, and each answers a specific question.

Let us start with Adapter. The problem: your domain expects a PaymentGateway interface, but each provider SDK has its own shape. The adapter class implements your interface, calls the third party API, and translates the request and the response. It is also an anti corruption layer, because the provider vocabulary stops at its boundary, and your domain never sees it.

Bridge. The problem: two independent axes of variation cause a class explosion, such as EmailAlert, SmsAlert, EmailReport, and SmsReport. Bridge splits them. A Channel interface, the implementor, has send. An abstract Message class, the abstraction, holds a channel. Alert and Report extend the message, and Email and Sms implement the channel. Now you add a new message type or a new channel without multiplying classes.

Composite. The problem: treat individual items and groups the same way. Examples are files and folders, menu items and submenus, permissions and permission groups, and bundle pricing. A PriceComponent interface has a price method. A Product returns its own price, and a Bundle sums the prices of its children, which can be bundles too. A design question: should the add method be on the shared interface? Putting it there, called transparency, lets clients treat all nodes alike, but forces leaves to throw. Keeping it on Bundle, called safety, is the usual TypeScript choice.

Decorator. Use it for caching, retries, and logging. Take a RateProvider interface. A CachedRates class implements the same interface, wraps an inner provider, and returns cached values when they are fresh. A retrying decorator can wrap the cached one, and you compose any combination at runtime. The follow up: why not subclass HttpRates? Subclassing fixes one combination at compile time, while decorators compose any combination at runtime. Pitfalls: identity checks fail, so instanceof HttpRates is false for a wrapped object, and deep stacks are hard to debug. Also note that TypeScript decorators with the at sign are a language feature for annotating classes and members. They can implement the pattern, but they are not the same thing.

Facade. A CheckoutFacade takes the cart service, inventory, payment gateway, order repository, and mailer, and offers a single checkout method that coordinates them. It gives callers a simple entry point to a complex subsystem. The risk: a facade that grows logic becomes a God object. Keep it as coordination only, and keep business rules in domain objects.

Flyweight. The problem: millions of similar objects, like map tiles, text glyphs, or game particles, waste memory by duplicating shared state. A tree type holds the intrinsic state, such as species and texture, and a factory with a pool returns the shared instance. Each tree object holds only its own position and a reference to the shared type. Flyweights must be immutable, or one change affects every user. JavaScript string interning and V8 hidden classes are engine level flyweights.

Proxy. There are several kinds: virtual, for lazy loading, protection, for authorisation, remote, as an RPC stub, caching, and logging. For example, an AuthorizedReportService implements the report service interface, holds the real service and the current user, checks permission, and then delegates. JavaScript also has a built in Proxy object that intercepts property access at runtime, used by Vue reactivity, MobX, and Immer. It is a metaprogramming tool that can implement the pattern.

Proxy versus Decorator is a favourite question. The structure is the same. Proxy controls whether and when the real call happens, and usually manages the real object's lifecycle. Decorator adds behaviour, and is meant to be stacked by the client.

Here is a short interview summary. Adapter converts, Bridge separates two axes, Composite treats groups like items, Decorator adds behaviour, Facade simplifies, Flyweight shares, and Proxy controls access.
passage:
Structural patterns describe how objects are composed. An Adapter makes a third party API fit a domain interface and acts as an anti corruption layer, so provider vocabulary stays at the boundary. A Bridge separates two independent axes of variation, such as message type and delivery channel, to avoid a class explosion. A Composite lets clients treat single items and groups through the same interface, as with products and bundles.

A Decorator wraps an object with the same interface to add behaviour such as caching, retries, or logging, and decorators can be combined at runtime, unlike subclasses that fix a combination at compile time. A Facade offers a simple entry point to a complex subsystem, but must contain only coordination to avoid becoming a God object.

A Flyweight shares immutable intrinsic state among many similar objects to save memory. A Proxy stands in for a real object to control access, for example lazily loading it or checking authorisation. Proxy and Decorator share a structure, but a Proxy controls whether and when the real call happens, while a Decorator adds behaviour that clients stack.
prompt: Compare the Decorator and Proxy patterns: they have the same structure, so explain how their intent differs. Then explain why you would use decorators for caching and retries instead of subclassing.

title: Behavioral Design Patterns
shadowText:
Today we will talk about behavioral design patterns: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Chain of Responsibility, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, and Visitor. They describe how objects communicate and share work.

Let us start with Strategy. The problem: an algorithm varies, such as discounts, pricing, routing, or sorting, and you do not want a growing if and else. Define a DiscountStrategy interface with an apply method, and create strategies like none, percent, and member only. The order takes one. Strategy versus State: both swap an object behind an interface. In Strategy, the client picks the algorithm. In State, the object itself switches as its state changes.

Observer. The problem: when one object changes, unknown others must react, without the subject depending on them. An event bus with on and emit methods is the typical form. The pitfalls interviewers probe: memory leaks from never unsubscribing, called the lapsed listener problem. One listener throwing stops the rest. Ordering assumptions. And synchronous cascades that re enter the subject. Pub sub differs by putting a broker between the publisher and the subscriber, often across processes.

Command, with undo. A command object has execute and undo. For a text document, an InsertText command stores the position and the string, inserts on execute, and removes on undo. Uses include undo and redo, job queues, macros, audit logs, and transactional outboxes. Commands are data, so they can be serialised and replayed.

State. An order has a state object, such as Pending, Paid, or Shipped. The order delegates pay, ship, and cancel to its current state, and each state decides what is allowed and what the next state is. The trade off: for three to five states, a transition table, a map from state and event to the next state, is shorter, data driven, and easy to persist. Use State classes when each state carries substantial behaviour, not just allowed transitions.

Template Method. A DataImport base class has a run method that fixes the skeleton: parse, validate, save, and then an after import hook. Subclasses fill in the steps. It is the inheritance based sibling of Strategy. Its weakness is that subclasses depend on the base's internal call order, which is the fragile base class problem. The composition alternative passes parse, validate, and save as strategies into one class.

Chain of Responsibility. A chain of handlers, each receiving the request and a next function. Each handler can handle the request, pass it on, or both. Express and Koa middleware work this way. The risk: a request falls off the end silently, so always define a terminal handler.

Iterator. JavaScript builds this into the language with Symbol.iterator and generators. A paginated class can implement async iteration, fetching pages with a cursor and yielding items one by one, so callers use a simple for await loop.

Mediator. Objects talk through a mediator instead of to each other, turning an N by N web into a star. Examples are a chat room, an air traffic controller, form fields whose enabled state depends on each other, and in process command buses like MediatR in .NET. The risk: the mediator becomes a God object.

Memento. Capture an object's internal state so it can be restored, without exposing that state. An editor can return a frozen memento from save, which is opaque to the caretaker, the history list. The main trade off is memory. Command based undo stores diffs instead of snapshots.

Visitor. The problem: add new operations over a stable class hierarchy without editing each class. It uses double dispatch: the element picks the visitor method by its own type. The trade off is the expression problem. Visitor makes new operations cheap and new types expensive, because every visitor changes. Polymorphic methods are the reverse. In TypeScript, a discriminated union with an exhaustive switch is the idiomatic Visitor, and Java 21 sealed interfaces with pattern matching switch play the same role.

Here is a short interview summary. Strategy swaps an algorithm, State swaps behaviour by state, Observer notifies, Command makes a request an object, Template Method fixes a skeleton, and Chain of Responsibility passes a request along. For each, I name when I would not use it.
passage:
Behavioral patterns describe how objects collaborate. Strategy swaps an algorithm chosen by the client, while State lets an object switch its own behaviour as its state changes, and for a few states a transition table can be simpler. Observer notifies unknown listeners without the subject depending on them, with pitfalls such as leaks from missing unsubscribes and one failing listener stopping the others.

Command turns a request into an object that can be executed, undone, queued, serialised, and replayed. Template Method fixes an algorithm's skeleton in a base class, but it creates fragile base class risks, and composition with strategies is the alternative. Chain of Responsibility passes a request through handlers, as middleware does, and needs a terminal handler.

Iterator is built into JavaScript through generators and async iteration. A Mediator centralises communication among objects but may become a God object. A Memento captures state for restoring it, trading memory for simplicity, while a Visitor adds operations over a stable hierarchy through double dispatch, making new operations cheap and new types expensive.
prompt: Explain the Strategy, State, and Template Method patterns and how they differ. Then explain the pitfalls of the Observer pattern and how you would avoid them.

title: Enterprise and Application Patterns
shadowText:
Today we will talk about enterprise and application patterns: dependency injection, repository, unit of work, specification, DTO, application services, domain services, and domain events.

Let us start with a quick guide. Pick a pattern from the symptom in the code. A switch on a type code repeated in many places suggests Strategy or polymorphism. Boolean flags like isPaid and isShipped with illegal combinations suggest State, or a transition table. Notify X, Y, and Z when this changes suggests Observer or domain events. Undo, queueing, or audit of actions suggests Command. Ordered checks where any step may stop the request suggests Chain of Responsibility. Many objects tightly wired to each other suggest a Mediator. And a small grammar for filters, like price greater than a thousand and category equals electronics, can use the Interpreter pattern, with a class for each rule. It is appropriate only for simple grammars. For anything larger, use a parser generator or an existing expression language, and never eval user input.

Dependency Injection. Dependencies arrive through the constructor, which is preferred, a method parameter, or a property. Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and objects valid on creation. You can do manual DI in a composition root, with no container: create the pool, the repository, the adapter, and the use case, and wire them in one place. Containers such as NestJS, InversifyJS, and tsyringe, or Spring and the .NET DI, automate wiring and lifetimes, which are singleton, scoped per request, and transient. The anti pattern is the service locator, where business code asks a container for its dependencies. It hides dependencies and makes tests depend on global setup.

Repository. A collection like interface for aggregates, defined in domain terms, that hides the database. For example, an order repository with byId, save, and nextId. Senior notes: one repository per aggregate root, not per table. Return domain objects, not ORM rows. Avoid a generic repository with a findAll that takes any filter, because it leaks query concerns back into callers. A repository over an ORM that already is a repository is justified only if you want domain shaped methods or to keep the ORM out of the domain layer.

Unit of Work. It tracks changes made during a business transaction and commits them atomically. A run method takes a function that receives the repositories and executes inside one database transaction. ORMs implement this for you, such as the Hibernate session, EF Core SaveChanges, and the TypeORM entity manager transaction.

Specification. A business rule as a composable object, with isSatisfiedBy, and and or combinators, usable both in memory and translated to queries. DTO, or Data Transfer Object. A behaviour free shape for crossing a boundary such as HTTP, a queue, or a process. DTOs decouple the API contract from the domain model, so you can refactor one without breaking the other. Validate DTOs at the edge with a library such as zod, then map them to domain objects. Do not add business logic to DTOs, and do not return domain entities directly from controllers.

Service layer, or application services. A thin layer that defines the application's operations: load aggregates, call domain behaviour, save, and publish events. It owns transactions and authorisation, not business rules. A PlaceOrder use case runs inside a unit of work. One trade off to mention: charging inside a database transaction holds locks during a network call. Production systems usually reserve and commit first, then charge, then confirm, as a saga. The smell to watch for is services full of if statements over entity fields, while entities are bags of getters. That is the anemic domain model.

Domain services. Domain logic that does not naturally belong to one entity, usually because it spans several, such as a transfer between two accounts, or a pricing calculation using customer tier, product, and promotion. They are stateless, named in the domain's language, and have no infrastructure.

Domain events. A record of something that happened in the domain, named in the past tense, like OrderPlaced and PaymentCaptured. Aggregates record events, and the application layer publishes them after commit. For reliability, note that publishing after commit can still lose events if the process crashes in between. The transactional outbox pattern writes events to an outbox table in the same transaction, and a relay publishes them.

Here is a short interview summary. I inject dependencies from a composition root, keep repositories per aggregate root, keep application services thin, put rules in the domain, and use an outbox for reliable events.
passage:
Enterprise patterns organise application code. Dependency injection passes dependencies, preferably through constructors, from a composition root, whereas a service locator hides them. A repository gives collection like access to aggregates in domain terms, one per aggregate root, and a unit of work commits a business transaction atomically. A specification expresses a business rule as a composable object.

Data transfer objects carry data across boundaries without behaviour, and are validated at the edge and mapped to domain objects. Application services define use cases, load aggregates, call domain behaviour, save, and publish events, owning transactions and authorisation but not business rules. If rules live in services and entities only hold data, the domain model is anemic. Domain services hold stateless domain logic that spans several entities.

Domain events record meaningful past facts such as OrderPlaced. Because publishing after a commit can lose events on a crash, the transactional outbox stores events in the same transaction and a relay publishes them later. A symptom based guide helps choose among behavioral patterns, and the Interpreter pattern suits only small grammars.
prompt: Explain the repository, unit of work, and application service patterns, and how they fit together in one use case. Then explain why domain events need a transactional outbox.

title: CQRS, Event Sourcing and Language Differences
shadowText:
Today we will talk about three advanced design ideas, DDD factories, CQRS, and event sourcing, and then compare what TypeScript, JavaScript, Java, and C sharp enforce.

Let us start with the DDD factory. It encapsulates creation of a complex aggregate with its invariants, such as Order.place or a loan application created from a form. Unlike GoF factories, the motivation is valid construction, not choosing a subclass.

CQRS means Command Query Responsibility Segregation. You have separate models for writes, which are commands that enforce invariants, and reads, which are queries shaped for screens. It can be as simple as two sets of classes over one database, or as complex as separate read stores fed by events. Use it when reads and writes have very different shapes or load, such as dashboards over a transactional core. Avoid it when the app is CRUD, because you double the code and add eventual consistency for nothing.

Event sourcing. State is stored as an append only sequence of events, and the current state is a fold over them. For a wallet, you store Credited and Debited events, and the balance is computed by applying them in order. The gains: a full audit trail, time travel, and the ability to rebuild projections. The costs: event schema versioning, snapshots for long streams, eventual consistency, harder queries, and GDPR deletion. It is usually paired with CQRS. Recommend it for ledgers and audit heavy domains, not by default.

Now the language comparison. Classes exist in all four. Interfaces in TypeScript are erased at runtime. JavaScript has no interfaces, while Java and C sharp have real types. Abstract classes are checked by TypeScript and then erased. JavaScript has no keyword, and you emulate it with a new.target check. For private, TypeScript's keyword is checked only and accessible at runtime, while JavaScript's hash field is truly private. Java and C sharp enforce private, though reflection can bypass it. Protected is checked only in TypeScript, and has no equivalent in JavaScript. Readonly in TypeScript is checked only. Java final fields are enforced, and C sharp has readonly and init accessors. Method overloading in TypeScript is signatures only with one implementation. JavaScript has none, and the last definition wins. Java and C sharp have true overloads resolved at compile time. For generics, TypeScript's are structural and erased, JavaScript has none, Java erases them, and C sharp keeps them reified at runtime. TypeScript typing is structural, JavaScript is dynamic duck typing, and Java and C sharp are nominal. For value equality types, Java has records and C sharp has records and structs. For sealed hierarchies, TypeScript uses discriminated unions, and Java and C sharp have sealed.

Structural versus nominal typing. In TypeScript, if you declare classes Usd and Bdt with the same shape, you can assign a Bdt to a variable of type Usd, because the shape matches. Java and C sharp reject this, since types are equal by name and declaration. To get nominal behaviour in TypeScript, add a private member or a brand, such as a number intersected with a readonly brand property.

Interfaces versus abstract classes in TypeScript. Use an interface for a contract between modules, with zero runtime cost, and a class can implement many. Use an abstract class when you need shared code or state, a runtime instanceof check, or a template method. Also, a class can implement another class, taking its public shape, which is useful for test fakes.

Runtime type checks. Instanceof walks the prototype chain. It fails across realms, such as iframes and vm contexts, and for duplicated package copies. TypeScript interfaces cannot be checked at runtime, so write a type guard function or validate with a schema library like zod. Java generics are erased, so a list of strings and a list of integers are the same class at runtime. C sharp generics are reified, so they differ.

For equality, TypeScript and JavaScript use triple equals for reference equality and hand written equals for value equality. Java uses double equals for references and equals plus hashCode for values. C sharp uses Equals and GetHashCode, automatic for records. Deep immutability is manual in JavaScript, and records in Java and C sharp are only shallowly immutable.

Here is a short interview summary. CQRS and event sourcing are powerful but costly, so I use them only where the domain justifies it. And I know which guarantees are compile time in TypeScript and which are real at runtime in each language.
passage:
A domain factory encapsulates creation of a complex aggregate so that it is always valid. CQRS separates the model for writes, which enforce invariants, from the model for reads, which are shaped for screens. It helps when reads and writes differ greatly in shape or load, but doubles the code and adds eventual consistency in simple CRUD applications.

Event sourcing stores state as an append only sequence of events and derives the current state by applying them. It gives an audit trail, time travel, and rebuildable projections, but needs schema versioning, snapshots, and careful handling of queries and deletion, so it suits ledgers and audit heavy domains rather than being a default.

Languages differ in what they enforce. TypeScript checks private, readonly, and interfaces only at compile time, while JavaScript hash private fields are truly private. Java and C sharp have real interfaces, true overloading, and nominal typing, and C sharp keeps generics at runtime. TypeScript typing is structural, so nominal behaviour needs a brand or a private member. Runtime type checks need type guards or schema validation, and instanceof can fail across realms and duplicated packages.
prompt: Explain what CQRS and event sourcing are and when they are worth their cost. Then explain what is enforced at compile time versus runtime in TypeScript compared with JavaScript, Java, and C sharp.

title: OOP Traps and Paradigm Trade-offs
shadowText:
Today we will talk about two things. First, how object oriented, functional, and procedural styles compare. Second, reflection. And then a set of classic traps about constructors, static members, and copying objects.

Let us start with paradigms. Object oriented code is strong at encapsulating state and extending behavior through polymorphism. Its weaknesses are ceremony and hidden mutation. It fits rich domains with invariants and long lived state. Functional code has pure functions, is easy to test, and composes well. Its weaknesses are modeling stateful entities and the cost of copying data. It fits data transformation, pipelines, and user interface state. Procedural code is direct and simple, but scales poorly as the rules grow. It fits scripts, glue code, and small utilities. Here is a senior signal. Modern TypeScript code mixes all three. Inside, you use immutable value types and pure functions. At the boundaries, you use objects for state and polymorphism. Saying that in an interview shows maturity.

Now reflection. Reflection lets code inspect and call members at runtime. Frameworks depend on it, such as dependency injection containers, object relational mappers, serializers, and test runners. Application code should rarely use it, because it bypasses encapsulation and breaks rename refactoring. Languages differ. In Java and C sharp, you get full class metadata at runtime. In TypeScript and JavaScript, types are gone at runtime, so you only have the prototype chain and the constructor name. Java erases generic arguments, while C sharp keeps them. Private state is the interesting part. A JavaScript hash private field cannot be reached, but TypeScript's private keyword is trivially bypassed. Here is the interview point. Constructor injection containers need parameter types at runtime. Only the older experimental decorator metadata emits those. The newer standard decorators do not. That is why NestJS still requires the experimental flag. Without metadata, containers fall back to explicit tokens or manual wiring.

Now the traps. First trap. A base constructor calls an overridden method. The base class constructor calls init. The derived class overrides init to push into an items array, which is a field initialized in the derived class. What happens? You get a TypeError, because the array is undefined. Dispatch is dynamic, so the derived init runs during the base constructor. But derived fields are initialized only after the base constructor returns. In C sharp, the opposite order applies, so it would work. In Java, the same code throws a null pointer exception. The rule: never call overridable methods from a constructor.

Second trap. A derived class redeclares a field that the base constructor assigned, only to narrow its type. With modern class field semantics, which are the default for newer targets, the redeclaration re defines the field as undefined after the base constructor returns. So you read undefined, not the base value. The fix is the declare keyword, which is a type only redeclaration that emits nothing.

Third trap. A counting set overrides add to count additions. Constructing it with three items gives size three but a count of zero. The Set constructor calls add inside the base constructor, when the counter is not initialized yet. The increment produces NaN, and then the field initializer resets it to zero. Prefer wrapping a set instead of extending it.

Fourth trap. Static counters and inheritance. A static method increments this dot count. Calling it on a subclass twice, and on the parent once, gives parent one and child two. This in a static method is the class it was called on. The first call on the child reads the inherited value and writes a new own property on the child. After that, they count separately. Many people expect a single shared slot.

Fifth, a static factory using new this creates an instance of the class it was called on, so calling it on Circle returns a circle. Sixth, identity versus equality. Map keys and triple equals compare object identity, so looking up a new object literal finds nothing, and two arrays with the same content are not equal. Seventh, the spread syntax copies only one level, so nested arrays are shared. And eighth, spreading a class instance copies own properties only, not prototype methods. You get a plain object, and calling a method on it fails.

To summarize in an interview: I choose paradigms by problem, I avoid reflection outside frameworks, and I never call overridable methods in constructors, because initialization order is the source of many surprising bugs.
passage:
Object oriented, functional, and procedural styles each have strengths. Object oriented code encapsulates state and extends behavior through polymorphism, functional code favors pure functions and composition, and procedural code is direct but scales poorly. Modern TypeScript commonly uses immutable values and pure functions internally, with objects at the boundaries.

Reflection allows code to inspect and invoke members at runtime and is mainly used by frameworks. TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so dependency injection containers rely on emitted decorator metadata, which is why NestJS still needs the experimental decorator flag.

Several traps involve construction order. If a base constructor calls an overridden method, the derived fields are not yet initialized. Redeclaring a field in a subclass can reset it to undefined under modern class field semantics. Static members inherited by a subclass can silently create separate own properties. Object keys in maps compare identity, spread copies only one level, and spreading a class instance drops its prototype methods.
prompt: Explain why calling an overridable method from a base class constructor is dangerous, using the example of a derived class whose array field is still undefined. Mention how initialization order differs in TypeScript, Java and C sharp.

title: Encapsulation, Immutability and this
shadowText:
Today we will talk about immutability, privacy, and the this keyword in classes. Each topic comes with a classic trap question.

Let us start with freezing. Object dot freeze is shallow, and the readonly keyword in TypeScript exists only at compile time. Imagine a team class with a readonly members array. You freeze an instance. Pushing a name to the array still works, because the freeze only locks the object's own top level properties, and the array itself is a separate object. But assigning a new array to the property throws a TypeError in strict mode, and class code and modules are strict. So, for real safety, use a readonly array type for the compiler, and return copies at runtime.

Now privacy. TypeScript's private keyword is erased at runtime. A class with a private pin and a hash private key behaves very differently. The pin is a normal own property. You can read it with a cast, and it even shows up in JSON output. The hash private field lives in a private slot. It is not a property with that name, and it is not serialized. Then why use the TypeScript private keyword at all? It is easier to debug, it works with older targets, and it has a protected sibling that subclasses can use. Hash private fields have no equivalent, because a subclass cannot see a parent's hash fields.

Another trap: getters that return internal state. A cart class keeps a private array of items, and a getter returns that array directly. Then a caller can push to it and mutate the private state. The fix is to return a copy, or a readonly view, or better, to expose behavior such as add and count instead of exposing data.

Here is a question interviewers love. Are encapsulation and abstraction the same thing? No. Encapsulation protects state and invariants. It is a boundary. Abstraction exposes a simplified model and hides decisions. It is a view. A class can be perfectly encapsulated with all private fields and still have a poor abstraction, such as a class named data manager that does everything. And the reverse can be true.

Now the this keyword. A detached method trap. A counter class has a count field and an inc method. You pass the method directly to forEach. What happens? A TypeError: cannot read properties of undefined. The value of this is decided by the call site, not by where the method is defined. ForEach calls the function with no receiver, and class bodies are always in strict mode, so this is undefined. There are three fixes: wrap it in an arrow function, bind the method, or define it as an arrow function field.

But arrow fields have costs. A subclass overrides an arrow field with its own arrow field that calls super dot greet. This fails. TypeScript reports an error, and at runtime you get a TypeError. The reason is that an arrow field is an own property created per instance, not a method on the prototype. So super dot greet looks on the parent's prototype, where nothing exists. The trade offs of arrow fields are: this is automatically bound, but you create one function per instance, which costs memory, they cannot be overridden through super, and they are invisible to prototype spies in tests.

Last, a nested regular function. A timer class starts an interval with a regular function that increments this dot s. The callback's this is not the timer. TypeScript with strict settings flags it, and at runtime it is wrong. Use an arrow function, which captures the lexical this.

To summarize in an interview: freeze is shallow and readonly is compile time only. TypeScript private is not real privacy, but hash fields are. I return copies or behavior instead of internal state. And I remember that this depends on the call site, so I use arrows or bind carefully, knowing their costs.
passage:
Object dot freeze locks only the top level properties of an object, and the readonly keyword in TypeScript exists only at compile time, so an array held in a frozen object can still be modified. Real safety requires readonly types for the compiler and copies at runtime.

TypeScript's private keyword is erased, so the property is an ordinary own property that can be read and even serialized. Hash private fields are genuinely private and are not serialized, although subclasses cannot access them. A getter that returns an internal array exposes the state to mutation, so it should return a copy or provide behavior instead.

Encapsulation protects state and invariants, while abstraction presents a simplified model, so they are different ideas. The value of this depends on how a function is called, so a method passed as a callback loses it. Arrow function fields fix this but create one function per instance and cannot be called through super.
prompt: Explain why passing a class method directly to forEach throws a TypeError, and compare the three fixes: an arrow wrapper, bind, and an arrow function field. Mention one drawback of arrow fields.

title: TypeScript Type System Traps
shadowText:
Today we will talk about traps in the TypeScript type system, especially around structural typing and the difference between compile time and runtime.

Let us start with structural typing. Suppose you have a class Cat with a name, and a class Robot with a name. You assign a new Robot to a variable of type Cat. Does it compile? Yes. TypeScript compares shapes, not class names. But if you then check whether the variable is an instance of Cat, it prints false, because the instanceof operator checks the prototype chain at runtime. So a narrowing like if x instanceof Cat can disagree with what the type checker allowed. This is a good example of why types and runtime checks are two different worlds.

Next, method parameter bivariance. Say you have Animal, and Dog which extends Animal and has a bark method. A handler interface declares a handle method that takes an Animal. You create an object whose handle method takes a Dog and calls bark. This compiles! Then you call it with a plain Animal, and it crashes at runtime. Why? Even with strict function types turned on, parameters declared with method syntax are checked bivariantly. This is a deliberate unsoundness for compatibility, for example with browser types. The fix is to declare the member with property syntax, as a function type, which gives proper contravariant and sound checking.

Array covariance is another trap. You can assign an array of dogs to a variable typed as an array of animals. That is allowed. Then you push a plain animal into it, and later call bark on the first dog element, which fails at runtime. TypeScript arrays are covariant, which is unsound for writes. Java arrays are also covariant, but Java throws an array store exception at runtime. Java generic lists are invariant, so assigning a list of dogs to a list of animals does not compile. In TypeScript, when you only read, use a readonly array type.

Now, using instanceof with an interface. This does not compile. The error says the interface only refers to a type but is being used as a value. Interfaces do not exist at runtime. The solution is a custom type guard, a function that checks the shape, for example whether an object has a pay method that is a function, and returns a type predicate.

Abstract classes. Can plain JavaScript code create an instance of a TypeScript abstract class? Yes, because the abstract keyword is erased. If it matters, add a runtime guard in the constructor. Check whether the new target is the abstract class itself, and throw a TypeError.

Finally, excess property checks. If you assign an object literal with a misspelled extra property directly to a typed variable, TypeScript reports an error. But if you first put the same object in a variable, and then assign that variable, there is no error, because it is no longer a fresh literal. So the check only catches typos at the point of creating the literal. Do not rely on it as general protection.

A short mental model helps here. TypeScript checks your program before it runs, using shapes and declarations. The runtime knows nothing about those declarations. Whenever a check matters at runtime, such as validating input, branching on a kind of object, or protecting an abstract base class, you need real code that executes: a type guard, an instanceof check on a real class, a discriminant field, or a schema validator. When you explain a trap, say which side it lives on, the compile time side or the runtime side. That one habit makes most of these questions easy.

To summarize in an interview: TypeScript is structural, so instanceof and types can disagree. Method syntax is bivariant, arrays are covariant, interfaces and abstract keywords vanish at runtime, and excess property checks only apply to fresh literals. When runtime safety matters, I add explicit guards or validation.
passage:
TypeScript uses structural typing, so an object of one class is assignable to a type from another class if the shapes match, while the instanceof operator checks the runtime prototype chain, and the two can disagree. Parameters declared with method syntax are checked bivariantly even in strict mode, which can allow unsound handlers, whereas property syntax with a function type is checked soundly.

Arrays are covariant, so an array of a subtype can be assigned to an array of the supertype, which is unsound for writes. Readonly arrays avoid this when only reading. Java arrays are also covariant but fail at runtime, while Java generic lists are invariant.

Interfaces are erased at runtime and cannot be used with instanceof, so a custom type guard is needed. The abstract keyword is also erased, so a runtime check on the new target is required if instantiation must be prevented. Excess property checks apply only to fresh object literals and not to variables.
prompt: Explain structural typing in TypeScript using a Cat class and a Robot class with the same shape. Say why the assignment compiles, why instanceof returns false, and how you would check for an interface at runtime.

title: Inheritance and Dispatch Across Languages
shadowText:
Today we will talk about inheritance and method dispatch in Java, C sharp, and TypeScript. These are subtle questions that interviewers use to see whether you understand what the compiler and runtime really do.

Let us start with Java. Overload is not override. A class A has a method m that takes an Object. A subclass B adds a method m that takes a String. You create a B but store it in a variable of type A and call m with a string. What is printed? The A version. Resolution has two steps. At compile time, the static type A has only the Object version, so that signature is chosen. At runtime, Java looks for an override of that exact signature in B, and there is none, because the String version is only an overload. If you had put the override annotation on B's method, the compiler would have rejected it. The tempting wrong answer is that the object is a B, so the B method runs.

Static methods are hidden, not overridden. If a parent and a child both define a static method n, then calling it through a variable declared as the parent type calls the parent's version, even if the object is a child. Static calls bind to the declared type at compile time. Fields are also not polymorphic. If both classes have a field called name, then reading name through a parent typed variable gives the parent's field, while calling a method gives the child's version. The rule: never shadow fields.

C sharp has a similar trap. Methods are non virtual by default. If a base method is virtual and the derived method uses override, the call goes to the derived version. But if the derived method uses the new keyword, it hides rather than overrides, so a call through a base typed variable runs the base version. In the example, you get B then A, so the string BA.

Now the diamond problem with default methods in Java. If a class implements two interfaces that each provide a default method with the same name, the compiler reports an error. You fix it by overriding the method and choosing one explicitly, using the interface name followed by super. The conflict rules are: class methods win over interface defaults, a more specific interface wins, and otherwise the class must override. C plus plus solves the state diamond with virtual inheritance, and TypeScript or JavaScript mixins are resolved by linear order.

Covariant returns. An override can return a narrower type in Java, in C sharp since version nine, and in TypeScript. Narrower return types are safe. Wider parameter types would also be safe in theory, but Java and C sharp do not allow contravariant parameters in overriding. A wider parameter creates an overload instead.

Another trap is a circular import with extends. File A imports B and has a method that creates a B. File B imports A and defines a class that extends A. Loading A first starts loading B, which tries to extend A before A is defined. You get a ReferenceError in modules, or a TypeError saying the class extends undefined in CommonJS. Fix it by breaking the cycle, for example by moving the factory out of A, or by placing shared types in a third module.

Constructor overloading differs. Java and C sharp allow several real constructors chosen at compile time. TypeScript allows several signatures over one implementation, which must branch on runtime arguments. JavaScript allows exactly one constructor. Two constructors with the same parameter types, such as polar and cartesian coordinates, cannot be overloaded in any of them. Named static factories solve this and state the intent clearly.

Last, implementation inheritance has hidden protocols. If you extend Array and call map on your subclass, the result is also an instance of your subclass, because map builds its result through the species constructor. If your constructor required a special argument, map would break it. So prefer interface inheritance or holding an array privately.

To summarize in an interview: I explain dispatch as compile time signature selection plus runtime override lookup, I avoid hiding and shadowing, and I prefer composition over extending built in classes.
passage:
In Java, method resolution happens in two steps: the compiler selects a signature using the static type, and the runtime then finds the override of that exact signature. A method with a different parameter type is an overload and not an override, so the parent version may run. Static methods and fields are not polymorphic and are bound to the declared type.

In C sharp, methods are non virtual by default, and the new keyword hides a base method rather than overriding it. Conflicting default methods in two Java interfaces cause a compile error that must be resolved by overriding explicitly.

A circular import in which a class extends another class from the cyclic file fails at load time. Constructor overloading is real in Java and C sharp, but in TypeScript only the signatures are overloaded, while the single implementation must branch at runtime. Extending built in classes brings hidden protocols, such as the species mechanism that makes array methods construct instances of the subclass, so composition is often safer.
prompt: Explain why, in Java, calling an overload through a parent typed variable runs the parent method, using the example of m with Object in the parent and m with String in the child. Mention the role of the override annotation.

title: Design Principles and Scenario Design
shadowText:
Today we will talk about object oriented design questions that appear in senior interviews. We will cover relationships between objects, common myths about SOLID, premature abstraction, and how to approach design scenarios such as a wallet ledger and a plugin system.

Let us start with relationships. A car has an engine. Is that composition or aggregation? The honest answer is that it depends on lifecycle ownership in your domain. In a car manufacturing system, where the engine is built inside the car and both are scrapped together, it is composition. In a repair system, where engines are swapped between cars, it is aggregation. Ask what happens to the part when the whole is deleted. Another question: is a method parameter an association? No, it is a dependency. Association means an object holds a reference over time, like a field. Dependencies are easier to change.

A bidirectional link can drift. A team has a list of players, and each player has a team field. If you push a player into the team list, the player's team field is still empty. The fix is one method that owns both sides, such as add, which sets the player's team and pushes into the list, and the arrays are private. Or you make the link one directional and query in the other direction.

Now the myths about design principles. Single responsibility does not mean a class does one thing. It means one reason to change, one actor. A cohesive class may have many methods. Open closed does not mean never edit code. It targets anticipated variation, and bug fixes are fine. Square is a rectangle is only correct if the square honors the rectangle's behavioral contract, and mutable setters break it. Not every class needs an interface for dependency inversion. Abstractions belong at volatile boundaries, and one implementation interfaces are often noise. More small interfaces is not always better for interface segregation. Segregate by client role. Getters and setters are not encapsulation. Encapsulation means the object protects its invariants. Inheritance is for substitutability, not for code reuse. Reuse code with composition or functions. An anemic domain model scatters invariants, so any service can put an entity in an invalid state. It is acceptable only for simple CRUD apps. And a god object is about knowing and deciding too much, not line count.

Premature abstraction. Imagine a teammate created a user service interface, an implementation class, a factory, and a provider for one CRUD endpoint. A strong review says: four types, one behavior. Keep one class. Extract an interface only at a real seam, such as a second implementation, a module boundary, or an external dependency to fake. Name the costs: navigation, indirection, and false flexibility. Mention the rule of three before abstracting.

Now the wallet and ledger design. Requirements: balances never go negative, every change is auditable, transfers are atomic, retries never double post, and balances reconcile. The model is double entry. Every transaction has entries that sum to zero. The balance is derived from entries, or cached with a version check, and never edited directly. Store money in integer minor units, using big integers, because floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly. In the use case, within one database transaction, check the idempotency key with a unique index, load both accounts with optimistic locking, apply the debit and credit, insert the ledger transaction, and bump the versions. On a version conflict, retry. If you use pessimistic locks, lock accounts in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks. Reversals are new compensating transactions, never deletions.

Plugin system. Requirements: third parties add importers without changing the core, and plugins are discovered at startup, validated, versioned, and isolated. The plugin API is a published contract, so version it and keep it tiny. Give plugins a capability object, not the whole app. Untrusted plugins need process or worker isolation, not just interfaces. Patterns involved are Strategy, Registry, Abstract Factory, and Facade.

For any scenario, use a template: requirements, object model, one interface in code, one use case walk through, the patterns and principles you name, alternatives, tests, and follow up questions. Typical traps are hard coded switches per courier, floats for money, loading huge files into memory, overselling under concurrency, and big bang rewrites without characterization tests.

To refactor a god class, pin current behavior with tests, extract value objects and pure policies, introduce ports for side effects, add a use case, and keep the old class as a thin facade until callers migrate. To fix a Penguin that extends Bird but cannot fly, model capabilities, not taxonomy.

To summarize in an interview: I reason from lifecycle and change, I know the principles' real meaning, I avoid ceremony, and I present designs with a clear structure.
passage:
Whether a car and its engine are composition or aggregation depends on lifecycle ownership in the domain, and a method parameter is a dependency, not an association. Bidirectional links drift unless one method maintains both sides.

Design principles are often misquoted. Single responsibility means one reason to change, open closed addresses anticipated variation, and inheritance is for substitutability and not code reuse. Interfaces belong at volatile boundaries, and creating an interface, a factory, and a provider for one simple endpoint is premature abstraction.

A wallet ledger uses double entry, derives balances from entries, stores money as integer minor units, and combines idempotency keys with optimistic locking inside a database transaction. A plugin system exposes a small versioned contract and a limited capability object, and untrusted plugins need real isolation. A good scenario answer follows a template of requirements, model, interface, use case, patterns, alternatives, tests, and follow ups.
prompt: Design a wallet ledger for an interview. Explain double entry, why balances are derived from entries, why money is stored in integer minor units, and how you prevent double posting on retries and lost updates under concurrency.

title: Programming Paradigms and Design Approaches
shadowText:
Today we will talk about programming paradigms and how they relate to everyday JavaScript and TypeScript work. We will cover imperative and declarative styles, pure functions, immutability, higher order functions, choosing between object oriented and functional, composition over inheritance, reactive programming, principles that conflict, and application architecture.

Let us start with the main paradigms. Imperative or procedural code gives step by step instructions that change state. Object oriented code bundles state with the behavior that changes it. Functional code composes pure functions over immutable data. Declarative code describes what result you want, not how to get it, like SQL, HTML, CSS, and React JSX. Reactive or event driven code reacts to streams of events or changing values. JavaScript supports all of them. Good codebases mix them deliberately, with a functional core inside an object oriented or modular structure.

Imperative versus declarative. Imperative code manages the loop, the index, and the result array yourself. Declarative code filters and maps. The same is true in the user interface. With the imperative DOM you create elements and append them. With React you describe the interface for the current state, and React works out the DOM changes. Declarative code is shorter, easier to read, and harder to get wrong. Imperative code gives control over performance, like early exit. Declarative layers run imperative code underneath.

Pure functions. A pure function returns the same output for the same inputs and has no side effects. It does not mutate arguments or outside state, and it does no input and output, including time and random values. Why does it matter? It is testable without mocks, predictable, cacheable, and safe to run in any order. React relies on this, because it may render a component twice or abandon a render. You cannot remove side effects from a real program, so push them to the edges. The idea is a functional core with an imperative shell.

Immutability means you never change a value after creating it. To update, you create a new one, using spread and copying array methods. React and Redux detect changes by reference equality, so mutating the same object may skip a re render and show stale data. Tools include structuredClone, Immer, freeze, and readonly types. The costs are allocation and time on very large structures, and spread copies are shallow. Local mutation that nobody else sees is fine. What matters is not mutating shared state.

Higher order functions take or return functions. Currying and partial application fix some arguments now and supply the rest later. Composition builds bigger functions from smaller ones. They are useful for logging, retries, auth checks, and caching. But overusing deep currying hurts readability.

How do you choose between object oriented and functional? Object oriented code is organized around nouns, with encapsulated state. It makes adding new types easy. Functional code is organized around verbs, with immutable data. It makes adding new operations easy. This is the expression problem. Choose by which you expect to change more. In practice, mix them. A NestJS service class calls pure functions for pricing. A React app uses function components. A domain entity guards its invariants while reports use map and reduce. A good answer is: I use classes where something has identity and rules about how its state may change, and pure functions for calculations.

Composition over inheritance. Inheritance causes tight coupling, the fragile base class problem, and rigid hierarchies. Composition injects the parts. In React, composition is the main reuse tool, through children, render props, and custom hooks. Inheritance is fine for a genuine, stable is a relationship one level deep.
