Reactive programming. Callbacks handle many events. Promises handle one value. Observables handle many values with operators like debounce and switch map. Signals track dependencies automatically for fine grained updates. Choose the simplest one that fits.

Principles conflict. SOLID, DRY, KISS, and YAGNI pull against each other. Merging two similar functions with flags couples unrelated features. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction, so abstract on the third repetition. An interface for one implementation is speculative. The senior answer is judgement.

Finally, application architecture. Layered is good for most CRUD back ends. Clean or hexagonal puts domain logic at the center with adapters around it, which suits complex rules. Feature based slices suit front ends and modular monoliths. The dependency direction matters more than folder names. The trap is full clean architecture for a ten endpoint service.

To summarize in an interview: I mix paradigms deliberately, keep a pure core, avoid mutating shared state, prefer composition, and choose architecture by real complexity.
passage:
JavaScript supports several paradigms: imperative, object oriented, functional, declarative, and reactive. Good codebases combine them deliberately, often with a functional core inside an object oriented structure. Declarative code states what is wanted and is shorter and safer, while imperative code offers control over performance.

A pure function returns the same output for the same input without side effects, which makes it easy to test, cache, and re run, and React depends on this. Side effects should be pushed to the edges of the program. Immutability avoids mutating shared state and lets React and Redux detect changes through reference equality, although copies are shallow and have a cost.

Object oriented design makes new types easy to add, while functional design makes new operations easy to add, so the choice depends on what will change. Composition is preferred over inheritance because inheritance couples subclasses to their parents. Principles such as DRY, KISS, YAGNI, and SOLID can conflict, so judgement is needed. Architecture should match the complexity, whether layered, hexagonal, or feature based.
prompt: Compare object oriented and functional programming and explain how you decide between them for a feature. Mention the expression problem, immutability, and give one example of mixing both in a NestJS or React project.

title: Concurrency Models for JavaScript Engineers
shadowText:
Today we will talk about concurrency models, and especially how JavaScript compares with threads and actors. This is a common senior interview question, because many people confuse concurrency with parallelism.

Let us start with the four models. The first is the event loop, which is single threaded asynchronous code. There is one thread. Waiting for input and output is handed to the operating system or to libuv, and callbacks resume later. This is how browser JavaScript and Node dot js work. The advantage is that there are no data races on JavaScript objects. The risk is that long CPU work blocks everything.

The second model is threads with shared memory. Many threads read and write the same memory. The risk is data races, so you need locks or atomics. Java, C sharp, and Go goroutines work this way, although Go also encourages channels. In Node, worker threads can share memory through a SharedArrayBuffer.

The third model is message passing, often called the actor model. You have isolated units that communicate only by messages, so there is no shared state by design. Erlang and Elixir, Akka, and also Web Workers and Node workers with postMessage follow this idea.

The fourth model is multiple processes. Separate operating system processes often sit behind a load balancer. There is no shared memory, so they coordinate through a database or a queue. Node cluster, PM2, and containers are examples.

Here is the key point for JavaScript engineers. Async and await is concurrency, not parallelism. Requests overlap while waiting for input and output, but JavaScript code runs one piece at a time. So if you start ten network calls, they wait together, but your own computation does not run in parallel.

Second, CPU heavy work needs a different approach. Use worker threads in Node, Web Workers in the browser, or move the work to a separate service. If you leave a big loop on the main thread, every request waits.

Third, even without data races, you can still have race conditions in logic. Imagine two requests read a balance of one hundred. Both subtract eighty and both write twenty. No memory was corrupted, but the result is wrong, because the money was spent twice. JavaScript's single thread does not protect you across await points or across multiple server instances.

How do you fix this? There are several tools. Use database transactions so that the read and the write happen as one unit. Use atomic updates, for example an increment operator in a document database, or a SQL update that subtracts only when the balance is large enough, so the check and the change happen together. Use optimistic locking with a version field, so a conflicting write fails and can be retried. And use idempotency keys, so a retried request does not apply the same change twice.

When you answer in an interview, name the model, the risk of that model, and the mitigation. For the event loop, the risk is blocking. For shared memory threads, the risk is data races. For actors, the risk is message ordering and mailbox growth. For multiple processes, the risk is coordination and consistency.

Let us make the last point concrete with a payment example. A customer double clicks the pay button. Two requests arrive within a few milliseconds. Each one loads the order, sees that it is unpaid, and calls the payment provider. Nothing crashed, no thread conflict happened, and yet the customer was charged twice. The fix is not to add a lock in JavaScript, because a second server instance would not see it. The fix is to move the guarantee into shared storage. Claim an idempotency key with a unique constraint, or update the order status with a condition that only succeeds when it is still unpaid. Then only one request wins, and the other receives the stored result or a conflict response.

To summarize in an interview, I would say this. JavaScript uses a single threaded event loop, which gives concurrency without data races, but it does not give parallel computation. For CPU work I use workers, for scale I use more processes, and for correctness I use transactions, atomic updates, versioning, and idempotency.
passage:
JavaScript uses an event loop on a single thread. Waiting for input and output is handled by the operating system, and callbacks resume later. This avoids data races on JavaScript objects, but long CPU work blocks everything. Other models include threads with shared memory, which need locks or atomics, message passing between isolated actors, and multiple processes that coordinate through a database or a queue.

Async and await provides concurrency but not parallelism, because requests overlap while waiting, yet JavaScript code runs one piece at a time. CPU heavy work should be moved to worker threads, Web Workers, or a separate service.

Even without data races, logic races can occur, such as two requests reading the same balance and both subtracting from it. They are prevented with database transactions, atomic updates, optimistic locking with version fields, and idempotency keys. The correct guarantee must live in shared storage, not in process memory.
prompt: Explain the difference between concurrency and parallelism in JavaScript. Then describe a race condition that can happen even in single threaded code, such as two requests spending the same balance, and how you would prevent it.

title: React Fundamentals for Interviews
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the fundamentals of React that interviewers ask again and again. We will cover JSX, elements and components, props, re renders, conditional rendering, keys, controlled inputs, composition, and events.

Let us start with JSX. It is syntax sugar for creating React elements. With the modern automatic runtime, the compiler imports a function from the React JSX runtime for you, and your tag becomes a function call that returns a plain object. Here is the key point. An element is a cheap, immutable description. Creating one does not render anything. Lowercase tags become strings, and capitalized tags become component references, which is why component names must start with a capital letter. The key is pulled out of props, so a child cannot read it. In React nineteen, ref is a normal prop for function components, so forward ref is no longer needed.

Components, elements, and instances. A component is a function that returns elements. An element is a plain object describing what to render. The long lived internal record for a mounted component is called a fiber, created by React. State lives on the fiber, not in your function. Your function is called again on every render, and hooks read state back by call order.

Props are the arguments a parent passes, and they are read only. A component must be pure with respect to its props, state, and context. Mutating props breaks memoization and concurrent rendering, which may call your component more than once. Children are props too, and that is the basis of composition.

What causes a re render? Exactly four things. First, the component's own state changes to a value that is not the same by Object dot is. Second, its parent re renders, unless it is memoized and props are shallow equal. Third, a context it reads changes. Fourth, an external store it subscribes to changes. A common misconception is that changing props causes a re render. The better framing is that a parent render causes the child to render, and a non memoized child renders even when props are identical.

Conditional rendering has a famous trap. Rendering items dot length followed by double ampersand and a list shows a zero when the list is empty. False, null, undefined, and true render nothing, but zero and NaN render as text. Always coerce to a boolean, for example by comparing length to zero.

Why do lists need keys? Keys give each child a stable identity among its siblings, so React can match old and new children. Index keys break when items are inserted, removed, or reordered, because identity follows position, and state like input text or focus sticks to the wrong row. Use index keys only for static lists with stateless rows. Never use random values, because every row remounts on each render. A senior follow up: keys also work outside lists. Giving a profile component a key equal to the user ID forces a full reset when the user changes. That is the idiomatic way to reset state, instead of syncing props into state with an effect.

Controlled versus uncontrolled inputs. A controlled input has React state as its source of truth, and re renders on each keystroke. It suits live validation and dependent fields. An uncontrolled input uses the DOM as its source, read through a ref or form data on submit, and it suits simple forms and file inputs. Traps: a value without an onChange makes a read only field. Switching a value from undefined to a string flips from uncontrolled to controlled and logs a warning, so start with an empty string.

Composition over inheritance. Pass components or elements as children or named slot props. Passing elements down, instead of data, is the first fix for prop drilling. Reach for context only after composition fails.

Finally, events. Since React seventeen, listeners attach to the root container. Event pooling is gone. On change fires on every keystroke. And since eighteen, updates in any handler, timeout, or promise are batched. Also remember: a parent does not call a child. It returns an element, and React decides when to call the child. Calling a component as a plain function breaks hooks.

To summarize in an interview: JSX makes element descriptions, state lives on fibers, renders come from state, parent, context, or store, keys are identity, and composition comes first.
passage:
JSX compiles to calls that create plain element objects, which are cheap descriptions and do not render anything. A component is a function that returns elements, while the state of a mounted component lives on an internal record called a fiber, and hooks read it back by call order. Props are read only, and a component must be pure with respect to its props, state, and context.

A component re renders in exactly four cases: its own state changes, its parent renders, a context it reads changes, or an external store it subscribes to changes. When rendering a number in a condition, the value zero is displayed as text, so conditions should be coerced to booleans.

Keys give list items a stable identity, and index keys cause state to attach to the wrong row when the list changes. A key can also be used to reset a component. Controlled inputs keep their value in React state, whereas uncontrolled inputs keep it in the DOM. Composition through children and slot props is preferred over inheritance and often removes the need for context.
prompt: Explain what causes a React component to re render and why a changed prop is not the real cause. Then explain why index keys are a problem in a list that can be reordered, and how a key can be used to reset state.

title: React Security and Production Readiness
shadowText:
Today we will talk about running React applications safely in production. We will cover cross site scripting, authentication patterns, secure API use, error monitoring, accessibility, and search engine optimization.

Let us start with XSS. React escapes strings that you render as children and attribute values, so ordinary rendering is safe. But XSS can still happen in several ways. The first is the dangerously set inner HTML property. If you render user written HTML, sanitize it with a library such as DOMPurify, ideally on the server, or prefer rendering Markdown into a safe tree. The second is links with a javascript colon address. If a link takes a user supplied address, allow only http, https, and mailto. React nineteen blocks javascript URLs and warns. The third is spreading untrusted props onto an element. Never spread user controlled objects. The fourth is server rendered pages that inline JSON containing a closing script tag. Serialize with proper escaping, and use a Content Security Policy with nonces as defense in depth. The fifth is writing inner HTML through a ref. Avoid it, or sanitize first.

Authentication and authorization patterns. For token storage, prefer HTTP only, secure, same site cookies set by the server, because JavaScript cannot read them. Tokens in local storage can be stolen by any XSS. For cookie based changes, add CSRF protection with same site settings and a token or origin check. Here is the key point. Client side guards are only user experience. Hiding a button or redirecting from a route does not protect data. The API, or the server function, must authorize every request.

A typical pattern is an auth provider that exposes the user and a status of loading, authenticated, or anonymous. Route guards render nothing, or a skeleton, while loading, to avoid flashing protected content. For authorization, check permissions rather than scattering role names through components, and centralize the rules in a policy module shared with the server. For token refresh, keep a single in flight refresh promise, queue requests during the refresh, log out when refresh fails, and sync logout across tabs using a broadcast channel or the storage event.

Secure API interactions. Never ship secrets in client bundles. Anything with a public prefix in Next or Vite environment variables is public. Validate input on the server with a schema library, even if the client validated. Use the server only package and server components for code that touches secrets. Rate limit and authorize server functions like any endpoint. Do not leak internal error messages. Log them on the server and return a safe message. And keep dependencies patched, using audit tools and automated update bots.

Error monitoring. Use error boundaries at the app, route, and widget level, with useful fallbacks such as retry or go home. Report errors through the root error callbacks in React nineteen, and through window error and unhandled rejection handlers, to a service like Sentry. Upload source maps privately, tag releases, and attach user and session context without personal data. Track real user monitoring for Core Web Vitals, which are largest contentful paint, interaction to next paint, and cumulative layout shift, per route. Use structured logs with correlation IDs that link frontend errors to backend traces, and feature flags for safe rollout and quick kill switches.

Accessibility is a production requirement. Start with semantic HTML, such as buttons, links, labels, and landmarks. Keep visible focus styles, manage focus on route changes and in dialogs, and announce async updates with live regions. Keep text contrast at least four point five to one, and respect the reduced motion preference. WCAG two point two level AA is the usual contractual bar.

For SEO, client only pages risk incomplete indexing and poor link previews, so use server rendering or static generation for public pages. React nineteen can render title, meta, and link tags anywhere in the tree and hoists them into the head. Use real anchor links, canonical URLs, structured data, and a fast largest contentful paint.

To summarize in an interview: React escapes by default, the dangers are raw HTML, URLs, prop spreading, and inline data, authorization lives on the server, and accessibility and SEO are not polish.
passage:
React escapes rendered strings, but cross site scripting can still occur through raw HTML rendering, user controlled link addresses, spreading untrusted props, inline server data, and direct writes to inner HTML. Defenses include sanitizing HTML, allowing only safe URL schemes, avoiding prop spreading of untrusted objects, and adding a Content Security Policy.

Tokens are safer in HTTP only, secure, same site cookies than in local storage, and cookie based mutations need CSRF protection. Client side route guards only improve the user experience, because the server must authorize every request. Secrets must never be placed in client bundles, and server inputs must be validated.

In production, error boundaries, root error callbacks, private source maps, and real user monitoring of Core Web Vitals help detect problems. Accessibility needs semantic HTML, focus management, sufficient contrast, and support for reduced motion. Public pages should be server rendered or statically generated so that they are indexed and previewed correctly.
prompt: Explain how React prevents XSS by default and name three ways it can still happen, with a defense for each. Then explain where you would store authentication tokens and why client side route guards are not security.

title: React State and Effect Traps, Part One
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the first set of tricky React questions. They all test whether you understand that state is a snapshot, that effects capture values, and that identity matters.

Let us start with three setters and a log. A click handler calls set count with count plus one, three times, and then logs count. What is logged and what does the button show? It logs zero, and the button shows one. In this render, count is a constant zero in the closure. Each call enqueues replace with one, so the queue holds one, one, one. The log reads the closure's zero, because setters never change the local variable. After the handler, React batches and renders once, giving one. To get three, use updater functions, where each receives the previous queued result.

Mixing values and updaters. Starting from zero, add one with an updater, then set five, then add one with an updater. The result is six. Updates apply in order, and a plain value discards everything queued before it.

Mutating state in place. A user object has a tags array. A handler pushes a tag into the array, then calls set user with the same object. Does the UI update? Usually not. React compares with Object dot is, sees the same reference, and bails out. The mutation happened, but nothing re renders. If something else re renders later, the tag suddenly appears, which makes the bug intermittent. React never deep compares state. The fix is to create a new object and a new array.

The stale alert. A click handler schedules an alert in three seconds, showing the count. You click it, then increase the count three times. The alert says zero. The timeout closed over the render where count was zero. Is this a bug? Not necessarily. It may be correct, the count when I clicked. If you need the latest value, read it from a ref updated in an effect.

The stuck interval. An effect with an empty dependency array starts an interval that calls set count with count plus one. The counter shows one and stays there. The effect ran once with count equal to zero, so every tick sets one. The fix is the updater form, which needs no dependency. Adding count as a dependency works, but recreates the interval every second.

The infinite effect loop has three versions. One: no dependency array, and the effect sets state. It runs after every commit. Two: an object created during render is a dependency, and the effect fetches and sets items. A new object each render means the effect runs each time, and each result is a new array, so state changes and it repeats. That is even a network loop. Three: the same with a function. Fixes: depend on primitive values and build the object inside the effect, move the function inside, or use memoization as a last resort. Better still, use a query library.

A memo that never memoizes. A memoized child receives an inline click handler and an inline style object. Each parent render creates new references, so the shallow comparison fails, and the child renders every time. Fix it with callback memoization, hoist constants outside the component, or use the React Compiler. The same trap applies to children elements. Likewise, a memoized value that depends on a freshly created array never caches.

Index keys and stateful rows. Two items, B and C, each with an input. You type hello in B's input, then prepend A. Where does hello appear? Next to A. React matches by key, so key zero's input is reused with the new label A, and a fresh empty input is created at the end. The fix is to use the item ID as the key.

Resetting state from props. An edit form initializes state from a user prop. When the selected user changes from Ada to Grace, the input still shows Ada. The initial value is used only on mount, and the component is at the same position, so state persists. Fix it with a key equal to the user ID. An effect that copies props into state renders a stale frame first and can overwrite edits.

To summarize in an interview: state is a snapshot, updaters chain, mutation is invisible, closures capture their render, objects created in render break dependencies, and keys control identity.
passage:
In React, state is a snapshot for each render, so a handler that calls the setter several times with the current value queues the same replacement repeatedly, and a log shows the old value. Updater functions chain on the previous queued result, and a plain value discards earlier queued updates.

Mutating state in place and passing the same reference causes React to bail out, because it compares with Object dot is and never deep compares. Closures capture the values of their render, so a timer shows the count from when it was created, and an interval with an empty dependency array gets stuck unless it uses the updater form.

Objects and functions created during render are new on every render, so they cause effects to loop and defeat memoization. Index keys move DOM state to the wrong row when items are added in front. State initialized from props does not change when the prop changes, and the idiomatic reset is to give the component a key based on the identity of the data.
prompt: A click handler calls setCount with count plus one three times and then logs count. Explain what is logged, what the button shows, and why. Then show how updater functions change the result.

title: React State and Effect Traps, Part Two
shadowText:
Today we will talk about the second set of tricky React questions. They cover context and memo, controlled inputs, Strict Mode, mutation during render, hydration, races, and refs.

Let us start with context and memo. A provider passes an object containing the theme, built inline, and a counter changes in the same parent. A middle component is memoized and has no props. A leaf component reads the context. When the counter changes, does the leaf re render? Yes. The parent re renders and builds a new context object, so the value has changed by Object dot is. The memoized middle component is skipped. But React still finds every component below the provider that reads the context and schedules it directly. So memo on the middle does not protect the leaf. Memo compares props only, and context updates bypass it. The fix is to memoize the value, or pass a primitive such as the theme string.

Controlled input traps. A value without an onChange gives a read only field and a warning. A value taken from async user data is undefined at first, so the input starts uncontrolled and later becomes controlled, with a warning. Fix it with a fallback to an empty string.

Strict Mode double effects. In development, with Strict Mode, an effect that logs subscribe and returns a cleanup that logs unsubscribe shows subscribe, unsubscribe, subscribe on mount. React simulates an unmount and a remount to prove that the effect is resilient. In production, only subscribe. It is not a React bug, and removing Strict Mode is the wrong fix. The double run reveals effects that would break on real remounts, such as fast refresh or navigating back. Using a ref flag to run once just hides real bugs.

Mutating props during render. A parent holds players in join order. One list component shows join order. A leaderboard component sorts the players array in place. What does the join order list show after a refresh? The score order. The in place sort changed the parent's state array. Nothing re rendered at first, so the bug was invisible. After a refresh, the same sorted array is passed down. Strict Mode would not catch it, because sorting twice gives the same result. And React freezes only the props object in development, not the arrays inside. The fix is to use a copying method such as to sorted, or copy before sorting. The rule is that render must not mutate anything that existed before the render started.

Hydration mismatch. A footer renders the current time. With server rendering, the server and the client render different times, so React reports a mismatch. The boundary falls back to client rendering, which loses the server rendering benefit and may cause layout shift. Fixes: render the time after mount in an effect, use the suppress hydration warning attribute if the difference is acceptable, or format on the server with a fixed time zone and pass the string.

Fetch race on fast prop changes. A profile effect fetches a user whenever the user ID changes. ID one starts a slow request of eight hundred milliseconds. Then ID two starts a fast request. The fast one finishes and sets user two. Then the slow one finishes and overwrites it with user one. The wrong user is shown. Fix it with an ignore flag or an abort controller in the cleanup. React runs your cleanup, but it cannot cancel promises you started.

A component defined inside a component. An input component is declared inside a form component. Each render creates a new function, which is a new component type, so React unmounts and remounts the input on every keystroke, and focus is lost. Declare components at module level.

Refs do not render. Incrementing a ref on click does not schedule a render, so the button still shows zero. Use state for anything displayed.

Callback memoization with empty dependencies freezes the state it uses. Adding three items with a callback that spreads the old items list results in one item, because the list is stuck at empty. Use the updater form.

Layout effect versus effect. A tooltip measures its height in a normal effect and then sets its position. The user sees a jump, because it first paints at the top and then moves. Use the layout effect, so measuring and the re render happen before paint.

To summarize in an interview: context bypasses memo, Strict Mode exposes missing cleanup, render must stay pure, async work needs cleanup, and measuring before paint needs a layout effect.
passage:
Context updates bypass memoization, because memo compares only props. If a provider creates a new value object on each render, every consumer below it re renders, even when a memoized parent is skipped. Memoizing the value or passing a primitive avoids this.

Strict Mode runs effects twice in development to expose missing cleanup, and the fix is to correct the cleanup instead of removing the check. Render must not mutate existing data, such as sorting a state array in place, because the bug can stay invisible until another render. Time dependent output causes hydration mismatches, which are fixed by rendering such values after mount.

Effects that fetch must clean up, using an ignore flag or an abort controller, otherwise the slowest response can overwrite the newest one. Components declared inside other components are recreated on every render, which remounts them and loses focus. Refs do not trigger renders, callback memoization with empty dependencies freezes state, and measurements that affect layout belong in a layout effect to avoid flicker.
prompt: Explain why a memoized middle component does not stop a context consumer from re rendering when the provider value is a new object. Then explain how you would fix a fetch effect that sometimes shows the wrong user when the ID changes quickly.

title: React Hooks Deep Dive
shadowText:
Today we will talk about React hooks in depth. We will cover the rules of hooks, state, effects, layout effects, refs, reducers, memoization, context, and a few newer hooks.

Let us start with the rules. Call hooks only at the top level, not inside conditions, loops, nested functions, or after an early return. And call them only from components or custom hooks. Why? On each render, React walks an ordered list of hook slots. If the first render calls state, effect, state, and the second skips the effect, then the second state call reads the effect's slot. State gets corrupted, and React throws an error about rendering fewer or more hooks. There is one exception in React nineteen. The use function can be called conditionally and in loops.

useState. Using a direct value versus an updater is a favorite question. If you call set count with count plus one three times, all three queue the same replacement, and you get one. Count is a constant captured by this render. Setters do not mutate it. They enqueue updates processed on the next render. Use the updater whenever the next value depends on the previous one. Also, a lazy initializer, which is a function passed to useState, runs only once. If you pass the result of a function call instead, it runs on every render and the result is thrown away. And setting the same value, by Object dot is, usually skips re rendering the children.

useEffect. Effects synchronize a component with an external system: network, subscriptions, timers, DOM APIs, and non React widgets. The effect runs after paint, usually, and does not block the browser. Cleanup runs before the next effect run, with the old values, and on unmount. Dependencies are compared with Object dot is. No array means every commit. An empty array means mount only, and in development Strict Mode that becomes mount, cleanup, mount. You probably do not need an effect when you are deriving data from props or state, because you can compute it during render. You do not need one for responding to a user event, because you use the handler. And for resetting state when a prop changes, use a key.

useLayoutEffect versus useEffect. The layout effect runs after DOM changes but before paint, synchronously, and it blocks paint. Use it for measuring layout and positioning tooltips, to avoid flicker. The normal effect is for data, subscriptions, and logging. If you set state inside a layout effect, React re renders synchronously before paint, so the user never sees the intermediate frame. There is also a special insertion effect, only for CSS in JS libraries.

useRef returns a stable mutable box that persists across renders. Changing its current value does not trigger a render. Use it for DOM nodes, timer IDs, previous values, and any instance value that the interface does not display. Do not read or write the current value during render, except for lazy initialization, because it makes rendering impure. In React nineteen, a callback ref can return a cleanup function.

useReducer is better when the next state depends on several fields, many event types update the same state, or you want transitions testable as a pure function. Seniors like it because dispatch is stable, so you can pass it through context without causing re renders.

useMemo caches a value, and useCallback caches a function. They help in three cases: the calculation is measurably expensive, the value is passed to a memoized child, or it is a dependency of another hook. They cost memory and readability, and they are hints, not guarantees. With the React Compiler enabled, most manual memoization becomes unnecessary, and interviewers increasingly ask about that.

useContext reads the nearest provider's value. When it changes, every consumer re renders, even through memoized parents. In React nineteen you can render the context object directly as a provider.

useId generates an ID that is stable across server and client, so it is safe for hydration. Use it for label and aria links, but not for list keys.

useEffectEvent, stable in nineteen point two, solves the problem of needing the latest value inside an effect without re running the effect. Call effect events only from inside effects, never pass them to other components, and do not list them as dependencies.

To summarize in an interview: hooks are ordered slots, state is a snapshot, effects are for external systems, and updaters, reducers, and effect events fix most stale value problems.
passage:
Hooks must be called at the top level of components or custom hooks, in the same order on every render, because React stores them as an ordered list of slots. Calling them conditionally corrupts state. The use function in React nineteen is the exception.

With useState, the setter queues an update for the next render, so an updater function should be used when the next value depends on the previous one, and a lazy initializer avoids repeated expensive work. Effects synchronize a component with external systems, run after paint, and clean up before re running and on unmount. Derived data, event responses, and state resets usually do not need effects.

The layout effect runs before paint and is used to measure layout without flicker. Refs hold mutable values that do not trigger renders and should not be read during render. A reducer suits state with many transitions. Memoization hooks are performance hints and are largely replaced by the React Compiler. The effect event hook gives effects access to the latest values without re running them.
prompt: Explain the Rules of Hooks and why they exist, then describe when you would use useEffect and when you would not. Give two examples of things that do not need an effect.

title: Custom Hooks, Stale Closures and Rendering
shadowText:
Today we will talk about more hooks, stale closures, and how React renders. We will cover the use hook, other hooks to recognize, custom hooks, the stale closure model, the render and commit phases, the virtual DOM, reconciliation, Fiber, and batching.

Let us start with the use function in React nineteen. It reads a promise or a context during render. With a promise, the component suspends until it resolves. The nearest Suspense boundary shows the fallback, and the nearest error boundary catches rejections. The promise must be cached or stable, for example created in a server component, a loader, or a cache. Creating a new promise inside the same component's render causes an infinite suspend loop.

Other hooks to recognize: use transition marks updates as non urgent and gives a pending flag. Use deferred value renders with a lagging copy of a value. Use sync external store subscribes to an external store without tearing. Use imperative handle exposes a custom ref API. Use action state, use form status, and use optimistic support forms and actions. Use debug value labels hooks in dev tools.

A custom hook is a function that starts with use and calls other hooks. It shares logic, not state. Each component that calls it gets its own state. Good custom hooks have a focused purpose, such as online status, not a vague name like use mount. They return stable references, clean up everything they start, and document server behavior.

Now the core mental model for dependencies and stale closures. Every render creates new functions that capture that render's props and state. An effect, timeout, or callback created in render N sees render N's values forever. That is a stale closure when it outlives render N. A classic example is an interval that calls set count with count plus one and has an empty dependency array. The count is always zero, so the display is stuck at one. The fixes, in order of preference: use an updater, move logic into a reducer and dispatch, use an effect event, or add the dependency honestly, accepting that the interval restarts. Never silence the exhaustive dependencies lint rule. If a dependency seems wrong, change the code so it is no longer needed.

Now rendering internals. What are the render and commit phases? First, a trigger, such as the initial render or a state update, schedules work on a priority lane. Second, the render phase. React calls components from where the update happened, building a work in progress tree and diffing it with the current one. This phase must be pure, with no DOM writes and no subscriptions, because in concurrent mode React can pause, resume, restart, or throw work away. Third, the commit phase, which is synchronous and uninterruptible. It does the DOM mutations, detaches and attaches refs, and runs layout effects. Then the browser paints. Then passive effects run, which are the normal effects. Rendering can be thrown away and redone, but committing cannot, which is why render must be pure.

Is the virtual DOM faster than the DOM? Not inherently. It is a tree of elements that describes the interface. React diffs the new description against the old and applies minimal DOM operations. Its value is a declarative model with good enough performance, and a layer where React can schedule, batch, and prioritize. Frameworks like Svelte and Solid show that fine grained reactivity can skip diffing altogether. That is a good senior talking point.

Reconciliation uses two heuristics to get linear time instead of cubic. Different element types produce different trees, so changing a div to a section, or one component type to another, unmounts the old subtree and destroys its state. And keys identify children across renders. Same type at the same position keeps the fiber and its state. State is tied to position in the tree. A classic bug is defining a component inside another component, which creates a new type on every render and remounts it.

Fiber is the reconciler architecture introduced in React sixteen. Each fiber is an object for one component with pointers, props, the hook list, effect flags, priorities, and an alternate copy. The old stack reconciler recursed synchronously, so a big update could block the main thread. Fiber turns recursion into a loop over a linked list, so React can stop after any unit of work and yield to the browser. It uses double buffering, where the current tree is on screen and a work in progress tree is built off screen. Lanes are priorities, so urgent work can interrupt low priority work.

Finally, automatic batching. Since React eighteen, multiple state updates in the same tick are batched into one render, in event handlers, promises, timeouts, and native listeners. That is why logging state right after a setter shows the old value. To opt out, rarely, use flush sync.

To summarize in an interview: closures capture their render, render is pure and interruptible, commit is atomic, and Fiber makes it all possible.
passage:
The use function in React nineteen reads a promise or a context during render. A promise makes the component suspend until it resolves, and it must be stable or cached, otherwise it causes an endless suspend loop. A custom hook is a function that calls other hooks and shares logic, not state, so each caller gets its own state.

Every render creates functions that capture that render's props and state, so effects and timers that outlive a render see stale values. The preferred fixes are updater functions, reducers, and effect events, and the dependency lint rule should never be silenced.

React works in a render phase and a commit phase. The render phase must be pure, because it can be paused, restarted, or discarded, while the commit phase applies DOM changes atomically and cannot be interrupted. Reconciliation matches elements by type and key, and state is tied to position in the tree. Fiber replaced recursion with an interruptible loop and priority lanes, and since React eighteen, updates in the same tick are batched into one render.
prompt: Explain the stale closure problem using an interval that increments a counter, and list the fixes in order of preference. Then explain why the render phase must be pure while the commit phase is atomic.

title: Concurrent React, Suspense and Boundaries
shadowText:
Today we will talk about advanced React features. We will cover concurrent rendering, transitions, Strict Mode, scheduling, context performance, portals, refs, error boundaries, Suspense, and lazy loading.

Let us start with concurrent rendering. It means React can prepare multiple versions of the interface and interrupt a render in progress. It is not multithreading. It is cooperative scheduling on the main thread, and React yields roughly every five milliseconds. You opt in per update through start transition, use transition, use deferred value, or Suspense. Everything else stays urgent. There are consequences. Components may render more than once before committing, so keep render pure. Reading mutable external sources during render can tear, so use the sync external store hook. And work in progress may be thrown away, so no side effects in render.

Use transition versus use deferred value. With use transition, you own the state setter. You wrap the update, such as setting the active tab, in start transition, so a heavy render stays interruptible, and you get a pending flag. With use deferred value, you wrap the value, which is useful when it comes from props or a parent. You compare the value with the deferred one to know it is pending. For a text input, never wrap the input's own state. Defer the expensive consumer instead. Here is the key insight. Transitions do not make code faster. They keep the interface responsive by letting urgent updates, like typing, interrupt non urgent ones, like re rendering ten thousand rows. The slow list must be memoized for use deferred value to help. In React nineteen, start transition accepts async functions, called actions, and the pending flag stays true until they settle.

What does Strict Mode do? It is development only. It double invokes component bodies, initializers, reducers, and updater functions to expose impure logic. It mounts, unmounts, and remounts effects to expose missing cleanup. It double invokes ref callbacks. And it warns about deprecated APIs. If you see two fetches on mount in development, your effect lacks proper cleanup or cancellation, and that is the point.

How does React schedule work? The reconciler asks the scheduler package for time slices using a message channel, not request idle callback, which fires too rarely. The work loop does units of work until it should yield, and then returns control to the browser. Urgent discrete events skip yielding.

Now context performance. A consumer re renders when the nearest provider's value changes by Object dot is, regardless of memo on parents between them. Problems and fixes: a value object created inline makes all consumers re render, so memoize the value. One big context re renders everyone on any field change, so split contexts, for example state from dispatch, or theme from auth. High frequency values like mouse position or keystrokes should use a store with selectors. Context has no selectors, which is its core limitation. Rule of thumb: context is dependency injection for low frequency values, like theme, locale, the current user, and feature flags. It is not a state manager.

Portals render children into a different DOM node, often the body, to escape overflow and stacking problems for modals, tooltips, and toasts. The trap: events bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree. A click in a portaled modal bubbles to the React parent's click handler. Context also flows through portals.

Refs. In React nineteen, ref is a regular prop. With use imperative handle you expose a narrow handle, such as play and pause, only for actions that state cannot express.

Error boundaries catch errors during render, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of descendants, and then show a fallback. They do not catch errors in event handlers, async code, server rendering, or the boundary itself. There is still no hook based boundary, so you write a class or use a library. React nineteen adds root options for caught, uncaught, and recoverable errors for central reporting.

Suspense lets a component wait and declares the loading interface at a boundary. Things that can suspend include lazy components, the use hook with a cached promise, and Suspense aware libraries and frameworks. Siblings inside one boundary reveal together, and nested boundaries reveal outside in. If an already visible boundary suspends during a transition, React keeps the old interface instead of showing a fallback.

For lazy loading, declare lazy at module top level, because declaring it inside a component resets state every render. The module needs a default export. Split at route level first, and preload on hover or intent.

To summarize in an interview: concurrent rendering is interruptible scheduling, transitions keep input responsive, context is for low frequency values, and boundaries decide what users see on errors and loading.
passage:
Concurrent rendering lets React prepare several versions of the interface and interrupt a render in progress. It is cooperative scheduling on the main thread, not multithreading, and it requires pure rendering. Transitions and deferred values keep urgent updates such as typing responsive by letting them interrupt non urgent work, but they do not make code faster.

Strict Mode in development double invokes render logic and re runs effects to expose impurity and missing cleanup. Context consumers re render whenever the provider value changes, even through memoized parents, so values should be memoized, contexts split, and high frequency data placed in a store with selectors.

Portals render into another DOM node while events still bubble through the React tree. Error boundaries catch errors during render, lifecycle methods, and constructors, but not in event handlers or asynchronous code. Suspense declares loading states at boundaries, and lazy loading splits code, with the lazy declaration placed at module level so state is not reset.
prompt: Explain the difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue, and why transitions do not make code faster. Then explain what error boundaries catch and what they do not.

title: React Patterns and Newer Features
shadowText:
Today we will talk about React component patterns, a few newer features, and legacy class lifecycles that some interviewers still ask about.

Let us start with compound components. These are components that share implicit state through context, and give consumers a flexible, declarative API. A tabs component, for example, holds the selected value, and provides a list, a trigger, and a panel as parts. Consumers control layout and markup without a giant prop API, where you would pass an array of labels, contents, icons, and disabled flags. Libraries like Radix and React Aria use this pattern.

HOCs, render props, and hooks. A higher order component wraps another component, such as with auth. It is good for cross cutting concerns at boundaries, but can cause wrapper hell, prop name collisions, and opaque trees. A render prop passes a function as a child. It gives explicit data flow but can create nesting pyramids. A custom hook is composable, explicit, and adds no extra tree nodes, but it can only share logic, not markup. The modern default is hooks for logic and components for markup. Higher order components are still fine for route guards or instrumentation, and render props still help when a library must hand back render time data, as in virtualizers.

The controlled or uncontrolled pattern. Reusable components should support both modes, like native inputs. A helper hook keeps an internal state and uses the value from props when it is defined. Do not switch between modes during a component's lifetime, and warn in development if the value flips between defined and undefined.

The Activity component, stable in nineteen point two. When its mode is hidden, it hides a subtree while preserving its state and DOM, unmounting its effects, and rendering updates at low priority. Use it for tabs, back navigation, and pre rendering likely next screens. Compared with conditionally rendering a tab, scroll position and input state survive tab switches. Compared with hiding with CSS, effects like subscriptions and timers are cleaned up while hidden.

View Transition and Fragment refs, stable in nineteen point three. The View Transition component wraps the browser's View Transition API. It animates its children as they enter, exit, or update, but only when the change happens inside a transition, such as start transition, use deferred value, or a Suspense reveal. A plain urgent state update does not animate. You can label a transition with a type, such as forward or back, to apply different animation classes. Fragment refs let you attach a ref to a fragment and work with its DOM children as a group, without adding a wrapper div that would break flex or grid layouts. The interview angle: before this, you would say add a wrapper div or use a ref per child. For animations, the old answer was a library or manual browser calls. Now React coordinates it with transitions and Suspense.

Now class lifecycles, which are legacy but still asked. On mount: constructor, get derived state from props, render, DOM commit, then component did mount. On update: get derived state from props, should component update, render, get snapshot before update, DOM commit, then component did update. On unmount: component will unmount. For errors: get derived state from error to render a fallback, and component did catch to log.

The hook equivalents. Constructor and state map to use state with a lazy initializer. Component did mount maps to an effect with an empty array, and Strict Mode runs it twice in development. Component did update maps to an effect with dependencies. Component will unmount maps to effect cleanup, which also runs before each re run. Should component update and pure component map to memo, or the React Compiler. Get derived state from props is usually replaced by computing during render, or resetting with a key. Get snapshot before update has no direct hook. The closest is a layout effect with a ref, for example preserving scroll position in a chat list. And error boundaries still need a class, or a library.

Traps: the set state callback runs after commit, like an effect. The unsafe will mount, will receive props, and will update methods are deprecated, because they run in the render phase, which concurrent rendering may repeat. And forgetting to bind methods makes this undefined in handlers.

Two follow ups. Does an error boundary catch an error from an effect? Yes, because effects run as part of the commit lifecycle. Errors inside an async callback started by the effect do not. And can you lazy load a named export? Only by mapping it to the default export.

To summarize in an interview: I prefer compound components and hooks, I know the new Activity and View Transition features, and I can map class lifecycles to hooks.
passage:
Compound components share implicit state through context, giving consumers flexible markup without a large prop API, and libraries such as Radix use this pattern. Hooks are now the default for sharing logic, while higher order components and render props remain useful for route guards, instrumentation, and libraries that hand back render time data.

Reusable components should support both controlled and uncontrolled use, without switching between modes during their lifetime. The Activity component hides a subtree while preserving its state and DOM and cleaning up its effects, which suits tabs and back navigation. The View Transition component animates changes that occur inside transitions, and Fragment refs allow working with a group of children without a wrapper element.

Class lifecycles map to hooks: component did mount to an effect with an empty array, component did update to an effect with dependencies, will unmount to cleanup, and should component update to memo. Error boundaries still require a class or a library, and the legacy unsafe lifecycle methods are deprecated because concurrent rendering can repeat the render phase.
prompt: Compare higher order components, render props and custom hooks for sharing logic in React. Say which one you choose by default and name one case where each of the others is still a good choice.

title: React State Management Choices
shadowText:
Today we will talk about state management in React. The key question is not which library to use, but where each kind of state should live.

Let us start with how to decide. Go through the kinds of state, and stop at the first yes. Local interface state, like a dropdown being open or input text, belongs in useState in the component. State shared by siblings, like a selected row and a detail panel, is lifted to the nearest common parent. Shareable or bookmarkable state, like filters, sort, page, and tab, belongs in the URL search parameters. Low frequency app wide values, like theme, locale, and the current user, belong in context. High frequency or complex client state, like an editor, a cart, a canvas, or a wizard, belongs in a store such as Zustand, Redux Toolkit, or Jotai. Server data, like users, orders, and products, belongs in a query library, a framework loader, or server components. Form state belongs in a form library, or in uncontrolled inputs with actions. And derived values like totals and filtered lists are not state at all. Compute them in render. Most state in a typical app ends in the first four answers. The principle is state colocation: keep state as close as possible to where it is used. Lifting too high makes everything re render and couples unrelated components.

Why is duplicated or derived state a bug? Imagine keeping the items in one state, the total in another, and an effect that updates the total when items change. There are two sources of truth that can drift, plus an extra render. Compute the total during render. Store IDs, not copies of objects.

Context versus a state library. Context has no selector, so every consumer re renders when the value changes. With frequent updates or large trees, that becomes the bottleneck. Stores built on the sync external store hook let each component subscribe to a slice and re render only when that slice changes.

Redux Toolkit is the official modern way to write Redux. It gives you configure store, create slice with Immer powered reducers that look like mutation, async thunks, entity adapters, and RTK Query for server state. Choose Redux when large teams need strict conventions, you want time travel debugging and an action log, many features read and write shared client state, or middleware such as undo, sync, and analytics matters. Watch the selector trap: a selector that filters and returns a new array each time causes a re render on every store change. Use a memoized selector, or return primitives.

Zustand is popular because it is a tiny store with hooks and selectors, no provider, and no boilerplate. The trade offs: less structure than Redux, so teams must agree conventions, and global module stores need care with server rendering. In Next, create a store per request and provide it through context. Others to name are Jotai, which is atomic, Valtio, which is proxy based, MobX, which is observable, and XState for explicit state machines.

Server state versus client state. Server state is a cache of data you do not own. It can go stale, be changed by others, and needs deduplication, retries, background refresh, pagination, and invalidation. Putting it in Redux or useState means rebuilding all of that. A query library handles it with key concepts: query keys as cache identity, stale time for how long data is fresh, garbage collection time for how long unused data stays cached, invalidation after mutations, refetch on focus or reconnect, and request deduplication.

Optimistic updates. Update the interface before the server confirms, then reconcile. On mutate, cancel in flight queries so they do not overwrite you, snapshot the previous data, and apply the change. On error, roll back. On settle, refetch. React nineteen's use optimistic hook does this at component level. Risks include rollback flicker, conflicting concurrent mutations, irreversible actions like payments, which should never be optimistic, and silent rollbacks that confuse users, so always show an error.

Finally, immutability. React detects change with Object dot is, and memo does shallow comparison. Mutating keeps the same reference, so React skips the render. Use spread for objects, spread or filter or map for arrays, to sorted for sorting, or Immer.

To summarize in an interview: classify the state first, never store derived values, use a query library for server data, and use a selector based store when context is not enough.
passage:
State should be classified before choosing a tool. Local interface state stays in useState, shared state is lifted to the nearest common parent, shareable state goes into the URL, low frequency app wide values go into context, complex or high frequency client state goes into a store, server data goes into a query library, and derived values are computed during render instead of being stored. Keeping state close to where it is used avoids needless re renders.

Context has no selectors, so every consumer re renders on any change, whereas stores built on the sync external store hook let components subscribe to slices. Redux Toolkit suits large teams that want strict conventions, while Zustand offers a lightweight store without boilerplate.

Server state is a cache of data the client does not own and needs keys, staleness rules, invalidation, and deduplication, which query libraries provide. Optimistic updates show the result before the server confirms, with rollback on error, but they are unsuitable for irreversible actions such as payments. React requires immutable updates because it detects change by reference.
prompt: Walk me through how you decide where each kind of state lives in a React app. Include local state, URL state, context, a client store, and server state, and explain why derived values should not be stored.

title: React Forms and Data Fetching
shadowText:
Today we will talk about forms and data fetching in React. We will cover form state, React nineteen actions, optimistic updates, fetch races, fetching patterns, loading states, and form libraries.

Let us start with form state and validation. There are three tiers, in order of complexity. First, uncontrolled inputs with form data and native validation, using attributes like required, email type, and pattern. This is the smallest and fastest option, and it works with React nineteen form actions and progressive enhancement. Second, controlled inputs with state or a reducer, for live validation, dependent fields, and formatting masks. Third, a form library. React Hook Form is uncontrolled first, with few re renders. TanStack Form is type safe and headless. Formik is older, controlled, and re renders more. Pair a library with a schema validator, like Zod, Valibot, or Yup, and share the schema with the server.

Validation experience rules: for most fields, validate on blur or on submit, not on every keystroke. After the first error, re validate on change. Show errors next to fields, with aria invalid and aria described by. Focus the first invalid field on submit. And always re validate on the server.

React nineteen actions. An action is an async function run in a transition. When you pass a function to a form's action attribute, React handles the pending state, errors, and form reset. The use action state hook gives you the last returned state, such as an error message, a wrapped action, and a pending flag. Facts interviewers check: the use form status hook must be called in a component rendered inside the form, not in the component that renders the form. Uncontrolled fields reset automatically after a successful form action. With a server function as the action, as in Next dot js, the form submits even before JavaScript loads. And actions are queued sequentially per use action state.

Use optimistic. You give it the real list and a function that produces the optimistic list, for example adding a message marked as sending. The optimistic value lives only while the action is pending. Afterward, React renders the real messages. If the parent did not update them, the item disappears, and that is your rollback.

Fetching in an effect correctly. Here is the race. The user types re, then react. The request for re resolves after the request for react and overwrites the correct results. The fix: create an abort controller in the effect, pass its signal to the request, abort in the cleanup, and ignore abort errors. Why both abort and ignore? Aborting saves bandwidth, and the error check ensures no stale write. If the API cannot be aborted, use an ignore flag set in cleanup. A senior answer adds that effect based fetching has no caching, no deduplication, and creates waterfalls, where a parent fetches, renders a child, and the child fetches. In production, prefer a framework loader, server components, or a query library.

Data fetching patterns compared. Fetch on render in an effect is simple but has waterfalls, races, no cache, and spinner soup. Fetch then render with a route loader avoids waterfalls and runs in parallel, but the whole route waits for the slowest request. Render as you fetch with Suspense starts the fetch early and reads with the use hook, giving parallel and progressive reveal, but needs a cache or framework. Server components fetch on the server during render, with no client JavaScript for data and streaming, but need a framework. A query library gives caching, deduplication, retries, and stale while revalidate, but is another dependency.

Loading and error states that do not lie. Model status explicitly as a union of idle, loading, success, and error, not three booleans that can disagree. Distinguish the initial load, which gets a skeleton, from a refetch, where you keep data and show a subtle indicator. An empty state is not an error, and an error state should offer retry. Avoid spinner flash by delaying the spinner or using transitions. Layout stable skeletons prevent layout shift.

To summarize in an interview: start uncontrolled, add control only when needed, validate on both sides, clean up every fetch effect, and prefer loaders, server components, or a query library.
passage:
Form state can be handled in three tiers: uncontrolled inputs with form data and native validation, controlled inputs for live validation and dependent fields, and a form library such as React Hook Form paired with a schema validator shared with the server. Validation should usually happen on blur or submit, with accessible error messages, and it must always be repeated on the server.

React nineteen actions are async functions run in a transition, and passing one to a form action lets React manage pending state, errors, and resets. The form status hook must be used in a child of the form, and the optimistic hook shows a temporary value that disappears if the real data is not updated.

A fetch in an effect needs an abort controller or an ignore flag in its cleanup, otherwise a slow older response can overwrite a newer one. Effect based fetching also lacks caching and creates waterfalls, so loaders, server components, or query libraries are preferred. Loading state should be modeled as a union of statuses, keeping stale data visible during refetches.
prompt: Explain the race condition when fetching in useEffect as a user types a search query, and how you fix it with an abort controller. Then say why effect based fetching is not what you would choose in production.

title: React Performance Optimization
shadowText:
Today we will talk about React performance. The golden rule is to measure first, and to try cheaper fixes before you reach for memoization.

Let us start with finding out why a component re renders. Use the React DevTools profiler and enable the option to record why each component rendered. Look at the flame graph for components that are wide, which means slow, and frequent, which means many commits. In Chrome's performance panel, React nineteen point two adds performance tracks, so you can see React's scheduler and components work next to browser work. For a quick check, use a console count in the component, or the Profiler component with an on render callback. In production, measure interaction to next paint and largest contentful paint with real user monitoring, not just development profiles.

How does React memo work, and when does it fail? Memo skips re rendering when props are shallow equal, using Object dot is for each prop. It silently fails when a parent passes inline objects or arrays, such as a style object or a filtered list. It fails with inline functions, such as an arrow function click handler. And it fails with children, because JSX creates a new element object every render. The fix is to memoize callbacks and values, so references are stable. A custom comparator is possible, but risky, because forgetting a prop causes stale interfaces.

Now the cheaper fixes before memoization. First, move state down. If typing in an input re renders an expensive chart because both live in the same parent, move the input and its state into a small component of its own. Second, lift content up. Pass slow subtrees as children. A scroll tracker component that updates state on scroll can render its children without re rendering them, because the children were created by the parent and keep the same element reference.

What does the React Compiler change? It is stable at version one point zero, a build time plugin that works with React seventeen and later, best with nineteen. It analyzes components and hooks, and automatically memoizes values, callbacks, and JSX at a finer grain than you would by hand. It requires code that follows the Rules of React: pure render, no mutation of props or state, and no reading refs in render. Violations make it skip that component. A lint plugin flags these violations, and you can opt a component out with a directive. Existing memo hooks can stay, but new code needs far fewer. The interview framing: the compiler removes re render cost, not render cost. A genuinely slow component, with ten thousand rows or heavy calculations, still needs virtualization, better algorithms, or moving work to the server.

Virtualization. Rendering ten thousand DOM rows costs memory, layout, and paint. Virtualization renders only the visible rows plus some overscan, and uses spacing for the rest. A library such as TanStack Virtual helps. The trade offs: find in page cannot find off screen rows, screen readers see a partial list, so use row count and row index attributes, dynamic heights need measurement, and sticky headers and keyboard focus need care. Alternatives are pagination, a load more button, or the CSS content visibility property.

Bundle size and code splitting. Analyze with a bundle analyzer or source map explorer. Split by route first, then by heavy, rarely used widgets such as editors, charts, and maps. Prefer ES modules and tree shakeable libraries, and import narrowly. Move non interactive interface to server components, which ship zero client JavaScript. Preload on intent, prefetch likely next routes, and set a performance budget in continuous integration.

Avoiding unnecessary effects. Every effect that sets state causes an extra render pass and a frame of stale interface. Instead of an effect that filters items into state, derive the filtered list during render, memoizing it if it is expensive.

Keeping interactions responsive. Wrap expensive non urgent updates in start transition. Use deferred value with memo for expensive consumers of fast input. Break long tasks, and move heavy computation to a web worker. Debounce or throttle high frequency events. And avoid layout thrashing by batching DOM reads before writes.

To summarize in an interview: profile first, move state down and lift content up, know why memo fails, use the compiler where possible, and virtualize or split what is genuinely big.
passage:
React performance work should begin with measurement, using the DevTools profiler with the option to record why each component rendered, browser performance tools, and real user monitoring of interaction to next paint. React memo skips rendering when props are shallow equal, and it fails when parents pass inline objects, inline functions, or children, because those create new references on every render.

Cheaper fixes come first: move fast changing state down into a small component, and lift slow content up by passing it as children so that its element reference stays the same. The React Compiler automatically memoizes values and callbacks, but it removes re render cost and not render cost, so slow components still need better algorithms, virtualization, or server work.

Virtualization renders only the visible rows of long lists, with trade offs for find in page and accessibility. Bundles are reduced by route based splitting, narrow imports, and server components. Derived data should be computed during render instead of through effects, and transitions and deferred values keep interactions responsive.
prompt: A parent component re renders a heavy child whenever the user types in an input. Explain how you would diagnose it and fix it, starting with the cheapest options before using memo, and mention what the React Compiler changes.

title: SSR, Hydration and Server Components
shadowText:
Today we will talk about modern React rendering strategies. We will cover CSR, SSR, static generation, streaming, hydration, React Server Components, Server Functions, and Next dot js caching.

Let us start with the strategies. Client side rendering produces HTML in the browser after JavaScript loads. It suits dashboards behind a login, but it has slow first paint and weak SEO. Server side rendering produces HTML on each request. It suits personalized pages, SEO, and fresh data, but costs server time, and the first byte depends on the slowest data. Static generation produces HTML at build time. It suits docs, marketing, and blogs, but is stale until rebuilt. Incremental regeneration regenerates static pages on an interval or on demand, which suits catalogues and CMS pages. Streaming SSR sends HTML in chunks as data resolves, and needs Suspense boundaries. Partial pre rendering combines a static shell with dynamic holes streamed per request.

What is hydration? React attaches to server rendered HTML. It renders the same tree on the client, walks the existing DOM, and attaches event listeners and state, but does not recreate nodes. The user sees content early, but can only interact with a boundary after it hydrates. With streaming, the server sends the HTML shell immediately with fallbacks. As each boundary's data resolves, the server streams its HTML plus a tiny inline script that swaps it into place, before any React JavaScript has loaded. Then the client hydrates boundaries independently. With selective hydration, if the user clicks inside a boundary that has not hydrated yet, React prioritizes hydrating that one first and replays the event.

Hydration mismatches. The client's first render must match the server's. Common causes are current time and locale formatting, random values, branches that check whether window exists, reading local storage during render, browser extensions that inject DOM, invalid HTML nesting such as a div inside a paragraph, and different data on the server and client. The standard fix is to render the client only value after hydration, in an effect. For unavoidable text differences like a timestamp, use the suppress hydration warning attribute on that one element. React nineteen shows a single diff style error, and tolerates unexpected tags injected into head and body by extensions. React nineteen point three adds a browser function that marks a Suspense subtree as browser only, so the server renders the fallback. Use it for genuinely browser only interface, because overusing it gives up the SEO and first paint benefits.

React Server Components run only on the server. Their code never ships to the browser. They can be async, read databases and files directly, and pass rendered output and serializable props to client components. A server component can run in a client component's children, because the page renders it and passes it in. A server component cannot use state, effects, or browser APIs. A client component can, but never touches databases or secrets. Rules interviewers probe: the use client directive marks a module boundary. That file and everything it imports become client code. It does not mean client only rendering, because client components are still server rendered. A client component cannot import a server component, but it can receive one as children. Props crossing the boundary must be serializable: primitives, plain objects, dates, maps, sets, promises, JSX, and server functions, but not class instances or ordinary functions. Push the directive to the leaves to minimize client JavaScript, and use the server only package to make accidental client imports of secret modules fail at build.

Are RSC and SSR the same? No. SSR turns components into HTML for the first load, and the components still ship and hydrate. RSC produces a serialized component tree whose server parts are never shipped as JavaScript or hydrated. Next dot js uses both.

Server functions. A function marked with use server runs on the server but can be called from the client. Used as a form action, it is a server action. Here is the senior point: every server function is a public HTTP endpoint. Never trust arguments, check authentication and authorization inside each one, validate input, and never close over secrets. Keep React and the framework patched.

Next dot js caching differs between versions, so state the version you used. A route becomes dynamic when it reads request data, and revalidation can be time based or on demand. Middleware can gate auth, but never as the only check.

To summarize in an interview: SSR is HTML first and still hydrates, RSC ships no JavaScript for server parts, streaming reveals content progressively, and server functions need authorization.
passage:
Rendering strategies differ in when HTML is produced: in the browser for client side rendering, on each request for server side rendering, at build time for static generation, and in chunks for streaming. Hydration attaches React to server rendered HTML without recreating nodes, and with streaming, boundaries hydrate independently, with selective hydration prioritizing the part the user interacts with.

Hydration mismatches occur when the first client render differs from the server output, for example because of time, random values, browser checks, or invalid HTML nesting, and they are fixed by rendering client only values after mount.

React Server Components run only on the server, never ship their code, and can read data directly, while client components handle state and browser APIs. The use client directive marks a module boundary, and props crossing it must be serializable. SSR and RSC are different: SSR produces HTML and still hydrates, whereas RSC output is never hydrated. Every server function is a public endpoint, so it must authenticate, authorize, and validate input.
prompt: Explain the difference between server side rendering and React Server Components, and what the use client directive really means. Then say why every server function must check authorization.

title: Testing React Applications
shadowText:
Today we will talk about testing React applications. We will cover the overall strategy, React Testing Library, mocking with MSW, hooks and timers, server components, accessibility testing, and debugging tools.

Let us start with the strategy. A helpful model is the testing trophy. At the base, static analysis is always on: TypeScript and ESLint, with hook rules, accessibility rules, and compiler rules. They catch typos, wrong props, and hook mistakes. Next, unit tests with Vitest or Jest cover pure functions, reducers, and hooks with logic. They are a small share. The biggest share is integration tests, using React Testing Library with Mock Service Worker. They test a feature through its interface with a mocked network. On top are end to end tests with Playwright or Cypress, few in number, covering critical journeys in a real browser against a real backend. And visual or accessibility checks, with tools like Storybook and axe, are targeted at design system regressions.

React Testing Library has a guiding principle: test the way users use the interface. Query the way users find things. Prefer get by role, then get by label text, then get by text, and use get by test ID only as a last resort. Use user event for realistic interactions. Use find queries for things that appear asynchronously. A typical test renders a form, types an invalid email, clicks submit, and asserts that an error message appears and the submit handler was not called. Anti patterns include asserting on state values or component instances, snapshotting whole trees, using container query selectors, wrapping everything in act manually, because the library already does, and using wait for with side effects inside.
