Mocking APIs with MSW. Mock at the network layer, so the component, the fetch code, and the cache library all run for real. You define handlers for routes, set up a server in the test environment, start it before all tests, reset handlers after each, and close it after all. The same handlers can power Storybook and local development. The principle: mock the network, not your own modules.

Testing custom hooks, async code, and timers. Use the render hook helper. For a debounce hook, use fake timers, render with an initial value, re render with a new value, advance the timers, and assert on the result. When combining user event with fake timers, pass the timer advance function to the user event setup. When testing components that use a query library, wrap them in a fresh query client for each test, with retries turned off, so tests do not share a cache.

Testing server components and server functions. Async server components are not yet well supported by Testing Library and jsdom. The practical split: unit test the data and server function logic as plain async functions, with authentication, validation, and database calls mocked. Test client components with Testing Library. And cover the full server component flow with Playwright.

Accessibility testing has layers. Lint with the JSX accessibility plugin. Run automated checks with axe in component tests and in end to end tests, which catch roughly a third of issues. Then do manual checks: a keyboard only pass using Tab, Enter, Space, Escape, and arrows, a screen reader smoke test with VoiceOver or NVDA, zoom to two hundred percent, and reduced motion. Querying by role in Testing Library is itself an accessibility test: if getting a button by role and name fails, a screen reader would fail too.

Debugging tools include React DevTools for components, props, hooks, and the profiler, the browser performance panel with React tracks, the network panel, state library dev tools, source maps in production, and React nineteen owner stacks in error messages, which show which component rendered the faulty one.

To summarize in an interview: mostly integration tests with Testing Library and MSW, a few critical end to end tests, queries by role, a mocked network, and accessibility checked both automatically and manually.
passage:
A balanced React testing strategy follows the testing trophy. Static analysis with TypeScript and lint rules is always on, unit tests cover pure logic and reducers, integration tests with React Testing Library and a mocked network form the largest share, and a few end to end tests with Playwright cover critical journeys.

React Testing Library encourages querying elements the way users find them, preferring roles and labels over test IDs, and using user event for realistic interactions. Anti patterns include asserting on internal state, snapshotting entire trees, and wrapping everything manually in act. Mock Service Worker mocks the network layer, so the components and data fetching code run for real.

Custom hooks are tested with a render hook helper, and timers with fake timers. Query library tests need a fresh client with retries disabled. Server component logic is split into plain functions that can be unit tested, with browser tests covering the full flow. Accessibility combines linting, automated axe checks that find about a third of issues, and manual keyboard and screen reader testing.
prompt: Describe your testing strategy for a React app using the testing trophy. Explain why integration tests with React Testing Library and a mocked network get the largest share, and how you would query elements.

title: Making Technical Decisions Like a Senior
shadowText:
Today we will talk about how to make and explain technical decisions. This is the heart of a senior interview. We will cover a decision frame, architecture decision records, then common choices: database, architecture style, rendering, state, API style, build versus buy, caching, and hosting.

Let us start with the frame. Use a repeatable structure so the interviewer can follow you. First, context and constraints: who are the users, what scale in a year, the team size and skills, the deadline, budget, and compliance. Second, options: at least two real ones, including doing the simple thing, and not building it at all. Third, ranked criteria: time to deliver, operating cost, team familiarity, performance, consistency, security, and how hard it is to reverse. Fourth, the decision, and why it wins on the criteria that matter most here. Fifth, risks and an exit plan: what could go wrong, how you would notice, and what signal would make you revisit.

Reversibility matters most. Think of one way doors and two way doors. A two way door, like a UI library, a cache, or a feature flag, can be decided fast and changed later. A one way door, like the primary database, the public API shape, the auth provider, or the data model for money, deserves a written proposal and a review. That brings us to the architecture decision record, or ADR. It is a short document stored with the code that records one significant decision: the context, the choice, and the consequences. One decision per record. Never edit an accepted one. Write a new record that supersedes it.

Database choice. Default to PostgreSQL unless you have a specific reason not to. Relationships, joins, reporting, money, inventory, and strong constraints point to PostgreSQL. Documents read and written whole, with varying shapes, like CMS content, point to MongoDB, or to PostgreSQL jsonb. Very high write throughput with simple access patterns points to MongoDB, DynamoDB, or Cassandra. And if the team already knows one well, that is often decisive. The real question is your access patterns. Also, MongoDB has had multi document transactions since version four, so saying it cannot do transactions is outdated. And schemaless really means the schema lives in application code.

Monolith or microservices? Start with a modular monolith in almost every new project built by one team. Microservices solve an organizational problem, many teams blocking each other, at a large technical cost. Signals to split: a separate team owns it, it has very different scaling or reliability needs, or it needs a different runtime. Keep clear module boundaries from day one, so a later split is cheap. The trap is doing microservices because a famous company does.

Rendering choice. Decide per route, by freshness and personalization. Marketing and docs are static. Product pages with hourly prices use incremental revalidation. Search results needing SEO use server rendering with streaming. A dashboard behind a login uses server components for the shell and client components for the interactive parts. Real time pages use a server rendered shell plus WebSocket or server sent events. Then measure Core Web Vitals.

State management. Split by kind first. Server state goes to React Query or server components. URL state goes in the URL. Form state goes to a form library or native forms with server actions. Local state uses useState. Shared client state uses context if it rarely changes, or Zustand or Redux Toolkit if it changes often or is large.

API style. REST with an OpenAPI spec for public APIs. GraphQL when several clients need different shapes of data. tRPC or server actions inside a TypeScript monorepo. gRPC between internal services. Settle error format, cursor pagination, versioning, and idempotency early.

Build versus buy. Buy anything that is not your differentiator and is risky to get wrong: authentication, payments, email delivery. Reduce lock in with a thin interface in front of the vendor, and state the exit cost.

Caching. Add a cache only when measurement shows repeated, expensive reads that tolerate staleness. Layers from cheapest: CDN and HTTP cache, framework data cache, in process memory, then Redis. Decide invalidation up front, and name the risks: stale data, stampedes, and caching personalized data under a shared key.

Hosting. Serverless suits Next dot js front ends. Containers on a managed platform suit APIs, workers, and WebSockets. Kubernetes is overkill for one team. A VM is cheap but you own everything.

To summarize in an interview: I frame decisions with context, options, criteria, a decision, and an exit plan, I write ADRs for one way doors, and I tie every choice to a constraint.
passage:
A technical decision should follow a repeatable frame: context and constraints, at least two real options, ranked criteria, a decision with reasons, and the risks with an exit plan. Reversibility matters most, since one way doors such as the primary database, the public API, or the money data model deserve a written proposal, while two way doors can be decided quickly. An architecture decision record captures one decision with its context and consequences, and a later record supersedes it instead of editing it.

PostgreSQL is a sensible default, with MongoDB suited to whole documents with varying shapes. A modular monolith is the right start for one team, because microservices solve an organizational problem at a high technical cost. Rendering is chosen per route, state is split by kind, and API style follows the clients.

Authentication, payments, and email should usually be bought behind a thin interface. Caches are added only after measurement, with an invalidation strategy, and hosting follows the team's operations skills and traffic shape.
prompt: Describe how you make and present a technical decision, for example choosing between PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Cover context, options, criteria, the decision, risks, and why reversibility and an ADR matter.

title: Decision Scenarios and Design Exercises
shadowText:
Today we will talk about more decision scenarios and a few design exercises you may get in a senior interview. We will cover synchronous versus asynchronous design, slow APIs, risky changes, estimation, a model scenario, and then exercises on an orders API, schemas, components, refactoring, and architecture smells.

Let us start with sync versus queue. Use a synchronous call when the caller needs the result now. Use a queue when the work is slow, when it can fail and retry without the user waiting, when you need to smooth spikes, or when several consumers react to one fact, like an order placed. The cost of async is at least once delivery, so handlers must be idempotent, plus retries with backoff, a dead letter queue, monitoring, ordering limits, and eventual consistency in the interface. To publish events reliably after a database write, use the transactional outbox: write the event row in the same transaction, and a relay publishes it.

When your API is slow, measure before changing anything. Define the target: which endpoint, which percentile, and the goal, such as p95 under three hundred milliseconds. Find where time goes with tracing. The usual culprits, most common first: missing indexes or bad queries, N plus one queries, sequential external calls that could run in parallel, returning too much data, and CPU heavy work on the event loop. Only then consider caching, and after that scaling out. Verify on the same metric and add an alert.

Planning a risky change without downtime. Make it incremental and reversible. For schema changes, expand, migrate, contract. Add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, switch reads, and remove the old one later. Use feature flags with a kill switch. Use the strangler pattern for rewrites. Write a rollback plan, watch dashboards during rollout, and communicate the plan. The trap is renaming a column in a single deploy, because old code still running breaks immediately.

Estimating with unclear requirements. Clarify the outcome, not just the feature. Break the work into tasks of a day or two, turning unknowns into time boxed spikes. Estimate as a range with assumptions, including review, testing, and deployment. Do the riskiest part first. Propose a smaller first version. And re estimate early. Push back with options, not a simple yes or no.

A model scenario for a learning platform: a modular monolith in Next dot js, MongoDB for varied content documents, bought authentication with an approval state, static public pages and dynamic signed in pages, an AI coach with an admin chosen key and a daily limit, Vercel plus Atlas for low operations burden, and decisions recorded as short ADRs. Every choice is tied to a constraint and has a condition that would change it.

Now the exercises. Orders API. Creating an order uses a post with an idempotency key, returning created. Listing uses cursor pagination. Getting someone else's order returns not found, not forbidden, so IDs cannot be enumerated. Cancel is an explicit action that returns conflict if shipped. Payment returns accepted, with the final result arriving by webhook. Use one error shape, money as integer minor units, and a version in the path. Common mistakes are a patch that accepts any status, floats for money, a 200 with an error body, and offset pagination.

Schema and indexes. Store a copy of the unit price in order items, so history survives price changes. Index customer, then created date descending, then ID for the cursor. Index status then created date for the admin view. Do analytics through a rollup table, not the transactional path. Avoid an index per column, and avoid unbounded arrays in MongoDB.

Frontend hierarchy for a product listing with fifty thousand products. Render the first page on the server for SEO. Keep filters, sort, and page in the URL. Keep server data in a query library. Make only the interactive leaves client components. Mention accessibility without being asked.

Refactoring a coupled service. Name the mixed responsibilities: persistence, payment, notification, and caching. Introduce ports and adapters, move logic into the entity, and write an outbox row so a worker sends the email. An email failure then retries instead of failing checkout.

Architecture smells. A shared database across services is a distributed monolith. A synchronous chain of three services multiplies failure. A shared package with business logic forces lockstep releases. Cron on every instance runs jobs many times. In memory sessions break scaling. One Redis used for cache and queue risks eviction of queue keys. Fix by risk, and do not propose a rewrite.

To summarize in an interview: measure first, make changes reversible, push back with options, and always tie a design to its consequences.
passage:
Synchronous calls are used when the caller needs the result immediately, and queues are used for slow, retryable, or fan out work, at the cost of idempotent handlers, retries, dead letter queues, and eventual consistency. The transactional outbox publishes events reliably after a database write.

A slow API is fixed by measuring percentiles, using tracing to find where time goes, and addressing the usual causes in order: missing indexes, N plus one queries, sequential external calls, oversized responses, and CPU work on the event loop. Risky changes are made incremental and reversible with expand, migrate, contract, feature flags, and a tested rollback plan.

Design exercises test concrete habits. An orders API needs idempotency keys, correct status codes, cursor pagination, one error format, and money in integer minor units. Indexes should trace back to queries, with equality columns before sort columns. Tightly coupled services are refactored with ports and adapters and an outbox, and architecture reviews should pair every smell with its consequence and a low risk fix.
prompt: Your API is slow. Walk me through how you decide what to fix first, from defining the target and using tracing to checking indexes and N plus one queries, and say when you would add caching or scale out.

title: Production Scenarios and Failure Handling
shadowText:
Today we will talk about practical production scenarios. We will cover slow queries, rate limiting, caching, idempotency, queue retries, failure points, ADRs, and several senior questions about slowness, traffic spikes, and outages.

Let us start with a slow query. A table with twenty million orders has an index only on created date, and the slowest requests take two and a half seconds. The query filters on lower case email and a status list, sorts by created date, and uses a large offset. First, measure with explain analyze. Second, wrapping the column in lower prevents a plain index on email from being used. Add an expression index, or use a case insensitive type, or better, filter by customer ID. Third, a large offset reads and discards thousands of rows, so switch to keyset pagination. Fourth, select only the needed columns. Then re run explain and compare. In MongoDB, build a compound index following the ESR rule: equality, then sort, then range. Verify that keys examined are close to documents returned. And remember that every index slows writes.

Rate limiting. Limit login to five attempts per minute and the public API to one hundred per minute per key, with three Node instances. The counter must live in Redis so all instances share it. In memory counters would let users get triple the limit. Fixed windows allow a double burst at the boundary, sliding windows are more precise, and token buckets allow controlled bursts. Make the operation atomic, with a single Lua script, since increment then expire as two calls can leave a key with no expiry. Return a 429 with a Retry After header. When Redis is down, fail open for the general API and fail closed for login.

Caching a product page with fifty thousand reads per minute. Use cache aside with a TTL plus random jitter. On a price update, commit to the database first, then delete the key. Protect against stampedes with a short lock so only one request rebuilds, and cache not found results briefly.

Idempotency for payments. Keep a table with a unique constraint on user and key. Insert the row as in progress before doing work. On a duplicate, return the stored response if completed, a conflict if still in progress, and an error if the request hash differs. The database constraint is the source of truth, because Redis alone can lose keys.

Queue consumer and retry policy. An email worker with a provider limit of ten requests per second. Delivery is at least once, so record the order and template under a unique constraint before sending, and use a deterministic job ID. Classify errors: timeouts, 429, and server errors are retryable, while an invalid address is permanent and should not retry. Use exponential backoff with jitter. Keep the provider timeout well under the job lock duration. Keep failed jobs as a dead letter queue, alert on it, and keep a replay tool.

Reviewing a single VPS architecture. Rank by likelihood and impact. Priority one: backups on the same disk and no monitoring. Priority two: the whole stack on one host, uploads on local disk, and Redis holding sessions and queue with unknown persistence. Priority three: shared resources and no circuit breaker around SMS. The path is incremental: off site backups and alerts first, object storage next, a managed database after, and a second app node later. Do not jump to Kubernetes.

An ADR for a team of three building a multi tenant MVP in four months. The decision is a modular monolith with one database, with modules per bounded context and no cross module table access. Rejected options include microservices and serverless, with reasons. The consequences include the downsides, and the revisit triggers are observable.

Senior questions. When a system is slow, scope it first, measure along the path, find the biggest span, test one hypothesis, and verify. When traffic rises ten times, database connections usually break first, then the event loop, then third party limits, and retry storms amplify the problem. When Redis goes down, list its roles and mitigate each, with tight timeouts. When the database goes down during a payment, record an intent first, use gateway retries and reconciliation, and never trust the browser redirect alone. When events are delivered twice, make effects idempotent with a processed events table.

To summarize in an interview: I measure, I make effects idempotent, I name failure behavior, and I rank problems by impact.
passage:
A slow query is improved by measuring with explain, fixing expressions that prevent index use, replacing large offsets with keyset pagination, selecting fewer columns, and choosing compound indexes in the right order. Rate limiters need shared atomic state in Redis, a clear algorithm, a 429 response with Retry After, and an explicit decision to fail open or closed.

Caches use random expiry jitter, delete keys after the database commit, and protect against stampedes. Idempotency relies on a database constraint and stored responses, since Redis alone can lose keys. Queue consumers must be idempotent, classify errors as retryable or permanent, use backoff with jitter, and keep a dead letter path with alerts.

Architecture reviews should rank failure points by likelihood and impact, starting with off site backups and monitoring. When traffic rises or Redis fails, the answer depends on what each component does, and retry storms amplify load. When a database fails during a payment, a recorded intent and reconciliation protect the user.
prompt: Redis goes down in your production system. List the roles Redis may play, such as cache, sessions, queue, rate limiter and locks, and explain the effect and mitigation for each, including fail open versus fail closed.

title: Scaling, Migration and Cost Scenarios
shadowText:
Today we will talk about more senior scenario questions. We will cover mass notifications, migrating from a monolith to microservices, cache stampedes, consistency across services, breaking API changes, large uploads, debugging latency, and cutting infrastructure costs.

Let us start with sending millions of notifications. Separate pipelines, so transactional messages like one time codes and receipts never queue behind a marketing blast. Use separate queues with priority. Batch the fan out. A campaign job enqueues batches of about a thousand recipients, and workers expand them. Do not create millions of jobs up front. Use one queue per channel, such as email, SMS, and push, each rate limited to its provider's quota. Use batch APIs where they exist, for example push multicast supports up to five hundred tokens per call. Before sending, check preferences, opt outs, and quiet hours, and deduplicate. After sending, record delivery status asynchronously, prune invalid device tokens, and alert on queue depth and the age of the oldest job. The senior signal is naming the provider quota, not your servers, as the real bottleneck.

Migrating a monolith to microservices. Ask why first. Valid reasons are team scaling, an independent deploy cadence, or one part with very different scaling needs. If none applies, modularize instead. Modularize in place, enforce module boundaries, and stop modules reading each other's tables. Extract one edge context first, one with clear boundaries and low coupling, such as notifications. Use the strangler pattern, routing its traffic through a gateway to the new service. The new service owns its tables, and you sync through the outbox during the cutover. Before the first split, you need CI and CD per service, centralized logs, tracing, and contract tests. State the costs you are buying: network latency, distributed consistency, and more operations work.

Preventing cache stampedes. Use single flight rebuilds, where one request takes a short lock and rebuilds while others wait or get stale data. Use stale while revalidate. Use early probabilistic refresh. Add jitter to expiry times. Warm the cache after deploys, and use CDN request coalescing. A cold cache after a Redis outage is the same problem at full scale.

Keeping data consistent across services. Decide per operation. Anything that must be strongly consistent belongs in one service and one database. If it spans two services, the boundary is probably wrong. The rest is eventually consistent, using the outbox, events, and idempotent consumers. Multi step workflows use a saga with a compensation per step. Orchestration is easier to follow, and choreography couples less. Avoid two phase commit across services, because it blocks on the coordinator and hurts availability. Use reconciliation jobs, and show pending states honestly. The senior signal is redrawing the boundary first.

Safely deploying a breaking API change. Avoid the break if you can, using additive changes and expand and contract. If it is unavoidable, release a new version and run both side by side. Send deprecation and sunset headers, and track old version traffic per client. Remove the old version only when its traffic is near zero. Mobile apps linger for months, so set a minimum supported app version. Catch breaks before release with contract tests.

Large file uploads. The preferred design is that the browser uploads directly to object storage using a presigned URL, with multipart and resumable uploads. The API only issues the URL and receives a completion callback. Process the file asynchronously, streaming it, never loading it whole. If it must pass through your server, stream it, and avoid memory storage. Remember that edge proxies cap request bodies. The senior signal is getting file bytes off the app servers entirely.

Debugging latency across layers. Break the request into phases: DNS, connection, first byte, download, and render. High first byte time points to server or network. Low first byte with slow largest contentful paint points to the frontend. Connect layers with a trace ID, and expose backend timing with the Server Timing header. Use edge and proxy numbers to separate network from application. Then go deep in the slow layer. Segment by device, region, and endpoint before averaging.

Cutting infrastructure cost. Measure cost per component and utilization. Right size instances. Cache and compress at the edge. Trim idle environments, unused volumes, and verbose logs. Treat service level objectives as hard limits, change one thing at a time, and never cut backups or redundancy on the critical path.

To summarize in an interview: I tie every scaling move to a measured reason, state the cost I am buying, and keep changes reversible.
passage:
Sending millions of notifications requires separate pipelines for transactional and marketing messages, batched fan out, one rate limited queue per channel, and attention to the provider quota, which is the real bottleneck. Migrating a monolith should begin with the question of why, then modularize in place, extract one low coupling context with the strangler pattern, and prepare tracing, logs, and contract tests first.

Cache stampedes are prevented with single flight rebuilds, stale while revalidate, early refresh, and jittered expiry. Consistency across services is handled by keeping strongly consistent operations inside one service, using the outbox, idempotent consumers, and sagas elsewhere, and avoiding two phase commit.

Breaking API changes are avoided with additive changes or released as a new version, with deprecation headers and traffic tracking. Large uploads go directly to object storage with presigned URLs. Latency is debugged by splitting the request into phases and following a trace ID, and cost is reduced by measuring, right sizing, and never cutting backups.
prompt: Explain how you would migrate a monolith toward microservices. Cover why you should ask for the reason first, modularizing in place, extracting one edge context with the strangler pattern, and what must exist before the first split.
